events.enhanced_description: On November 11, 1912, William Lawrence Bragg presented his derivation of Bragg's law at the Geological Society of London. This groundbreaking work laid the foundation for the field of x-ray crystallography, which would later enable the imaging of DNA's double helix structure.
events.name: Bragg's Law Presentation

events.enhanced_description: On November 25, 1912, 'Românul de la Pind', the longest-running newspaper by and about Aromanians, ceased publication. This marked the end of an important cultural voice for the Aromanian community until World War II.
events.name: Cease of Publication of Românul de la Pind

events.enhanced_description: On November 28, 1912, Albania declared its independence from the Ottoman Empire in the city of Vlorë. This declaration was a pivotal moment in the Balkan region, leading to the establishment of Albania as a sovereign state.
events.name: Albania Declares Independence

events.enhanced_description: On December 3, 1912, Bulgaria, Montenegro, and Serbia signed an armistice with the Ottoman Empire at Çatalca, temporarily halting the First Balkan War. This ceasefire was short-lived, as hostilities resumed shortly thereafter.
events.name: Armistice at Çatalca

events.enhanced_description: On December 18, 1912, the fossil known as Piltdown Man was presented to the Geological Society of London, initially believed to be a significant discovery in human evolution. It was later revealed to be a hoax in 1953, casting doubt on the scientific community's methods at the time.
events.name: Presentation of Piltdown Man

events.enhanced_description: On December 24, 1912, Merck filed patent applications in Germany for the synthesis of MDMA (Ecstasy), developed by chemist Anton Köllisch. This marked the beginning of the drug's complex history in both therapeutic and recreational contexts.
events.name: Merck Files Patent for MDMA

events.enhanced_description: In January 1913, Joseph Stalin traveled to Vienna to study Marxism and the National Question. During this period, he was among several influential figures, including Hitler and Trotsky, residing in the city.
events.name: Stalin's Research Trip to Vienna

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1913, Canberra was officially designated as the capital of the Commonwealth of Australia, chosen for its location between Sydney and Melbourne. The city was purpose-built to serve as the political center of Australia, reflecting the nation's aspirations for a distinct identity.

image.caption: Panoramic view of Canberra from Mount Ainslie Lookout.
image.credit: The 3B's — https://www.flickr.com/photos/3-bs/52072528695/
image.date_qualification: A later view of Canberra’s site and cityscape, not a photograph of its designation as capital. Image date: 2022-05-07 10:23:02.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Canberra becomes the capital of Australia

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1913, Venustiano Carranza announced his Plan of Guadalupe, which called for the overthrow of Victoriano Huerta's government during the Mexican Revolution. This plan became a rallying point for constitutionalists and marked the beginning of a significant rebellion against Huerta's regime.
events.name: Announcement of the Plan of Guadalupe

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Adrianople concluded in 1913 when Bulgarian forces captured the city from the Ottoman Empire during the Balkan Wars. This victory was pivotal in the conflict, significantly weakening Ottoman control in the region.
events.name: Siege of Adrianople ends

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1913, Norway became one of the first countries in the world to grant women the right to vote in parliamentary elections, marking a significant milestone in the global suffrage movement. This achievement was largely driven by the efforts of activists such as Gina Krog, who campaigned tirelessly for women's rights.
events.name: Women's suffrage is enacted in Norway

events.enhanced_description: From June 10 to June 15, 1913, the Battle of Bud Bagsak took place in the Philippines, where U.S. troops led by General John J. Pershing engaged in a fierce four-day battle against Moro rebels. The conflict ended with a decisive victory for the U.S. forces, but at a high cost, as many rebels were killed in a final desperate charge.
events.name: Battle of Bud Bagsak

events.enhanced_description: In 1913, Death Valley, California, recorded a scorching temperature of 134 °F (56.7 °C), which remains one of the highest temperatures ever recorded on Earth. This extreme weather event has been a subject of scientific study and debate regarding its validity.

image.caption: A NASA photograph of Death Valley taken from the Space Shuttle Columbia.
image.credit: NASA — http://nix.nasa.gov/info?id=STS073-E-5119&orgid=3
image.date_qualification: A photograph of the site, not the 1913 heat event; image date: 1995-10-25.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Death Valley, California hits 134 °F (~56.7 °C)

events.enhanced_description: In 1913, Imperial Russian Army pilot Pyotr Nesterov became the first person to perform a loop in an airplane, flying a Nieuport IV monoplane over Syretzk Aerodrome near Kiev. This daring maneuver showcased the evolving capabilities of early aviation.

image.caption: Pyotr Nesterov’s sketch of his looping maneuver, with inscriptions noting heights.
image.credit: Pyotr Nesterov — https://www.thisdayinaviation.com/tag/nesterovs-loop/
image.date_qualification: Dated 1913 in the supplied image metadata; this is the image’s stated date, not an independently verified date of the depicted flight.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Imperial Russian Army pilot Pyotr Nesterov loops an airplane

events.enhanced_description: In 1913, the Helgoland Island air disaster occurred when the Imperial German Navy Zeppelin LZ 14 was forced down into the North Sea during a thunderstorm, resulting in the deaths of 16 of the 22 men on board. This incident marked one of the first fatalities in airship history.
events.name: Helgoland Island air disaster

events.enhanced_description: In 1913, Yuan Shikai was elected as the President of the Republic of China, marking a pivotal moment in the country's transition from imperial rule to a republic. His presidency was marked by political strife and attempts to consolidate power, ultimately leading to significant changes in Chinese governance.
events.name: Yuan Shikai Elected President of the Republic of China

events.enhanced_description: In 1913, the Ford Motor Company introduced the first moving assembly line, revolutionizing the manufacturing process by drastically reducing assembly time. This innovation not only transformed the automotive industry but also set a precedent for mass production across various sectors.
events.name: Ford Motor Company Introduces the Moving Assembly Line

events.enhanced_description: In 1913, Crete, having gained self-rule from Turkey after the First Balkan War, was officially annexed by Greece. This event marked a significant step in the unification of Greek territories and the establishment of modern Greece.
events.name: Annexation of Crete by Greece

events.enhanced_description: In 1913, the Buenos Aires Underground, the first subway system in South America, was opened to the public. This landmark development revolutionized urban transportation in Buenos Aires and set a precedent for future public transit systems in the region.
events.name: Opening of Buenos Aires Underground

events.enhanced_description: In the aftermath of the First Balkan War, the newly-established Greek authorities deported a group of Bulgarian teachers and priests, including Gligor Zisov, to Bulgaria. Tragically, they were intercepted and killed by Greek soldiers, highlighting the tensions and violence that persisted in the region following the war.
events.name: Bulgarian Deportations by Greek Authorities

events.enhanced_description: The Ahmadiyya Muslim Community was established in Bengal Province, marking a significant development in Islamic thought and practice. Founded by Mirza Ghulam Ahmad, this movement aimed to promote a peaceful interpretation of Islam and has since grown into a global community.
events.name: Establishment of the Ahmadiyya Muslim Community

events.enhanced_description: The America Cultural Center was inaugurated in Salta, Argentina, serving as a hub for cultural exchange and artistic expression. This center aimed to foster a deeper understanding of American culture within the local community.
events.name: Inauguration of America Cultural Center

events.enhanced_description: French physicist Georges Sagnac conducted a groundbreaking experiment demonstrating that light propagates at a speed independent of the speed of its source. This work laid the foundation for future developments in the field of relativity and optics.
events.name: Georges Sagnac's Light Propagation Experiment

events.enhanced_description: R. J. Reynolds introduced Camel cigarettes in the United States, marking the launch of the first packaged cigarettes. This innovation transformed the tobacco industry and significantly influenced smoking culture in America.
events.name: Introduction of Camel Cigarettes

events.enhanced_description: Prada was established as a leather goods dealer in Milan by Mario Prada and his brother. This company would eventually evolve into a leading luxury fashion brand known worldwide.

image.caption: Prada shop in Milan, Italy.
image.credit: Pavel Gromov ( Pagan ) — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photograph of a Prada shop in Milan, made in 2007; it depicts the brand’s site, not its establishment in 1913.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Establishment of Prada

events.enhanced_description: Astra, a predecessor of the global healthcare and pharmaceutical brand AstraZeneca, was founded in Södertälje, Sweden. This company would play a significant role in the development of pharmaceuticals and healthcare solutions.
events.name: Foundation of Astra

events.enhanced_description: In 1913, the value of world trade reached approximately $38 billion, reflecting the global economic conditions and trade dynamics of the time. This milestone indicated the increasing interconnectedness of economies worldwide.
events.name: World Trade Value Reaches $38 Billion

events.enhanced_description: On January 3, 1913, during the First Balkan War, Greece completed its capture of the eastern Aegean island of Chios, marking the surrender of the last Ottoman forces on the island. This victory solidified Greek control over the Aegean Sea.
events.name: Capture of Chios

events.enhanced_description: On January 13, 1913, Edward Carson founded the first Ulster Volunteer Force by unifying several existing loyalist militias. This organization was established to resist home rule for Ireland and played a significant role in the political landscape of the time.
events.name: Founding of the Ulster Volunteer Force

events.enhanced_description: On January 23, 1913, Enver Pasha orchestrated a coup d'état in the Ottoman Empire, consolidating power and marking a significant shift in the political landscape of the empire. This event set the stage for further military and political changes in the region.
events.name: Ottoman Coup d'état

events.enhanced_description: On February 1, 1913, Grand Central Terminal reopened after extensive renovations, establishing itself as the world's largest railroad station. This iconic structure became a symbol of New York City's transportation network and architectural grandeur.
events.name: Grand Central Terminal Reopens

events.enhanced_description: On February 3, 1913, the Sixteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution was ratified, granting Congress the power to impose and collect income taxes on all sources of income. This amendment fundamentally changed the federal government's revenue system and taxation policy.
events.name: Ratification of the Sixteenth Amendment

events.enhanced_description: The 1913 Great Meteor Procession was a significant astronomical event observed over the Atlantic Ocean, where numerous meteors were seen streaking across the sky. This event contributed to the study of meteors and their origins, captivating both scientists and the public.
events.name: 1913 Great Meteor Procession

events.enhanced_description: On February 9, 1913, the Mexican Revolution saw the onset of 'La Decena Trágica', a rebellion led by military chiefs against President Francisco I. Madero. This pivotal moment marked a significant escalation in the conflict that would reshape Mexico's political landscape.
events.name: La Decena Trágica Begins

events.enhanced_description: On February 13, 1913, Thubten Gyatso, the 13th Dalai Lama, declared Tibet's independence from the Qing dynasty of China. This declaration was a significant assertion of Tibetan sovereignty during a tumultuous period in Asian geopolitics.
events.name: Tibet Declares Independence

events.enhanced_description: On February 18, 1913, during the Mexican Revolution, President Francisco I. Madero and Vice President José María Pino Suárez were forced to resign following a coup led by General Victoriano Huerta. This event marked a critical turning point in the revolution.
events.name: Madero and Pino Suárez Resign

events.enhanced_description: On February 22, 1913, former President Francisco I. Madero and Vice President José María Pino Suárez were assassinated, marking a tragic end to their leadership during the Mexican Revolution. Their deaths intensified the conflict and led to further violence in the country.
events.name: Assassination of Madero and Pino Suárez

events.enhanced_description: On February 23, 1913, Joseph Stalin was arrested by the Russian secret police, the Okhrana, in Petrograd and subsequently exiled to Siberia. This event marked a significant moment in Stalin's early political career, foreshadowing his later rise to power.
events.name: Stalin Arrested

events.enhanced_description: In March 1913, the House of Romanov celebrated its 300th anniversary of succession to the Russian throne, amidst a wave of monarchist sentiment. This event highlighted the enduring legacy of the Romanov dynasty in Russian history.
events.name: 300th Anniversary of the House of Romanov

events.enhanced_description: Around March 1, 1913, the British steamship Calvados mysteriously disappeared in the Sea of Marmara, with 200 passengers on board. The incident raised concerns about maritime safety and the perils of sea travel during that era.
events.name: Calvados Disappearance

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1913, the Woman Suffrage Procession took place in Washington, D.C., led by activist Inez Milholland on horseback. This event was a pivotal moment in the women's suffrage movement, drawing attention to the fight for women's voting rights.
events.name: Woman Suffrage Procession

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1913, Woodrow Wilson was sworn in as the 28th President of the United States. His presidency would be marked by significant domestic reforms and involvement in World War I.
events.name: Woodrow Wilson Sworn In

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1913, during the First Balkan War, forces of the Kingdom of Greece captured the forts of Bizani, strategically covering the approaches to Ioannina from the Ottoman Empire. This victory was crucial in the Greek campaign against Ottoman forces.
events.name: Battle of Bizani

events.enhanced_description: On March 7, 1913, the British freighter Alum Chine exploded in the harbor of Baltimore, Maryland, while carrying 343 tons of dynamite. The explosion caused significant destruction and raised concerns about the safety of transporting explosives.
events.name: Alum Chine Explosion

events.enhanced_description: On March 13, 1913, Pancho Villa returned to Mexico from his self-imposed exile in the United States. His return marked a significant moment in the Mexican Revolution, as he would become a key figure in the ongoing conflict.
events.name: Pancho Villa Returns

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1913, the Military Aviation Academy (Escuela de Aviación Militar) was founded in Montevideo, Uruguay. This institution would later evolve into the Uruguayan Air Force, marking a significant development in the country's military aviation capabilities.
events.name: Military Aviation Academy Founded

events.enhanced_description: On March 18, 1913, King George I of Greece was assassinated after 50 years on the throne, leading to the ascension of his son, Constantine I. This event had profound implications for Greece during a period of national turmoil.
events.name: Assassination of King George I

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1913, Sung Chiao-jen, a prominent founder of the Chinese nationalist party (Kuomintang), was wounded in an assassination attempt and died two days later. His death significantly impacted the political landscape in China during the early Republican period.
events.name: Sung Chiao-jen Assassination Attempt

events.enhanced_description: On March 23, 1913, supporters of Phan Xích Long initiated a revolt against colonial rule in French Indochina. This uprising was part of the broader struggle for independence from French colonialism in Vietnam.
events.name: Phan Xích Long Revolt

events.enhanced_description: On March 25, 1913, the Great Dayton Flood occurred after four days of heavy rain in the Miami Valley, resulting in over 360 fatalities and the destruction of 20,000 homes, primarily in Dayton, Ohio. This disaster prompted significant changes in urban planning and flood management.
events.name: Great Dayton Flood

events.enhanced_description: On March 26, 1913, Venustiano Carranza announced his Plan of Guadalupe, marking the beginning of his rebellion against Victoriano Huerta's government as the leader of the Constitutionals. This plan was pivotal in the ongoing Mexican Revolution.
events.name: Plan of Guadalupe Announced

events.enhanced_description: In April 1913, Bernhard Kellermann's novel 'Der Tunnel' was published, exploring themes of technology and human ambition. The book gained significant attention and is regarded as a precursor to modern science fiction literature.
events.name: Publication of Der Tunnel

events.enhanced_description: On April 5, 1913, the United States Soccer Federation was established, marking a significant step in the organization and promotion of soccer in the United States. This federation would later play a crucial role in the development of the sport across the nation.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Formation of the United States Soccer Federation

events.enhanced_description: On April 8, 1913, the Seventeenth Amendment to the United States Constitution was ratified, establishing the direct election of U.S. senators by popular vote. This amendment aimed to reduce corruption and increase democratic participation in the political process.
events.name: Passage of the Seventeenth Amendment

events.enhanced_description: On April 21, 1913, the RMS Aquitania, a Cunard ocean liner, was launched from the River Clyde in Clydebank, Scotland. Known for its size and luxury, the Aquitania would become one of the most famous ocean liners of its time.
events.name: Launch of RMS Aquitania

events.enhanced_description: On April 24, 1913, the Woolworth Building was officially opened in New York City. Designed by architect Cass Gilbert, it stood as the tallest building in the world at the time, symbolizing the architectural ambitions of the early 20th century.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Opening of the Woolworth Building

events.enhanced_description: On May 3, 1913, 'Raja Harishchandra,' the first full-length Indian feature film, was released, marking the inception of the Indian film industry. Directed by Dadasaheb Phalke, this silent film laid the foundation for future cinematic endeavors in India.
events.name: Release of Raja Harishchandra

events.enhanced_description: On May 14, 1913, New York Governor William Sulzer approved the charter for the Rockefeller Foundation, which began operations with a substantial donation of $100 million from John D. Rockefeller. The foundation aimed to promote the well-being of humanity.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Approval of the Rockefeller Foundation charter

events.enhanced_description: On May 24, 1913, Princess Victoria Louise of Prussia married Prince Ernest Augustus of Hanover in Berlin. This union ended a long-standing rift between the Houses of Hohenzollern and Hanover and was notable for being one of the last grand gatherings of European royalty.
events.name: Marriage of Princess Victoria Louise and Prince Ernest Augustus

events.enhanced_description: On May 25, 1913, Adolf Hitler moved from Vienna to Munich, a significant step in his life that would eventually lead to his rise in German politics. This move marked the beginning of his involvement in the nationalist movements in Germany.
events.name: Adolf Hitler moves to Munich

events.enhanced_description: On May 26, 1913, Igor Sikorsky became the first person to pilot a four-engine fixed-wing aircraft, showcasing advancements in aviation technology. This achievement marked a significant milestone in the development of larger aircraft capable of carrying more passengers and cargo.
events.name: Igor Sikorsky pilots a 4-engine aircraft

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1913, Igor Stravinsky's ballet 'The Rite of Spring' premiered at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris, conducted by Pierre Monteux and choreographed by Vaslav Nijinsky. Its avant-garde style incited one of the most famous riots in classical music history.
events.name: Premiere of The Rite of Spring

events.enhanced_description: On May 30, 1913, the Treaty of London was signed, officially ending the First Balkan War. The treaty recognized the independence of Albania and granted Greece additional territories in southern Epirus.
events.name: Signing of the Treaty of London

events.enhanced_description: On June 1, 1913, the Greek-Serbian Treaty of Alliance was signed, establishing a military alliance between Greece and Serbia. This treaty was a crucial step in the lead-up to the Second Balkan War.
events.name: Signing of the Greek-Serbian Treaty of Alliance

events.enhanced_description: On June 4, 1913, British suffragette Emily Davison ran in front of the King's horse at The Derby, resulting in her being trampled. She died four days later, becoming a martyr for the women's suffrage movement in the UK.

locations.name: Epsom Downs, Surrey, England, United Kingdom

events.name: Emily Davison's protest at The Derby

events.enhanced_description: On June 8, 1913, the Deutsches Stadion in Berlin was dedicated in front of an audience of 60,000 people, featuring the release of 10,000 pigeons. The stadium was built in anticipation of the 1916 Summer Olympics, which were later canceled due to World War I.
events.name: Dedication of the Deutsches Stadion

events.enhanced_description: On June 11, 1913, Norway enacted women's suffrage, granting women the right to vote and marking a significant milestone in the country's social and political history. This legislation was part of a broader movement for women's rights in Europe.
events.name: Women's suffrage enacted in Norway

events.enhanced_description: On June 13, 1913, the predecessor of the Aldi store chain opened in Essen, Germany. This marked the beginning of a significant retail revolution in Germany, leading to the establishment of one of the largest discount supermarket chains in the world.
events.name: Opening of the predecessor of Aldi

events.enhanced_description: On June 18, 1913, the Arab Congress convened in Istanbul, where Arab nationalists gathered to discuss reforms under the Ottoman Empire. This congress was a pivotal moment in the Arab nationalist movement.

image.caption: Plaque marking the Société de Géographie on Boulevard Saint-Germain in Paris.
image.credit: Heurtelions — Own work
image.date_qualification: The plaque identifies the venue associated with the congress; it is a site marker, not a photograph of the congress. No image date is supplied.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Opening of the Arab Congress of 1913

events.enhanced_description: On June 19, 1913, the Parliament of South Africa passed the Natives Land Act, which restricted land ownership for black South Africans to designated areas. This act laid the groundwork for institutionalized racial segregation in South Africa.

locations.name: Cape Town, Western Cape, South Africa

events.name: Passage of the Natives Land Act in South Africa

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1913, Joseph Cook was appointed as the 6th Prime Minister of Australia. His leadership came during a time of significant change and development for the nation, particularly in its foreign policy and national identity.
events.name: Joseph Cook becomes Prime Minister of Australia

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1913, the Second Balkan War began, following tensions between the Balkan League members over the division of territories gained from the Ottoman Empire. This conflict would further destabilize the region and set the stage for future conflicts in Europe.
events.name: Beginning of the Second Balkan War

events.enhanced_description: On July 10, 1913, Furnace Creek in California recorded the highest temperature ever documented on Earth at 134°F (56.7°C). This record has been a subject of study and debate among meteorologists and climate scientists, highlighting extreme weather phenomena.
events.name: highest temperature recorded on Earth

events.enhanced_description: On July 10, 1913, Romania officially declared war on Bulgaria, marking the beginning of hostilities in the Second Balkan War. This declaration was driven by territorial disputes and the desire to expand Romanian influence in the region.
events.name: Romania declares war on Bulgaria

events.enhanced_description: On July 11, 1913, a significant industrial strike occurred in the Black Country of England, involving 25,000 workers demanding a minimum wage of 23 shillings. This strike threatened the naval and steel industries' preparations for World War I.

locations.name: Black Country, West Midlands, United Kingdom

events.name: Major industrial strike in the Black Country

events.enhanced_description: On July 13, 1913, a cholera outbreak began among the Romanian Army during the Second Balkan War, exacerbating the already dire conditions faced by soldiers. The outbreak highlighted the challenges of military logistics and public health during wartime.
events.name: The 1913 Romanian Army cholera outbreak during the Second Balkan War starts

events.enhanced_description: On July 27, 1913, the town of San Javier was founded in Uruguay by Russian settlers, contributing to the diverse cultural tapestry of the region. This settlement reflected the broader trends of immigration and agricultural development in early 20th-century Uruguay.
events.name: The town of San Javier, Uruguay, is founded by Russian settlers

events.enhanced_description: On August 2, 1913, Swiss mountaineers Daniel Baud-Bovy and Frédéric Boissonnas, guided by Christos Kakkalos, achieved the first known ascent of Mount Olympus, the highest mountain in Greece and a site of great mythological significance. This ascent marked a notable achievement in the history of mountaineering.
events.name: The first known ascent of Mount Olympus in Greece

events.enhanced_description: On August 4, 1913, the city of Chungking (modern-day Chongqing) declared its independence from the central government of the Republic of China. This declaration was part of a larger wave of regional unrest and rebellion against the central authority during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Chungking declares independence

events.enhanced_description: On August 10, 1913, the Treaty of Bucharest was signed, officially ending the Second Balkan War. The treaty resulted in significant territorial changes, including the division of Macedonia and the assignment of Northern Epirus to Albania.

image.caption: Map of Bulgarian territories in Southern Dobruja ceded to Romania under the Treaty of Bucharest.
image.credit: Ikonact — Map of Bulgaria after Bucharest Treaty 1913 South Dobruja-bg.svg
image.date_qualification: Map published/dated 2018-08-21; depicts territorial changes associated with the 1913 treaty, not the signing event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Second Balkan War: The Treaty of Bucharest is signed

events.enhanced_description: On August 13, 1913, Harry Brearley, a British metallurgist, invented stainless steel in Sheffield, England. This groundbreaking development revolutionized various industries by providing a corrosion-resistant material that is still widely used today.
events.name: Harry Brearley invents stainless steel

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1913, French aviator Adolphe Pégoud made history by becoming the first person to successfully bail out from an airplane and land safely after his aircraft failed at an altitude of 900 feet. This remarkable feat marked a significant milestone in aviation safety.
events.name: Adolphe Pégoud becomes the first person to bail out from an airplane

events.enhanced_description: On August 23, 1913, the iconic Little Mermaid statue was completed in Copenhagen, Denmark. Created by sculptor Edvard Eriksen, this statue has since become a symbol of the city and a popular tourist attraction.
events.name: The Little Mermaid statue is finished

events.enhanced_description: On August 26, 1913, members of James Larkin's Irish Transport and General Workers' Union began strike action in Dublin, Ireland, in response to the dismissal of union members by the Dublin United Tramways Company. This marked the beginning of the Dublin Lock-out, a pivotal moment in Irish labor history.

image.caption: Ernest Kavanagh’s satirical cartoon “The Demon of Death,” depicting William Martin Murphy.
image.credit: Ernest Kavanagh (1884–1916) — http://multitext.ucc.ie/d/test5e ( archived copy )
image.date_qualification: Published 6 September 1913; the supplied evidence does not establish the date the cartoon was created.
image.image_date: published on 6 September 1913 in Irish Worker (bibliographic reference taken out of the monography of Thomas Morrissey: William Martin Murphy , ISBN 0-85221-132-5 )
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Dublin Lock-out: Members of the Irish Transport and General Workers' Union begin strike action

events.enhanced_description: On August 31, 1913, the Dublin Lock-out escalated into violence during an event known as 'Bloody Sunday,' when the Dublin Metropolitan Police clashed with demonstrators, resulting in the death of one protester and injuries to over 400 others. This incident underscored the tensions between labor movements and authorities in early 20th-century Ireland.
events.name: Dublin Lock-out: Bloody Sunday

events.enhanced_description: On September 7, 1913, the Fourth Congress of the International Psychoanalytical Association took place in Munich, marking the last occasion when Carl Jung and Sigmund Freud would meet. This congress was significant for the development of psychoanalysis and the relationship between these two influential figures.
events.name: Fourth Congress of the International Psychoanalytical Association

events.enhanced_description: On September 9, 1913, BASF inaugurated the world's first plant for the production of fertilizer using the Haber-Bosch process in Ludwigshafen, Germany. This innovation revolutionized agriculture by enabling the mass production of nitrogen fertilizers, significantly impacting global food production.
events.name: BASF starts the world's first plant for the production of fertilizer based on the Haber-Bosch process

events.enhanced_description: On September 10, 1913, Jean Sibelius's tone poem 'Luonnotar' premiered at Gloucester Cathedral, featuring soprano Aino Ackté. This work is notable for its lyrical beauty and connection to Finnish mythology, showcasing Sibelius's unique compositional style.
events.name: Jean Sibelius's tone poem Luonnotar is premiered

events.enhanced_description: On September 17, 1913, the Anti-Defamation League of B'nai B'rith was founded in Chicago, Illinois, with Sigmund Livingston serving as its first president. The organization was established to combat anti-Semitism and promote justice and fair treatment for all citizens.
events.name: Anti-Defamation League of B'nai B'rith is founded

events.enhanced_description: On September 23, 1913, French aviator Roland Garros made a historic flight by crossing the Mediterranean Sea from Fréjus, France, to Bizerte, Tunisia. This achievement was a significant milestone in early aviation and demonstrated the potential for long-distance air travel.
events.name: Roland Garros crosses the Mediterranean

events.enhanced_description: On September 29, 1913, the Treaty of Constantinople was signed in Istanbul, marking the end of the Second Balkan War between the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria. This treaty resulted in significant territorial adjustments and was a pivotal moment in the history of the Balkans.
events.name: Second Balkan War: The Treaty of Constantinople is signed

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1913, during the Mexican Revolution, Pancho Villa's troops captured the city of Torreón after a three-day battle, forcing government troops to retreat. This victory was a significant moment in Villa's campaign against the Mexican government.
events.name: Mexican Revolution: Pancho Villa's troops take Torreón

events.enhanced_description: On October 7, 1913, the Ford Motor Company's Highland Park Plant in Highland Park, Michigan, became the first automobile production facility in the world to implement the moving assembly line. This revolutionary method significantly reduced production time for the Model T, transforming the automotive industry and paving the way for mass production.
events.name: Implementation of the Moving Assembly Line at Ford Motor Company

events.enhanced_description: On October 9, 1913, the Canadian-owned ocean liner SS Volturno caught fire in a North Atlantic gale while en route from Rotterdam to New York City. Despite the tragedy that claimed 136 lives, the quick response of nearby ships, alerted by SOS messages, saved 521 passengers and crew members.
events.name: SS Volturno Fire

events.enhanced_description: On October 10, 1913, U.S. President Woodrow Wilson triggered the explosion of the Gamboa Dike, marking a significant milestone in the construction of the Panama Canal. This event symbolized the completion of a crucial phase in one of the most ambitious engineering projects of the early 20th century.
events.name: Explosion of the Gamboa Dike

events.enhanced_description: On October 11, 1913, the Philadelphia Athletics clinched the 1913 World Series by defeating the New York Giants 3-1 in the deciding game. This victory marked the Athletics' third championship title, solidifying their place in baseball history.
events.name: Deciding Game of the 1913 World Series

events.enhanced_description: On October 14, 1913, an explosion at the Universal Colliery in Senghenydd, Wales, resulted in the deaths of 439 miners, making it the worst mining disaster in the United Kingdom's history. The tragedy highlighted the dangerous conditions in coal mines and led to significant reforms in mining safety regulations.
events.name: Senghenydd Colliery Disaster

events.enhanced_description: On October 16, 1913, the British Royal Navy launched HMS Queen Elizabeth at Portsmouth Dockyard, marking a significant advancement in naval technology as the first oil-fired battleship. This innovation represented a shift in naval warfare and the future of battleship design.
events.name: Launch of HMS Queen Elizabeth

events.enhanced_description: On October 18, 1913, the Monument to the Battle of the Nations in Leipzig, Germany, was completed. This monumental structure commemorates the decisive battle of 1813, where the coalition forces defeated Napoleon, symbolizing German unity and national pride.

locations.name: Monument to the Battle of the Nations

events.name: Completion of the Monument to the Battle of the Nations

events.enhanced_description: On October 19, 1913, the German Life-Saving Society (DLRG) was founded to promote water safety and rescue services in Germany. This organization has played a crucial role in reducing drowning incidents and enhancing public awareness of water safety.

image.caption: Logo of the German Life Saving Association (DLRG).
image.credit: Deutsche Lebens-Rettungs-Gesellschaft e.V. — dlrg.de
image.date_qualification: Logo dated 2024-05-05; founding event dated 1913-10-19.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False; Restrictions: trademarked

events.name: Founding of the DLRG

events.enhanced_description: On October 26, 1913, Victoriano Huerta was elected as the President of Mexico amidst a backdrop of political turmoil and revolution. His presidency was characterized by authoritarian rule and conflict with revolutionary factions, leading to significant instability in the country.
events.name: Victoriano Huerta Elected President of Mexico

events.enhanced_description: On October 28, 1913, the Zabern Affair erupted in Alsace-Lorraine, where acts of aggression by the Prussian garrison provoked widespread political debate across the German Empire. This incident highlighted tensions between military authority and civil rights, leading to significant political discourse.
events.name: Zabern Affair

events.enhanced_description: On October 31, 1913, the Lincoln Highway, the first automobile road across the United States, was dedicated. This landmark event marked a significant advancement in American transportation, facilitating cross-country travel and commerce.
events.name: Dedication of the Lincoln Highway

events.enhanced_description: The Second Revolution in Mexico, occurring in 1913, was a revolt led by various factions against the government of Victoriano Huerta. This conflict was part of the broader Mexican Revolution, which sought to address issues of land reform and social justice.
events.name: Second Revolution

events.enhanced_description: On November 5, 1913, King Otto of Bavaria was deposed by his cousin, Prince Regent Ludwig, who subsequently assumed the title Ludwig III. This event marked a significant shift in Bavarian leadership during a period of political upheaval in Germany.
events.name: Deposition of King Otto of Bavaria

events.enhanced_description: On November 6, 1913, Mohandas Gandhi was arrested while leading a march of Indian miners in South Africa. This event was a pivotal moment in Gandhi's activism, highlighting the struggles against racial discrimination and injustice.
events.name: Gandhi's Arrest in South Africa

events.enhanced_description: On November 7, 1913, the Great Lakes Storm claimed 19 ships and over 250 lives, making it one of the deadliest storms in the region's history. The storm's ferocity highlighted the dangers of maritime navigation on the Great Lakes.
events.name: Great Lakes Storm of 1913

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1913, the Ford Motor Company introduced the first moving assembly line, drastically reducing chassis assembly time from over 12 hours to just 2 hours and 40 minutes. This innovation not only revolutionized automobile manufacturing but also set the stage for modern mass production techniques.
events.name: Introduction of the Moving Assembly Line by Ford

events.enhanced_description: On December 12, 1913, Vincenzo Peruggia was arrested in Florence while attempting to sell the stolen Mona Lisa. This incident brought international attention to the theft of the iconic painting and highlighted issues of art theft and cultural heritage.
events.name: Vincenzo Peruggia Arrested for Selling the Mona Lisa

events.enhanced_description: On December 19, 1913, President Woodrow Wilson signed the Raker Act, allowing the City of San Francisco to dam Hetch Hetchy Valley in Yosemite National Park. This controversial decision sparked debates about environmental conservation and urban development.

image.caption: Portrait of John E. Raker, U.S. Representative from California.
image.credit: Harris & Ewing — This image is available from the United States Library of Congress 's Prints and Photographs division under the digital ID cph.3c11671 . This tag does not indicate the copyright status of the attached work. A normal copyright tag is still required. See Commons:Licensing .
image.date_qualification: Portrait of the Raker Act’s chief sponsor, not a depiction of the signing. Image date is approximate: circa 1911.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Signing of the Raker Act

events.enhanced_description: On December 23, 1913, the Federal Reserve System was established as the central banking system of the United States through the signature of President Woodrow Wilson on the Federal Reserve Act. This landmark legislation aimed to provide the country with a safer and more flexible monetary and financial system.
events.name: Creation of the Federal Reserve System

events.enhanced_description: On December 24, 1913, the Italian Hall disaster occurred in Calumet, Michigan, where a stampede during a Christmas party resulted in the deaths of 73 people, mostly striking mine workers and their families. This tragic event underscored the dangers faced by laborers and their communities during a time of industrial strife.
events.name: Italian Hall Disaster

events.enhanced_description: On December 30, 1913, Italy returned the Mona Lisa to France, following its theft by Vincenzo Peruggia in 1911. This event marked the end of a significant chapter in art history and highlighted the importance of cultural heritage.
events.name: Return of the Mona Lisa to France

events.enhanced_description: The St. Petersburg–Tampa Airboat Line commenced operations, becoming the first airline to provide scheduled commercial passenger services using heavier-than-air aircraft. Tony Jannus, the first federally licensed pilot, transported passengers, marking a significant milestone in aviation history.
events.name: St. Petersburg–Tampa Airboat Line Begins Services

events.enhanced_description: The Karluk, flagship of the Canadian Arctic Expedition, sank after being crushed by ice. This incident underscored the dangers faced by explorers in the harsh Arctic environment.
events.name: Sinking of the Karluk

events.enhanced_description: The film 'Tess of the Storm Country', starring Mary Pickford, premiered in 1914 and significantly boosted her fame, marking a pivotal moment in the rise of modern celebrity culture in the film industry.
events.name: Film Tess of the Storm Country is released

events.enhanced_description: In response to the escalating tensions following the Tampico Affair, President Woodrow Wilson requested Congress to authorize military force in Mexico, reflecting the U.S. government's increasing involvement in Mexican affairs during this tumultuous period.
events.name: President Wilson asks Congress to use military force in Mexico

events.enhanced_description: In June 1914, Blaise Diagne of Senegal made history by becoming the first Black African representative in the French Parliament, symbolizing a significant step towards greater political representation for Africans in colonial powers.
events.name: Blaise Diagne becomes first Black African representative in French Parliament

events.enhanced_description: The funeral of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria took place at Artstetten Castle, marking a pivotal moment in history as his assassination had triggered the outbreak of World War I.
events.name: Funeral of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria

events.enhanced_description: In 1914, an anarchist bomb intended for John D. Rockefeller exploded prematurely in New York City, resulting in the deaths of four individuals and highlighting the tensions of the era.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Lexington Avenue bombing

events.enhanced_description: The USS Nevada, the United States Navy's first 'super-dreadnought' battleship, was launched in 1914, representing a significant advancement in naval technology during the early 20th century.

image.caption: USS Nevada (BB-36), painted orange as a target ship for the Operation Crossroads Able nuclear weapons test.
image.credit: USNavy — USNavy Photo via https://www.navsource.net/archives/01/36g.htm
image.date_qualification: 1946; 32 years after the 1914 launch
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Launch of USS Nevada

events.enhanced_description: In 1914, over 5,000 people gathered in Union Square, Manhattan, for a rally organized by the Anti-Militarist League to commemorate the anarchists killed in the Lexington Avenue bombing, reflecting the growing anti-war sentiment in the United States.

locations.name: Union Square, Manhattan, New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Anti-Militarist League rally

events.enhanced_description: In 1914, the Signal Corps of the United States Army established an Aviation Section, marking the formal recognition of military aviation and laying the groundwork for future air combat operations.
events.name: Establishment of Aviation Section in the U.S. Army

events.enhanced_description: In 1914, King George V reviewed the British Fleet at Spithead, showcasing the naval power of the United Kingdom just before the outbreak of World War I.
events.name: British Fleet review by George V

events.enhanced_description: In 1914, Mahatma Gandhi departed from South Africa for the last time, marking a significant transition in his life as he moved towards leading the Indian independence movement.

locations.name: Cape Town, Western Cape, South Africa

events.name: Mahatma Gandhi leaves South Africa

events.enhanced_description: In early August 1914, France ordered a general mobilization of its military forces in response to the growing threat from Germany, setting the stage for its involvement in World War I.
events.name: France orders general mobilization

events.enhanced_description: In 1914, the New York Stock Exchange closed its doors due to the outbreak of World War I in Europe, reflecting the global economic impact of the conflict.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: New York Stock Exchange closes due to war

events.enhanced_description: In 1914, Marcus Garvey established the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA) in Kingston, Jamaica, aiming to promote unity and self-reliance among people of African descent worldwide. The organization became a significant force in the Pan-African movement and laid the groundwork for future civil rights activism.
events.name: Marcus Garvey founds the Universal Negro Improvement Association in Jamaica

events.enhanced_description: In early 1914, a secret treaty was signed between the Ottoman Empire and the German Empire, ensuring Ottoman neutrality at the onset of World War I. This alliance would later shift as the Ottomans entered the war on the side of the Central Powers.
events.name: A secret treaty between the Ottoman Empire and German Empires secures Ottoman neutrality

events.enhanced_description: In 1914, the Imperial German Navy, commanded by Rear-Admiral Wilhelm Souchon, bombarded the French Algerian ports of Bône and Philippeville, showcasing Germany's naval capabilities early in World War I.
events.name: Bombardment of Bône and Philippeville

events.enhanced_description: In 1914, the Ittihad Alexandria Sports Club was founded in Alexandria, Egypt, becoming one of the prominent sports clubs in the region and contributing to the development of sports culture in the country.
events.name: Foundation of Ittihad Alexandria Sports Club

events.enhanced_description: In 1914, the first electric traffic light was installed at the intersection of Euclid Avenue and East 105 Street in Cleveland, Ohio, marking a significant advancement in urban traffic management.
events.name: First electric traffic light installation

events.enhanced_description: In 1914, the first engagement between British and German light cruisers occurred in the West Indies when HMS Bristol pursued SMS Karlsruhe, which managed to escape, highlighting the naval tensions of World War I.
events.name: First engagement between British and German light cruisers

events.enhanced_description: In 1914, German colonial forces executed Martin-Paul Samba for high treason, reflecting the tensions and conflicts arising in the colonies during World War I.
events.name: Execution of Martin-Paul Samba

events.enhanced_description: In 1914, Sir Ernest Shackleton's Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition set sail from Britain aboard the Endurance, aiming to cross Antarctica, which would later become one of the most famous survival stories in exploration history.

image.caption: A Times of London newspaper article reporting Ernest Shackleton’s return from his Antarctic expedition.
image.credit: Journalist working for The Times (London, 1916) — https://www.newspapers.com/image/32828121 (newspaper clipping from 1916)
image.date_qualification: Newspaper dated 2 June 1916; it documents the expedition’s aftermath, not its 1914 departure.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Shackleton's Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition

events.enhanced_description: In 1914, during the Mexican Revolution, troops under Venustiano Carranza and General Álvaro Obregón entered Mexico City, marking a significant moment in the struggle for power in Mexico.
events.name: Mexican Revolution: Carranza's troops enter Mexico City

events.enhanced_description: In 1914, a brief naval battle occurred on Lake Nyasa between British and German forces, where Captain Edmund Rhoades commanded the British steamship SS Gwendolen to disable the German vessel Hermann von Wissmann, marking an early naval engagement in Africa during World War I.
events.name: Naval battle on Lake Nyasa

events.enhanced_description: The Togoland Campaign concluded in August 1914 with the surrender of the German colony of Togoland to British and French forces. This campaign was significant as it marked one of the first military actions in Africa during World War I.
events.name: The Togoland Campaign ends

events.enhanced_description: In September 1914, the Austro-Hungarian city and fortress of Lemberg fell to Russian troops during World War I. This event was part of the Eastern Front campaigns and marked a significant loss for the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

image.caption: Map of the Eastern Front.
image.credit: Department of Military Art and Engineering, at the U.S. Military Academy (West Point) — West Point web site at: http://www.dean.usma.edu/history/web03/atlases/great%20war/great%20war%20%20pages/great%20war%20map%2028.htm
image.date_qualification: The map’s stated coverage is through September 26, 1914; no separate creation or depicted date is supplied.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Fall of Lemberg to Russian troops

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1914, Giacomo della Chiesa was elected as Pope Benedict XV, succeeding Pope Pius X. His papacy would be marked by efforts to promote peace during World War I and to address the challenges faced by the Catholic Church in a rapidly changing world.
events.name: Pope Benedict XV succeeds Pope Pius X

events.enhanced_description: William, Prince of Albania, fled the country on January 1, 1914, after facing significant opposition to his rule from various factions within Albania. His departure marked a critical moment in the early political instability of the newly established Albanian state.
events.name: William, Prince of Albania leaves the country

events.enhanced_description: The London Agreement, established on January 1, 1914, was a crucial pact among the members of the Triple Entente—Britain, France, and Russia—prohibiting any of them from seeking a separate peace with the Central Powers during World War I. This agreement aimed to maintain unity among the Allies in the face of growing hostilities.
events.name: London Agreement

events.enhanced_description: The First Battle of the Masurian Lakes, which took place from September 9 to September 14, 1914, was a significant German offensive that successfully pushed the Russian First Army back across its entire front. This battle demonstrated the effectiveness of German military strategy early in World War I.

image.caption: Map of the Eastern Front, prepared by the Department of Military Art and Engineering at the U.S. Military Academy.
image.credit: Department of Military Art and Engineering, at the U.S. Military Academy (West Point) — West Point web site at: http://www.dean.usma.edu/history/web03/atlases/great%20war/great%20war%20%20pages/great%20war%20map%2028.htm
image.date_qualification: The map depicts the Eastern Front to September 26, 1914; no original image date is supplied. It provides geographic and campaign context for the battle, rather than depicting the battle itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: First Battle of the Masurian Lakes

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1914, Andrew Fisher was sworn in as Prime Minister of Australia for the third time. His leadership during a tumultuous period included navigating the challenges of World War I and advocating for social reforms.

image.caption: Portrait of Andrew Fisher, Prime Minister of Australia.
image.credit: National Library of Australia — This image has been extracted from another file
image.date_qualification: The image is dated 1912, before Fisher's third term began in 1914.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Andrew Fisher becomes Prime Minister of Australia for the third time

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1914, the Flying Squadron of America was established to promote the temperance movement across the United States. This organization aimed to raise awareness about the dangers of alcohol consumption and advocate for prohibition.
events.name: The Flying Squadron of America established

events.enhanced_description: In January 1914, a significant earthquake struck the region of Burdur in Turkey, causing considerable damage and loss of life. This natural disaster highlighted the seismic activity prevalent in the area.
events.name: Burdur earthquake occurs in Turkey

events.enhanced_description: In 1914, the Manifesto of the Ninety-Three was signed by prominent German academics, expressing support for the German war effort in World War I. This document reflected the nationalistic fervor and the intellectual community's alignment with the government during the early stages of the conflict.
events.name: The Manifesto of the Ninety-Three is signed

events.enhanced_description: The First Battle of Ypres commenced in October 1914, marking a critical phase in the Western Front of World War I. This battle was characterized by fierce fighting and significant casualties as Allied forces sought to hold their positions against German advances.
events.name: The First Battle of Ypres begins

events.enhanced_description: The Race to the Sea, a series of maneuvers by both the Allies and Central Powers, effectively concluded in late 1914 with the front lines reaching the Belgian coast. This marked a shift to trench warfare that would dominate the Western Front for years.
events.name: The Race to the Sea effectively ends

events.enhanced_description: The British super-dreadnought battleship HMS Audacious was sunk off Tory Island, Ireland, in 1914 after hitting a minefield laid by the German merchant-cruiser Berlin. This incident underscored the dangers of naval warfare during World War I.
events.name: HMS Audacious is sunk off Tory Island

events.enhanced_description: In 1914, the Greek army occupied Northern Epirus with the approval of the Allies, amidst the backdrop of World War I. This occupation was part of Greece's efforts to expand its territory and influence in the region.
events.name: The Greek army occupies Northern Epirus

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Penang, fought in 1914, saw the German cruiser Emden sink a Russian cruiser and a French destroyer before escaping. This naval engagement highlighted the effectiveness of the Emden in disrupting Allied shipping in the Indian Ocean.
events.name: Battle of Penang

events.enhanced_description: In 1914, the participants in the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria were sentenced in Sarajevo. Gavrilo Princip, being underage, received a 20-year prison sentence, while others faced harsher penalties.
events.name: Participants in the Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria are sentenced

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Tanga concluded in late 1914, with the British Indian Expeditionary Force B failing to capture German East Africa defenses. This battle was part of the East African Campaign during World War I.
events.name: Battle of Tanga ends

events.enhanced_description: In 1914, Alpha Phi Delta was founded as a social fraternity at Syracuse University in New York. This organization has since grown to become a significant part of the university's social and cultural life.
events.name: Alpha Phi Delta founded

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1914, Mohandas Gandhi departed from England, sailing back to India with his wife, Kasturba. This journey marked a significant moment in Gandhi's life as he began to immerse himself in the Indian independence movement.
events.name: Mohandas Gandhi leaves England for India

events.enhanced_description: In 1914, the capital of Guangxi Province in China was officially moved from Guilin to Nanning. This change was part of administrative reforms aimed at improving governance and regional development.
events.name: Capital of Guangxi Province moved from Guilin to Nanning

events.enhanced_description: In 1914, oxymorphone, a powerful narcotic analgesic closely related to morphine, was first developed in Germany. This drug would later become significant in pain management and medical treatments.
events.name: Oxymorphone developed in Germany

events.enhanced_description: In 1914, the first everyday items made of stainless steel began to circulate in public. This innovation marked a significant advancement in materials science, leading to the widespread use of stainless steel in various applications.
events.name: First everyday items made of stainless steel come into public circulation

events.enhanced_description: In 1914, the Port of Orange in Texas was dredged to facilitate the fabrication of vessels for the United States Navy. This development was part of the broader mobilization efforts during World War I.

locations.name: Port of Orange, Texas, United States

events.name: Port of Orange, Texas dredged

events.enhanced_description: In 1914, Phi Sigma, a local undergraduate classical club, was founded by a group of students in the Greek Department at the University of Chicago. This organization aimed to promote the study of classical languages and literature.

locations.name: University of Chicago, Illinois, United States

events.name: Phi Sigma founded at University of Chicago

events.enhanced_description: In 1914, watchmaker Glycine Watch SA was founded by Eugène Meylan in Switzerland. The company would go on to become known for its innovative watch designs and contributions to the horology industry.
events.name: Glycine Watch SA founded in Switzerland

events.enhanced_description: In 1914, the fashion and perfumes company Puig was founded in Barcelona, Spain. The company has since grown to become a significant player in the global fashion and fragrance industry.
events.name: Fashion and perfumes company Puig founded in Barcelona

events.enhanced_description: In 1914, Woodman's of Essex, a famous family-owned clam shack, opened on Boston's North Shore in Massachusetts. It has since become a beloved institution known for its fried clams and seafood.

image.caption: Sign outside Woodman's of Essex.
image.credit: Paul Keleher — originally posted to Flickr as woodmans of essex
image.date_qualification: A site/sign photograph dated 2007, not a photograph of the restaurant’s 1914 opening.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Woodman's of Essex opened

events.enhanced_description: The Sakurajima volcano in Japan began to erupt, becoming effusive after a significant earthquake on January 13. The eruption caused the island to be linked to the Ōsumi Peninsula, altering the geography of the region.
events.name: Eruption of Sakurajima Volcano

events.enhanced_description: The Luxembourg national football team achieved its first victory by defeating France 5-4 in a friendly match, marking a historic moment in Luxembourg's football history.
events.name: Luxembourg National Football Team's First Victory

events.enhanced_description: The first stone of the Lincoln Memorial was laid in Washington, D.C., marking the beginning of the construction of this iconic tribute to President Abraham Lincoln. The memorial would later become a symbol of American history and civil rights.
events.name: First Stone of Lincoln Memorial Laid

events.enhanced_description: The American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers (ASCAP) was established in New York City to protect the copyrighted musical compositions of its members. This organization played a crucial role in the music industry, advocating for the rights of creators.
events.name: Establishment of ASCAP

events.enhanced_description: Karl Staaff resigned as Prime Minister of Sweden following the Courtyard Crisis, a political scandal that shook the government. He was succeeded by Hjalmar Hammarskjöld, the father of future UN Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjöld.
events.name: Karl Staaff Resigns as Prime Minister

events.enhanced_description: The ocean liner that would become HMHS Britannic, sister to the RMS Titanic, was launched at the Harland and Wolff shipyards in Belfast. This vessel would later serve as a hospital ship during World War I before sinking in the Aegean Sea.

image.caption: Britannic’s funnel being transported to the Harland and Wolff shipyard in Belfast.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — http://paquebot-titanic.e-monsite.com
image.date_qualification: Image dated 1914; the article dates Britannic’s launch to 26 February 1914, but the image is of funnel transport, not the launch itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Launch of HMHS Britannic

events.enhanced_description: The Autonomous Republic of Northern Epirus was proclaimed by ethnic Greeks in Northern Epirus, reflecting the ongoing ethnic tensions and aspirations for autonomy in the region during this period.
events.name: Proclamation of the Autonomous Republic of Northern Epirus

events.enhanced_description: Prince William of Wied arrived in Albania to begin his reign as the country's monarch. His rule would be marked by political instability and challenges in establishing a stable government.
events.name: Prince William of Wied Arrives in Albania

events.enhanced_description: Suffragette Mary Richardson damaged Velázquez's painting Rokeby Venus in London's National Gallery using a meat chopper. This act of vandalism was a protest against the treatment of women and highlighted the suffragette movement's struggle for rights.

image.caption: Diego Velázquez’s painting *The Toilet of Venus* (*Rokeby Venus*).
image.credit: Diego Velázquez — Key facts . The National Gallery, London. Retrieved on 25 June 2013 .
image.date_qualification: The image_date field gives 1644, while the article dates the painting to between 1647 and 1651; neither date is the 1914 event date. The discrepancy is unresolved.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Mary Richardson Damages Rokeby Venus

events.enhanced_description: On Saint Patrick's Day, Thomas H. Curtin invented green beer, showcasing a festive twist on the traditional beverage. This innovation has since become a popular drink during St. Patrick's Day celebrations.
events.name: Invention of Green Beer

events.enhanced_description: During the Curragh Incident, British Army officers stationed at the Curragh Camp in Ireland resigned their commissions rather than be ordered to act against Unionist Ulster Volunteers if the Government of Ireland Act was passed. This event highlighted the tensions surrounding Irish home rule and the military's role in political conflicts.
events.name: Curragh Incident

events.enhanced_description: Belgian surgeon Albert Hustin performed the first successful non-direct blood transfusion using anticoagulants, marking a significant advancement in medical practices and blood transfusion techniques.
events.name: First Successful Non-Direct Blood Transfusion

events.enhanced_description: Katherine Routledge and her husband arrived on Easter Island to conduct the first true study of the island's culture and archaeology. Their research would contribute significantly to the understanding of Rapa Nui history and society.
events.name: Katherine Routledge Arrives on Easter Island

events.enhanced_description: On September 27, 1914, the SS Komagata Maru sailed from India to Canada, but was denied entry into Vancouver due to restrictive immigration laws aimed at excluding Asian immigrants. The incident highlighted the racial discrimination prevalent in Canadian immigration policy at the time.
events.name: Komagata Maru incident

events.enhanced_description: The Tampico Affair in April 1914 was a diplomatic incident between the United States and Mexico, triggered by the arrest of U.S. sailors in Tampico. The misunderstanding escalated tensions and led to a breakdown in diplomatic relations, prompting U.S. military intervention.
events.name: Tampico Affair

events.enhanced_description: On April 11, 1914, Margaret C. MacDonald was appointed Matron-in-Chief of the Canadian Nursing Service, becoming the first woman in the British Empire to achieve the rank of major, marking a significant advancement for women in military roles.
events.name: Margaret C. MacDonald appointed Matron-in-Chief

events.enhanced_description: The first International Criminal Police Congress was held in Monaco on April 14, 1914, bringing together representatives from 24 countries to discuss international cooperation in law enforcement and crime prevention.
events.name: First International Criminal Police Congress

events.enhanced_description: On April 20, 1914, the Colorado National Guard attacked a tent colony of striking coal miners in Ludlow, Colorado, resulting in the deaths of 24 people. This tragic event highlighted the violent struggles between labor unions and mining companies during the Colorado Coalfield War.
events.name: Ludlow Massacre

events.enhanced_description: On April 21, 1914, U.S. Navy sailors and Marines landed in Veracruz, Mexico, as part of a military intervention that lasted over six months. This occupation was a response to the ongoing political instability in Mexico and aimed to enforce an arms embargo.
events.name: United States occupation of Veracruz

events.enhanced_description: On April 22, 1914, Mexico officially severed diplomatic relations with the United States in response to the U.S. occupation of Veracruz, marking a significant deterioration in bilateral relations during a period of political turmoil.
events.name: Mexico ends diplomatic relations with the United States

events.enhanced_description: On April 23, 1914, Cornelis Jacobus Langenhoven addressed the English caucus of the Cape Provincial Council, leading to the official recognition of the Afrikaans language. This event was a significant milestone in the cultural and linguistic identity of South Africa.
events.name: Afrikaans language receives official recognition

events.enhanced_description: On April 23, 1914, the Chicago Federals hosted the Kansas City Packers in the first game played at Weeghman Park, which would later be known as Wrigley Field, marking an important moment in the history of Major League Baseball.
events.name: MLB Chicago Federals host the Kansas City Packers

events.enhanced_description: On April 24, 1914, a significant arms shipment of 35,000 rifles and over 3 million rounds of ammunition was landed at Larne, Bangor, and Donaghadee in Ulster for the Unionist Ulster Volunteers, escalating tensions in the lead-up to the Irish War of Independence.
events.name: Larne Gun Running

events.enhanced_description: The Exposition Internationale was held in Lyon, France, on November 1, 1914, showcasing advancements in technology and culture from around the world, although it was overshadowed by the onset of World War I shortly thereafter.
events.name: Exposition Internationale

events.enhanced_description: The Jubilee Exhibition (Jubilæumsutstillingen) was held in Oslo, Norway, on October 11, 1914, to commemorate the centennial of the Norwegian constitution, celebrating national pride and cultural heritage.
events.name: Jubilee Exhibition in Kristiania

events.enhanced_description: On May 8, 1914, W. W. Hodkinson founded Paramount Pictures as a national film distributor in the United States, which would go on to become one of the most influential film studios in Hollywood history.
events.name: Paramount Pictures is created

events.enhanced_description: On May 9, 1914, J. T. Hearne became the first bowler in cricket history to take 3,000 first-class wickets, a remarkable achievement that underscored his skill and longevity in the sport.
events.name: J. T. Hearne takes 3,000 first-class wickets

events.enhanced_description: The Protocol of Corfu, established on May 17, 1914, granted autonomy to the provinces of Korçë and Gjirokastër in Northern Epirus under nominal Albanian sovereignty, reflecting the complex ethnic and political landscape of the Balkans.

image.caption: Newspaper illustration depicting negotiations in Corfu related to the Protocol of Corfu.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Newspaper "Nea Ellas", Issue: May 9, 1914/Εφημερίδα "Νέα Ελλάς, 9 Μαΐου, 1914.
image.date_qualification: Depicted date: May 1914, as recorded in the image metadata. The image is described as an illustration, not a photograph.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Protocol of Corfu

events.enhanced_description: On May 25, 1914, the House of Commons of the United Kingdom passed the Government of Ireland Act 1914, also known as the Irish Home Rule Bill, which aimed to provide self-governance for Ireland amidst ongoing political tensions.
events.name: Government of Ireland Act 1914

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1914, the ocean liner RMS Empress of Ireland sank in the Gulf of St. Lawrence after colliding with another vessel, resulting in the tragic loss of 1,012 lives, marking one of the worst maritime disasters in Canadian history.
events.name: RMS Empress of Ireland sinks

events.enhanced_description: On May 30, 1914, the RMS Aquitania embarked on her maiden voyage from Southampton, England, marking the beginning of her service as one of the largest and most luxurious ocean liners of her time.
events.name: RMS Aquitania makes her maiden voyage

events.enhanced_description: On June 1, 1914, Edward Mandell House, an envoy for President Woodrow Wilson, met with Kaiser Wilhelm II in Berlin, discussing diplomatic relations and the growing tensions in Europe leading up to World War I.
events.name: Edward Mandell House meets Kaiser Wilhelm II

events.enhanced_description: On June 8, 1914, the Brazilian Football Confederation was founded in Rio de Janeiro, with Álvaro Zamith as its first president, marking a pivotal moment in the organization and promotion of football in Brazil.
events.name: Brazilian Football Confederation is founded

events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1914, Honus Wagner, a legendary shortstop for the Pittsburgh Pirates, became the first player in the twentieth century to achieve 3,000 career hits in Major League Baseball, marking a significant milestone in baseball history.
events.name: Honus Wagner achieves 3,000 career hits

events.enhanced_description: The 1914 Kenwood House ball was a lavish social event attended by members of the British aristocracy, reflecting the opulence and social dynamics of the time. This event occurred just before the onset of World War I, marking a significant moment in British social history.
events.name: 1914 Kenwood House ball

events.enhanced_description: On June 12, 1914, during the Greek genocide, Ottoman Greeks in Phocaea were massacred by Turkish irregular troops, reflecting the ethnic tensions and violence that characterized the period leading up to World War I.
events.name: Massacre of Ottoman Greeks in Phocaea

events.enhanced_description: On June 18, 1914, during the Mexican Revolution, the Constitutionalists led by Venustiano Carranza captured San Luis Potosí, further undermining the regime of President Victoriano Huerta and escalating the conflict in Mexico.

locations.name: San Luis Potosí, San Luis Potosí, Mexico

events.name: Constitutionals take San Luis Potosí

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1914, Kaiser Wilhelm II reopened the Kaiser-Wilhelm-Kanal after deepening, while the British Fleet, under Admiral Sir George Warrender, visited, showcasing the naval cooperation and tensions in pre-World War I Europe.
events.name: Reopening of the Kaiser-Wilhelm-Kanal

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1914, a significant downtown fire in Manchester, New Hampshire, caused $400,000 in damages and injured 19 firefighters, highlighting the risks and challenges faced by urban centers during this period.
events.name: Manchester downtown fire

events.enhanced_description: On June 28, 1914, Serbian nationalist Gavrilo Princip assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria and his wife, Duchess Sophie, in Sarajevo, an event that triggered the July Crisis and ultimately led to the outbreak of World War I.

locations.name: Sarajevo, Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bosnia and Herzegovina

events.name: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1914, the Secretary of the Austro-Hungarian Legation in Belgrade sent a dispatch to Vienna suggesting Serbian complicity in the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, escalating tensions between Austria-Hungary and Serbia.
events.name: Dispatch from Austro-Hungarian Legation

events.enhanced_description: On June 30, 1914, prominent figures including Lords Crewe and Lansdowne, along with Prime Minister Herbert Asquith and Andrew Bonar Law, addressed the UK Parliament regarding the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, reflecting the gravity of the situation.
events.name: Parliament addresses assassination of Archduke

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1914, the Emperor of Austria-Hungary received the report of the investigation into the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, which fueled anti-Serbian sentiment and set the stage for the impending conflict.
events.name: Austro-Hungarian investigation report

events.enhanced_description: On July 10, 1914, Nicholas Hartwig, the Russian Minister to Serbia, died of a heart attack while visiting the Austrian minister in Belgrade, a significant event amidst the rising tensions in the Balkans.
events.name: Death of Nicholas Hartwig

events.enhanced_description: On July 11, 1914, Babe Ruth made his major league debut with the Boston Red Sox, marking the beginning of a legendary career that would transform the sport of baseball.
events.name: Babe Ruth's major league debut

events.enhanced_description: On July 13, 1914, reports emerged of a projected Serbian attack on the Austro-Hungarian Legation in Belgrade, further escalating the already tense relations between the two nations.
events.name: Projected Serbian attack on Austro-Hungarian Legation

events.enhanced_description: On July 14, 1914, the Government of Ireland Bill completed its passage through the House of Lords in the UK, allowing Ulster counties to vote on Home Rule, although the outbreak of war would prevent its implementation.
events.name: Government of Ireland Bill passage

events.enhanced_description: On July 15, 1914, Victoriano Huerta resigned from the presidency of Mexico and fled to Coatzacoalcos, Veracruz, marking a significant turning point in the Mexican Revolution.
events.name: Victoriano Huerta resigns

events.enhanced_description: On July 18, 1914, the Signal Corps of the United States Army established an Aviation Section, marking the formal recognition of military aviation and setting the stage for its future role in warfare.
events.name: Establishment of Aviation Section

events.enhanced_description: On July 19, 1914, King George V summoned a conference to discuss the Irish Home Rule problem, which met from July 21-24 but failed to reach a consensus amidst the growing tensions in Europe.
events.name: George V summons conference on Irish Home Rule

events.enhanced_description: On July 23, 1914, Austria-Hungary presented Serbia with an unconditional ultimatum, a critical step that escalated tensions and set the stage for the outbreak of World War I.
events.name: Austria-Hungary presents July Ultimatum

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1914, Serbia responded to an ultimatum from Austria-Hungary, accepting some demands but rejecting others. This response led to the severance of diplomatic ties and the mobilization of Austrian forces, marking a significant escalation towards World War I.
events.name: Serbia responds to the ultimatum from the 23rd

events.enhanced_description: On July 26, 1914, Erskine Childers and his wife Molly successfully landed 2,500 rifles in Howth, Ireland, for the Irish Volunteers, a nationalist group. This event escalated tensions between the British authorities and Irish nationalists, culminating in the Bachelor's Walk massacre.
events.name: Howth gun-running

events.enhanced_description: On July 27, 1914, Felix Ysagun Manalo officially registered the Iglesia ni Cristo (Church of Christ) with the Philippine government, marking the establishment of a significant religious movement in the country.
events.name: Felix Ysagun Manalo registers the Iglesia ni Cristo
