events.enhanced_description: The Charge at Haritan represented the final engagement between units of the Desert Mounted Corps and Ottoman forces during World War I. This battle underscored the effectiveness of cavalry in the desert warfare of the Middle East.
events.name: WWI: Charge at Haritan

events.enhanced_description: Czechoslovakia declared its independence from Austria-Hungary in 1918, a pivotal moment in Central European history that led to the establishment of a new nation-state. This declaration was fueled by nationalist sentiments and the desire for self-determination among Czechs and Slovaks.
events.name: Czechoslovakia declares its independence from Austria-Hungary

events.enhanced_description: The Wilhelmshaven mutiny marked a critical moment in the German High Seas Fleet during the final days of World War I, as sailors protested against the war and demanded an end to hostilities. This mutiny was indicative of the growing unrest and desire for change within Germany.
events.name: The Wilhelmshaven mutiny of the German High Seas Fleet breaks out

events.enhanced_description: The Martin Declaration, published on October 30, 1918, marked a significant step in the formation of the Czechoslovak state, asserting the inclusion of Slovakia as a key component. This declaration was a pivotal moment in the national awakening of Slovaks and their quest for independence from Austro-Hungarian rule.

image.caption: Protected monument at the Tatra banka headquarters in Martin, Slovakia.
image.credit: User:Darwinek — Own work
image.date_qualification: A 2011 photograph of a protected monument at the Tatra banka site associated with the Martin Declaration; it is not a photograph of the 1918 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: The Martin Declaration is published, including Slovakia in the formation of the Czecho-Slovak state

events.enhanced_description: The Armistice of Mudros, signed on October 30, 1918, marked the end of hostilities between the Ottoman Empire and the Allies in World War I. This agreement led to significant territorial changes and the eventual disintegration of the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: The Armistice of Mudros ends conflict between the Ottoman Empire and the Allies of World War I

events.enhanced_description: On October 31, 1918, a revolution in Hungary led to the overthrow of the pro-Habsburg government, significantly contributing to the dissolution of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. This event was part of a broader wave of national movements across Central and Eastern Europe following World War I.
events.name: Revolution overthrows the pro-Habsburg government in Hungary, effectively dissolving the Austro-Hungarian Empire

events.enhanced_description: In late 1918, the Czechoslovak army successfully retook the Czech Borderland, asserting control over the region following the collapse of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. This event was crucial in the establishment of Czechoslovakia as an independent nation.
events.name: Retaking Czech Borderland (1918)

events.enhanced_description: The Polish–Ukrainian War began in November 1918 with the proclamation of the West Ukrainian People's Republic in Lviv, leading to a conflict over territorial claims in Eastern Europe. This war was part of the broader chaos following World War I and the collapse of empires.
events.name: The Polish–Ukrainian War is inaugurated by the proclamation of the West Ukrainian People's Republic

events.enhanced_description: The Armistice of Villa Giusto, signed on November 3, 1918, marked the cessation of hostilities between Austria-Hungary and the Allies on the Italian Front. This agreement was a crucial step towards the end of World War I in Europe.
events.name: WWI: The Armistice of Villa Giusto is signed between Austria-Hungary and the Allies near Padua

events.enhanced_description: The Armistice of Villa Giusti came into effect on November 4, 1918, officially ending the warfare between Italy and Austria-Hungary on the Italian Front. This armistice was a significant moment in the conclusion of World War I.
events.name: WWI: The Armistice of Villa Giusti comes into effect, ending warfare between Italy and Austria-Hungary

events.enhanced_description: On November 6, 1918, a new Polish government was proclaimed in Lublin, marking a significant step towards Polish independence following the end of World War I. This event was part of the broader national revival in Poland.
events.name: A new Polish government is proclaimed in Lublin

events.enhanced_description: On November 7, 1918, King Ludwig III of Bavaria fled Munich amid the revolutionary upheaval that swept through Germany at the end of World War I. His departure marked the end of the monarchy in Bavaria and the rise of republican sentiments.
events.name: King Ludwig of Bavaria flees his country

events.enhanced_description: On November 7, 1918, Kurt Eisner, the Minister-President of the Provisional National Council, declared Bavaria a republic. This declaration was part of the broader wave of revolutionary changes sweeping through Germany following World War I, leading to the establishment of a democratic government in Bavaria.
events.name: Bavaria declared a republic

events.enhanced_description: On November 8, 1918, the German army withdrew its support for Kaiser Wilhelm II, signaling a critical turning point in the German Revolution. This event led to the Kaiser’s abdication and the establishment of a republic in Germany.
events.name: The German army withdraws its support of the Kaiser

events.enhanced_description: On November 9, 1918, Kaiser Wilhelm II of Germany abdicated the throne amid the turmoil of the German Revolution and the end of World War I. He subsequently chose to live in exile in Doorn, Netherlands, where he lived until his death in 1941, marking the end of the German monarchy.
events.name: Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicates

events.enhanced_description: On November 9, 1918, Philipp Scheidemann proclaimed the establishment of the German Republic from the balcony of the Reichstag in Berlin. This declaration came in the wake of the abdication of Kaiser Wilhelm II and marked a significant shift from imperial rule to a democratic government in Germany.
events.name: The German Republic is proclaimed

events.enhanced_description: On November 9, 1918, the British battleship HMS Britannia was sunk by a German submarine off Cape Trafalgar, marking the last major naval engagement of World War I. The attack resulted in the loss of around fifty lives and underscored the ongoing naval conflict even as the war was drawing to a close.
events.name: HMS Britannia sunk

events.enhanced_description: On November 10, 1918, communist forces in Luxembourg City initiated a rebellion, marking the beginning of the Luxembourg rebellions. This uprising was part of the broader revolutionary wave in Europe following World War I, as workers and soldiers sought to establish a socialist government.
events.name: Luxembourg rebellions begin

events.enhanced_description: On November 11, 1918, Germany signed an armistice agreement with the Allies in the 'Compiègne Wagon', marking the official end of World War I. The signing took place between 5:12 AM and 5:20 AM, and it became effective at the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month, symbolizing the cessation of hostilities.
events.name: End of WWI: Armistice signed

events.enhanced_description: On November 12, 1918, Austria was officially declared a republic following the collapse of the Austro-Hungarian Empire at the end of World War I. Karl Renner, a prominent political figure, played a crucial role in this transition, leading the new government during a time of significant upheaval.
events.name: Austria becomes a republic

events.enhanced_description: On November 13, 1918, the Allied Occupation of Constantinople began, following the end of World War I. This occupation was part of the Allies' strategy to control the remnants of the Ottoman Empire and set the stage for the eventual establishment of the Republic of Turkey under Mustafa Kemal Atatürk.
events.name: Allied Occupation of Constantinople begins

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1918, Czechoslovakia was declared a republic, marking a significant moment in Central European history. This declaration followed the collapse of the Austro-Hungarian Empire and was led by key figures such as Tomáš Masaryk, who became the first president of the new republic.
events.name: Czechoslovakia becomes a republic

events.enhanced_description: On November 16, 1918, the Hungarian Democratic Republic was declared, marking Hungary's independence from Austria following the end of World War I. Mihály Károlyi, a prominent politician, became the first Prime Minister of the new republic, advocating for democratic reforms.
events.name: Hungarian Democratic Republic declared

events.enhanced_description: On November 18, 1918, Latvia declared its independence from Russia, following the chaos of World War I and the Russian Revolution. Jānis Čakste, a key figure in the independence movement, later became the first President of Latvia.
events.name: Latvia declares independence

events.enhanced_description: On November 20, 1918, U-boats began to rendezvous off Harwich as part of the surrender of the High Seas Fleet to the British Royal Navy. This marked a significant moment in the aftermath of World War I, as German naval power was effectively neutralized.
events.name: U-boats surrender to British Royal Navy

events.enhanced_description: On November 21, 1918, Polish troops and volunteers perpetrated a massacre in Lwów, Galicia, resulting in the deaths of at least 320 Ukrainian Christians and Jews. This tragic event highlighted the ethnic tensions and violence that erupted in the region following the end of World War I.
events.name: Lwów pogrom

events.enhanced_description: On November 22, 1918, the Belgian royal family returned to Brussels after the end of World War I, with King Albert I having commanded the Allied army group during the liberation of Belgium. This marked a significant moment of national pride and recovery for the Belgian people.
events.name: Belgian royal family returns to Brussels

events.enhanced_description: On November 23, 1918, the British military government of Palestine was established following the end of World War I. This marked the beginning of British administration in the region, which would last until the establishment of the State of Israel in 1948.
events.name: British military government of Palestine begins

events.enhanced_description: On November 25, 1918, the Great People's Assembly convened in Novi Sad, bringing together representatives of Serbs, Bunjevci, and other Slavic groups to discuss their political future following World War I. This assembly played a significant role in the formation of new national identities in the post-war period.
events.name: Great People's Assembly of Serbs, Bunjevci and other Slavs in Banat, Bačka and Baranja

events.enhanced_description: On November 25, 1918, General Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck, the German commander in German East Africa, signed a ceasefire at Abercorn in Northern Rhodesia. This event marked the end of hostilities in the region, concluding the German campaign in Africa during World War I.
events.name: Ceasefire signed in Northern Rhodesia

events.enhanced_description: On November 26, 1918, the Podgorica Assembly voted for a 'union of the people' between the kingdoms of Montenegro and Serbia, effectively ending Montenegro's status as a sovereign state. This decision led to the deposition of the exiled King Nicholas I and the integration of Montenegro into the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes.
events.name: Podgorica Assembly votes for union

events.enhanced_description: On November 28, 1918, the Red Army invaded Estonia, marking the beginning of the Estonian War of Independence. This conflict arose as Estonia sought to establish its sovereignty following the collapse of the Russian Empire, leading to the establishment of the Commune of the Working People of Estonia as a Soviet puppet state.
events.name: Estonian War of Independence begins

events.enhanced_description: On November 29, 1918, Serbia formally annexed Montenegro, effectively suspending its existence as a sovereign state for nearly 88 years. This annexation was part of the broader unification efforts in the region following World War I, led by King Alexander I of Serbia.
events.name: Serbia annexes Montenegro

events.enhanced_description: On November 30, 1918, conductor Ernest Ansermet led the first concert of the Orchestre de la Suisse Romande in Geneva, marking a significant cultural event in post-war Switzerland. This orchestra would go on to become one of the leading symphonic ensembles in the country.
events.name: First concert by Orchestre de la Suisse Romande

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1918, the Danish–Icelandic Act of Union was enacted, granting Iceland independence while maintaining a personal union with the King of Denmark. This significant step marked Iceland's transition towards full sovereignty after centuries of foreign rule.
events.name: By the Danish–Icelandic Act of Union, Iceland regains independence

events.enhanced_description: On December 4, 1918, President Woodrow Wilson departed from New York City by ship to attend the Paris Peace Conference, becoming the first sitting U.S. president to travel to Europe while in office. His participation was pivotal in shaping the post-war order and establishing the League of Nations.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: President Woodrow Wilson departs by ship to the Paris Peace Conference

events.enhanced_description: On December 5, 1918, during the Estonian War of Independence, the British light cruiser HMS Cassandra struck a mine and sank near Saaremaa, resulting in the deaths of 11 sailors. This incident highlighted the ongoing conflicts in the region as Estonia sought to assert its independence.
events.name: Estonian War of Independence: The British light cruiser HMS Cassandra strikes a mine and sinks

events.enhanced_description: On December 6, 1918, a magnitude 7.2 earthquake struck British Columbia, causing significant geological activity in the region. This event was part of the ongoing tectonic processes affecting the Pacific Northwest.
events.name: A magnitude (Mw) 7.2 earthquake shakes British Columbia

events.enhanced_description: On December 14, 1918, Prince Frederick Charles of Hesse renounced his claim to the Finnish throne, a decision that came in the wake of Finland's declaration of independence from Russia. His abdication marked a significant moment in Finland's transition to sovereignty.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Prince Frederick Charles of Hesse renounces the Finnish throne

events.enhanced_description: On December 16, 1918, Vincas Mickevičius-Kapsukas declared the formation of the Lithuanian Soviet Socialist Republic, a move orchestrated by the Russian SFSR to justify its involvement in the Lithuanian–Soviet War. This declaration was part of the broader struggle for control and influence in the region following World War I.
events.name: Vincas Mickevičius-Kapsukas declares the formation of the Lithuanian Soviet Socialist Republic

events.enhanced_description: On December 17, 1918, disaffected workers marched on Government House in Darwin, demanding the resignation of the Administrator of the Northern Territory, John A. Gilruth. This protest, known as the Darwin Rebellion, highlighted the social and political tensions in Australia following World War I.

image.caption: Black-and-white photograph of demonstrators marching through Darwin toward Government House.
image.credit: Creator unknown. — Source credit: Northern Territory Archives Service
image.date_qualification: The image description dates the march to 17 December 1918; supported display date is 1918.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Darwin Rebellion in Australia

events.enhanced_description: On December 20, 1918, Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk returned to Prague, marking a significant moment in the establishment of Czechoslovakia as an independent republic following the collapse of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. His leadership was pivotal in shaping the new nation's democratic foundations.
events.name: Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk returns to the Czechoslovak Republic

events.enhanced_description: On December 21, 1918, the Red Army captured Tartu, a key city in Estonia, during the Estonian War of Independence. This event marked a significant escalation in the conflict as Estonian forces sought to establish their sovereignty against Soviet influence.
events.name: Estonian War of Independence: The Red Army captures Tartu, Estonia

events.enhanced_description: On December 25, 1918, Der Stahlhelm, Bund der Frontsoldaten, was established in Germany as a nationalist veterans' organization. It aimed to unite former soldiers and promote nationalist sentiments in the post-World War I era.
events.name: Der Stahlhelm, Bund der Frontsoldaten, is formed in Germany

events.enhanced_description: On December 27, 1918, the Greater Poland Uprising began, sparked by a patriotic speech from pianist and politician Ignacy Jan Paderewski in Poznań. This uprising was a crucial step towards Polish independence from German rule.
events.name: Greater Poland Uprising (1918–19)

events.enhanced_description: On December 28, 1918, Sinn Féin achieved a landslide victory in the Irish general election, winning 73 out of 105 seats. This victory led to the establishment of the First Dáil in Dublin, marking a pivotal moment in the struggle for Irish independence.
events.name: Sinn Féin landslide victory in Irish general election

events.enhanced_description: On December 31, 1918, a British-brokered ceasefire was established, ending two weeks of fighting in the Georgian–Armenian War. This ceasefire aimed to stabilize the region amidst the chaos following World War I.
events.name: British-brokered ceasefire in the Georgian–Armenian War

events.enhanced_description: The Fremantle Wharf riot in 1919 was a significant workers' strike at Fremantle Harbour, reflecting the labor unrest and demands for better working conditions in post-World War I Australia. This event highlighted the growing strength of labor movements in the country.
events.name: 1919 Fremantle Wharf riot

events.enhanced_description: The Khaibalikend Massacre in 1919 involved the mass killing of Armenian civilians in Nagorno-Karabakh, part of the broader context of violence against Armenians during and after World War I. This tragic event is a reminder of the ethnic conflicts that plagued the region during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Khaibalikend Massacre

events.enhanced_description: In early 1919, the Czechoslovak Legions occupied much of the self-proclaimed 'free city' of Pressburg, enforcing its incorporation into the newly established republic of Czechoslovakia. This action was part of the broader struggle for national self-determination in Central Europe.
events.name: Czechoslovak Legions occupy Pressburg

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1919, the HMY Iolaire sank off the coast of the Hebrides, resulting in the tragic deaths of 201 people, primarily servicemen returning home to Lewis and Harris. This disaster remains one of the worst maritime tragedies in Scottish history.

image.caption: A lifeboat from the wrecked HMY Iolaire lies against rocks at Stornoway.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — https://beeldbank.spaarnestadphoto.com/search.pp?flush=1&multikeyword=SFA022806673&searchtype=0#ctr-thumbnails
image.date_qualification: The source dates the image to 1919; no more precise depicted date is supplied.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: HMY Iolaire disaster

events.enhanced_description: The Spartacist uprising began in Berlin in early January 1919, led by the Marxist Spartacus League, which included the newly formed Communist Party of Germany. The uprising aimed to establish a socialist government but was violently suppressed within a week, leading to the deaths of key leaders Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht.
events.name: Spartacist uprising in Berlin

events.enhanced_description: In 1919, the German Workers' Party (Deutsche Arbeiterpartei, DAP) was formed in Munich through the merger of Anton Drexler's Committee of Independent Workmen and Karl Harrer's Political Workers' Circle. This party would later evolve into the National Socialist German Workers' Party (Nazi Party).

image.caption: Logo of the German Workers’ Party (Deutsche Arbeiterpartei).
image.credit: LH658 — Own work
image.date_qualification: The logo file is dated 2023-01-19; it represents the 1919–1920 party and does not depict the 1919 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Formation of the German Workers' Party

events.enhanced_description: In early 1919, Friedrich Ebert, the Chancellor of Germany, ordered the Freikorps into action in Berlin to suppress leftist uprisings and maintain order during the chaotic aftermath of World War I. This decision reflected the tensions between the Weimar government and radical socialist movements.
events.name: Friedrich Ebert orders Freikorps into action

events.enhanced_description: During the Estonian War of Independence, the Battle of Tapa took place in early 1919, where Estonian forces successfully liberated the town from the Red Army. This battle was crucial in establishing Estonia's independence from Soviet influence.
events.name: Battle of Tapa

events.enhanced_description: In early 1919, a group of socialist and liberal deputies in Luxembourg City tabled a motion to establish Luxembourg as a republic. This political movement was met with resistance, leading to a confrontation with the French Army that quelled the rebellion.
events.name: Luxembourg Republic motion

events.enhanced_description: In 1919, the Georgian genocide occurred in Alagir, where significant violence was inflicted upon the Georgian population. This tragic event is part of the broader context of ethnic conflicts and political upheaval in the region during this period.
events.name: Georgian genocide in Alagir

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1919, the Great Molasses Flood occurred in Boston, Massachusetts, when a large storage tank burst, releasing a wave of molasses that swept through the streets, killing 21 people and injuring 150. This bizarre disaster highlighted the industrial hazards of the time.
events.name: Great Molasses Flood

events.enhanced_description: In 1919, renowned pianist Ignacy Jan Paderewski was appointed as the second Prime Minister of Poland, playing a crucial role in the country's post-World War I reconstruction and international diplomacy. His leadership was instrumental in establishing Poland's sovereignty after over a century of partitions.
events.name: Ignacy Jan Paderewski becomes Prime Minister of Poland

events.enhanced_description: In early 1919, Estonian forces liberated Narva, expelling the Red Army from Northern Estonia during the Estonian War of Independence. This victory was significant in the struggle for Estonia's independence and sovereignty.
events.name: Estonian forces liberate Narva

events.enhanced_description: In 1919, Bentley Motors Limited was founded in Crewe, England, by W. O. Bentley. The company quickly gained a reputation for producing high-quality luxury automobiles and became synonymous with British automotive excellence.
events.name: Founding of Bentley Motors Limited

events.enhanced_description: The Communist International, also known as the Comintern, was founded in 1919 to promote worldwide communism and coordinate the activities of communist parties across the globe. This organization played a crucial role in the spread of communist ideology throughout the 20th century.
events.name: Founding of the Communist International

events.enhanced_description: During the Russian Civil War, the White forces in Siberia, led by Admiral Alexander Kolchak, launched a Spring Offensive against the Red Army. This campaign resulted in significant territorial gains for the Whites, including the capture of key cities.
events.name: Spring Offensive in Russian Civil War

events.enhanced_description: The arrest of Saad Zaghloul by British authorities in Egypt marked the beginning of the Egyptian Revolution of 1919. His exile to Malta galvanized nationalist sentiments and led to widespread protests against British colonial rule.
events.name: Arrest of Saad Zaghloul

events.enhanced_description: Eugene V. Debs, a prominent socialist leader and labor activist, was imprisoned for opposing U.S. involvement in World War I and speaking out against conscription. His imprisonment became a significant event in the labor movement and highlighted the tensions between civil liberties and national security during wartime.
events.name: Eugene V. Debs enters prison

events.enhanced_description: The Bauhaus, a revolutionary school of art and design, was founded in Weimar, Germany, by Walter Gropius. It aimed to unify art, craft, and technology, influencing modern architecture and design principles worldwide.
events.name: Founding of the Bauhaus

events.enhanced_description: Anzac Day was observed for the first time in Australia, commemorating the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps (ANZAC) who fought at Gallipoli during World War I. This day has since become a national day of remembrance in Australia and New Zealand.
events.name: First observance of Anzac Day

events.enhanced_description: Pancho Villa, a prominent Mexican revolutionary general, captured the city of Parral in Chihuahua, Mexico, and executed the mayor and his two sons. This act was part of Villa's ongoing campaign against the Mexican government and its officials.

image.caption: Portrait of Mexican revolutionary Pancho Villa.
image.credit: Unlnown — Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division Washington, D.C. 20540 USA [1]
image.date_qualification: Image date: 1910. This predates the event; the supplied evidence does not establish that the portrait was made at Parral or during the event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Pancho Villa takes Parral

events.enhanced_description: The eruption of Kelud Volcano in East Java, Indonesia, resulted in the deaths of approximately 5,000 people. This catastrophic event was marked by explosive eruptions and pyroclastic flows, devastating nearby communities and altering the landscape.
events.name: Kelud Volcano Eruption

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Spin Boldak occurred during the Third Anglo-Afghan War, marking a significant military engagement where British forces attempted to secure their position against Afghan resistance. This battle was notable as it was the last instance of the British Army employing escalade tactics.
events.name: Siege of Spin Boldak

events.enhanced_description: The Republic of Prekmurje declared its independence from Hungary in the aftermath of World War I, reflecting the shifting national boundaries and the rise of new states in Central Europe. This declaration was part of a broader trend of national self-determination in the region.
events.name: Declaration of Independence of Prekmurje

events.enhanced_description: Earl W. Bascom and his father John W. Bascom designed the first reverse-opening side-delivery bucking chute in Lethbridge, Alberta, which became the standard in rodeo events. This innovation significantly improved safety and efficiency in rodeo competitions.
events.name: Invention of the Reverse-Opening Bucking Chute

events.enhanced_description: In 1919, Admiral Ludwig von Reuter ordered the scuttling of the German fleet interned at Scapa Flow, Scotland, to prevent its capture by the Allies. This dramatic act resulted in the sinking of numerous ships and the death of nine German sailors.
events.name: Scuttling of the German Fleet at Scapa Flow

events.enhanced_description: The White Army's capture of Kyiv marked a pivotal moment in the Southern Front of the Russian Civil War, reflecting the intense conflict between the Bolsheviks and their opponents in the region.
events.name: Russian Civil War, Southern Front: Kyiv captured by the White Army

events.enhanced_description: The establishment of the Communist Party of America marked a significant development in American political history, as it sought to promote Marxist ideology and organize workers in the wake of the Russian Revolution.

image.caption: The Communist Party USA Workers’ Bookshop at its New York headquarters, with political posters in the window.
image.credit: Marjory Collins — This image is available from the United States Library of Congress 's Prints and Photographs division under the digital ID fsa.8d08139 . This tag does not indicate the copyright status of the attached work. A normal copyright tag is still required. See Commons:Licensing .
image.date_qualification: A 1942 photograph of the party’s bookshop in New York, not a photograph of the party’s 1919 establishment in Chicago.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The Communist Party of America is established

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1919, Nancy Astor, Viscountess Astor, made history by becoming the first woman to take her seat in the House of Commons of the United Kingdom, following her election on November 28, 1918, marking a significant milestone in women's political representation.

locations.name: House of Commons, London, United Kingdom

events.name: Nancy Astor Takes Her Seat

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1919, XWA, located in Montreal, became the first public radio station in North America to go on the air, marking a significant development in the field of broadcasting and communication.
events.name: First Public Radio Station in North America

events.enhanced_description: In 1919, Germany experienced severe inflation, with the value of the Papiermark plummeting from 12 marks to 47 marks against the United States dollar by December, reflecting the economic turmoil following World War I.
events.name: German Inflation

events.enhanced_description: On January 2, 1919, the Red Army's Caspian-Caucasian Front initiated the Northern Caucasus Operation against the White Army during the Russian Civil War. This operation aimed to secure strategic territories but faced significant challenges.
events.name: Russian Civil War: Northern Caucasus Operation begins

events.enhanced_description: On January 3, 1919, the Faisal–Weizmann Agreement was signed, establishing a framework for Arab-Jewish cooperation in the development of a Jewish homeland in Palestine and an Arab nation in the Middle East. This agreement reflected the complex political dynamics of the post-World War I era.

image.caption: Signature page of the Faisal–Weizmann Agreement with T. E. Lawrence’s translation of Faisal’s caveat.
image.credit: Faisal bin Hussein and Chaim Weizmann — Faisal Weizmann agreement 1919
image.date_qualification: Document page from 1919 associated with the agreement signed on 3 January 1919; it is not a photograph of the signing meeting.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Faisal–Weizmann Agreement signed

events.enhanced_description: On January 9, 1919, Friedrich Ebert ordered the Freikorps into action in Berlin to suppress leftist uprisings. This decision was part of the broader struggle for control in post-World War I Germany.
events.name: Freikorps action ordered in Berlin

events.enhanced_description: On January 10, 1919, the Freikorps launched an attack against Spartacist supporters in Berlin, marking a violent confrontation during the Spartacist uprising. This event underscored the intense political strife in Germany during this period.
events.name: Freikorps attacks Spartacist supporters

events.enhanced_description: In 1919, Romania formally annexed Transylvania, a region with a complex ethnic and political history. This annexation was part of the broader territorial changes in Eastern Europe following World War I and was met with varying degrees of acceptance among the local population.
events.name: Romania annexes Transylvania

events.enhanced_description: On January 12, 1919, during the Russian Civil War, the Armed Forces of South Russia under General Anton Denikin engaged in fierce fighting against the Red Army for control of the strategic Donbass region. This conflict was part of the larger struggle for dominance in post-revolutionary Russia.
events.name: Russian Civil War: Donbass region conflict

events.enhanced_description: On January 13, 1919, workers' councils in Berlin officially ended the general strike, marking the conclusion of the Spartacist uprising. This uprising was a significant event in the struggle between leftist factions and the Weimar government.
events.name: End of the Spartacist uprising

events.enhanced_description: On January 14, 1919, Estonian forces successfully liberated Tartu from the Red Army during the Estonian War of Independence. This victory was a crucial step in Estonia's struggle for sovereignty.
events.name: Estonian forces liberate Tartu

events.enhanced_description: Following the Spartacist uprising in early 1919, prominent socialist leaders Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht were murdered in Berlin. Their deaths symbolized the brutal suppression of leftist movements in post-war Germany and had lasting impacts on the political landscape.
events.name: Murder of Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht

events.enhanced_description: In 1919, the Eighteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution was ratified, establishing Prohibition and prohibiting the manufacture, sale, and transportation of alcoholic beverages. This marked a significant shift in American social policy and led to widespread changes in society.
events.name: Ratification of the Eighteenth Amendment

events.enhanced_description: The Paris Peace Conference commenced on January 18, 1919, at the Palace of Versailles, where delegates from 27 nations gathered to negotiate peace treaties following World War I. The conference aimed to establish a new world order and address the geopolitical landscape altered by the war.

image.caption: Photograph of the Japanese delegation at the Paris Peace Conference.
image.credit: 1919 photo, unknown author — Photographed by me at the Japan Foreign Office Archives in 2009
image.date_qualification: Image dated 1919; the source gives only the year, not a specific date within it.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The Paris Peace Conference opens

events.enhanced_description: On January 19, 1919, the Red Army initiated a counter-offensive in the Perm area during the Russian Civil War, aiming to reclaim territory from the White forces. This marked a significant escalation in the conflict as the Bolsheviks sought to consolidate their power.
events.name: Red Army counter-offensive in Perm

events.enhanced_description: On January 19, 1919, the Monarchy of the North was established in Northern Portugal, a short-lived political entity that emerged during the tumultuous post-World War I period in Portugal. This monarchy was part of the broader instability that characterized the region during this time.
events.name: Establishment of the Monarchy of the North

events.enhanced_description: Dáil Éireann convened for the first time on January 21, 1919, at the Mansion House in Dublin, comprising Sinn Féin members who had been elected in the 1918 general election. This assembly declared an independent Irish Republic, marking a pivotal moment in Ireland's struggle for independence.
events.name: First meeting of Dáil Éireann

events.enhanced_description: On January 23, 1919, during the Khotyn Uprising, partisans captured the city of Khotyn in what is now Ukraine, as they sought to assert control over the region amidst the chaos of post-World War I territorial disputes. This event highlighted the ongoing struggles for power in Eastern Europe.
events.name: Khotyn Uprising

events.enhanced_description: The League of Nations was founded on January 25, 1919, in Paris, France, as part of the peace settlement following World War I. It aimed to promote international cooperation and prevent future conflicts, although it ultimately faced significant challenges in achieving its goals.
events.name: Founding of the League of Nations

events.enhanced_description: On January 31, 1919, the Battle of George Square occurred in Glasgow, Scotland, as the British Army was called in to quell riots during negotiations over working hours. This event underscored the social unrest and labor disputes prevalent in post-war Britain.
events.name: Battle of George Square

events.enhanced_description: On February 1, 1919, Estonian forces successfully liberated the towns of Valga and Võru from the Red Army, marking a significant step in the Estonian War of Independence. This event was crucial in establishing Estonia's sovereignty following the chaos of World War I.
events.name: Estonian War of Independence: Estonian forces liberate Valga and Võru

events.enhanced_description: On February 3, 1919, Soviet troops occupied Ukraine, solidifying their control over the region during the tumultuous period of the Russian Civil War. This occupation was part of a broader strategy to extend Bolshevik influence across former territories of the Russian Empire.
events.name: Russian Civil War: Soviet troops occupy Ukraine

events.enhanced_description: On February 4, 1919, Pressburg, now known as Bratislava, was designated as the capital of Slovakia. This decision was part of the broader reorganization of Central European states following the end of World War I and the dissolution of the Austro-Hungarian Empire.
events.name: Pressburg (Bratislava) becomes the capital of Slovakia

events.enhanced_description: On February 5, 1919, United Artists was incorporated in Los Angeles by prominent filmmakers D. W. Griffith, Charlie Chaplin, Mary Pickford, and Douglas Fairbanks. This studio was established to provide greater creative control and financial independence to its founders in the burgeoning film industry.
events.name: Incorporation of United Artists

events.enhanced_description: On February 10, 1919, the Inter-Allied Women's Conference convened in Paris to address women's issues and advocate for their inclusion in the post-war peace negotiations. This conference was a significant step in the women's rights movement, emphasizing the need for gender equality in the new world order.
events.name: Inter-Allied Women's Conference

events.enhanced_description: On February 11, 1919, Friedrich Ebert was elected as the first President of Germany by the Weimar National Assembly. His presidency marked the beginning of the Weimar Republic, a period characterized by political instability and economic challenges in post-war Germany.
events.name: Friedrich Ebert elected President of Germany

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1919, ethnic Germans and Hungarians in Pressburg protested against the city's incorporation into Czechoslovakia. The protest turned violent when Czechoslovak Legions opened fire on the demonstrators, highlighting the ethnic tensions in the newly formed state.
events.name: Protest in Pressburg against incorporation into Czechoslovakia

events.enhanced_description: On February 13, 1919, a revolt in Porto led by civilians and members of the National Republican Guard resulted in the end of the Monarchy of the North in Portugal. This event was part of the broader republican movement that swept through Portugal in the aftermath of World War I.
events.name: End of Portugal's Monarchy of the North

events.enhanced_description: On February 14, 1919, the Polish–Soviet War began with the Battle of Bereza Kartuska. This conflict arose from territorial disputes following World War I and would shape the borders and political landscape of Eastern Europe for years to come.
events.name: Beginning of the Polish–Soviet War

events.enhanced_description: On February 16, 1919, a rebellion by uniformed peasants occurred in Saaremaa during the Estonian War of Independence. The Estonian government forces swiftly crushed the uprising, resulting in over 200 casualties, underscoring the internal conflicts within Estonia during its fight for independence.
events.name: Saaremaa Rebellion during Estonian War of Independence

events.enhanced_description: On February 25, 1919, Oregon became the first U.S. state to impose a gasoline tax of one cent per gallon. This legislative move aimed to fund road construction and maintenance, setting a precedent for future transportation funding mechanisms across the country.
events.name: Oregon's gasoline tax

events.enhanced_description: On February 26, 1919, an act of the United States Congress established most of the Grand Canyon as a National Park. This designation was a significant step in the conservation movement, aimed at preserving the natural beauty and ecological integrity of this iconic American landmark.
events.name: Establishment of Grand Canyon National Park

events.enhanced_description: On February 28, 1919, Amānullāh Khān ascended to the throne as King of Afghanistan. His reign was marked by efforts to modernize the country and assert its independence from British influence, culminating in the Third Anglo-Afghan War.
events.name: Amānullāh Khān becomes King of Afghanistan

events.enhanced_description: The Rowlatt Act, passed by the Imperial Legislative Council, allowed the British government to suppress dissent in India by extending emergency measures from the Defence of India Act 1915. This act sparked widespread protests and was a significant factor leading to the Indian independence movement.
events.name: The Rowlatt Act is passed

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, members of the American Expeditionary Forces gathered in Paris for the first American Legion caucus, marking the establishment of a veterans' organization aimed at advocating for the rights and benefits of American soldiers returning from World War I.
events.name: First American Legion caucus

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, the Commonwealth of the Philippines was established, marking a significant step towards independence from American colonial rule. This political transition aimed to prepare the nation for full sovereignty while establishing a democratic government.
events.name: Birth of the Commonwealth of the Philippines

events.enhanced_description: On March 21, Béla Kun proclaimed the establishment of the Hungarian Soviet Republic, a short-lived communist state that sought to implement radical socialist reforms in Hungary following World War I. The republic faced significant opposition and was ultimately overthrown later that year.
events.name: Hungarian Soviet Republic established

events.enhanced_description: On March 23, Benito Mussolini founded the Italian Fascist political movement in Milan, advocating for a nationalist and authoritarian regime. This movement would later lead to the establishment of a totalitarian state in Italy and significantly impact European politics.
events.name: Founding of Italian Fascist movement

events.enhanced_description: On March 24, Charles I, the last Emperor of Austria, left his homeland for exile in Switzerland, following the collapse of the Austro-Hungarian Empire after World War I. His departure marked the end of imperial rule in Austria and the beginning of a new political era.
events.name: Charles I goes into exile

events.enhanced_description: On March 26, Queen of the South F.C. was formed in Dumfries, Scotland, becoming one of the prominent football clubs in the region. The club has since played a significant role in Scottish football history.
events.name: Formation of Queen of the South F.C.

events.enhanced_description: On March 27, the name Bratislava was officially adopted for the city previously known as Pressburg. This change reflected the national identity shift following World War I and the dissolution of the Austro-Hungarian Empire.
events.name: Bratislava officially adopted as city name

events.enhanced_description: On April 5, during the Polish-Soviet War, the Polish Army executed 35 Jews in Pinsk, accusing them of Bolshevism without trial. This tragic event highlighted the violence and ethnic tensions during the tumultuous period following World War I.
events.name: Pinsk massacre

events.enhanced_description: On April 6, the Bavarian Soviet Republic was founded in Munich, establishing a short-lived socialist government in the aftermath of World War I. The republic aimed to implement radical reforms but faced opposition and was dissolved within months.
events.name: Bavarian Soviet Republic founded

events.enhanced_description: On April 10, Mexican Revolution leader Emiliano Zapata was ambushed and killed in Morelos. His assassination marked a significant turning point in the revolution, leading to the decline of agrarian reform efforts in Mexico.
events.name: Assassination of Emiliano Zapata

events.enhanced_description: The International Labour Organization (ILO) was established in 1919 as an agency of the League of Nations, aimed at promoting social justice and fair labor standards worldwide. It was the first specialized agency of the United Nations and continues to play a crucial role in labor rights.
events.name: The International Labour Organization (ILO) is established

events.enhanced_description: On April 12, notorious French serial killer Henri Désiré Landru was arrested in Paris. His crimes, which included the murder of multiple women, shocked the nation and led to a highly publicized trial.
events.name: Arrest of Henri Désiré Landru

events.enhanced_description: On April 13, the Amritsar Massacre occurred when British troops, under the command of Reginald Dyer, opened fire on a peaceful gathering at Jallianwala Bagh, killing hundreds of unarmed Sikh civilians. This brutal act intensified Indian resentment towards British colonial rule and became a pivotal moment in the struggle for independence.
events.name: Amritsar Massacre

events.enhanced_description: On April 15, the Save the Children Fund was established in the UK to provide relief for children affected by the aftermath of World War I, particularly in Germany and Austria. This organization has since grown into a global movement advocating for children's rights and welfare.
events.name: Creation of Save the Children Fund

events.enhanced_description: On April 20, the French Army blew up the bridge over the Dniester River at Bender, Moldova, as a strategic move to protect the city from advancing Bolshevik forces during the Russian Civil War. This action was part of the broader conflict involving multiple factions in the region.
events.name: Destruction of bridge in Bender

events.enhanced_description: On April 23, the Estonian Constituent Assembly convened its first session, marking a significant step in Estonia's path to independence following World War I. This assembly was tasked with drafting a constitution and establishing a democratic government.
events.name: Estonian Constituent Assembly convenes

events.enhanced_description: On April 25, the Bauhaus architectural and design movement was founded in Weimar, Germany, by Walter Gropius. This influential movement sought to unify art, craft, and technology, significantly impacting modern architecture and design.

image.caption: The Bauhaus building in Dessau.
image.credit: Spyrosdrakopoulos — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photograph of the Dessau Bauhaus site, made in 2014; it depicts a later site, not the 1919 founding in Weimar.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Founding of the Bauhaus movement

events.enhanced_description: On April 30, the first wave of anarchist bombings occurred in the United States, with several bombs sent by followers of Italian anarchist Luigi Galleani intercepted by authorities. This series of bombings reflected the growing tensions and fears of radicalism in post-World War I America.
events.name: First wave of anarchist bombings in the U.S.

events.enhanced_description: Weimar Republic troops, along with Freikorps units, occupied Munich to suppress the Bavarian Soviet Republic. This military action was part of the broader conflict between leftist and nationalist forces in post-World War I Germany.
events.name: Occupation of Munich

events.enhanced_description: Amānullāh Khān, the King of Afghanistan, launched an attack against the British government in India, reflecting the growing nationalist sentiments in the region. This event was part of the broader struggle for independence from colonial rule.
events.name: Amānullāh Khān attacks British government

events.enhanced_description: The May Fourth Movement erupted in China as a response to the decision made at the Paris Peace Conference to transfer German concessions in Jiaozhou Bay to Japan instead of returning them to China. This movement marked a significant turning point in Chinese nationalism and intellectual thought.
events.name: May Fourth Movement erupts in China

events.enhanced_description: The Third Anglo-Afghan War began as Afghanistan sought to regain its independence from British influence. This conflict was marked by a series of military engagements and ultimately led to the recognition of Afghanistan's sovereignty.

image.caption: Afghan peace delegates.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — https://collection.nam.ac.uk/detail.php?acc=1963-09-633-39
image.date_qualification: Dated 1919; described as following the war, not as a photograph of its beginning.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Beginning of the Third Anglo-Afghan War

events.enhanced_description: The United States Navy's Curtiss flying boat NC-4, commanded by Albert Cushing Read, completed the first transatlantic flight, departing from Naval Air Station Rockaway and arriving in Lisbon. This historic flight marked a significant achievement in aviation history.
events.name: First transatlantic flight by NC-4

events.enhanced_description: A new electoral law was introduced in Belgium, establishing universal manhood suffrage and granting voting rights to certain classes of women. This reform was a significant step towards gender equality in the political sphere.
events.name: New electoral law in Belgium

events.enhanced_description: The University College of Wales in Aberystwyth established what is likely the world's first chair in International Politics, endowed by David Davies and his sisters in honor of Woodrow Wilson. Alfred Eckhard Zimmern was appointed as the first professor, marking a significant development in the academic study of international relations.

image.caption: The Aberystwyth University International Politics building.
image.credit: Uwa786 at English Wikipedia — Transferred from en.wikipedia to Commons.
image.date_qualification: The image date is given as “13 September 2007 (original upload date)”; it does not establish when the building was photographed.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Establishment of chair in International Politics

events.enhanced_description: The Hellenic Army landed at Smyrna, supported by ships of the British Royal Navy, as part of the Greco-Turkish War. This military action was aimed at expanding Greek territory following World War I.
events.name: Greek landing at Smyrna

events.enhanced_description: Mustafa Kemal Atatürk landed at Samsun on the Anatolian Black Sea coast, marking the beginning of the Turkish War of Independence. This event is commemorated annually as a day of youth and sports in Turkey.
events.name: Mustafa Kemal Atatürk lands at Samsun

events.enhanced_description: The University of California opened its second campus in Los Angeles, initially known as the Southern Branch of the University of California. This institution would later be renamed the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), becoming a major center for higher education.

locations.historical_name: Southern Branch of the University of California
locations.name: University of California, Los Angeles

events.name: Opening of the University of California, Los Angeles

events.enhanced_description: During the Estonian War of Independence, Estonian forces captured the city of Pskov from the Red Army and subsequently handed it over to White forces. This event was part of the broader struggle for independence in the region.
events.name: Estonian forces capture Pskov

events.enhanced_description: Fyodor Raskolnikov, a Russian revolutionary, was exchanged for 14 British prisoners of war during the tumultuous period following World War I. This exchange highlighted the complex political dynamics and negotiations occurring in the aftermath of the war.
events.name: Exchange of Fyodor Raskolnikov

events.enhanced_description: The Eddington experiment tested Einstein's theory of general relativity by observing the bending of light during a total solar eclipse. Conducted by Arthur Eddington in Príncipe and Andrew Crommelin in Sobral, Brazil, the results confirmed Einstein's predictions and revolutionized modern physics.
events.name: Eddington experiment

events.enhanced_description: By agreement with the United Kingdom, Belgium was granted a mandate over part of German East Africa, specifically Ruanda-Urundi, which would later become Rwanda and Burundi. This mandate was confirmed by the League of Nations and marked a significant change in colonial governance in East Africa.
events.name: Belgium receives mandate over Ruanda-Urundi

events.enhanced_description: In June 1919, a series of anarchist bombings occurred in the United States, where eight mail bombs were sent to prominent figures. This wave of violence reflected the heightened tensions and fears of radicalism in post-World War I America.
events.name: United States Anarchist Bombings

events.enhanced_description: On June 4, 1919, the United States Congress approved the Nineteenth Amendment, which guaranteed women the right to vote. This landmark decision marked a significant victory in the women's suffrage movement and set the stage for ratification by the states.
events.name: Nineteenth Amendment Approval

events.enhanced_description: On June 5, 1919, the pro-German Baltische Landeswehr initiated hostilities against Estonia in Northern Latvia, marking a significant moment in the Estonian and Latvian Wars of Independence. This conflict was part of the broader struggle for national sovereignty following World War I.
events.name: Estonian and Latvian Wars of Independence

events.enhanced_description: On June 6, 1919, the Hungarian Red Army launched an attack on the Republic of Prekmurje, intensifying the conflict in the region during the post-World War I upheaval. This military action was part of the broader struggle for control and influence in Central Europe.
events.name: Hungarian Red Army Attack

events.enhanced_description: On June 7, 1919, British troops opened fire on a protesting mob in Valletta, Malta, resulting in the deaths of four individuals. This tragic event underscored the tensions between the colonial government and the Maltese population during a period of unrest.
events.name: Sette Giugno on Malta

events.enhanced_description: On June 8, during the Russian Civil War, the Cossacks of the Upper Don revolted against Bolshevik rule in the Vyoshenskaya Uprising, aligning themselves with the White forces. This rebellion was part of the larger conflict between the Red and White factions during the civil war.

image.caption: Map of the area of the Vyoshenskaya Uprising.
image.credit: Adolf Marks — Настольный атлас А. Ф. Маркса, 1903 год
image.date_qualification: A 1903 atlas map showing the uprising's area, not a photograph of the 1919 uprising.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Vyoshenskaya Uprising

events.enhanced_description: On June 14, 1919, British aviators John Alcock and Arthur Whitten Brown completed the first nonstop transatlantic flight, traveling from St. John's, Newfoundland, to Clifden, Ireland. This historic achievement marked a significant milestone in aviation history and demonstrated the potential for long-distance air travel.

locations.name: St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada

events.name: First Nonstop Transatlantic Flight

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1919, the Epsom Riot erupted when Canadian troops clashed with local police, resulting in the death of English Police Sergeant Thomas Green. This incident highlighted the tensions between returning soldiers and civilians in post-war Britain.
events.name: Epsom Riot by Canadian Troops

events.enhanced_description: On June 18, 1919, Liga Deportiva Alajuelense, one of the most popular football clubs in Costa Rica, was founded. This establishment marked a significant development in the country's sports culture and contributed to the growth of football in the region.
events.name: Foundation of Liga Deportiva Alajuelense

events.enhanced_description: On June 20, during the Russian Civil War, the Red Army launched a counteroffensive on the Siberian Front, where General Gaya Gai led a decisive victory against White forces near Orenburg. This battle marked a turning point in the conflict, pushing the Whites back behind the Ural Mountains.
events.name: Counteroffensive of Eastern Front

events.enhanced_description: On June 20, 1919, during the Russian Civil War, the White Volunteer Army achieved a decisive victory over the exhausted Red forces in the Kharkiv Operation, capturing the industrial city of Kharkiv. This battle was a critical moment in the ongoing conflict.
events.name: Kharkiv Operation

events.enhanced_description: On June 21, 1919, during the Winnipeg General Strike, the Royal North-West Mounted Police fired into a crowd of unemployed war veterans, resulting in two deaths. This tragic event underscored the tensions between labor movements and authorities in post-war Canada.
events.name: Bloody Saturday of the Winnipeg General Strike

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1919, during the Estonian and Latvian Wars of Independence, the Estonian army achieved a significant victory against the pro-German Baltische Landeswehr at the Battle of Cēsis. This battle forced the enemy to retreat towards Riga and is celebrated as Victory Day in Estonia.
events.name: Battle of Cēsis

events.enhanced_description: On June 26, 1919, British officials St John Philby and T. E. Lawrence arrived in Cairo to discuss Arab unrest in Egypt. Their discussions were crucial in shaping British policy in the region following the end of World War I.
events.name: Arrival of St John Philby and T. E. Lawrence in Cairo

events.enhanced_description: On June 28, 1919, the Treaty of Versailles was signed, formally ending World War I. This treaty imposed significant reparations and territorial losses on Germany, shaping the geopolitical landscape of Europe for decades to come.
events.name: Signing of the Treaty of Versailles

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Versailles was signed on June 28, 1919, marking the formal end of World War I. The treaty imposed heavy reparations and territorial losses on Germany, which led to significant political and economic turmoil in the country in the years that followed.
events.name: The Treaty of Versailles is signed, formally ending World War I

events.enhanced_description: The Perm Operation, part of the Russian Civil War, commenced in July 1919, where the Red Army aimed to recapture the city of Perm from White forces. This operation was significant in consolidating Bolshevik control over the region.
events.name: Perm Operation begins on the Siberian Front

events.enhanced_description: On July 2, 1919, the Syrian National Congress convened in Damascus, where Arab nationalists proclaimed Syria's independence from Ottoman rule. This event marked a significant step towards Arab nationalism and the quest for self-determination in the region.
events.name: The Syrian National Congress in Damascus announces independence

events.enhanced_description: On July 2, 1919, the British airship R34 completed the first successful transatlantic flight by dirigible, traveling from RAF East Fortune in Scotland to Mineola, New York. This historic flight demonstrated the potential of air travel for long distances.
events.name: British airship R34 makes the first transatlantic flight

events.enhanced_description: On July 3, 1919, the pro-German Baltische Landeswehr signed a peace treaty with Estonia and Latvia, marking a significant moment in the Estonian and Latvian Wars of Independence. This event led to the resignation of Latvian Prime Minister Andrievs Niedra and the takeover of Riga by Latvian forces.
events.name: Baltische Landeswehr signs a peace treaty with Estonia and Latvia

events.enhanced_description: On July 5, 1919, during the Russian Civil War, the Red Army successfully captured the city of Ekaterinburg from the White forces led by Admiral Alexander Kolchak. This victory was crucial for the Bolsheviks in their campaign against the White Army.
events.name: Red Army captures the city of Ekaterinburg

events.enhanced_description: On July 7, 1919, the United States Army initiated a convoy across the continental U.S. starting from Washington, D.C., to evaluate the feasibility of cross-country road travel. This endeavor highlighted the need for improved infrastructure, as the U.S. Highway System was still in its infancy.
events.name: The United States Army sends a convoy across the continental U.S.

events.enhanced_description: On July 11, 1919, the Netherlands enacted legislation establishing the eight-hour workday and a free Sunday for workers. This law was a significant advancement in labor rights and reflected the growing labor movement's influence in post-war Europe.
events.name: The eight-hour day and free Sunday become law for workers in the Netherlands

events.enhanced_description: The Longview Race Riot occurred on July 12, 1919, in Longview, Texas, where racial tensions escalated into violence, resulting in the lynching of an African American man. This event highlighted the pervasive racial discrimination and violence that characterized the post-World War I era in the United States.
events.name: Longview Race Riot

events.enhanced_description: On July 19, 1919, the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic established its Foreign Ministry, marking a significant step in the country's efforts to assert its sovereignty and engage in international diplomacy following its independence.

image.caption: Map of the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic.
image.credit: Golden — Own work . events.name: The Foreign Ministry of the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic is established

events.enhanced_description: On July 21, 1919, the dirigible Wingfoot Air Express caught fire over downtown Chicago, resulting in the deaths of two passengers, one crew member, and ten people on the ground. This tragic incident raised concerns about the safety of air travel during the early years of aviation.
events.name: Wingfoot Air Express crash

events.enhanced_description: The Chicago Race Riot of 1919 erupted on July 27, 1919, following a racially charged incident where a white man threw stones at a group of Black teenagers. This violent confrontation marked the beginning of a week-long riot that highlighted racial tensions in the United States during the post-World War I era.
events.name: The Chicago Race Riot of 1919 begins

events.enhanced_description: On July 28, 1919, the International Astronomical Union (IAU) was founded in Paris, France, to promote international cooperation in astronomy. The IAU has since played a critical role in the advancement of astronomical research and the standardization of astronomical nomenclature.
events.name: The International Astronomical Union is founded

events.enhanced_description: On July 31, 1919, British police in London and Liverpool went on strike demanding recognition of the National Union of Police and Prison Officers. The strike resulted in the dismissal of over 2,000 officers and highlighted the growing labor unrest in post-war Britain.
events.name: British police strikes in London and Liverpool

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1919, the Hungarian Soviet Republic, led by Béla Kun, collapsed after a series of military defeats. This marked the end of a short-lived communist government in Hungary and led to the re-establishment of a conservative regime.
events.name: Béla Kun's Hungarian Soviet Republic collapses

events.enhanced_description: On August 3, 1919, the Romanian army entered Timișoara, asserting control over the city during the post-World War I territorial realignments in Eastern Europe. This move was part of Romania's efforts to secure its borders and influence in the region.
events.name: The Romanian army enters Timișoara

events.enhanced_description: On August 4, 1919, the Romanian army occupied Budapest, further consolidating its control over Hungary following the collapse of the Hungarian Soviet Republic. This occupation was part of the broader geopolitical shifts in Eastern Europe after World War I.
events.name: The Romanian army occupies Budapest

events.enhanced_description: On August 8, 1919, the Anglo-Afghan Treaty was signed in Rawalpindi, ending the Third Anglo-Afghan War. The treaty recognized Afghanistan's right to conduct its own foreign affairs, marking a significant step towards Afghan independence from British influence.

image.caption: Map of the Emirate of Afghanistan and surrounding regions.
image.credit: Weaveravel — Own work
image.date_qualification: A retrospective map depicting the region around the 1919 Rawalpindi Treaty; created in 2021.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: The Anglo-Afghan Treaty of 1919 is signed

events.enhanced_description: On August 11, 1919, the Weimar Constitution was ratified in Germany, establishing a democratic framework for the newly formed Weimar Republic. This constitution aimed to provide a stable government following the upheaval of World War I and the abdication of the Kaiser.
events.name: The Weimar Constitution is ratified in Germany

events.enhanced_description: On August 14, 1919, during the Russian Civil War, the Red Army launched a counteroffensive against the White Volunteer Army led by General Anton Denikin. Despite their efforts, the Red Army was defeated, illustrating the ongoing struggle for control in post-revolutionary Russia.
events.name: Russian Civil War: Southern Front counteroffensive

events.enhanced_description: On August 16, 1919, the First Silesian Uprising began as Polish nationalists in Upper Silesia rose against German rule. This uprising was part of a series of conflicts aimed at securing Polish autonomy and control over the region.
events.name: First Silesian Uprising

events.enhanced_description: On August 18, 1919, during the Russian Civil War, British Royal Navy Coastal Motor Boats and military aircraft launched a combined operation that significantly damaged the Bolshevik fleet at Kronstadt, which was protecting Petrograd. This intervention highlighted the international dimensions of the conflict.
events.name: Russian Civil War: North Russia intervention

events.enhanced_description: On August 21, 1919, Friedrich Ebert was inaugurated as the first President of Germany under the Weimar Constitution. His leadership was pivotal during the early years of the Weimar Republic as it faced numerous challenges, including political extremism and economic instability.
events.name: Friedrich Ebert becomes the first President of Germany

events.enhanced_description: Louis Botha, the first Prime Minister of the Union of South Africa, succumbed to the Spanish flu while in office, marking a significant moment in South African politics as he was a key figure in the establishment of the Union in 1910.

locations.name: Cape Town, Western Cape, South Africa

events.name: Louis Botha dies in office of 'Spanish flu'

events.enhanced_description: During the Russian Civil War, the Red Army successfully captured the city of Pskov from the White forces, marking a strategic victory that contributed to the Bolshevik consolidation of power in the region.
events.name: Red Army captures Pskov from White forces

events.enhanced_description: The Knoxville Riot of August 31, 1919, erupted from racial tensions in Knoxville, Tennessee, leading to violence and the destruction of property. This incident was part of a broader pattern of racial unrest across the United States during this period.
events.name: Knoxville Riot of 1919

events.enhanced_description: In a significant event of the Russian Civil War, the White Army captured Kyiv, a vital city, from the Red forces, showcasing the ongoing struggle for control in Ukraine during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Kyiv captured by the White Army

events.enhanced_description: Admiral Alexander Kolchak's final offensive in the Tobolsk operation represented a desperate attempt by the White forces to regain momentum against the Red Army during the Russian Civil War.
events.name: Admiral Alexander Kolchak launches final offensive in Tobolsk operation

events.enhanced_description: Jan Smuts was appointed as the second Prime Minister of South Africa, succeeding Louis Botha, and played a crucial role in shaping the country's policies during the post-World War I era.

locations.name: Cape Town, Western Cape, South Africa

events.name: Jan Smuts becomes the second prime minister of South Africa

events.enhanced_description: The U.S. Army expedition, which traversed North America, concluded in San Francisco, highlighting the military's role in exploration and the consolidation of territories in the post-war period.
events.name: U.S. Army expedition across North America ends in San Francisco

events.enhanced_description: The devastating Florida Keys hurricane resulted in the loss of approximately 600 lives, making it one of the deadliest natural disasters in U.S. history at the time.
events.name: Florida Keys hurricane kills 600

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Saint-Germain was signed, officially ending World War I with Austria-Hungary and leading to the dissolution of its empire, significantly altering the political landscape of Central Europe.
events.name: Treaty of Saint-Germain signed

events.enhanced_description: Gabriele D'Annunzio, an Italian nationalist poet and war hero, led a march into Fiume, asserting Italian claims to the city and igniting a wave of nationalist fervor in post-war Italy.
events.name: Gabriele D'Annunzio marches into Fiume

events.enhanced_description: Following World War I, German South West Africa was placed under South African administration, marking a significant shift in colonial governance in the region.
events.name: German South West Africa placed under South African administration

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Petrograd saw White general Nikolai Yudenich's forces approach the city with 18,500 soldiers, but they were ultimately defeated by the Red Army's defense, organized by Leon Trotsky, marking a crucial turning point in the Russian Civil War.

image.caption: A young defender of Petrograd, photographed by Yakov Vladimirovich Steinberg.
image.credit: Yakov Vladimirovich Steinberg — russiainphoto.ru
image.date_qualification: Contemporary image associated with the 1919 Battle of Petrograd; the saved image date is 1919.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Petrograd

events.enhanced_description: The Steel strike of 1919 marked a significant labor movement across the United States, as workers protested for better wages and working conditions in the steel industry, reflecting broader social tensions in the post-war era.
events.name: Steel strike of 1919 begins across the United States

events.enhanced_description: The withdrawal of the last British Army troops from Arkhangelsk marked the end of foreign intervention in the Russian Civil War, leaving the conflict to be resolved by Russian factions.
events.name: Last British Army troops leave Arkhangelsk

events.enhanced_description: The Elaine massacre was a tragic event in which an estimated 100 to 800 African Americans were killed by white mobs and vigilante militias, assisted by federal troops, marking one of the deadliest racial confrontations in U.S. history.
events.name: Elaine massacre

events.enhanced_description: President Woodrow Wilson suffered a debilitating stroke, which rendered him an invalid for the remainder of his life, significantly impacting his ability to lead the nation during a critical post-war period.
events.name: Woodrow Wilson suffers serious stroke

events.enhanced_description: KLM, the Dutch airline, was founded in 1919 and has since become the world's oldest airline still operating under its original name, marking a significant development in the history of aviation.
events.name: KLM founded

events.enhanced_description: On October 8, 1919, Hugo Haase, a prominent German politician and member of the USPD (Independent Social Democratic Party), was assassinated in Mitte, Berlin. His murder underscored the political violence and instability that plagued the Weimar Republic in its early years.
events.name: Assassination of Hugo Haase

events.enhanced_description: The Cincinnati Reds won the World Series against the Chicago White Sox, a notable event in Major League Baseball history, especially as it was later revealed that some White Sox players had intentionally lost the series.
events.name: Cincinnati Reds win the World Series

events.enhanced_description: Estonia implemented a radical land reform that nationalized 97% of agrarian lands, primarily affecting the Baltic German nobility, as part of its efforts to establish a new social order following independence.
events.name: Estonia adopts radical land reform

events.enhanced_description: The Convention relating to the Regulation of Aerial Navigation was signed in Paris, establishing international standards for aviation and marking a significant step in the development of global air travel regulations.
events.name: Convention relating to the Regulation of Aerial Navigation signed

events.enhanced_description: Adolf Hitler delivered his first speech for the German Workers' Party (DAP) in Munich, marking the beginning of his political career and the rise of the party that would later become the National Socialist German Workers' Party.
events.name: Adolf Hitler gives first speech for the German Workers' Party

events.enhanced_description: The 1919 Luxembourg general election was notable for being the first in the duchy to include female suffrage, following constitutional amendments earlier that year, representing a significant advancement in women's rights.
events.name: 1919 Luxembourg general election

events.enhanced_description: The passage of the Volstead Act by the United States Congress, overriding President Woodrow Wilson's veto, laid the groundwork for Prohibition, which would go into effect in January 1920, fundamentally altering American society.
events.name: Prohibition in the United States: Volstead Act passed

events.enhanced_description: The First Annual Meeting of the International Labour Conference was held in Geneva, addressing labor issues and setting the stage for international cooperation on workers' rights in the post-war era.
events.name: First Annual Meeting of the International Labour Conference

events.enhanced_description: The Coal Strike of 1919, led by the United Mine Workers under John L. Lewis, marked a significant labor dispute in the United States, advocating for better wages and working conditions. The strike began on November 1, 1919, and concluded with a final agreement on December 10, 1919.
events.name: The Coal Strike of 1919

events.enhanced_description: On November 7, 1919, the first of the Palmer Raids was conducted, targeting suspected communists and anarchists in the United States. Over 10,000 individuals were arrested across 23 cities, reflecting the heightened fear of radicalism following the Russian Revolution.

image.caption: People arrested in New York City-area raids arrive at Ellis Island.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Corbis Images for Education database
image.date_qualification: The image is dated January 3, 1920, and depicts arrivals after raids the previous night; it is not a photograph of the first raids on November 7, 1919.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The first of the Palmer Raids

events.enhanced_description: Felix the Cat made his debut in the animated short 'Feline Follies' on November 9, 1919. Created by Otto Messmer, Felix became one of the first animated characters to gain widespread popularity, marking a significant milestone in the history of animation.
events.name: Felix the Cat debuts in Feline Follies

events.enhanced_description: The first national convention of the American Legion was held in Minneapolis from November 10-12, 1919. This gathering of World War I veterans aimed to establish a national organization to advocate for veterans' rights and benefits.
events.name: The first national convention of the American Legion

events.enhanced_description: On November 10, 1919, the Supreme Court of the United States upheld the conviction of Jacob Abrams for inciting resistance to the war effort against Soviet Russia. This case highlighted the tension between national security and free speech during the Red Scare.
events.name: Abrams v. United States

events.enhanced_description: The Centralia Massacre on November 11, 1919, involved a violent confrontation between American Legionnaires and members of the Industrial Workers of the World (IWW) in Centralia, Washington. This conflict reflected the intense labor struggles and anti-radical sentiments of the post-war period.
events.name: Centralia Massacre

events.enhanced_description: On November 11, 1919, during the Russian Civil War, General Nikolai Yudenich's Northwestern Army retreated to Estonia and was subsequently disarmed. This marked a significant defeat for the White forces in their struggle against the Red Army.
events.name: Russian Civil War: Retreat of the Northwestern Army

events.enhanced_description: The first Remembrance Day was observed in the British Empire on November 11, 1919, with a two-minute silence at 11:00 hours. This day was established to honor the soldiers who died in World War I.
events.name: First Remembrance Day observed

events.enhanced_description: The Centralia Massacre occurred on November 11, 1919, during an Armistice Day parade in Centralia, Washington.
