This event exemplified the ongoing conflict and resistance against British rule in Ireland.
events.name: Irish War of Independence: Headford Ambush

events.enhanced_description: In early 1921, the British government returned control of coal mines from wartime state management to private owners, leading to demands for wage cuts and subsequent strike actions by miners. This decision sparked significant labor unrest and was a precursor to the coal miners' strike later that year.
events.name: The British government returns the coal mines from wartime control to private owners

events.enhanced_description: In 1921, Coco Chanel launched Chanel No. 5, a revolutionary perfume that would become an iconic symbol of luxury and sophistication. Its unique blend of floral and aldehydic notes set a new standard in the fragrance industry.
events.name: Chanel No. 5 launch

events.enhanced_description: In 1921, Bessie Coleman became the first African American woman to obtain a pilot's license in France, breaking racial and gender barriers in aviation. Her achievement inspired future generations of aviators and highlighted the importance of diversity in the field.
events.name: Bessie Coleman obtains pilot's license

events.enhanced_description: The coal strike in the United Kingdom concluded with the Miners' Federation of Great Britain forced to accept pay cuts, highlighting the economic struggles and labor disputes in post-World War I Britain.
events.name: UK Coal Strike Ends

events.enhanced_description: The first BCG vaccination against tuberculosis was administered in Paris to a newborn child, marking a significant advancement in preventive medicine and the fight against infectious diseases.
events.name: First BCG Vaccination

events.enhanced_description: In 1921, a severe heat wave struck Europe, with temperatures reaching 39 degrees Celsius in Wrocław (then Breslau), Poland. This extreme weather event was part of a broader pattern of rising temperatures affecting various regions across the continent.
events.name: Heat Wave in Breslau

events.enhanced_description: Following the assassination of former Finance Minister Matthias Erzberger by right-wing terrorists in 1921, the German government declared martial law to restore order and address the escalating violence.
events.name: Martial Law Declared in Germany

events.enhanced_description: In 1921, during the Battle of Jafarabad, Simko Shikak, leader of the Shikak tribe, killed Iranian commander Colonel Mohammad Taqi Pessian. This marked the beginning of Shikak's rebellion against the Iranian government.
events.name: Battle of Jafarabad

events.enhanced_description: The Link River Dam, part of the Klamath Project, was completed in 1921, playing a crucial role in water management and irrigation in southern Oregon. This infrastructure project significantly impacted agriculture and water supply in the region.

image.caption: Link River Dam complex in Klamath Falls, Oregon.
image.credit: User:bobjgalindo — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed 12 June 2013; the event is described as occurring in 1921.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

locations.name: Link River Dam, Klamath Falls, Oregon, United States

events.name: Completion of the Link River Dam

events.enhanced_description: In 1921, Agnes Macphail made history by becoming the first woman elected to the Canadian Parliament. Her election marked a significant milestone in the fight for women's rights and representation in Canada.
events.name: Agnes Macphail elected to Parliament

events.enhanced_description: In 1921, luxury goods brand Gucci was founded in Florence, Italy, by Guccio Gucci. The brand would go on to become a symbol of high fashion and luxury, known for its craftsmanship and iconic designs.

image.caption: Exterior of Gucci’s New York City flagship on Fifth Avenue.
image.credit: Ajay Suresh from New York, NY, USA — Gucci NYC Flagship
image.date_qualification: A 2019 photograph of a Gucci store in New York City; it depicts a later retail site, not Gucci’s 1921 founding in Florence.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Gucci founded

events.enhanced_description: On January 2, 1921, Cruzeiro Esporte Clube was founded in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, originally as the multi-sports club Palestra Italia by Italian expatriates. The club has since become one of Brazil's most successful football teams.
events.name: Founding of Cruzeiro Esporte Clube

events.enhanced_description: On January 16, 1921, the Marxist Left in Slovakia and the Transcarpathian Ukraine held its founding congress in Ľubochňa. This congress marked a significant moment in the political landscape of the region, as it sought to unify leftist movements.
events.name: Founding Congress of the Marxist Left

events.enhanced_description: On January 17, 1921, English stage magician P. T. Selbit performed the first recorded public performance of the illusion 'sawing a woman in half' at the Finsbury Park Empire variety theatre in London. This performance became a classic in the world of magic and illusion.
events.name: First Performance of 'Sawing a Woman in Half'

events.enhanced_description: On January 20, 1921, the British K-class submarine HMS K5 sank in the English Channel during a training exercise, resulting in the tragic loss of all 57 crew members on board. The sinking highlighted the challenges and dangers faced by submarines during this era.
events.name: British K-class submarine HMS K5 sinks

events.enhanced_description: On January 21, 1921, Charlie Chaplin's silent comedy-drama film 'The Kid' premiered in the United States. The film, which starred Chaplin as the iconic Tramp character and Jackie Coogan as the child, received critical acclaim and is considered a landmark in film history.
events.name: Release of The Kid

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Kars was signed on January 23, 1921, establishing the borders between Turkey and the Armenian, Azerbaijani, and Georgian Soviet Republics. This treaty was significant in defining the territorial boundaries in the aftermath of World War I and the subsequent Turkish War of Independence.
events.name: The Treaty of Kars

events.enhanced_description: On January 23, 1921, Hjalmar Branting, leader of the Swedish Social Democratic Party, returned to the position of Prime Minister following significant electoral gains for his party. His leadership marked a pivotal moment in Swedish politics, emphasizing social welfare and labor rights.
events.name: Hjalmar Branting becomes Prime Minister

events.enhanced_description: On January 25, 1921, the Italian battleship Leonardo da Vinci was successfully righted in Taranto Harbour after having capsized in 1916. This event marked a significant moment in naval history as it demonstrated advancements in salvage operations.
events.name: Italian battleship Leonardo da Vinci is righted

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1921, the Red Army invaded the Democratic Republic of Georgia, marking the beginning of a military campaign that would lead to the establishment of a Soviet regime in the country. This invasion was part of the broader strategy of the Bolshevik government to expand its influence in the Caucasus region.
events.name: Red Army invasion of Georgia

events.enhanced_description: On February 19, 1921, the French Third Republic and the Second Polish Republic formed a defensive alliance aimed at countering the threat posed by Germany and the Soviet Union in post-World War I Europe. This alliance was significant in shaping the geopolitical landscape of the interwar period.
events.name: Defensive alliance between France and Poland

events.enhanced_description: On February 20, 1921, the Young Communist League of Czechoslovakia was founded as a youth organization aligned with the Communist Party. This organization played a crucial role in mobilizing young people in support of communist ideals during the interwar period.
events.name: Foundation of the Young Communist League of Czechoslovakia

events.enhanced_description: On February 21, 1921, Reza Khan and Zia'eddin Tabatabaee staged a coup d'état in Iran, leading to the overthrow of the Qajar dynasty. This coup set the stage for Reza Khan's rise to power and the eventual establishment of the Pahlavi dynasty.
events.name: 1921 Persian coup d'état

events.enhanced_description: On February 23, 1921, Oscar von Sydow took over the premiership of Sweden from Baron Louis De Geer the Younger. His leadership marked a period of moderate conservatism in Swedish politics during the early 1920s.
figures: Baron Louis De Geer the Younger
events.name: Oscar von Sydow becomes Prime Minister of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On February 25, 1921, the Red Army entered Tbilisi, the capital of Georgia, effectively occupying the country and establishing a Soviet government. This event was a critical moment in the Bolshevik expansion into the Caucasus region.
events.name: Red Army occupies Tbilisi

events.enhanced_description: On February 27, 1921, a Socialist congress concluded in Vienna, resulting in the founding of the International Working Union of Socialist Parties. This congress aimed to unify socialist movements across Europe in the aftermath of World War I.
events.name: Socialist congress in Vienna

events.enhanced_description: On February 28, 1921, the Kronstadt rebellion was initiated by sailors of the Soviet Navy's Baltic Fleet, who protested against the Bolshevik government. This uprising was significant as it represented a major challenge to the authority of the Soviet regime.
events.name: Kronstadt rebellion begins

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1921, the city of Kiryū was founded in Gunma Prefecture, Japan. The establishment of Kiryū marked an important development in the region's urbanization and economic growth.
events.name: Foundation of Kiryū

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1921, Warren G. Harding was inaugurated as the 29th President of the United States. His presidency would be marked by a return to normalcy following World War I and significant domestic challenges.
events.name: Inauguration of Warren G. Harding

events.enhanced_description: On March 5, 1921, during the Irish War of Independence, a force of approximately 100 members of the Irish Republican Army ambushed a British Army convoy in Clonbanin, resulting in several casualties, including the death of Brigadier General Cumming. This event underscored the intensity of the conflict in Ireland.
events.name: Clonbanin ambush during Irish War of Independence

events.enhanced_description: On March 6, 1921, the Allied Powers formally enforced reparations on Germany as part of the Treaty of Versailles, which had significant economic and political implications for the Weimar Republic. This decision contributed to the instability that would later lead to World War II.
events.name: Allied Powers enforce reparations on Germany

events.enhanced_description: On March 8, 1921, Spanish Premier Eduardo Dato e Iradier was assassinated while exiting the parliament building in Madrid. His assassination was a significant political event that reflected the turmoil and instability in Spain during this period.
events.name: Assassination of Eduardo Dato e Iradier

events.enhanced_description: On March 9, 1921, the Cilicia Peace Treaty was signed between the French Third Republic and the Turkish National Movement, aiming to end the Franco-Turkish War. This treaty was pivotal in shaping the post-war landscape in the region.
events.name: Cilicia Peace Treaty signed

events.enhanced_description: On March 12, 1921, the İstiklâl Marşı (Independence March) was officially adopted as the national anthem of Turkey. This anthem became a symbol of national pride and resistance during the Turkish War of Independence.
events.name: Adoption of the İstiklâl Marşı

events.enhanced_description: On March 13, 1921, the Russian White Army captured Mongolia from China, with Roman von Ungern-Sternberg declaring himself ruler. This occupation was part of the broader conflict involving the Russian Civil War and had lasting implications for Mongolia's sovereignty.
events.name: Occupation of Mongolia by Russian White Army

events.enhanced_description: On March 14, 1921, Armenian Soghomon Tehlirian assassinated Mehmed Talaat, the former Interior Minister of the Ottoman Empire, in Charlottenburg, Berlin. This assassination was a significant act of vengeance for the Armenian Genocide and highlighted the ongoing tensions between Armenians and Turks.

image.caption: Portrait of Talaat Bey.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Forty Years in Constantinople. The Recollections of Sir Edwin Pears 1873-1915 with 16 Illustrations. Herbert Jenkins Limited, London 1916.
image.date_qualification: The image is dated 1916, five years before the 1921 assassination; it is not a photograph of the event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Assassination of Mehmed Talaat

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Moscow, signed on March 16, 1921, established diplomatic relations between the Grand National Assembly of Turkey and the Russian Socialist Federative Soviet Republic, marking a significant step in post-World War I geopolitics. This treaty laid the groundwork for future cooperation between the two nations, particularly in opposition to Western imperialism.
events.name: Treaty of Moscow establishes friendly relations between the Government of the Grand National Assembly of Turkey and the Russian Socialist Federative Soviet Republic

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1921, the Red Army decisively defeated the Kronstadt rebellion, a major uprising by sailors who had previously supported the Bolsheviks but were now demanding political reforms and greater freedoms. The suppression of the rebellion marked a turning point in the Russian Civil War, consolidating Bolshevik power but also highlighting dissent within the revolutionary ranks.

image.caption: Archival photograph depicting Red Army soldiers attacking Kronstadt across the ice of the Gulf of Finland.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — https://www.marxists.org/history/ussr/events/kronstadt/index.htm
image.date_qualification: The saved image description identifies an attack during the suppression of the Kronstadt mutiny. Its stated date is after 6 March and before 18 March 1921; it is not supported as a specific date. Pixels were not supplied or inspected.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The Red Army crushes the Kronstadt rebellion, and a number of sailors flee to Finland

events.enhanced_description: The second Peace of Riga, signed on March 18, 1921, concluded the Polish–Soviet War, establishing a permanent border between Poland and the Soviet Union. This treaty not only solidified Poland's independence but also marked a significant geopolitical shift in Eastern Europe, influencing future relations between the two nations.

image.caption: Official Polish document of the Treaty of Riga.
image.credit: official document of Poland — Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Poland) Archive
image.date_qualification: The image is described as the treaty document; its saved image date is 1921-03-18, the date the treaty was signed.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The second Peace of Riga ends the Polish–Soviet War

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1921, a plebiscite was held in Upper Silesia, where the local population voted for re-annexation to Germany, reflecting the complex ethnic and national identities in the region. This vote was part of the aftermath of World War I and the Treaty of Versailles, which had significant implications for the borders and governance of Central Europe.
events.name: Upper Silesia votes for re-annexation to Germany

events.enhanced_description: The New Economic Policy (NEP), introduced on March 21, 1921, marked a significant shift in Soviet economic policy, allowing for a degree of private enterprise and market mechanisms to revive the economy after the devastation of the Civil War. This policy aimed to stabilize the economy and gain popular support for the Bolshevik regime.
events.name: The New Economic Policy starts in Soviet Russia

events.enhanced_description: The 1921 Women's Olympiad, held in Monte Carlo starting March 24, 1921, was the first international sports event exclusively for women, showcasing female athletic talent and promoting gender equality in sports. This event was a pivotal moment in the history of women's athletics, paving the way for future competitions.

image.caption: Photograph associated with the 1921 Women's Olympiad in Monte Carlo.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — https://www.vivremaville.mc/uploads/images/original/6pAsfx9O9R1YTaKuLZWo7Ah9EPxSKUAEiLdY0UOT.jpg
image.date_qualification: Dated 1921; the saved evidence does not establish a more specific day.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The 1921 Women's Olympiad begins in Monte Carlo

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1921, Abkhazia was declared the Socialist Soviet Republic of Abkhazia, becoming a part of the Soviet Union. This event was significant in the context of Soviet nationalities policy, as it aimed to integrate various ethnic groups into the Soviet framework.
events.name: Abkhazia becomes the Socialist Soviet Republic of Abkhazia

events.enhanced_description: The Russian famine of 1921–22 began in the spring of 1921, resulting in the deaths of approximately 5 million people due to starvation and disease. This famine was exacerbated by the civil war and the policies of the Bolshevik government, leading to widespread suffering.
events.name: Russian famine of 1921–22 begins

events.enhanced_description: On April 11, 1921, the Emirate of Transjordan was established under British Mandate, with Abdullah I appointed as emir. This event was significant in shaping the political landscape of the Middle East and laid the groundwork for the future Kingdom of Jordan.
events.name: The Emirate of Transjordan is created under British Mandate

events.enhanced_description: On April 15, 1921, the event known as 'Black Friday' occurred in Britain when transport union members of the 'Triple Alliance' refused to support a national strike called by coal miners. This refusal highlighted divisions within the labor movement and had significant implications for labor relations in the UK.
events.name: "Black Friday" in Britain: transport union members refuse to support national strike action

events.enhanced_description: On April 20, 1921, Ferenc Molnár's play 'Liliom' was first produced in English on Broadway, marking a significant moment in American theater. The play would later inspire the musical 'Carousel,' showcasing the enduring impact of Molnár's work on the performing arts.

image.caption: Photograph of Joseph Schildkraut as Liliom, Evelyn Chard as Louise, and Eva Le Gallienne as Julie in the Theatre Guild production of Liliom.
image.credit: Theatre Guild, Ira D. Schwartz, photographer — Source
image.date_qualification: Dated 1921; the image description identifies the Theatre Guild production, not a specific performance date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Ferenc Molnár's play Liliom is first produced in English on Broadway

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1921, riots erupted in Jaffa, Mandatory Palestine, resulting in the deaths of 47 Jews and 48 Arabs. These violent clashes were indicative of the growing tensions between Jewish and Arab communities in the region, foreshadowing future conflicts.
events.name: Jaffa riots result in 47 Jewish and 48 Arab deaths

events.enhanced_description: On May 2, 1921, the Third Silesian Uprising began as Polish nationalists in Upper Silesia rose against German rule. This uprising was part of a series of conflicts that sought to determine the region's national affiliation following World War I and the Treaty of Versailles.

image.caption: Polish insurgents during the Third Silesian Uprising.
image.credit: unknown-anonymous — Centralne Archiwum Wojskowe
image.date_qualification: Contemporary image of insurgents during the uprising; the original image date is given as 1921-05, not a more precise day.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Third Silesian Uprising: Poles in Upper Silesia rise against the Germans

events.enhanced_description: On May 3, 1921, the province of Northern Ireland was officially created as part of the United Kingdom, following the Government of Ireland Act 1920. This marked a significant moment in Irish history, establishing a separate political entity that would lead to decades of conflict and division.
events.name: Creation of Northern Ireland

events.enhanced_description: On May 5, 1921, the London Schedule of Payments was established, outlining reparations of 132 billion gold marks to be paid by Germany and other successor states of the Central Powers following World War I. This agreement had significant implications for the post-war economy and international relations.
events.name: London Schedule of Payments

events.enhanced_description: On May 6, 1921, the German-Soviet Provisional Agreement was signed, marking the formal recognition of the Soviet government by Germany. This agreement was pivotal in establishing diplomatic relations between the two nations during a time of significant political upheaval.
events.name: German-Soviet Provisional Agreement

events.enhanced_description: On May 14, 1921, a significant geomagnetic storm occurred, impacting communication systems and electrical infrastructure across the globe. This event highlighted the vulnerability of technology to solar activity and spurred further research into space weather.
events.name: May 1921 geomagnetic storm

events.enhanced_description: On May 14, 1921, violent anti-European riots erupted in Cairo and Alexandria, fueled by nationalist sentiments against colonial rule. These riots were part of a broader wave of unrest in Egypt during the post-World War I period, reflecting the growing demand for independence.
events.name: Anti-European riots in Egypt

events.enhanced_description: On May 16, 1921, the Communist Party of Czechoslovakia was founded in Prague, marking a significant moment in the country's political landscape. The party would go on to play a crucial role in Czechoslovak politics, especially during the interwar period.
events.name: Founding of the Communist Party of Czechoslovakia

events.enhanced_description: On May 19, 1921, the United States Congress passed the Emergency Quota Act, establishing national quotas on immigration. This legislation significantly restricted immigration from Eastern Europe, influencing Jewish migration patterns towards Palestine.
events.name: Emergency Quota Act

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1921, the United States triumphed over the United Kingdom in the first international golf match, winning 9 rounds to 3. This event marked a significant moment in the history of golf, showcasing the growing popularity of the sport across the Atlantic.
events.name: First golf international match

events.enhanced_description: On May 23, 1921, the Leipzig War Crimes Trials were held in Germany, addressing the actions of German military leaders during World War I. These trials were significant in the context of post-war justice and accountability.
events.name: Leipzig War Crimes Trials

events.enhanced_description: On May 24, 1921, the first general election for the new Parliament of Northern Ireland was held, resulting in a decisive victory for the Ulster Unionists, who won 40 out of 52 seats. This election established a dominant-party system that would last for fifty years.
events.name: First Northern Ireland general election

events.enhanced_description: On May 25, 1921, during the Irish War of Independence, the Irish Republican Army occupied and burned The Custom House in Dublin, a key government building. The attack resulted in the deaths of five IRA members and the capture of over 80 by British forces.
events.name: Burning of The Custom House

events.enhanced_description: On May 26, 1921, a general strike began in Norway, reflecting widespread labor unrest and demands for better working conditions. This strike was part of a larger wave of labor movements occurring across Europe in the aftermath of World War I.
events.name: General strike in Norway

events.enhanced_description: On May 31, 1921, the Tulsa Race Massacre occurred when mobs of white residents attacked the prosperous black community of Greenwood in Tulsa, Oklahoma. The violence resulted in the destruction of over 1,250 homes and a death toll that may have reached as high as 300, marking one of the worst incidents of racial violence in U.S. history.
events.name: Tulsa Race Massacre

events.enhanced_description: On June 3, 1921, Sweden abolished the death penalty, marking a significant shift in the country's approach to justice and punishment. This decision reflected broader trends in Europe towards more humane legal practices.
events.name: Death penalty abolished in Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On June 10, 1921, representatives from the Armenian, Azerbaijani, and Georgian Socialist Soviet Republics proclaimed their independence in a Paris declaration. This declaration aimed to establish a customs union and military alliance, although it was not recognized internationally.
events.name: Paris declaration of Transcaucasia

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1921, the SS Paris, a liner of Compagnie Générale Transatlantique, made her maiden voyage from Le Havre, France, to New York City. This event marked an important moment in transatlantic travel and commerce.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Maiden voyage of SS Paris

events.enhanced_description: On June 21, 1921, the International Hydrographic Bureau was established as an agency of the League of Nations, tasked with ensuring the safety of navigation and the efficiency of maritime operations. It continues to play a vital role in international maritime affairs.
events.name: Establishment of International Hydrographic Bureau

events.enhanced_description: On June 22, 1921, the Third Congress of the Communist International convened in Moscow, focusing on the strategies and policies of communist movements worldwide. This congress was significant in shaping the direction of international communism.
events.name: Third Congress of the Communist International

events.enhanced_description: On June 27, 1921, the first signings of Treaty 11 took place at Fort Providence, an agreement between King George V of Canada and various First Nations. This treaty aimed to address land rights and governance issues in the region.
events.name: Signing of Treaty 11

events.enhanced_description: On June 28, 1921, the Constitutional Assembly of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes passed the Vidovdan Constitution, despite a boycott by communist and nationalist parties. This constitution established a parliamentary system and was a key moment in the formation of the Yugoslav state.

locations.historical_name: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes
locations.name: Belgrade, Serbia

events.name: Vidovdan Constitution passed

events.enhanced_description: The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) was founded in Shanghai, marking a significant turning point in Chinese politics and the beginning of a movement that would lead to the establishment of the People's Republic of China in 1949.
events.name: Founding of the Chinese Communist Party

events.enhanced_description: U.S. President Warren G. Harding signed a joint congressional resolution declaring an end to America's state of war with Germany, Austria, and Hungary, formally concluding hostilities from World War I.
events.name: End of State of War with Germany

events.enhanced_description: Ivanoe Bonomi formed a new conservative government in Italy, amidst rising political tensions and the threat of fascism, marking a significant moment in Italy's interwar political landscape.
events.name: Formation of New Italian Government

events.enhanced_description: The Irish War of Independence concluded with a truce effective at noon between the British Army and the Irish Republican Army, leading to negotiations that would eventually result in the Anglo-Irish Treaty.
events.name: End of the Irish War of Independence

events.enhanced_description: A Massachusetts jury found Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo Vanzetti guilty of first-degree murder after a highly publicized trial, a verdict that would ignite protests and debates over justice and political bias worldwide.
events.name: Sacco and Vanzetti Verdict

events.enhanced_description: The Republic of Mirdita was proclaimed near the Albanian-Serbian border with Yugoslav support, reflecting the complex ethnic and political dynamics in the Balkans during the early 20th century.
events.name: Proclamation of the Republic of Mirdita

events.enhanced_description: During the Rif War, Spanish troops suffered a devastating defeat at the Battle of Annual against the forces led by Abd el-Krim, which significantly weakened Spanish influence in Morocco and emboldened the Rifian resistance.
events.name: Battle of Annual

events.enhanced_description: The 1st National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party convened in Shanghai, marking a pivotal moment in Chinese history as the party began to organize and strategize for its future role in Chinese politics.
events.name: 1st National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party

events.enhanced_description: U.S. President Warren G. Harding received Princess Fatima of Afghanistan, an event marked by the presence of an imposter, Stanley Clifford Weyman, highlighting the complexities of diplomatic relations during the period.
events.name: Warren G. Harding Receives Princess Fatima

events.enhanced_description: Researchers at the University of Toronto, led by biochemist Frederick Banting, announced the discovery of insulin, a breakthrough that would revolutionize the treatment of diabetes and save countless lives.
events.name: Discovery of Insulin

events.enhanced_description: Adolf Hitler was appointed Führer of the Nazi Party in Germany, solidifying his control and setting the stage for the party's rise to power and the subsequent impact on Germany and the world.
events.name: Adolf Hitler Becomes Führer of the Nazi Party

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Blair Mountain commenced in Logan County, West Virginia, marking the largest labor uprising in U.S. history and a pivotal moment in the labor movement as miners fought for their rights against coal operators.

locations.name: Logan County, West Virginia, United States

events.name: Battle of Blair Mountain Begins

events.enhanced_description: On August 25, 1921, Franklin D. Roosevelt was diagnosed with polio while vacationing on Campobello Island, Canada. This illness would lead to his permanent disability, profoundly impacting his political career and public image.
events.name: Franklin D. Roosevelt's Paralytic Illness

events.enhanced_description: In 1921, rising prices led to significant social unrest in Munich, Germany, resulting in major riots. These disturbances reflected the economic turmoil and dissatisfaction prevalent in post-World War I Germany.
events.name: Riots in Munich

events.enhanced_description: In September 1921, during the Poplar Rates Rebellion, nine members of the borough council of Poplar, London, were arrested. This event highlighted the struggle against austerity measures and local government funding issues.
events.name: Poplar Rates Rebellion Arrests

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1921, 16-year-old Margaret Gorman won the Golden Mermaid trophy at a beauty pageant in Atlantic City, New Jersey, later recognized as the first Miss America. This event marked the beginning of a significant cultural phenomenon in the United States.
events.name: First Miss America Pageant

events.enhanced_description: On September 13, 1921, the first White Castle hamburger restaurant opened in Wichita, Kansas, marking the foundation of the world's first fast food chain. This establishment revolutionized the fast food industry and American dining culture.
events.name: Opening of White Castle

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1921, a catastrophic explosion occurred at BASF's nitrate factory in Oppau, Germany, resulting in the deaths of approximately 500 to 600 people. This disaster highlighted the dangers of industrial processes and led to changes in safety regulations.

image.caption: Photograph of damage from the Oppau Explosion, credited to Popular Mechanics Magazine.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Popular Mechanics Magazine , 1921
image.date_qualification: The source gives the image date as 1921; it does not establish the precise date the photograph was taken.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Oppau Explosion

events.enhanced_description: On September 28, 1921, the Sauerländer Heimatbund was founded in Meschede, Germany. This organization aimed to promote regional culture and heritage in the Sauerland region.
events.name: Sauerländer Heimatbund Founded

events.enhanced_description: On October 5, 1921, the World Series baseball game was first broadcast on the radio by Newark station WJZ and Pittsburgh station KDKA, among others. This event marked a significant milestone in sports broadcasting and media history.

image.caption: Photograph of infielder Mike McNally stealing home during Game 1 of the 1921 World Series at the Polo Grounds.
image.credit: Bain News Service, publisher — Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division, LC-DIG-ggbain-33188 (digital file from original negative)
image.date_qualification: Depicted date: October 5, 1921, as stated in the source metadata; the image documents a World Series game rather than the broadcast act.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: First Radio Broadcast of World Series

events.enhanced_description: On October 7, 1921, Simko Shikak launched an attack on the Savujbulak district of Mahabad, Iran, during his first rebellion. With a force of approximately 3,900, he killed around 400 Gendarmes and looted the local population.
events.name: Simko Shikak's Attack on Savujbulak

events.enhanced_description: On October 8, 1921, the first Sweetest Day was celebrated in Cleveland, Ohio. This day was established to promote kindness and appreciation, particularly towards loved ones.
events.name: First Sweetest Day

events.enhanced_description: On October 10, 1921, teaching began at the University of Szeged in Hungary. This institution played a significant role in the educational landscape of the country.
events.name: University of Szeged Teaching Begins

events.enhanced_description: On October 11, 1921, the Irish Treaty Conference opened in London, aiming to negotiate the terms of Irish independence from British rule. This conference was pivotal in shaping the future of Ireland.
events.name: Irish Treaty Conference Opens

events.enhanced_description: On October 13, 1921, the Treaty of Kars was signed between the Government of the Grand National Assembly of Turkey and the Armenian, Azerbaijani, and Georgian Socialist Soviet Republics. This treaty established common boundaries and aimed to stabilize the region.
events.name: Treaty of Kars Signed

events.enhanced_description: On October 19, 1921, a massacre known as 'Bloody Night' occurred in Lisbon, resulting in the deaths of Portuguese Prime Minister António Granjo and several other politicians. This event underscored the political instability in Portugal during this period.
events.name: Bloody Night in Lisbon

events.enhanced_description: On October 20, 1921, the Treaty of Ankara was signed between the French Third Republic and the Government of the Grand National Assembly of Turkey, effectively ending the Franco-Turkish War. This treaty marked a significant shift in regional power dynamics.
events.name: Treaty of Ankara Signed

events.enhanced_description: On October 21, 1921, George Melford's silent film 'The Sheik' premiered in Los Angeles, catapulting its leading actor Rudolph Valentino to international stardom. This film became a cultural phenomenon and significantly influenced the film industry.
events.name: Premiere of The Sheik

events.enhanced_description: On October 24, 1921, during the ongoing Rif War, the Spanish Army achieved a significant victory against rifkabyl rebels in Morocco. This conflict was part of Spain's efforts to maintain control over its North African territories.
events.name: Spanish Army Defeats Rifkabyl Rebels

events.enhanced_description: On October 29, 1921, an incident occurred at the Link River Dam in Oregon, United States. This event highlighted the ongoing challenges related to infrastructure and water management in the region.
events.name: Link River Dam Incident

events.enhanced_description: In a historic upset on October 29, 1921, Centre College's football team, led by quarterback Bo McMillin, defeated Harvard University 6-0, ending Harvard's five-year winning streak. This match is often referred to as 'football's upset of the century' and remains a celebrated moment in college football history.
events.name: Centre College defeats Harvard

events.enhanced_description: In July 1922, hyperinflation in Germany escalated dramatically, with the exchange rate reaching 563 marks for a single American dollar. This economic crisis was a consequence of the reparations imposed after World War I and led to severe social and economic instability.
events.name: Hyperinflation in Germany

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1921, after a speech by Adolf Hitler at the Hofbräuhaus in Munich, members of the Sturmabteilung (SA), also known as the brownshirts, violently assaulted his political opponents. This event highlighted the growing tensions and political violence in Germany during the rise of the Nazi Party.
events.name: Hitler's speech and assault by the SA

events.enhanced_description: On November 9, 1921, the National Fascist Party (Partito Nazionale Fascista) was founded in Italy, marking a significant moment in the rise of fascism in Europe. This party would go on to play a crucial role in Italian politics under the leadership of Benito Mussolini.
events.name: Founding of the National Fascist Party

events.enhanced_description: On November 11, 1921, during an Armistice Day ceremony, President Warren G. Harding dedicated the Tomb of the Unknowns at Arlington National Cemetery. This solemn event honored the unidentified soldiers who died in World War I and has since become a symbol of national remembrance.

locations.name: Arlington National Cemetery, Arlington, Virginia, United States

events.name: Dedication of the Tomb of the Unknowns

events.enhanced_description: On November 14, 1921, the Spanish Communist Party was founded, marking a significant development in the political landscape of Spain. This party would later play a crucial role in the Spanish Civil War and the broader European communist movement.
events.name: Founding of the Spanish Communist Party

events.enhanced_description: On November 23, 1921, President Warren G. Harding signed the Sheppard–Towner Act, which provided federal funding for maternity and child care. This legislation was a landmark in public health policy and women's rights in the United States.
events.name: Sheppard–Towner Act signed

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1921, rising prices and economic instability led to riots in Vienna, reflecting the broader social and economic turmoil in post-World War I Europe. These events highlighted the struggles faced by citizens in the wake of hyperinflation and political unrest.
events.name: Riots in Vienna

events.enhanced_description: On December 6, 1921, the Anglo-Irish Treaty was signed in London, establishing the Irish Free State as an independent nation comprising 26 of Ireland's 32 counties. This treaty marked a significant turning point in Irish history, leading to the eventual establishment of a sovereign state.
events.name: Signing of the Anglo-Irish Treaty

events.enhanced_description: On December 13, 1921, the Four-Power Treaty was signed by Japan, the United States, the United Kingdom, and France, agreeing to recognize the status quo in the Pacific. This treaty aimed to prevent conflict and maintain peace in the region following World War I.
events.name: Four-Power Treaty on Insular Possessions

events.enhanced_description: On December 23, 1921, Rabindranath Tagore founded Visva-Bharati College in Santiniketan, India, with the vision of creating a global center for education and culture. This institution became a significant cultural hub, promoting the arts and humanities.
events.name: Founding of Visva-Bharati College

events.enhanced_description: On December 29, 1921, William Lyon Mackenzie King was appointed as Canada's tenth Prime Minister. He would serve three non-consecutive terms, shaping Canadian policy during a pivotal time in the country's history.
events.name: William Lyon Mackenzie King becomes Prime Minister

events.enhanced_description: From February 17 to 23, 1922, the Modern Art Week in São Paulo showcased groundbreaking works that heralded the beginning of Modernism in Brazil. This event featured prominent artists and writers, including Mário de Andrade and Anita Malfatti, and challenged traditional artistic norms, influencing Brazilian culture for decades.
events.name: Modern Art Week in São Paulo marks the start of Modernism in Brazil

events.enhanced_description: In 1922, the Five Power Naval Disarmament Treaty was signed in Washington, D.C., between the United States, United Kingdom, Japan, France, and Italy. This treaty aimed to prevent an arms race by limiting naval construction and was a significant step towards international cooperation in military matters.
events.name: Five Power Naval Disarmament Treaty signed

events.enhanced_description: In 1922, the Cheka, the Soviet Union's secret police, was reorganized and renamed the Gosudarstvennoye Politicheskoye Upravlenie (GPU), a precursor to the NKVD. This change reflected the evolving nature of state security and repression in the early years of the Soviet regime.
events.name: Cheka becomes the GPU

events.enhanced_description: In 1922, Baragoola, the last of the Binngarra class Manly ferries, was launched in Balmain, New South Wales. This event marked a significant moment in the history of public transportation in Sydney, as these ferries played a crucial role in connecting the city with its suburbs.
events.name: Baragoola launched at Balmain

events.enhanced_description: The British Civil Aviation Authority was established to regulate civil aviation in the United Kingdom, ensuring safety and efficiency in air travel. This marked a significant step in the development of aviation governance in the post-World War I era.
events.name: The British Civil Aviation Authority is established

events.enhanced_description: The Syrian Federation was established by an arrêté issued by French High Commissioner Henri Gouraud in 1922, marking a significant step in the French mandate over Syria. This federation aimed to unify various regions under a single administrative framework while maintaining French control.
events.name: Constitution of the Syrian Federation

events.enhanced_description: In January 1922, The Sun News-Pictorial was founded in Melbourne, Australia, serving as a precursor to the Herald Sun. This newspaper played a crucial role in the evolution of Australian journalism.
events.name: The Sun News-Pictorial founded

events.enhanced_description: In January 1922, the League of Nations approved the Mandate of Palestine, establishing a framework for British administration in the region. This decision had lasting implications for the geopolitical landscape of the Middle East.

image.caption: Front page of the Mandate for Palestine and Transjordan memorandum.
image.credit: British government — Archive.org
image.date_qualification: Image depicts a document presented in December 1922; image_date is 2012-02-06 and is not the depicted date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Mandate of Palestine approved

events.enhanced_description: In 1922, the Red Army occupied Vladivostok, solidifying Bolshevik control over the region during the Russian Civil War. This occupation was crucial for the establishment of Soviet power in the Far East.
events.name: The Red Army occupies Vladivostok

events.enhanced_description: The Rose Bowl sports stadium officially opened in Pasadena, California, in 1922, becoming an iconic venue for college football and other events. It has since become a symbol of American sports culture.
events.name: Rose Bowl officially opens

events.enhanced_description: In 1922, the United Kingdom introduced a broadcast receiving licence requiring citizens to pay a fee of ten shillings to legally receive radio broadcasts. This marked a significant step in the regulation of broadcasting and the establishment of public broadcasting standards.
events.name: A broadcast receiving licence with a fee of ten shillings is introduced in the United Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: During a three-day general strike in Guayaquil, Ecuador, police and military forces opened fire on protestors, resulting in the deaths of at least 300 individuals. This tragic event highlighted the tensions between the government and labor movements during a period of social unrest.
events.name: Guayaquil general strike

events.enhanced_description: On January 7, 1922, Dáil Éireann, the parliament of the Irish Republic, ratified the Anglo-Irish Treaty by a narrow vote of 64 to 57. This decision was pivotal in the establishment of the Irish Free State and marked a significant moment in Irish history.
events.name: Dáil Éireann ratifies the Anglo-Irish Treaty

events.enhanced_description: On January 10, 1922, Arthur Griffith was elected President of Dáil Éireann, following the resignation of Éamon de Valera. Griffith's leadership came at a crucial time as Ireland transitioned to a new political landscape after the ratification of the Anglo-Irish Treaty.
events.name: Arthur Griffith elected President of Dáil Éireann

events.enhanced_description: On January 11, 1922, Frederick Banting successfully administered the first insulin treatment for diabetes in Toronto, Canada. This groundbreaking medical advancement revolutionized the treatment of diabetes and saved countless lives.
events.name: First successful insulin treatment

events.enhanced_description: On January 15, 1922, Michael Collins was appointed as the Chairman of the Provisional Government of the Irish Free State. His leadership was critical during the transitional period following the Anglo-Irish Treaty.
events.name: Michael Collins becomes Chairman of the Provisional Government

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1922, Italian forces occupied Misrata, Libya, marking the beginning of the reconquest of Libya. This military action was part of Italy's efforts to reassert control over its former colonies in North Africa.
events.name: Italian forces occupy Misrata, Libya

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1922, Achille Ratti was elected as Pope Pius XI, succeeding Pope Benedict XV. His papacy would later be marked by significant events, including the Lateran Treaty, which established the Vatican City as an independent sovereign entity.
events.name: Pope Pius XI succeeds Pope Benedict XV

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1922, President Warren G. Harding made history by introducing the first radio in the White House, marking a significant moment in the integration of modern technology into political life. This event symbolized the growing influence of radio as a medium for communication and information dissemination in American society.
events.name: Warren G. Harding introduces the first radio in the White House

events.enhanced_description: On February 14, 1922, Finnish Minister of the Interior Heikki Ritavuori was assassinated by Ernst Tandefelt, an act that underscored the political tensions in post-independence Finland. This assassination highlighted the struggles within the Finnish government and the challenges of maintaining order during a tumultuous period.

image.caption: Portrait of Finnish Minister of the Interior Heikki Ritavuori.
image.credit: valok. Atelier Rembrandt (Suomen Kuvalehti 25.2.1922) — https://www.magnuslonden.net/ , https://digi.kansalliskirjasto.fi/aikakausi/binding/877837?page=7
image.date_qualification: Portrait made before 1922; it is not a depiction of the assassination itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Assassination of Heikki Ritavuori

events.enhanced_description: On February 15, 1922, the inaugural session of the Permanent Court of International Justice (PCIJ) was held in The Hague, marking a significant step in the establishment of international law and justice. The court aimed to resolve disputes between nations peacefully, reflecting the post-World War I desire for stability and cooperation.
events.name: Inaugural session of the Permanent Court of International Justice

events.enhanced_description: On February 26, 1922, the Supreme Court of the United States ruled in Leser v. Garnett, affirming the constitutionality of the Nineteenth Amendment, which granted women the right to vote. This landmark decision was a pivotal moment in the women's suffrage movement, solidifying the legal foundation for gender equality in voting rights.
events.name: Leser v. Garnett Supreme Court case

events.enhanced_description: On February 28, 1922, the United Kingdom issued the Unilateral Declaration of Egyptian Independence, ending its protectorate over Egypt and granting the country nominal independence while retaining control over military and diplomatic matters. This declaration was a significant step towards Egypt's full sovereignty and reflected the growing nationalist sentiments in the region.
events.name: Unilateral Declaration of Egyptian Independence

events.enhanced_description: On March 2, 1922, an ice mass broke the Oder Dam in Wrocław, causing significant flooding and damage. This natural disaster highlighted the vulnerabilities of infrastructure to extreme weather conditions and the importance of disaster preparedness.
events.name: Ice mass breaks the Oder Dam

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1922, the silent horror film Nosferatu premiered at the Berlin Zoological Garden, directed by Friedrich Wilhelm Murnau. This film is considered a landmark in cinema history, as it introduced a new level of artistry and storytelling in the horror genre.
events.name: Premiere of Nosferatu

events.enhanced_description: On March 10, 1922, Mahatma Gandhi was arrested in Mumbai for sedition, a pivotal moment in the Indian independence movement. His arrest sparked widespread protests and highlighted the growing resistance against British colonial rule in India.
events.name: Mahatma Gandhi arrested for sedition

events.enhanced_description: On March 13, 1922, Edward, Prince of Wales, inaugurated the Prince of Wales Royal Indian Military College in Dehradun, India. This event marked a significant step towards the Indianization of the officer cadre in the Indian Army, reflecting the changing attitudes towards colonial governance.
events.name: Inauguration of the Prince of Wales Royal Indian Military College

events.enhanced_description: On March 15, 1922, Fuad I was proclaimed King of Egypt following the country's attainment of self-government from British rule. His reign would be marked by efforts to modernize Egypt and navigate the complexities of post-colonial governance.
events.name: Fuad I becomes King of Egypt

events.enhanced_description: On March 16, 1922, the Rand Rebellion, which began as a strike by white South African mine workers, was suppressed by the government. This event highlighted the tensions between labor movements and state authority in post-World War I South Africa.
events.name: Suppression of the Rand Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On March 18, 1922, Mahatma Gandhi was sentenced to six years in prison for sedition, although he would serve only two years. This sentence drew international attention to the Indian independence movement and Gandhi's philosophy of nonviolent resistance.
events.name: Mahatma Gandhi sentenced to prison

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1922, the USS Langley was commissioned as the first aircraft carrier in the United States Navy. This marked a pivotal development in naval warfare, as aircraft carriers would become central to military strategy in the years to come.
events.name: Commissioning of the USS Langley

events.enhanced_description: On March 22, 1922, radio station WLW in Cincinnati began broadcasting, becoming one of the first radio stations in the United States to operate at a high power. This event marked a significant advancement in mass communication and entertainment.
events.name: WLW Radio begins broadcasting

events.enhanced_description: On March 23, 1922, Queensland, Australia, abolished its Legislative Council, marking a significant change in the state's governance structure. This decision reflected broader trends towards more democratic forms of government in Australia.
events.name: Queensland abolishes the Legislative Council

events.enhanced_description: On March 26, 1922, the German Social Democratic Party was founded in Poland, reflecting the political dynamics and the influence of socialist movements in the region during the interwar period. This party aimed to represent the interests of the German-speaking population in Poland.
events.name: German Social Democratic Party founded in Poland

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1922, six members of the Gruber family were murdered at their remote farm in Hinterkaifeck, Bavaria, in a case that remains one of Germany's most infamous unsolved crimes. The brutal nature of the murders and the mystery surrounding them have captivated public interest for decades.
events.name: Hinterkaifeck murders

events.enhanced_description: On April 1, 1922, South African Railways assumed control over all railway operations in South West Africa, consolidating its influence in the region. This move was part of South Africa's broader administrative control over the territory, which had been mandated by the League of Nations after World War I.
events.name: South African Railways takes control of all railway operations in South West Africa

events.enhanced_description: Joseph Stalin was appointed General Secretary of the Central Committee of the Soviet Communist Party on April 3, 1922. This position would enable him to consolidate power and eventually lead the Soviet Union through significant political and social changes.
events.name: Joseph Stalin is appointed General Secretary of the Central Committee of the Soviet Communist Party

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1922, the first midair collision between airliners occurred over Poix-de-Picardie, France, involving a Daimler Airway de Havilland DH.18 and a Grands Express Aériens Farman Goliath. This incident highlighted the growing need for aviation regulations and safety measures as air travel became more common.
events.name: 1922 Picardie mid-air collision

events.enhanced_description: The Genoa Conference, held on April 10, 1922, brought together representatives from 34 countries to discuss monetary economics in the aftermath of World War I. This conference aimed to address economic instability and foster international cooperation.
events.name: Genoa Conference

events.enhanced_description: On April 12, 1922, the United Kingdom's Prince of Wales arrived in Yokohama aboard HMS Renown, marking the beginning of a one-month visit to Japan. This visit was significant in strengthening diplomatic and cultural ties between the UK and Japan.
events.name: The United Kingdom's Prince of Wales arrives in Japan

events.enhanced_description: On April 13, 1922, the State of Massachusetts opened all public offices to women, marking a significant advancement in gender equality and women's rights in the United States. This decision reflected the changing attitudes towards women's roles in society following the suffrage movement.
events.name: The State of Massachusetts opens all public offices to women

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Rapallo, signed on April 16, 1922, marked a significant rapprochement between the Weimar Republic of Germany and Bolshevik Russia. This treaty aimed to normalize relations and foster economic cooperation between the two nations.
events.name: The Treaty of Rapallo

events.enhanced_description: On April 24, 1922, the first portion of the Imperial Wireless Chain was opened, establishing a strategic international wireless telegraphy network intended to link the British Empire. This development was crucial for improving communication across vast distances.
events.name: The first portion of the Imperial Wireless Chain is opened

events.enhanced_description: On May 8, 1922, in Moscow, eight priests, two laymen, and one woman were sentenced to death for opposing the Soviet government's confiscation of church property. This event underscored the tensions between the Soviet regime and religious institutions during this period.
events.name: In Moscow, priests and laymen sentenced to death

events.enhanced_description: On May 18, 1922, a historic meeting took place at the Hotel Majestic in Paris, where prominent figures such as Sergei Diaghilev, Igor Stravinsky, Pablo Picasso, Marcel Proust, James Joyce, Erik Satie, and Clive Bell dined together. This gathering represented a unique convergence of influential artists and intellectuals of the time.
events.name: Cultural meeting in Paris

events.enhanced_description: On May 19, 1922, the All-Russian Young Pioneer Organisation was established in Moscow, aiming to promote communist ideology among the youth. This organization played a significant role in the education and indoctrination of children in the Soviet Union.
events.name: The All-Russian Young Pioneer Organisation is established

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1922, British Liberal MP Horatio Bottomley was sentenced to seven years in prison for fraud. This scandal highlighted issues of corruption and accountability in British politics during the early 20th century.
events.name: Horatio Bottomley jailed for fraud

events.enhanced_description: On May 30, 1922, the Lincoln Memorial was dedicated in Washington, D.C., honoring the legacy of President Abraham Lincoln. This iconic structure has since become a symbol of American democracy and civil rights.
events.name: Lincoln Memorial is dedicated

events.enhanced_description: On June 1, 1922, Bolshevik forces achieved a significant victory over Basmachi troops led by Enver Pasha in Central Asia. This conflict was part of the broader struggle against anti-Bolshevik forces in the region.
events.name: Bolshevik forces defeat Basmachi troops

events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1922, Åland's Regional Assembly convened for its first plenary session in Mariehamn, marking a significant step in self-governance for the Åland Islands. This day is celebrated as Self-Government Day in Åland.
events.name: Åland's Regional Assembly convenes

events.enhanced_description: On June 11, 1922, Robert J. Flaherty's 'Nanook of the North' premiered in New York City, becoming the first commercially successful feature-length documentary film. This groundbreaking work showcased the life of an Inuit family and set a precedent for future documentary filmmaking.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Nanook of the North premieres

events.enhanced_description: On June 14, 1922, President Warren G. Harding made his first speech on the radio, marking a new era in political communication. This event demonstrated the growing importance of radio as a medium for reaching the public.
events.name: Warren G. Harding makes first radio speech

events.enhanced_description: On June 22, 1922, Irish Republican Army agents assassinated British Army field marshal Sir Henry Wilson in London. This assassination was part of the ongoing conflict between Irish republicans and British authorities.
events.name: Assassination of Sir Henry Wilson

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1922, Weimar Republic foreign minister Walther Rathenau was assassinated in Berlin. His murder was a significant event that highlighted the political instability and violence in Germany during the early 1920s.
events.name: Assassination of Walther Rathenau

events.enhanced_description: On June 26, 1922, Louis Honoré Charles Antoine Grimaldi became Reigning Prince Louis II of Monaco. His reign would see significant developments in the principality, including modernization and increased tourism.

image.caption: Portrait photograph of Prince Louis II of Monaco.
image.credit: Georges Detaille — This image is available from the United States Library of Congress 's Prints and Photographs division under the digital ID ggbain.05670 . This tag does not indicate the copyright status of the attached work. A normal copyright tag is still required. See Commons:Licensing .
image.date_qualification: Portrait of Louis II, who became Reigning Prince on 26 June 1922. The image is dated before 1923, so it may precede or follow his accession.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Louis II of Monaco becomes Reigning Prince

events.enhanced_description: The Irish Civil War and the Battle of Dublin began on June 28, 1922, when the Irish National Army bombarded the anti-Treaty Irish Republican Army forces occupying the Four Courts in Dublin. This conflict marked a pivotal moment in Irish history, leading to a bitter civil war.
events.name: The Irish Civil War and Battle of Dublin begin

events.enhanced_description: The Irish Civil War began on June 28, 1922, with the Irish National Army's bombardment of the Four Courts in Dublin, where anti-Treaty Irish Republican Army forces were entrenched. The conflict, rooted in disagreements over the Anglo-Irish Treaty, led to significant casualties and political upheaval in Ireland.

image.caption: The Four Courts in Dublin after an explosion of stored munitions; photograph by the National Library of Ireland.
image.credit: National Library of Ireland on The Commons — Flickr : Conflagration
image.date_qualification: 30 June 1922; aftermath during the Battle of Dublin, not the opening bombardment on 28 June.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Irish Civil War and Battle of Dublin

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1922, Subhi Barakat was appointed president of the Syrian Federation, a short-lived political entity that aimed to unify the various regions of Syria. His presidency was marked by challenges in governance and regional stability.
events.name: Subhi Barakat becomes president of the Syrian Federation

events.enhanced_description: The Hollywood Bowl, an iconic open-air music venue, officially opened on July 11, 1922, in Los Angeles, California. Known for its distinctive shell-shaped stage and natural acoustics, it has since become a premier location for concerts and cultural events.

image.caption: Photograph of the Hollywood Bowl amphitheatre.
image.credit: Alan Light — Hollywood Bowl Uploaded by MaybeMaybeMaybe
image.date_qualification: Photograph dated 1990; decades after the 1922 opening.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Opening of the Hollywood Bowl

events.enhanced_description: On July 17, 1922, the final signings of Treaty 11 took place at Fort Liard, Canada, between King George V and various First Nations. This treaty was significant in defining land rights and governance for Indigenous peoples in the region.
events.name: Final Signings of Treaty 11

events.enhanced_description: On July 20, 1922, the former German protectorate of Togoland was divided into French Togoland and British Togoland under the League of Nations mandates. This division marked a significant change in colonial administration in West Africa.
events.name: Division of Togoland

events.enhanced_description: The Cherkess Autonomous Oblast was established within the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic on July 27, 1922. This administrative division aimed to provide a degree of self-governance for the Cherkess people.
events.name: Establishment of Cherkess Autonomous Oblast

events.enhanced_description: On August 2, 1922, the Swatow typhoon struck Shantou, China, resulting in the deaths of over 5,000 people. This devastating natural disaster highlighted the vulnerability of coastal cities to severe weather events.
events.name: Swatow Typhoon

events.enhanced_description: General Michael Collins, a key figure in the Irish Civil War, was assassinated on August 22, 1922, in West Cork. His death marked a pivotal moment in the conflict and had lasting implications for the future of Ireland.
events.name: Assassination of Michael Collins

events.enhanced_description: On August 23, 1922, Morocco revolted against Spanish colonial rule, marking the beginning of a series of uprisings in the Rif region. This revolt was part of the broader struggle for independence and self-determination in North Africa.
events.name: Morocco Revolts Against Spain

events.enhanced_description: On August 26, 1922, Turkish forces launched a large-scale attack against Greek troops in Afyon, leading to a decisive Turkish victory on August 30. This battle was a significant event in the Greco-Turkish War, contributing to the eventual withdrawal of Greek forces from Anatolia.
events.name: Turkish Attack on Greek Forces

events.enhanced_description: On August 28, 1922, Japan agreed to withdraw its troops from Siberia, marking the end of its military presence in the region following the Russian Civil War. This decision was part of Japan's broader strategy to focus on its interests in East Asia.
events.name: Japan Withdraws Troops from Siberia

events.enhanced_description: The Autodromo Nazionale di Monza, the world's third purpose-built motorsport race track, officially opened on September 3, 1922, in Monza, Italy. This venue has since become a historic site for motorsport events, including the Italian Grand Prix.
events.name: Opening of Autodromo Nazionale di Monza

events.enhanced_description: On September 9, 1922, Turkish forces entered İzmir, effectively ending the Greco-Turkish War (1919–1922). This event marked a significant turning point in the conflict, leading to the establishment of Turkish sovereignty in the region.
events.name: Turkish Forces Enter İzmir

events.enhanced_description: The Sun News-Pictorial, a predecessor of the Herald Sun, was founded on September 11, 1922, in Melbourne, Australia. This publication played a significant role in the Australian media landscape and continues to be influential today.
events.name: Founding of The Sun News-Pictorial

events.enhanced_description: On September 13, 1922, the Polish Parliament passed the Gdynia Seaport Construction Act, which aimed to develop Gdynia as a major seaport. This act was crucial for Poland's economic development and maritime trade.
events.name: Gdynia Seaport Construction Act

events.enhanced_description: On September 13, 1922, the Great Fire of Smyrna devastated much of İzmir, leading to widespread destruction and loss of life. The causes of the fire remain disputed, with various parties blamed for the disaster.
events.name: Great Fire of Smyrna

events.enhanced_description: On September 17, 1922, Dutch cyclist Piet Moeskops became the world champion sprinter, marking a significant achievement in the world of cycling. His victory contributed to the popularity of the sport in the Netherlands and beyond.
events.name: Piet Moeskops Becomes World Champion Sprinter

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1922, the Kingdom of Hungary officially joined the League of Nations, signaling its commitment to international cooperation and peace following the tumultuous aftermath of World War I.
events.name: Hungary Joins the League of Nations

events.enhanced_description: On September 24, 1922, the September 11 Revolution occurred in Greece, leading to significant political changes in the country. This revolution was part of the broader instability in Greece following the end of the Greco-Turkish War.
events.name: September 11 Revolution in Greece

events.enhanced_description: On September 29, 1922, Bertolt Brecht's play 'Drums in the Night' premiered at the Munich Kammerspiele, marking the first staging of his work. This event was significant in the development of modern theater and Brecht's career as a playwright.
events.name: Drums in the Night (Trommeln in der Nacht) staged

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1922, G. I. Gurdjieff opened his Institute for the Harmonious Development of Man in Fontainebleau, France. This institute aimed to promote a unique blend of spiritual and physical development, influencing many seekers of knowledge.
events.name: G. I. Gurdjieff opens Institute

events.enhanced_description: On October 3, 1922, Rebecca Latimer Felton was appointed as the first female U.S. senator from Georgia, filling the vacancy left by the death of Senator Thomas Watson. Her appointment marked a significant milestone in women's political representation in the United States.
events.name: Rebecca Latimer Felton becomes first female U.S. senator

events.enhanced_description: The Greco-Turkish War, which lasted from 1919 to 1922, concluded on October 11, 1922, with a decisive victory for Turkey. This conflict significantly altered the territorial and political landscape of the region.
events.name: Greco-Turkish War ends

events.enhanced_description: On October 15, 1922, T. S. Eliot established The Criterion magazine, which featured the first publication of his poem 'The Waste Land.' This magazine became a significant platform for modernist literature.
events.name: T. S. Eliot establishes The Criterion

events.enhanced_description: The British Broadcasting Company (BBC) was formed on October 18, 1922, in London, marking a pivotal moment in the history of broadcasting. The BBC would go on to become one of the world's leading public service broadcasters.
events.name: British Broadcasting Company formed

events.enhanced_description: On October 25, 1922, the Third Dáil enacted the Constitution of the Irish Free State, establishing a new political framework for Ireland following its independence from British rule. This constitution laid the groundwork for modern Irish governance.
events.name: Irish Free State Constitution enacted

events.enhanced_description: On October 27, 1922, a referendum in Southern Rhodesia resulted in a rejection of union with South Africa. This decision reflected the region's desire for self-governance and independence from colonial rule.
events.name: Southern Rhodesians reject union with South Africa

events.enhanced_description: On October 28, 1922, the March on Rome culminated in the National Fascist Party's rise to power under Benito Mussolini. This event marked the beginning of a fascist regime in Italy, which would last until the end of World War II.
events.name: March on Rome

events.enhanced_description: On October 31, 1922, Benito Mussolini was appointed as the youngest Prime Minister of Italy at the age of 39. His leadership marked the start of a totalitarian regime that would shape Italian politics for decades.
events.name: Benito Mussolini becomes Prime Minister

events.enhanced_description: On November 1, 1922, the Ottoman Empire was officially abolished after 600 years of rule, leading to the abdication of its last sultan, Mehmed VI. This marked the end of a significant era in Middle Eastern history.
events.name: Ottoman Empire abolished

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1922, English archaeologist Howard Carter and his team discovered the entrance to the tomb of Tutankhamun in the Valley of the Kings, a monumental find that would captivate the world and shed light on ancient Egyptian civilization.
events.name: Discovery of the tomb of Tutankhamun

events.enhanced_description: On November 12, 1922, Sigma Gamma Rho Sorority, Incorporated was founded by seven educators in Indianapolis, Indiana. This organization has since become a prominent national collegiate sorority, promoting scholarship and community service.
events.name: Sigma Gamma Rho Sorority founded

events.enhanced_description: On November 14, 1922, the British Broadcasting Company (BBC) began its radio service in the United Kingdom, broadcasting from station 2LO in London. This marked the beginning of a new era in mass communication.
events.name: BBC begins radio service

events.enhanced_description: The 1922 United Kingdom general election was held following the Conservative Party's withdrawal from the coalition government, resulting in a significant victory for the Conservatives. This election marked the first time Labour became the main opposition party, surpassing the divided Liberal Party.
events.name: 1922 United Kingdom general election

events.enhanced_description: On November 19, 1922, Abdülmecid II, the Crown Prince of the Ottoman Empire, was elected Caliph. This event occurred during a tumultuous period following the abolition of the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: Abdülmecid II elected Caliph

events.enhanced_description: On November 21, 1922, Rebecca Felton took the oath of office, formally becoming the first woman United States Senator. Her appointment was a landmark moment in the history of women's political participation in the U.S.
events.name: Rebecca Felton takes oath as senator

events.enhanced_description: On November 24, 1922, Erskine Childers, a popular author and anti-Treaty Republican, was executed by firing squad in Dublin after being convicted of unlawful possession of a firearm. His execution highlighted the intense political strife in post-Civil War Ireland.
events.name: Erskine Childers executed

events.enhanced_description: On November 26, 1922, archaeologist Howard Carter and Lord Carnarvon became the first individuals to enter the tomb of Pharaoh Tutankhamun (KV62) in over 3,000 years. This discovery sparked worldwide interest in ancient Egypt and significantly advanced the field of Egyptology.
events.name: Discovery of Tutankhamun's tomb

events.enhanced_description: On December 5, 1922, the British Parliament enacted the Irish Free State Constitution Act, which legally sanctioned the new Constitution of the Irish Free State. This act was a crucial step in the establishment of Irish self-governance following the Anglo-Irish Treaty.
events.name: Irish Free State Constitution Act

events.enhanced_description: On December 6, 1922, the Irish Free State officially came into existence, marking a significant moment in Irish history. George V became the monarch of the new state, while Tim Healy was appointed as its first Governor-General and W. T. Cosgrave as President of the Executive Council.
events.name: Establishment of the Irish Free State

events.enhanced_description: On December 9, 1922, Gabriel Narutowicz was elected as the first president of Poland, following the country's re-establishment after World War I. His presidency was marked by political instability and he faced significant opposition from various factions.
events.name: Gabriel Narutowicz elected president of Poland

events.enhanced_description: On December 11, 1922, the trial of Edith Thompson and Frederick Bywaters concluded at the Old Bailey in London, where both were found guilty of the murder of Thompson's husband. Their case garnered significant public attention and raised questions about justice and morality.
events.name: Trial of Edith Thompson and Frederick Bywaters

events.enhanced_description: On December 16, 1922, Gabriel Narutowicz, who had been sworn in as the first president of the Second Polish Republic just days earlier, was assassinated by a right-wing sympathizer in Warsaw. His assassination highlighted the political tensions in post-war Poland.
events.name: Assassination of Gabriel Narutowicz

events.enhanced_description: On December 20, 1922, Jean Cocteau's adaptation of Antigone premiered in Paris, featuring innovative settings by Pablo Picasso, music by Arthur Honegger, and costumes designed by Coco Chanel. This production was a significant cultural event that showcased the collaboration of prominent artists of the time.
events.name: Premiere of Antigone by Jean Cocteau

events.enhanced_description: On December 27, 1922, the Japanese aircraft carrier Hōshō was commissioned, becoming the first purpose-designed aircraft carrier in history. This marked a significant advancement in naval warfare and the development of aircraft carrier technology.
events.name: Commissioning of Hōshō aircraft carrier

events.enhanced_description: On December 30, 1922, Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, and the Transcaucasian Republics (Armenia, Azerbaijan, and Georgia) united to form the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR). This event marked the establishment of a new political entity that would have a profound impact on global politics.
events.name: Formation of the USSR

events.enhanced_description: In 1923, the Egyptian Constitution was adopted, introducing a parliamentary system of democracy in the country. This constitution marked a significant step towards modern governance in Egypt.
events.name: Egyptian Constitution of 1923 adopted

events.enhanced_description: In January 1923, Southeastern Michigan experienced an unprecedented snowfall, with 15 centimeters (5.9 inches) accumulating in a short period. This extreme weather event was part of a broader trend of severe winter conditions affecting the region.
events.name: Southeastern Michigan receives a record 15 centimetres (5.9 in) of snow

events.enhanced_description: The premiere of Bertolt Brecht's play 'In the Jungle' at the Residenztheater in Munich was notably interrupted by Nazi demonstrators, reflecting the tense political climate of the time. This incident highlighted the challenges faced by artists under rising authoritarian regimes.
events.name: The premiere of Bertolt Brecht's play In the Jungle (Im Dickicht)

events.enhanced_description: Stanley Baldwin's appointment as British Prime Minister in 1923 marked a significant moment in British politics, as he led the country through a period of economic challenges and political instability. His leadership style and policies would shape the Conservative Party's direction in the years to come.
events.name: Stanley Baldwin is appointed British Prime Minister
