events.enhanced_description: The establishment of Sabena Airlines in Belgium in 1923 marked the beginning of the country's national airline, which would play a crucial role in connecting Belgium to the rest of the world through air travel. Sabena became a symbol of Belgian aviation and international connectivity.
events.name: Belgium's Sabena Airlines is created

events.enhanced_description: In July 1923, hyperinflation in the Weimar Republic reached staggering levels, with the exchange rate soaring to 353,000 marks for a single American dollar. This economic crisis had profound social and political implications, contributing to the instability that would lead to the rise of extremist movements.

image.caption: Five-billion-mark German Papiermark banknote.
image.credit: Reichsbankdirektorium Berlin — Image by Godot13
image.date_qualification: The image metadata gives the banknote date as 1923; the upload date is 2015 and is not the depicted date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False; Restrictions: currency

events.name: Hyperinflation in the Weimar Republic (Germany)

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1923, the Great Kantō earthquake struck Tokyo and Yokohama, resulting in the deaths of over 100,000 people and widespread destruction. This catastrophic event led to significant changes in urban planning and disaster preparedness in Japan.
events.name: Great Kantō earthquake

events.enhanced_description: Following the Great Kantō earthquake in September 1923, the Kantō Massacre began, resulting in the deaths of thousands of ethnic Koreans due to unfounded rumors of crime and rebellion. This tragic event highlighted the racial tensions and societal unrest in Japan during this period.
events.name: Kantō Massacre

events.enhanced_description: The first American Track & Field championships for women took place in Newark, New Jersey, marking a significant milestone in the history of women's athletics in the United States. This event helped to promote women's participation in sports and laid the groundwork for future competitions.
events.name: The first American Track & Field championships for women are held in New Jersey

events.enhanced_description: The League of Nations Mandate for Palestine came into effect, establishing British administration over the region and aiming to provide a homeland for the Jewish people. This mandate also included the establishment of the Emirate of Transjordan under Abdullah I, shaping the political landscape of the Middle East.
events.name: The League of Nations Mandate for Palestine comes into effect

events.enhanced_description: In 1923, Ankara was officially designated as the capital of Turkey, replacing Istanbul (formerly Constantinople). This decision was part of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk's reforms to modernize and secularize the nation following the collapse of the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: Ankara replaces Istanbul as the capital of Turkey

events.enhanced_description: In 1923, meteorologists recorded the first instance of a storm crossing from the Eastern Pacific Ocean into the Atlantic Ocean, occurring near Oaxaca, Mexico. This event was significant for the study of weather patterns and the understanding of storm behavior.
events.name: First recorded storm crossing from the Eastern Pacific into the Atlantic occurs in Oaxaca

events.enhanced_description: In 1923, a rare meteorological event occurred when a sixth tropical storm developed in the Gulf of Mexico, coinciding with the presence of four active tropical storms simultaneously. This unusual occurrence highlighted the complexities of tropical storm formation and tracking.
events.name: A sixth tropical storm develops in the Gulf of Mexico

events.enhanced_description: In 1923, brothers Roy and Walt Disney founded what would become The Walt Disney Company, initially known as the Disney Brothers Studio. This company would grow to become a major player in the entertainment industry, revolutionizing animation and family entertainment.
events.name: Roy and Walt Disney found The Walt Disney Company

events.enhanced_description: On February 5, 1923, Australian cricketer Bill Ponsford scored an astonishing 429 runs, setting a new world record for the highest first-class cricket score at the Melbourne Cricket Ground. This remarkable achievement occurred during his third match at this level, contributing to the Victoria cricket team's total of 1,059 runs in the innings.
events.name: Bill Ponsford breaks first-class cricket record

events.enhanced_description: On February 9, 1923, Billy Hughes resigned as Prime Minister of Australia after the Country Party refused to form a coalition with his Nationalist Party. He was succeeded by Stanley Bruce, marking a significant shift in Australian political dynamics that would influence the country's governance for decades.

image.caption: Portrait of Prime Minister Billy Hughes smiling during celebrations on his return from the Paris Peace Conference in Sydney.
image.credit: Fairfax Corporation — National Library of Australia ( http://nla.gov.au/nla.obj-162944348/view )
image.date_qualification: Depicted in July 1919; it predates the resignation on 9 February 1923.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Billy Hughes resigns as Prime Minister of Australia

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1923, Eskom was established as the largest electricity producer in Africa, playing a crucial role in the development of South Africa's energy infrastructure. The company has since become a key player in the region's power generation and distribution.
events.name: Eskom established in South Africa

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1923, the first issue of TIME magazine was published, marking a significant moment in American journalism. TIME would go on to become one of the most influential news magazines in the world, shaping public discourse and opinion.

image.caption: Cover of the first issue of TIME magazine, depicting Joseph Gurney Cannon.
image.credit: William Oberhardt — TIME Magazine cover, 3 March 1923. Time magazine archive. [2]
image.date_qualification: The cover is dated March 3, 1923; the supplied evidence identifies it as the first issue’s cover, not a photograph of the publication event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: First issue of TIME magazine published

events.enhanced_description: On March 6, 1923, the Egyptian Feminist Union was founded at the home of activist Huda Sha'arawi, marking the establishment of the first nationwide feminist movement in Egypt. This organization played a pivotal role in advocating for women's rights and social reforms in the country.
events.name: Egyptian Feminist Union founded

events.enhanced_description: On March 9, 1923, Vladimir Lenin suffered his third stroke, which left him bedridden and unable to speak. This health crisis forced him to retire from his position as Chairman of the Soviet government, significantly impacting the future of Soviet leadership.
events.name: Vladimir Lenin suffers third stroke

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1923, Dobrolyot was established as the first Soviet civil aviation service, which would later become part of the flag carrier Aeroflot. This marked the beginning of organized civil aviation in the Soviet Union.
events.name: Dobrolyot formed as Soviet civil aviation service

events.enhanced_description: On March 28, 1923, the Regia Aeronautica, the air force of Fascist Italy, was founded. This establishment marked a significant development in Italy's military capabilities during the interwar period.
events.name: Regia Aeronautica founded

events.enhanced_description: On April 6, 1923, the first Prefects Board in Southeast Asia was formed at the Victoria Institution in Kuala Lumpur. This initiative aimed to foster leadership and responsibility among students in the region.
events.name: First Prefects Board in Southeast Asia formed

events.enhanced_description: On April 12, 1923, the Kandersteg International Scout Centre was established in Kandersteg, Switzerland. This center has since become a prominent location for international scouting events and gatherings.
events.name: Kandersteg International Scout Centre established

events.enhanced_description: On January 25, 1925, Hjalmar Branting resigned as Prime Minister of Sweden due to ill health, paving the way for Rickard Sandler to take over. Branting was a significant figure in Swedish politics, known for his social democratic policies.
events.name: Hjalmar Branting resigns as Prime Minister of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On April 23, 1923, the Gdynia seaport was inaugurated, located on the Polish Corridor. This development was crucial for Poland's maritime trade and economic growth in the interwar period.
events.name: Gdynia seaport inaugurated

events.enhanced_description: On April 26, 1923, Prince Albert, Duke of York, married Lady Elizabeth Bowes-Lyon at Westminster Abbey. This union would later lead to Albert becoming King George VI and Elizabeth becoming the Queen Mother.
events.name: Wedding of Prince Albert and Lady Elizabeth Bowes-Lyon

events.enhanced_description: On April 28, 1923, the original Wembley Stadium opened its doors to the public for the first time, hosting the FA Cup Final between Bolton Wanderers and West Ham United. This iconic venue would become synonymous with English football.
events.name: Wembley Stadium opens

events.enhanced_description: On May 9, 1923, Southeastern Michigan experienced a record snowfall of 15 centimeters (5.9 inches), following a dramatic drop in temperatures. This unusual weather event highlighted the region's unpredictable climate.
events.name: Record snowfall in Southeastern Michigan

events.enhanced_description: On May 20, 1923, British Prime Minister Bonar Law resigned due to ill health. His departure marked a pivotal moment in British politics, leading to a change in leadership during a challenging period.
events.name: Bonar Law resigns as British Prime Minister

events.enhanced_description: On May 23, 1923, Stanley Baldwin was appointed as British Prime Minister, succeeding Bonar Law. Baldwin's leadership would influence British politics during a time of economic and social change.
events.name: Stanley Baldwin appointed British Prime Minister

events.enhanced_description: On May 24, 1923, the Irish Civil War officially came to an end, concluding a brutal conflict that had divided the nation. The resolution of this war paved the way for the establishment of a more stable Irish government.
events.name: Irish Civil War ends

events.enhanced_description: On May 26, 1923, the first 24 Hours of Le Mans motor race took place, with drivers André Lagache and René Léonard emerging victorious. This endurance race has since become one of the most prestigious events in motorsport.
events.name: First 24 Hours of Le Mans motor race held

events.enhanced_description: On May 27, 1923, the Ku Klux Klan in the United States openly defied a law requiring the publication of its membership. This act of defiance highlighted the organization's ongoing influence and the challenges faced by law enforcement.
events.name: Ku Klux Klan defies membership publication law

events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1923, a military coup in Bulgaria ousted Prime Minister Aleksandar Stamboliyski, who would later be killed on June 14. This coup marked a significant turning point in Bulgarian politics, leading to a period of instability.
events.name: Bulgarian coup d'état of 1923

events.enhanced_description: On June 12, 1923, William Walton's Façade was performed for the first time in London. This work would become a significant contribution to British music and culture.
events.name: William Walton's Façade performed for the first time

events.enhanced_description: On June 13, 1923, President Li Yuanhong of China was forced to abandon his residence as a warlord surrounded the mansion, cutting off water and electricity supplies. This event underscored the political instability and power struggles in China during this period.
events.name: President Li Yuanhong abandons residence

events.enhanced_description: The storming of Ayan marked the conclusion of the Yakut Revolt, a significant uprising against Bolshevik rule during the Russian Civil War. This event underscored the complexities of regional resistance within the broader context of the civil conflict in Russia.
events.name: The storming of Ayan in Siberia concludes the Yakut Revolt and the Russian Civil War

events.enhanced_description: The eruption of Mount Etna in June 1923 resulted in widespread devastation, displacing approximately 60,000 people from their homes. This event highlighted the ongoing geological activity of one of the world's most active volcanoes and its impact on local communities.
events.name: Mount Etna erupts in Italy, making 60,000 homeless

events.enhanced_description: In July 1923, a severe hailstorm struck Rostov-on-Don, resulting in the tragic deaths of 23 individuals. This event underscored the dangers posed by extreme weather phenomena and their impact on urban populations.
events.name: Large hailstones kill 23 people in Rostov, Soviet Union

events.enhanced_description: The inauguration of the Hollywood Sign in 1923, originally reading 'Hollywoodland', marked the beginning of a cultural icon that would symbolize the American film industry. The sign has since become a globally recognized landmark representing cinema and entertainment.
events.name: The Hollywood Sign is inaugurated in California (originally reading Hollywoodland)

events.enhanced_description: The assassination of Pancho Villa on July 20, 1923, in Hidalgo del Parral, Chihuahua, marked the end of an era for the Mexican Revolution. Villa, a legendary figure and revolutionary leader, had a profound impact on Mexican history and his death signified the waning of revolutionary fervor.

image.caption: Gelatin silver photographic postcard depicting Pancho Villa on horseback, by D. W. Hoffman.
image.credit: D.W. Hoffman, an El Paso photographer — https://www.getty.edu/news/faces-of-the-mexican-revolution/
image.date_qualification: Portrait made circa 1912, about eleven years before Villa’s assassination; it is not a photograph of the assassination.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Pancho Villa is assassinated at Hidalgo del Parral, Chihuahua

events.enhanced_description: The signing of the Treaty of Lausanne on July 24, 1923, in Switzerland marked a pivotal moment in the establishment of modern Turkey and the reconfiguration of borders following World War I. This treaty effectively ended the Ottoman Empire's territorial claims and set the stage for the Republic of Turkey.
events.name: The Treaty of Lausanne (1923) is signed

events.enhanced_description: On August 2, 1923, Vice President Calvin Coolidge was sworn in as the 30th President of the United States following the death of President Warren G. Harding in San Francisco. Coolidge's presidency would be marked by a return to normalcy and economic prosperity during the Roaring Twenties.
events.name: Vice President Calvin Coolidge becomes the 30th president of the United States

events.enhanced_description: Calvin Coolidge was sworn in as President of the United States on August 3, 1923, in a ceremony conducted by his father in their family home in Plymouth Notch, Vermont. This unique setting underscored Coolidge's humble beginnings and connection to his roots.
events.name: President Calvin Coolidge is sworn in by his father

events.enhanced_description: In August 1923, the first major seagoing ship docked at Gdynia, marking the port's official opening and its significance as a key maritime hub for Poland. This event was crucial for the country's economic development and trade expansion.
events.name: The first major seagoing ship arrives at Gdynia, the newly constructed Polish seaport

events.enhanced_description: The inaugural British Track & Field championships for women took place in London on August 18, 1923, marking a significant milestone in the history of women's athletics. This event helped pave the way for greater recognition and participation of women in sports.
events.name: The first British Track & Field championships for women are held in London

events.enhanced_description: The 1923 hurricane season commenced with a tropical storm forming northeast of the Turks and Caicos Islands, signaling the start of a period known for its potential for severe weather events in the Caribbean. This season would be closely monitored for its impact on the region.
events.name: Hurricane season begins, with a tropical storm northeast of the Turks and Caicos Islands

events.enhanced_description: On August 31, 1923, the Italian navy occupied the island of Corfu in retaliation for the murder of an Italian officer, leading to international tensions and protests from the League of Nations. The occupation lasted until September 30, highlighting the fragile post-war geopolitical landscape.
events.name: The Italian navy occupies Corfu

events.enhanced_description: The Great Kantō earthquake struck on September 1, 1923, devastating Tokyo and Yokohama and resulting in the deaths of over 100,000 people. This catastrophic event led to widespread destruction and had lasting effects on urban planning and disaster preparedness in Japan.

image.caption: Photograph of Nihonbashi bridge.
image.credit: urbzoo — https://www.flickr.com/photos/urbzoo/3767766524/
image.date_qualification: Photograph of the current bridge, which the image description says survived the 1923 earthquake; taken in 2009, not a contemporary event photograph.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: The Great Kantō earthquake devastates Tokyo and Yokohama

events.enhanced_description: On September 4, 1923, the USS Shenandoah (ZR-1) made her inaugural flight at Naval Air Station Lakehurst, New Jersey. This airship was notable for containing most of the world's helium reserves at the time, representing a significant advancement in naval aviation technology.

locations.name: Naval Air Station Lakehurst, New Jersey

events.name: The United States Navy's first home-built rigid airship USS Shenandoah makes her first flight

events.enhanced_description: The Fukuda Village Incident on September 6, 1923, was a tragic event during the Kantō Massacre, where nine Japanese individuals were killed based on false accusations of being ethnic Koreans. This incident exemplified the xenophobia and violence that erupted in the aftermath of the Great Kantō earthquake.
events.name: The Fukuda Village Incident occurs as a part of the larger Kantō Massacre

events.enhanced_description: On September 7, 1923, the International Criminal Police Commission (ICPC), now known as Interpol, was established during the International Police Conference in Vienna. This organization aimed to facilitate international police cooperation and combat transnational crime.
events.name: The International Criminal Police Commission (ICPC), better known as Interpol, is set up

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1923, nine United States Navy destroyers ran aground during a naval exercise off the coast of California at Honda Point. This incident resulted in the loss of 23 sailors and significant damage to the ships, highlighting the challenges of navigation and communication in naval operations.

image.caption: Animated illustration depicting the wrecked destroyers at Honda Point.
image.credit: U.S. Navy, photographed from a plane assigned to USS Aroostook (CM-3). — US Navy
image.date_qualification: Animation uploaded 9 July 2009; depicts the September 1923 disaster. The underlying photograph date is not specified.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Honda Point disaster

events.enhanced_description: On September 9, 1923, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk founded the Republican People's Party (CHP) in Ankara, marking a significant step in the establishment of a secular and modern Turkish state following the collapse of the Ottoman Empire. The CHP would become the dominant political party in Turkey for decades, shaping the country's political landscape.
events.name: Founding of the Republican People's Party (CHP)

events.enhanced_description: On September 10, 1923, the Irish Free State officially joined the League of Nations, symbolizing its recognition as a sovereign state on the international stage. This membership marked a significant step in Ireland's post-independence diplomatic relations.
events.name: Irish Free State joins the League of Nations

events.enhanced_description: On September 11, 1923, Sun Yat-sen, the leader of the Nationalist Kuomintang party, decided to ally with the Comintern and the Chinese Communist Party in a bid to strengthen his position in southern China. This alliance aimed to unify China against warlord factions and foreign imperialism.
events.name: Sun Yat-sen allies with the Comintern

events.enhanced_description: On September 13, 1923, Miguel Primo de Rivera led a military coup in Spain, establishing a dictatorship that would last until 1930. His regime prohibited trade unions for a decade and sought to stabilize the country amid political turmoil.
events.name: Military coup in Spain

events.enhanced_description: On September 17, 1923, a devastating fire erupted in Berkeley, California, consuming approximately 640 structures, including 584 homes. The fire spread rapidly through densely populated neighborhoods, leading to significant loss of property and displacement of residents.
events.name: 1923 Berkeley fire

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1923, newspaper printers in New York City initiated a strike, protesting against poor working conditions and low wages. This labor action highlighted the growing tensions between labor unions and management in the early 20th century.
events.name: Newspaper printers strike in New York City

events.enhanced_description: On September 24, 1923, the second major hurricane of the Atlantic hurricane season struck north of Hispaniola, causing widespread damage and disruption. The storm's impact was felt across the Caribbean, exacerbating the region's vulnerability to natural disasters.
events.name: Hurricane strikes north of Hispaniola

events.enhanced_description: On September 26, 1923, Gustav Ritter von Kahr assumed dictatorial powers in Bavaria, effectively sidelining the democratic government. His rule would be marked by authoritarian measures and a crackdown on political dissent.
events.name: Gustav Ritter von Kahr takes dictatorial powers

events.enhanced_description: On September 29, 1923, the first American Track & Field championships for women were held in Newark, New Jersey. This event marked a significant milestone in the recognition of women's athletics in the United States.
events.name: First American Track & Field championships for women

events.enhanced_description: On September 30, 1923, Major Ernst Buchrucker and the Black Reichswehr attempted a putsch by seizing several forts near Küstrin. This coup attempt was part of a broader reaction against the Weimar Republic and highlighted the political instability in post-World War I Germany.
events.name: Küstrin Putsch

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1923, the Johor–Singapore Causeway was opened to public traffic, establishing a vital link between Malaysia and Singapore. This infrastructure development facilitated trade and movement between the two regions, significantly impacting their economies.

image.caption: The Johor–Singapore Causeway, photographed by Rainer Halama.
image.credit: Rainer Halama — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photograph of the causeway in 1973–74, decades after its 1923 opening; it documents the site, not the opening event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Opening of the Johor–Singapore Causeway

events.enhanced_description: On October 2, 1923, after two days of siege, Major Ernst Buchrucker and his men surrendered following the Küstrin Putsch. This event underscored the fragility of the Weimar Republic and the challenges it faced from extremist factions.
events.name: Küstrin Putsch surrender

events.enhanced_description: On October 6, 1923, the occupation of Constantinople by the Allied powers following World War I officially ended. This withdrawal marked a significant step in Turkey's transition to sovereignty and the establishment of the Republic of Turkey.
events.name: End of the Occupation of Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: On October 13, 1923, Ankara was officially declared the capital of Turkey, replacing Istanbul. This decision was part of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk's vision to modernize and centralize the new republic, reflecting a shift away from the Ottoman past.
events.name: Ankara replaces Istanbul as capital of Turkey

events.enhanced_description: On October 14, 1923, the fourth tropical storm of the year formed just north of Panama, contributing to the active Atlantic hurricane season. This storm was part of a series of weather events that affected the Caribbean and Gulf regions.
events.name: Formation of tropical storms

events.enhanced_description: On October 15, 1923, the fifth tropical storm of the Atlantic hurricane season formed north of the Leeward Islands. This storm added to the already active weather patterns affecting the region during this period.
events.name: Formation of the fifth tropical storm

events.enhanced_description: On October 16, 1923, a sixth tropical storm developed in the Gulf of Mexico, marking a rare occurrence where four active tropical storms were present simultaneously in the Atlantic basin. This unusual weather pattern raised concerns for coastal communities.
events.name: Sixth tropical storm develops in the Gulf of Mexico

events.enhanced_description: On October 23, 1923, the Hamburg Uprising occurred as Communists attempted a putsch in Hamburg, leading to violent street battles that lasted for two days. The uprising ultimately failed, reflecting the intense political strife in Germany during the Weimar Republic.
events.name: Hamburg Uprising

events.enhanced_description: On October 27, 1923, General Hans von Seeckt ordered the dissolution of the Social Democratic-Communist government of Saxony, which was resisting the authority of the Reich government. This action exemplified the increasing tensions between the military and civilian governments in post-war Germany.
events.name: Dissolution of the Saxony government

events.enhanced_description: On October 28, 1923, Reza Khan was appointed as prime minister of Persia under Ahmad Shah Qajar. This appointment marked the beginning of Reza Khan's rise to power, which would culminate in the establishment of the Pahlavi dynasty.
events.name: Reza Khan becomes prime minister

events.enhanced_description: On October 29, 1923, Turkey was officially declared a republic, marking the end of the Ottoman Empire. Mustafa Kemal Atatürk was elected as the first president, initiating a series of reforms aimed at modernizing the nation.
events.name: Turkey becomes a republic

events.enhanced_description: On October 30, 1923, İsmet İnönü was appointed as the first prime minister of the newly established Republic of Turkey. His leadership would play a crucial role in shaping the early years of the republic and implementing Atatürk's reforms.
events.name: İsmet İnönü appointed as prime minister

events.enhanced_description: In November 1923, Aero oy was established as the Finnish flag carrier airline, which would later be known as Finnair. This marked the beginning of commercial aviation in Finland, connecting the country to international destinations.
events.name: The Finnish flag carrier airline Finnair is started

events.enhanced_description: On November 8, 1923, Adolf Hitler led the Nazis in the Beer Hall Putsch, an unsuccessful coup attempt to overthrow the Bavarian government in Munich. The attempt was swiftly crushed by police and military forces, resulting in the deaths of 20 individuals.
events.name: Beer Hall Putsch

events.enhanced_description: Following the failed Beer Hall Putsch, Adolf Hitler was arrested on November 11, 1923, for his role in the coup attempt. His arrest would later lead to a trial that garnered significant public attention and provided a platform for his political ideology.
events.name: Adolf Hitler is arrested for his leading role in the Beer Hall Putsch

events.enhanced_description: On November 12, 1923, Princess Maud of Fife married Captain Charles Alexander Carnegie at Wellington Barracks in London. This royal union was celebrated in the British press and marked a significant event in the British royal family.
events.name: Princess Maud of Fife marries Captain Charles Alexander Carnegie

events.enhanced_description: In November 1923, hyperinflation in the Weimar Republic reached its peak, with the exchange rate soaring to 4.2 trillion Papiermark for one US dollar. Chancellor Gustav Stresemann introduced the Rentenmark to stabilize the economy, marking a pivotal moment in German financial history.

image.caption: Front of a 500,000-mark Leipzig banknote.
image.credit: Leipzig — scanned NobbiP
image.date_qualification: A 1923 banknote associated with the hyperinflation period; the saved image date is 2007-08 and is not the depicted date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Hyperinflation in the Weimar Republic reaches its height

events.enhanced_description: On November 23, 1923, the coalition government led by Gustav Stresemann collapsed amid the ongoing economic crisis in Germany. This political instability further complicated the challenges facing the Weimar Republic during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Gustav Stresemann's coalition government collapses in Germany

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1923, the Gleno Dam on the Gleno River in the Valle di Scalve, Bergamo, Italy, burst, resulting in a catastrophic flood that killed at least 356 people. This disaster highlighted the need for improved safety measures in dam construction and maintenance.

image.caption: Gleno Dam in Italy.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Book: "Il disastro del Gleno"
image.date_qualification: Image date stated as 1923; depicts the dam, but the evidence does not establish whether it was photographed before or after the collapse.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Gleno Dam bursts in Italy

events.enhanced_description: The 1923 United Kingdom general election, held on December 6, resulted in the governing Conservative Party, led by Stanley Baldwin, losing its majority status. This election marked a significant shift in British politics, with the Labour Party gaining ground as the second-largest party.
events.name: 1923 United Kingdom general election

events.enhanced_description: On December 21, 1923, the Nepal–Britain Treaty was signed, marking the first formal recognition of Nepal as an independent sovereign country. This treaty established diplomatic relations between Nepal and the British Empire, shaping the future of Nepal's foreign relations.
events.name: Nepal–Britain Treaty defines Nepal's international status

events.enhanced_description: On December 27, 1923, Crown Prince Hirohito of Japan survived an assassination attempt by communist student Daisuke Nanba in Tokyo. This incident raised concerns about political extremism in Japan and highlighted the tensions of the era.
events.name: Toranomon Incident: Assassination attempt on Crown Prince Hirohito

events.enhanced_description: On December 29, 1923, inventor Vladimir K. Zworykin filed his first patent in the United States for 'television systems.' This patent was a crucial step in the development of television technology, which would revolutionize communication and entertainment.
events.name: Vladimir K. Zworykin files patent for television systems

events.enhanced_description: The first revenue flight for Belgium's Sabena Airlines took place in 1924, marking the beginning of commercial aviation services in Belgium. This event contributed to the growth of air travel in Europe.
events.name: First revenue flight for Sabena Airlines

events.enhanced_description: In 1924, authorities of the British Raj arrested prominent Indian nationalist leader Subhas Chandra Bose, leading to his imprisonment for over two years. His arrest was part of the British efforts to suppress the growing independence movement in India.
events.name: Authorities of the British Raj arrest Subhas Chandra Bose

events.enhanced_description: The final raid of the Renegade period of the Apache Wars marked the end of a prolonged conflict between the United States and various Apache tribes. This event symbolized the conclusion of the American Indian Wars, which spanned over three centuries.
events.name: Final raid of the Renegade period of the Apache Wars

events.enhanced_description: In 1924, Iraq officially abolished slavery, marking a significant step towards modern human rights in the region. This decision was part of broader reforms in the post-Ottoman state as it sought to establish a new national identity.
events.name: Abolition of Slavery in Iraq

events.enhanced_description: The International Union of Official Organizations for Tourist Propaganda was established in 1924 to promote tourism and cultural exchange among nations. This organization aimed to enhance international cooperation in the tourism sector.
events.name: Establishment of the International Union of Official Organizations for Tourist Propaganda

events.enhanced_description: In 1924, Earl W. Bascom, a rodeo cowboy and artist, designed the first one-hand bareback rigging, revolutionizing rodeo equipment. This innovation significantly impacted the sport, enhancing both safety and performance.
events.name: Earl W. Bascom designs rodeo's first one-hand bareback rigging

events.enhanced_description: The League of Nations established the Temporary Slavery Commission in 1924 to address and combat slavery and forced labor globally. This initiative represented an early international effort to promote human rights.
events.name: Creation of the Temporary Slavery Commission by the League of Nations

events.enhanced_description: The first Winter Olympics were held in Chamonix, France, marking a significant milestone in the history of winter sports. This inaugural event featured athletes from 16 nations competing in various winter sports disciplines.
events.name: The first Winter Olympics

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1924, Petrograd was officially renamed Leningrad in honor of the deceased leader of the Bolshevik Revolution, Vladimir Lenin. This change reflected the political climate of the time and the influence of the Soviet regime.
events.name: Renaming of Petrograd to Leningrad

events.enhanced_description: On February 1, 1924, the United Kingdom formally recognized the Soviet Union, marking a significant shift in international relations following the Russian Revolution. This recognition was part of a broader effort to establish diplomatic ties with the new communist government.
events.name: Recognition of the Soviet Union by the United Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: On February 5, 1924, the Royal Greenwich Observatory broadcast the first radio time signal, revolutionizing timekeeping and synchronization across the globe. This innovation laid the groundwork for modern timekeeping practices.
events.name: First radio time signal broadcast

events.enhanced_description: On February 14, 1924, the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company (CTR) was renamed International Business Machines (IBM), marking a pivotal moment in the history of computing and business technology. This rebranding reflected the company's expanding focus on international markets and innovation.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Renaming of CTR to IBM

events.enhanced_description: On February 22, 1924, the Treaty of Rome was signed, resulting in the annexation of the Free State of Fiume by the Kingdom of Italy and the absorption of Sušak by the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes. This treaty was part of the post-World War I territorial adjustments in Europe.

image.caption: Map of the territory of the Free State of Fiume, with colored areas indicating territorial boundaries.
image.credit: No machine-readable author provided. Decius assumed (based on copyright claims). — Kirchner Reill, Dominique (2020) The Fiume Crisis: Life in the Wake of the Habsburg Empire , Cambridge, Massachusetts : Harvard University Press , pp. xii ISBN : 9780674244245 .
image.date_qualification: Map illustrating the territory connected with the Treaty of Rome; it is not a contemporary photograph of the signing. Image date: 2006-07-28.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Treaty of Rome

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1924, the Ottoman Caliphate was officially abolished, marking the end of a significant institution in Islamic governance. This event was part of the broader reforms initiated by Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, aimed at modernizing Turkey and separating religion from state affairs.
events.name: End of the Ottoman Caliphate

events.enhanced_description: On March 6, 1924, İsmet İnönü formed a new government in Turkey, succeeding the previous administration. His leadership was pivotal in navigating the early years of the Republic of Turkey following the abolition of the Ottoman Caliphate.
events.name: İsmet İnönü forms new government in Turkey

events.enhanced_description: On March 15, 1924, Horacio Vásquez won the general election in the Dominican Republic, marking the end of the United States military occupation that had begun in 1916. His presidency signified a return to national sovereignty.

locations.name: Santo Domingo, Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic

events.name: Horacio Vásquez wins Dominican Republic election

events.enhanced_description: On March 24, 1924, Finnish composer Jean Sibelius conducted the world premiere of his Symphony No. 7 in Stockholm, showcasing his innovative approach to symphonic form. This work is considered one of his most significant compositions.
events.name: World premiere of Sibelius's Symphony No. 7

events.enhanced_description: On March 25, 1924, the Second Hellenic Republic was proclaimed in Greece, following the abolition of the monarchy. This marked a significant shift in the political landscape of the country, emphasizing democratic governance.
events.name: Proclamation of the Second Hellenic Republic

events.enhanced_description: On March 29, 1924, Raymond Poincaré began his third ministry in France, navigating the complexities of post-World War I politics and economic challenges. His leadership was characterized by efforts to stabilize the French economy.
events.name: Formation of the Third Ministry of Raymond Poincaré

events.enhanced_description: On April 1, 1924, Adolf Hitler was sentenced to five years in Landsberg Prison for his role in the failed Beer Hall Putsch of 1923. He ultimately served less than nine months, during which he wrote 'Mein Kampf,' outlining his political ideology.
events.name: Adolf Hitler sentenced to Landsberg Prison

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 1924, Alexandra David-Néel, a Francophone explorer and former operatic soprano, disguised herself as a male pilgrim and spent two months in the forbidden city of Lhasa, Tibet. Her journey provided valuable insights into Tibetan culture and Buddhism, challenging Western perceptions of the region.
events.name: Francophone explorer Alexandra David-Néel's stay in Lhasa

events.enhanced_description: On April 6, 1924, the Italian general election resulted in a significant victory for the Fascist Party, led by Benito Mussolini, who secured a two-thirds majority. This election solidified Mussolini's power and marked a turning point in Italian politics.
events.name: Italian general election, 1924

events.enhanced_description: On April 13, 1924, a referendum in Greece favored the establishment of the Second Hellenic Republic, leading to the formal abolition of the monarchy. This event was pivotal in shaping modern Greek governance.
events.name: Greek republic referendum

events.enhanced_description: On April 17, 1924, the merger of Metro Pictures Corporation, Goldwyn Pictures, and Louis B. Mayer Productions resulted in the creation of Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer (MGM), which would become one of the most iconic film studios in Hollywood history.
events.name: Formation of Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer

events.enhanced_description: On April 23, 1924, the British Empire Exhibition opened in London, showcasing the achievements and cultures of 58 countries within the British Empire. This grand exhibition aimed to promote unity and cooperation among the empire's nations.

image.caption: Malta Pavilion at the British Empire Exhibition in Wembley, London.
image.credit: Campbell-Gray — Agius WW1 ; cf. [1] p. 13; cf. also this postcard: [2]
image.date_qualification: Dated 1924; the source does not give a more specific date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: British Empire Exhibition opens

events.enhanced_description: The opening ceremonies of the 1924 Summer Olympics were held in Paris on May 4, 1924, showcasing the spirit of international competition and athleticism. This event was notable for its grand scale and the participation of numerous countries.

image.caption: Map of the 1924 Summer Olympics in Paris.
image.credit: Shakki — self-made using p.73 of 1924 Summer Olympics official report and Image:Paris and inner ring.svg
image.date_qualification: Map depicting the Games, not a photograph of the opening ceremony. Image date: 2008-01.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Opening ceremonies of the 1924 Summer Olympics

events.enhanced_description: On May 8, 1924, Lithuania signed the Klaipėda Convention, which transferred the Klaipėda Region from East Prussia to Lithuania, granting it autonomous status. This agreement was significant for Lithuania's territorial integrity and national identity.
events.name: Klaipėda Convention signed

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1924, J. Edgar Hoover was appointed as the head of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), a position he would hold for nearly five decades. His leadership significantly shaped the agency's direction and its role in American law enforcement.
events.name: J. Edgar Hoover appointed head of FBI

events.enhanced_description: On May 11, 1924, the merging of companies owned by Gottlieb Daimler and Karl Benz led to the formation of Mercedes-Benz, a brand that would become synonymous with luxury and innovation in the automotive industry.
events.name: Formation of Mercedes-Benz

events.enhanced_description: Harry Grindell Matthews, an inventor, attempted to demonstrate his controversial 'death ray' to officials at the War Office in London. This event highlighted the intersection of science and military interest during the interwar period.
events.name: Harry Grindell Matthews attempts to demonstrate his "death ray"

events.enhanced_description: Italian socialist leader Giacomo Matteotti delivered a powerful speech denouncing the rise of Fascism in Italy. Just days later, he was kidnapped and murdered, an event that sparked outrage and highlighted the violent suppression of dissent under Mussolini's regime.
events.name: Giacomo Matteotti speaks out against Fascism

events.enhanced_description: U.S. President Calvin Coolidge signed the Indian Citizenship Act, which granted citizenship to all Native Americans born within the territorial limits of the United States. This landmark legislation was a significant step towards recognizing the rights of Indigenous peoples.
events.name: Indian Citizenship Act signed into law

events.enhanced_description: Ernst Alexanderson successfully sent the first facsimile transmission across the Atlantic Ocean from Schenectady, New York, to his father in Gothenburg, Sweden. This event marked a significant advancement in communication technology.
events.name: First facsimile sent across the Atlantic

events.enhanced_description: Rudolf Steiner delivered his influential Agriculture Course at Koberwitz, which laid the foundation for the organic agriculture movement. His teachings emphasized the importance of holistic farming practices and the connection between agriculture and spirituality.
events.name: Rudolf Steiner delivers Agriculture Course

events.enhanced_description: Mountaineers George Mallory and Andrew Irvine were last seen by teammate Noel Odell as they ascended Mount Everest, reportedly 'going strong for the top.' Their disappearance during this historic expedition remains one of the great mysteries of mountaineering.
events.name: George Mallory and Andrew Irvine last seen on Mount Everest

events.enhanced_description: The 'Wildkansas' tornado struck Hungary, causing widespread devastation over a path of 70 kilometers. With a width of 500 to 1500 meters, it completely destroyed the village of Páty, resulting in 9 fatalities and numerous injuries.
events.name: Wildkansas tornado strikes Hungary

events.enhanced_description: The Fédération Internationale des Échecs (FIDE) was founded in Paris, establishing an international governing body for chess. This organization has since played a crucial role in promoting and regulating chess competitions worldwide.
events.name: FIDE founded

events.enhanced_description: J. B. M. Hertzog was appointed as the third Prime Minister of South Africa, leading the country during a period marked by significant political changes and the consolidation of Afrikaner nationalism.
events.name: J. B. M. Hertzog becomes Prime Minister of South Africa

events.enhanced_description: Finnish athlete Paavo Nurmi achieved a remarkable feat at the Paris Olympics by winning both the 1,500 and 5,000 meter races within two hours. His extraordinary performance solidified his status as one of the greatest middle-distance runners in Olympic history.
events.name: Paavo Nurmi wins at the Paris Olympics

events.enhanced_description: The United States occupation of the Dominican Republic, which began in 1916, officially ended, leading to the establishment of a constitutional government under General Horacio Vázquez. This marked a significant shift in U.S.-Dominican relations.
events.name: End of U.S. occupation of the Dominican Republic

events.enhanced_description: The Napalpí massacre occurred in Argentina, where around 400 indigenous Toba people were killed in a brutal act of violence. This tragic event highlighted the severe repression faced by indigenous communities in the region.
events.name: Napalpí massacre

events.enhanced_description: The Dawes Plan was signed in Paris, providing a new framework for the payment of reparations by Germany following World War I. This agreement aimed to stabilize the German economy and improve international relations.
events.name: Dawes Plan signed

events.enhanced_description: The August Uprising in Georgia was a rebellion against Soviet rule that resulted in the deaths of several thousand people. This failed uprising underscored the tensions and struggles for independence within the Soviet Union.
events.name: August Uprising in Georgia

events.enhanced_description: The Hanapepe massacre occurred in Hanapepe, Hawaii, where tensions between local labor unions and law enforcement escalated into violence. This tragic event highlighted the struggles faced by workers in the early 20th century.
events.name: Hanapepe massacre

events.enhanced_description: The Kohat riots broke out in Kohat, India, reflecting the ethnic and communal tensions prevalent during the British colonial period. The riots resulted in significant violence and unrest in the region.
events.name: Kohat riots

events.enhanced_description: On September 25, 1924, Malcolm Campbell set a new land speed record at Pendine Sands in Wales, achieving a speed of 146.16 mph. This event marked a significant milestone in automotive history and showcased the advancements in engineering and speed.
events.name: 1924 land speed record at Pendine Sands

events.enhanced_description: U.S. Army pilots John Harding and Erik Nelson completed the first aerial circumnavigation of the globe, a journey that took 175 days and included 74 stops. Their achievement marked a significant milestone in aviation history.
events.name: First aerial circumnavigation of the globe

events.enhanced_description: Australia passed the Commonwealth Electoral (Compulsory Voting) Act 1924, making voting in federal elections compulsory. This legislation was championed by Tasmanian Nationalist senator Herbert Payne and marked a significant development in Australian democracy.
events.name: Compulsory voting in Australia

events.enhanced_description: The Zeppelin LZ-126 made a significant transatlantic delivery flight from Friedrichshafen, Germany, to Lakehurst, New Jersey. This flight was part of the post-World War I reparations and showcased the potential of airship travel.
events.name: Zeppelin LZ-126 transatlantic delivery flight

events.enhanced_description: On October 15, 1924, André Breton published the first Surrealist Manifesto in Paris, defining the movement as 'pure psychic automatism'. This manifesto laid the groundwork for Surrealism, influencing artists and writers to explore the unconscious mind and dream imagery.
events.name: The first Surrealist Manifesto is published

events.enhanced_description: On October 18, 1924, Hjalmar Branting took office as Prime Minister of Sweden, succeeding Ernst Trygger. This marked Branting's third and final government, reflecting the shifting political landscape in Sweden during the interwar period.
events.name: Sweden's Prime Minister Ernst Trygger replaced by Hjalmar Branting

events.enhanced_description: On October 19, 1924, Abdul Aziz Ibn Saud, the founder of modern Saudi Arabia, declared himself the protector of the holy places in Mecca. This declaration solidified his authority and the significance of Mecca in the Islamic world.

image.caption: Official portrait of King Abdulaziz, founder of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.
image.credit: Saudi Press Agency
image.date_qualification: Portrait from the 1940s, well after the 1924 declaration; it is contextual, not a depiction of the event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Abdul Aziz declares himself protector of holy places

events.enhanced_description: On October 25, 1924, the British press published the Zinoviev letter, which was purportedly a directive from Grigory Zinoviev, head of the Communist International, to the Communist Party of Great Britain. The letter had significant political implications, influencing public opinion against the Labour Party.
events.name: The British press publishes the Zinoviev letter

events.enhanced_description: On October 27, 1924, the Uzbek SSR was officially incorporated into the Soviet Union, marking a significant step in the consolidation of Soviet power in Central Asia. This event was part of the broader process of establishing Soviet republics in the region.
events.name: The Uzbek SSR joins the Soviet Union

events.enhanced_description: In November 1924, Colonel John R. White recorded the last known sighting of a California grizzly bear in Sequoia National Park. This event marked the decline of the species, which was declared extinct shortly thereafter.

locations.name: Sequoia National Park, California, United States

events.name: The last known sighting of a California grizzly bear

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1924, Nellie Tayloe Ross was elected as the first woman governor in the United States, representing Wyoming. Her election was a significant milestone in the women's suffrage movement and set a precedent for future female political leaders.
events.name: Nellie Tayloe Ross elected as the first woman governor in the United States

events.enhanced_description: On November 10, 1924, the Trial of the 149 commenced in Estonia, targeting communists and resulting in the conviction of 129 individuals, including several members of the Riigikogu. This trial reflected the political tensions and repressive measures against leftist movements in Estonia.
events.name: The Trial of the 149 begins in Estonia

events.enhanced_description: On November 19, 1924, Major-General Sir Lee Stack, the British Governor-General of the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan, was shot in Cairo by Egyptian nationalist students. He succumbed to his injuries the following day, escalating tensions between British authorities and Egyptian nationalists.
events.name: Major-General Sir Lee Stack is shot in Cairo

events.enhanced_description: On November 21, 1924, Ali Fethi Okyar formed a new government in Turkey, marking his third term in office. This government was part of the ongoing political restructuring in the early years of the Turkish Republic.
events.name: Ali Fethi Okyar forms a new government in Turkey

events.enhanced_description: On November 26, 1924, the Mongolian People's Republic was proclaimed, establishing a socialist state in Mongolia. This event marked a significant shift in the region's political landscape, aligning Mongolia more closely with the Soviet Union.

image.caption: Orthographic projection map of the Mongolian People's Republic.
image.credit: Elevatorrailfan — This vector image includes elements that have been taken or adapted from this file:
image.date_qualification: Map created 2015-02-05; it does not depict the 1924 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: The Mongolian People's Republic is proclaimed

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1924, a Soviet-backed communist coup d'état attempt failed in Estonia, highlighting the tensions between the government and leftist factions. The failure of this coup was significant in maintaining the independence of Estonia during a turbulent period.
events.name: A Soviet-backed communist coup d'état attempt fails in Estonia

events.enhanced_description: On December 19, 1924, Fritz Haarmann, a notorious German serial killer, was sentenced to death for the murder and dismemberment of at least 24 young males in Hanover. His crimes shocked the nation and highlighted issues of crime and justice in Weimar Germany.
events.name: German serial killer Fritz Haarmann is sentenced to death

events.enhanced_description: On December 20, 1924, Adolf Hitler was released from Landsberg Prison after serving nine months for his role in the Beer Hall Putsch of 1923. His release marked a pivotal moment in his political career, allowing him to re-enter the political arena in Germany.
events.name: Adolf Hitler is released from Landsberg Prison

events.enhanced_description: On December 24, 1924, an Imperial Airways de Havilland DH.34 crashed shortly after takeoff from Croydon Airport, killing all eight people aboard. This tragic incident led to the first public inquiry into a civil aviation accident in the United Kingdom.

locations.name: Croydon, Greater London, England, United Kingdom

events.name: Imperial Airways de Havilland DH.34 crash

events.enhanced_description: On December 30, 1924, American astronomer Edwin Hubble announced that Andromeda, previously thought to be a nebula, is actually another galaxy. This groundbreaking discovery expanded our understanding of the universe and established Hubble as a key figure in modern astronomy.

locations.name: Mount Wilson Observatory, California, United States

events.name: Edwin Hubble announces Andromeda is a galaxy

events.enhanced_description: The Franc affair, which emerged in 1925, involved a conspiracy by Hungarian nationalists to forge French bank notes. This plot highlighted the tensions and political intrigue in post-World War I Europe, particularly concerning national identity and economic stability.
events.name: Franc affair

events.enhanced_description: In 1925, the Syrian Federation was officially dissolved, leading to the establishment of the State of Syria. This political change was part of the broader reorganization of territories in the Middle East following World War I.
events.name: Dissolution of the Syrian Federation

events.enhanced_description: In 1925, Frank Heath embarked on an ambitious two-year journey across the United States on horseback, aiming to visit all 48 states. His journey not only showcased the spirit of adventure but also highlighted the changing landscapes and cultures of America during the Roaring Twenties.
events.name: Frank Heath's journey

events.enhanced_description: In 1925, the United States Patent and Trademark Office was transferred to the Department of Commerce, reflecting a shift in the government's approach to intellectual property and commerce. This move aimed to streamline operations and enhance the protection of inventions and trademarks.
events.name: Transfer of the Patent and Trademark Office

events.enhanced_description: In 1925, Barcelona Sporting Club was founded in Guayaquil, Ecuador, becoming one of the most successful and popular football clubs in the country. The club has since played a significant role in Ecuadorian sports culture and has a passionate fanbase.
events.name: Founding of Barcelona S.C.

events.enhanced_description: The All-China Federation of Trade Unions was founded in 1925 in Guangzhou, becoming the largest trade union organization in the world. This organization played a crucial role in advocating for workers' rights and labor reforms in China during a time of significant social and political change.
events.name: Founding of All-China Federation of Trade Unions

events.enhanced_description: In 1925, Göztepe S.K., a prominent Turkish sports club, was founded in Izmir, Turkey. The club has since become known for its achievements in various sports, particularly football, and has a dedicated fanbase.
events.name: Founding of Göztepe S.K.

events.enhanced_description: The Temporary Slavery Commission of the League of Nations submitted a comprehensive report on global slavery and the slave trade, which laid the groundwork for the 1926 Slavery Convention. This report highlighted the urgent need for international cooperation to combat slavery.
events.name: The Temporary Slavery Commission of the League of Nations files their report

events.enhanced_description: The first Surrealist art exhibition opened in Paris in 1925, showcasing works that challenged conventional artistic norms and explored the unconscious mind. This exhibition played a pivotal role in the development of the Surrealist movement.
events.name: The first Surrealist art exhibition opens in Paris

events.enhanced_description: In 1925, New York City surpassed London to become the largest city in the world, a status it has maintained since. This shift reflected the rapid growth of the city due to immigration, industrialization, and urbanization during the early 20th century.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: New York City becomes the largest city

events.enhanced_description: In 1925, President Mustafa Kemal Atatürk ordered the closure of Islamic Bektashi Order lodges in Turkey, leading to a significant shift in the religious landscape. The leadership of the order subsequently relocated to Albania, reflecting the broader secular reforms implemented by Atatürk.
events.name: Closure of Bektashi Order lodges

events.enhanced_description: In 1925, Lion Feuchtwanger's novel Jud Süß was published in Germany. The book, which explores themes of anti-Semitism and Jewish identity, became a significant work in German literature and was later adapted into a controversial film during the Nazi regime.
events.name: Publication of Jud Süß

events.enhanced_description: In 1925, Ernest Blythe, the Minister for Finance in the Irish Free State, arranged for an annual government subsidy of £850 for the Abbey Theatre in Dublin. This funding made the Abbey Theatre the first state-supported theatre in the English-speaking world, highlighting the importance of the arts in Irish society.
events.name: Abbey Theatre subsidy

events.enhanced_description: On January 3, 1925, Benito Mussolini delivered a pivotal speech in the Italian Chamber of Deputies, which is regarded as the beginning of his dictatorship. This speech marked a significant turning point in Italian politics, consolidating Mussolini's power.
events.name: Benito Mussolini's pivotal speech in the Italian Chamber of Deputies

events.enhanced_description: On January 5, 1925, Nellie Tayloe Ross was inaugurated as the first female governor in the United States, representing Wyoming. Her election marked a significant milestone in women's political participation in the country.
events.name: Nellie Tayloe Ross becomes the first female governor in the United States

events.enhanced_description: On February 1, 1925, the Great Race of Mercy, also known as the 1925 serum run to Nome, commenced to deliver diphtheria antitoxin by dog sled across Alaska. This heroic effort was crucial in combating a diphtheria epidemic threatening the town of Nome.
events.name: The 1925 serum run to Nome

events.enhanced_description: On February 25, 1925, Art Gillham recorded the first Western Electric masters to be commercially released, marking a significant advancement in the recording industry. This event contributed to the evolution of sound recording technology.
events.name: Art Gillham records first Western Electric masters

events.enhanced_description: On February 28, 1925, the Charlevoix–Kamouraska earthquake struck northeastern North America, causing significant damage and loss of life. This earthquake was one of the most powerful in Canadian history.
events.name: The 1925 Charlevoix–Kamouraska earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1925, the New York City Fire Department Rescue 2 was put into service in Brooklyn, enhancing the city's emergency response capabilities. This addition marked a significant development in urban firefighting services.
events.name: New York City Fire Department Rescue 2 is put in service

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1925, İsmet İnönü was appointed Prime Minister of Turkey, marking a significant moment in the early republican era. His leadership was pivotal in shaping modern Turkey's political landscape.

image.caption: Official portrait of İsmet İnönü.
image.credit: Unknown. Official photo of President. — http://www.tccb.gov.tr/sayfa/cumhurbaskanlarimiz/ismet_inonu/
image.date_qualification: 1938; later than the 4 March 1925 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: İsmet İnönü appointed Prime Minister of Turkey

events.enhanced_description: On March 6, 1925, Pionerskaya Pravda, one of the oldest children's newspapers in Europe, was founded in the Soviet Union. This publication aimed to educate and inform young readers about the ideals of communism.
events.name: Pionerskaya Pravda founded in the Soviet Union

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1925, during Pink's War, the British Royal Air Force bombarded the mountain strongholds of the Mahsud tribesmen in South Waziristan. This military action was part of the British efforts to maintain control over the region.
events.name: Pink's War: RAF bombards Mahsud tribesmen

events.enhanced_description: On March 15, 1925, the Phi Lambda Chi fraternity, originally named 'The Aztecs,' was founded on the campus of Arkansas State Teachers' College in Conway, Arkansas. This fraternity aimed to foster brotherhood and academic excellence among its members.
events.name: Founding of Phi Lambda Chi fraternity

events.enhanced_description: On March 18, 1925, the Tri-State Tornado, the deadliest in U.S. history, tore through Missouri, Illinois, and Indiana, killing 695 people and injuring over 2,000. This catastrophic event remains one of the most devastating tornadoes recorded.
events.name: Tri-State Tornado

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1925, the Bauhaus school closed its doors in Weimar and relocated to a new building in Dessau designed by Walter Gropius. This move marked a significant moment in the history of modern architecture and design.
events.name: Closure of the Bauhaus in Weimar

events.enhanced_description: Fritz Haarmann, known as the 'Butcher of Hanover', was executed by guillotine for the murder of 24 boys and young men, a series of crimes that shocked Germany in the early 20th century. His heinous acts and subsequent trial highlighted the social issues and fears surrounding crime in post-World War I Germany.
events.name: Fritz Haarmann's execution

events.enhanced_description: On April 16, 1925, a devastating communist assault on St Nedelya Church in Sofia resulted in the deaths of approximately 150 people. This tragic event underscored the violent political climate in Bulgaria during the interwar period, marked by conflict between various ideological factions.
events.name: St Nedelya Church attack

events.enhanced_description: Colo-Colo, one of the most famous football clubs in Chile, was founded in Macul, a suburb of Santiago, on April 19, 1925. The club has since become a symbol of Chilean football, known for its passionate fanbase and significant contributions to the sport in the country.
events.name: Founding of Colo-Colo

events.enhanced_description: On April 20, 1925, Iranian forces under Reza Shah occupied Ahvaz and arrested Sheikh Khaz'al Ibn Jabir, a prominent local leader. This event marked a significant step in Reza Shah's efforts to consolidate power and centralize authority in Iran during his reign.
events.name: Occupation of Ahvaz

events.enhanced_description: On April 28, 1925, during a budget presentation, Chancellor of the Exchequer Winston Churchill announced Britain's return to the gold standard. This decision aimed to stabilize the British economy post-World War I but faced criticism for its potential impact on economic recovery.
events.name: Winston Churchill announces return to the gold standard

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1925, King Ibn Saud ordered the destruction of the al-Baqi' mausoleums in Medina, which contained the graves of many prominent figures in early Islamic history. This act was part of a broader campaign against what he deemed un-Islamic practices, leading to significant controversy and debate within the Muslim world.

image.caption: Photograph of Jannat al-Baqi cemetery and its mausoleums.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — alnabi musium
image.date_qualification: Photograph dated to the 1910s; it predates the 1925 destruction and does not depict the demolition itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Destruction of al-Baqi' mausoleums

events.enhanced_description: On May 5, 1925, Japan passed the General Election Law, which extended suffrage to all males aged 25 and over. This law marked a significant step towards democratization in Japan, reflecting the changing political landscape of the country during the Taisho period.
events.name: General Election Law in Japan

events.enhanced_description: On May 8, 1925, African American Tom Lee heroically rescued 32 people from the sinking steamboat M.E. Norman on the Mississippi River. His brave actions earned him recognition and highlighted the themes of courage and selflessness in the face of disaster.
events.name: Tom Lee's rescue

events.enhanced_description: On May 16, 1925, the first modern performance of Claudio Monteverdi's opera 'Il ritorno d'Ulisse in patria' took place in Paris, reviving interest in early opera and showcasing the rich cultural heritage of the Baroque period. This performance marked a significant moment in the history of opera.
events.name: First modern performance of Il ritorno d'Ulisse in patria

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1925, English explorer Percy Fawcett sent a final telegram to his wife before disappearing in the Amazon rainforest. His mysterious disappearance sparked numerous expeditions and theories, contributing to his legacy as one of the most enigmatic explorers of the early 20th century.
events.name: Percy Fawcett's last telegram

events.enhanced_description: On June 6, 1925, Walter Chrysler founded the Chrysler Corporation in Detroit, Michigan, marking a significant moment in the American automotive industry. The company quickly became known for its innovative designs and engineering, contributing to the growth of the automobile market in the United States.
events.name: Founding of Chrysler Corporation

events.enhanced_description: On June 13, 1925, American engineer Charles Francis Jenkins achieved the first synchronized transmission of pictures and sound, marking a milestone in the development of television technology. This public demonstration of radiovision showcased Jenkins' pioneering work in the field and laid the groundwork for future advancements in broadcasting.
events.name: Charles Francis Jenkins' radiovision demonstration

events.enhanced_description: The Aristotle University of Thessaloniki was founded on June 14, 1925, in Thessaloniki, Greece, becoming one of the largest and most prestigious universities in the country. The institution has played a vital role in higher education and research in Greece and the Balkans.

image.caption: Aerial view of central Thessaloniki, showing Aristotle University’s campus and AHEPA Hospital.
image.credit: en:User:Salonica84 — Uploaded to en September 13 2006
image.date_qualification: The image is dated circa 2006, not to the university’s 1925 founding.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Founding of Aristotle University of Thessaloniki

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1925, a 6.8 magnitude earthquake struck Santa Barbara, California, causing widespread destruction and resulting in the deaths of 13 people. The earthquake highlighted the region's vulnerability to seismic activity and led to changes in building codes and disaster preparedness.
events.name: Santa Barbara earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On July 10, 1925, the Scopes Trial, also known as the 'Monkey Trial', took place in Dayton, Tennessee, where teacher John T. Scopes was accused of violating the Butler Act by teaching evolution. The trial became a focal point for the debate between science and religion in America, featuring prominent figures such as William Jennings Bryan and Clarence Darrow.

image.caption: Bust portrait of Clarence Darrow, photographed by Underwood & Underwood.
image.credit: Underwood & Underwood — This image is available from the United States Library of Congress 's Prints and Photographs division under the digital ID cph.3a44036 . This tag does not indicate the copyright status of the attached work. A normal copyright tag is still required. See Commons:Licensing .
image.date_qualification: Portrait of trial attorney Clarence Darrow at Dayton during the Scopes Trial; image date recorded as 1925.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Scopes Trial

events.enhanced_description: On July 10, 1925, Meher Baba, an Indian spiritual master, began a 44-year period of silence, communicating through gestures and writing. This decision was a significant aspect of his spiritual teachings and has drawn followers and interest from around the world.
events.name: Meher Baba's silence

events.enhanced_description: On July 18, 1925, Adolf Hitler published Volume 1 of his personal manifesto, 'Mein Kampf', in Munich, Germany. This book outlined his political ideology and future plans for Germany, laying the groundwork for the Nazi Party's rise to power and the subsequent events of World War II.
events.name: Publication of Mein Kampf

events.enhanced_description: On July 21, 1925, English racing motorist Malcolm Campbell became the first person to exceed 150 mph on land at Pendine Sands, Wales, driving a Sunbeam 350HP automobile. This achievement marked a significant milestone in automotive history and showcased the advancements in engineering and speed.

locations.name: Bonneville Salt Flats, Utah, United States

events.name: Malcolm Campbell's land speed record

events.enhanced_description: The Telegraph Agency of the Soviet Union, known as TASS, was established to serve as the official news agency of the Soviet government, providing news and information aligned with state policies. It played a crucial role in disseminating propaganda and shaping public perception during the Soviet era.
events.name: The Telegraph Agency of the Soviet Union (TASS) is established

events.enhanced_description: The incorporation of the New Cape Central Railway into the South African Railways marked a significant development in the railway infrastructure of South Africa, facilitating better transportation and trade across the region. This move was part of a broader effort to unify and modernize the country's rail system.
events.name: The New Cape Central Railway is incorporated into the South African Railways

events.enhanced_description: On August 8, 1925, the Ku Klux Klan held a massive parade in Washington, D.C., showcasing their influence with an estimated 30,000 to 35,000 marchers. This event highlighted the Klan's resurgence in the 1920s and its attempts to assert its presence in American society.
events.name: The Ku Klux Klan parade in Washington, D.C.

events.enhanced_description: The completion of the Hetch Hetchy Moccasin Powerhouse in California marked a significant achievement in hydroelectric power generation, providing electricity to San Francisco and surrounding areas. This facility was part of the Hetch Hetchy Project, which aimed to supply water and power to the growing city.
events.name: The original Hetch Hetchy Moccasin Powerhouse is completed

events.enhanced_description: The completion of the French evacuation from the Ruhr region in Germany marked the end of a significant chapter in post-World War I reparations and occupation. This event was part of the broader context of the Treaty of Versailles and the tensions that followed the war.
events.name: The French complete their evacuation of the Ruhr region

events.enhanced_description: Anthropologist Margaret Mead arrived in American Samoa to conduct fieldwork that would lead to her influential book 'Coming of Age in Samoa.' Her research challenged Western perceptions of adolescence and contributed significantly to the field of cultural anthropology.
events.name: Margaret Mead lands in American Samoa

events.enhanced_description: On September 3, 1925, the U.S. Navy dirigible Shenandoah tragically broke apart in a squall line near Caldwell, Ohio, resulting in the deaths of 14 crew members. This incident highlighted the dangers of airship travel during this era.
events.name: The U.S. Navy dirigible Shenandoah disaster

events.enhanced_description: On September 27, 1925, during the Feast of the Cross, a celestial cross appeared over Athens, Greece, while Greek police pursued a group of Old Calendarists. This phenomenon lasted for half an hour and was interpreted by many as a significant religious event.
events.name: Feast of the Cross celestial phenomenon

events.enhanced_description: In October 1925, the major forgery and fraud scheme orchestrated by Alves dos Reis was exposed in Portugal, revealing significant corruption within the banking system. This scandal had far-reaching implications for the Portuguese financial landscape.
events.name: Alves dos Reis forgery scandal exposed

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1925, the Mount Rushmore National Memorial was dedicated, featuring the carved faces of four U.S. presidents: George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt, and Abraham Lincoln. This monumental sculpture symbolizes American democracy and history.

locations.name: Mount Rushmore, South Dakota, United States

events.name: Mount Rushmore National Memorial is dedicated

events.enhanced_description: On October 2, 1925, John Logie Baird successfully transmitted the first television pictures with a greyscale image in London, marking a pivotal moment in the development of television technology. This achievement laid the groundwork for future advancements in broadcasting.
events.name: John Logie Baird transmits first television pictures

events.enhanced_description: On October 4, 1925, the Finnish S2 torpedo boat sank during a fierce storm near the coast of Pori in the Gulf of Bothnia, resulting in the loss of all 53 crew members aboard. This tragic event underscored the dangers faced by naval vessels in adverse weather conditions.
events.name: Finnish S2 torpedo boat disaster

events.enhanced_description: On October 5, 1925, the Locarno Treaties were negotiated, aiming to secure post-World War I territorial settlements in Europe. These agreements were significant in promoting peace and stability in the region during the interwar period.
events.name: The Locarno Treaties are negotiated

events.enhanced_description: Cubana de Aviación was founded on October 8, 1925, marking the establishment of Cuba's national airline. This company played a crucial role in the development of air travel in the Caribbean and Latin America.
events.name: Cubana de Aviación is founded

events.enhanced_description: On November 9, 1925, the Schutzstaffel (SS) was formally established as a personal bodyguard for Adolf Hitler in Germany. This organization would later evolve into one of the most powerful and feared institutions in Nazi Germany.
events.name: Foundation of the Schutzstaffel (SS)

events.enhanced_description: The 1925 Australian federal election took place on November 14, resulting in the re-election of Stanley Bruce's Nationalist/Country Coalition Government with an increased majority, defeating the Labor Party led by Matthew Charlton. This election reflected the political landscape of post-World War I Australia.

image.caption: Map showing results of the 1925 Australian federal election by electoral division.
image.credit: MsCosmicAsh — Own work
image.date_qualification: Created 2023-05-30; this is a later map of the 1925 election results, not a contemporary event photograph.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: 1925 Australian federal election

events.enhanced_description: The New Zealand and South Seas International Exhibition opened on November 17, 1925, in Dunedin, showcasing the culture, industry, and innovations of New Zealand and the South Seas. This world's fair attracted visitors from around the globe and promoted international cooperation.
events.name: New Zealand and South Seas International Exhibition opens
