events.enhanced_description: The silent film 'El Húsar de la Muerte' was released in Santiago, Chile, on November 24, 1925. This film is notable for its historical narrative and is considered one of the early examples of Chilean cinema.

image.caption: A newspaper advertisement in La Nación announcing the premiere of El Húsar de la Muerte.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — http://culturadigital.udp.cl/cms/wp-content/uploads/2018/03/LN_1925_11_24.pdf
image.date_qualification: Dated 24 November 1925; the source describes it as an advertisement published on the film's premiere date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Release of the silent film El Húsar de la Muerte

events.enhanced_description: On November 26, 1925, Prajadhipok was crowned as King of Siam, marking the beginning of his reign. His leadership would later be characterized by efforts to modernize the country and navigate the challenges of the 20th century.
events.name: Prajadhipok crowned as King of Siam

events.enhanced_description: The Grand Ole Opry, a weekly country music-variety radio program, was first broadcast on November 28, 1925, in Nashville, Tennessee, originally known as the 'WSM Barn Dance.' This program would become a cornerstone of American country music culture.
events.name: First broadcast of the Grand Ole Opry

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1925, the Locarno Treaties were signed in London, aimed at securing the post-war territorial settlement in Europe. These treaties were significant in promoting peace and stability in the region during the interwar period.
events.name: The Locarno Treaties are signed

events.enhanced_description: On December 11, 1925, Pope Pius XI promulgated the encyclical Quas primas, which established the Feast of Christ the King as a liturgical celebration. This encyclical emphasized the sovereignty of Christ over all aspects of life and was part of the Pope's efforts to address the secularization of society.
events.name: Pope Pius XI's encyclical Quas primas

events.enhanced_description: On December 12, 1925, the Milestone Mo-Tel opened in San Luis Obispo, California, marking the establishment of the first motel in the world. This innovative lodging concept provided travelers with convenient and affordable accommodations, paving the way for the modern motel industry.

locations.name: San Luis Obispo, California, United States

events.name: Opening of the first motel

events.enhanced_description: On December 15, 1925, Reza Shah was officially sworn in as the first Shah of Persia of the Pahlavi dynasty. His reign marked significant modernization efforts in Iran, including reforms in education, infrastructure, and the legal system.
events.name: Reza Shah takes the oath

events.enhanced_description: On December 25, 1925, IG Farben was formed through the merger of six major chemical companies in Germany. This conglomerate became one of the largest chemical manufacturers in the world and played a significant role in the industrialization of Germany during the interwar period.
events.name: Formation of IG Farben

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1926, Crown Prince Nguyễn Phúc Vĩnh Thụy ascended the throne as Bảo Đại, becoming the last monarch of the Nguyễn dynasty in Vietnam. His reign was marked by significant political changes and challenges during a time of colonial rule.
events.name: Crown Prince Nguyễn Phúc Vĩnh Thụy ascends the throne

events.enhanced_description: In 1926, Alan Cobham established the first commercial air route connecting the United Kingdom to South Africa, marking a significant milestone in aviation and international travel. This route facilitated greater connectivity between the two nations, paving the way for future commercial aviation developments.
events.name: The first commercial air route from the United Kingdom to South Africa is established by Alan Cobham

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1926, Henry Ford announced the implementation of the 8-hour workday and the 5-day work week for his employees, a revolutionary move that significantly improved labor conditions and influenced labor practices across the United States and beyond.
events.name: Henry Ford announced the 8-hour, 5-day work week

events.enhanced_description: In 1926, a decree was issued in Italy under Benito Mussolini's regime that prohibited women from holding public office, reflecting the authoritarian and patriarchal policies of the Fascist government during this period.
events.name: A decree in Italy bans women from holding public office

events.enhanced_description: The Fazal Mosque, the first purpose-built mosque in London and the first Ahmadiyya mosque in Britain, was completed in 1926, serving as a significant center for the Ahmadiyya Muslim community and promoting interfaith dialogue in the UK.
events.name: The Fazal Mosque is completed

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1926, the New York Philharmonic, conducted by Walter Damrosch, premiered Jean Sibelius's tone poem Tapiola. This performance marked the last major work Sibelius would publicly release for the next three decades, highlighting his evolving artistic journey.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: World premiere of Jean Sibelius's Tapiola

events.enhanced_description: Muthulakshmi Reddi made history in 1926 by becoming the first woman appointed to a legislature in India, specifically the Madras Legislative Council. Her appointment was a significant milestone in the fight for women's rights and representation in Indian politics.

image.caption: Portrait of Muthulakshmi Reddy as a medical student at Madras Medical College.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — http://www.iicdelhi.nic.in/ContentAttachments/Publications/DiaryFiles/22612January212013_IIC%20Occasional%20Publication%2044.pdf
image.date_qualification: Circa 1912, as stated in the image date; the appointment was in 1926.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Muthulakshmi Reddi appointed to Madras Legislative Council

events.enhanced_description: In 1926, archaeologist Stephen H. Langdon began excavations at Jemdet Nasr, uncovering proto-cuneiform clay tablets dating back to 3100–2900 BCE. This discovery provided valuable insights into early writing systems and the development of civilization in Mesopotamia.
events.name: Stephen H. Langdon begins excavations in Jemdet Nasr

events.enhanced_description: In 1926, phencyclidine (PCP), commonly known as angel dust, was first synthesized. Initially developed as an anesthetic, its later recreational use raised significant concerns about its safety and effects.
events.name: Phencyclidine (PCP) synthesized

events.enhanced_description: In 1926, rodeo cowboy and artist Earl W. Bascom designed and marked the first high-cut rodeo chaps in Stirling, Alberta. This innovation contributed to the evolution of rodeo attire and the culture surrounding this sport.
events.name: Earl W. Bascom designs rodeo chaps

events.enhanced_description: The International African Institute was founded in London in 1926 to promote the study of Africa and its peoples. The institute aimed to foster understanding and cooperation between Africa and the wider world through research and education.
events.name: The International African Institute founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1926, the Soviet Union's industrial output surpassed pre-World War I levels, specifically those of 1913. This achievement was a result of the rapid industrialization efforts initiated by the Bolshevik government following the revolution.
events.name: Industrial output surpasses 1913 levels in the USSR

events.enhanced_description: On January 3, 1926, Theodoros Pangalos declared himself dictator of Greece, marking a significant shift in the country's political landscape. His regime was characterized by authoritarian rule and attempts to centralize power, which ultimately led to his downfall.

image.caption: Soldiers on the streets of Athens during Theodoros Pangalos’s 1925 coup d’état.
image.credit: Agence de presse Meurisse — Bibliothèque nationale de France
image.date_qualification: Dated June 1925; this is associated with the coup, not specifically with the event dated January 3, 1926.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Theodoros Pangalos declares himself dictator

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1926, Ibn Saud was crowned as the ruler of the Kingdom of Hejaz. This event was significant in the context of the unification of the Arabian Peninsula under his leadership, which would culminate in the establishment of Saudi Arabia.
events.name: Ibn Saud crowned ruler

events.enhanced_description: On January 16, 1926, a radio play by Ronald Knox aired on the British Broadcasting Company, satirizing a workers' revolution in London. The broadcast caused panic among listeners who were unaware it was a satire, highlighting the power of media in shaping public perception.
events.name: Panic caused by BBC radio play

events.enhanced_description: On January 21, 1926, the Belgian Parliament accepted the Locarno Treaties, which aimed to secure post-World War I borders in Western Europe. This acceptance was a significant step towards stabilizing European relations and reducing the likelihood of future conflicts.
events.name: Belgian Parliament accepts Locarno Treaties

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1926, Scottish inventor John Logie Baird demonstrated a mechanical television system at his laboratory in London. This groundbreaking demonstration was a pivotal moment in the development of television technology, showcasing the potential for visual broadcasting.
events.name: John Logie Baird demonstrates television

events.enhanced_description: On January 31, 1926, British and Belgian troops withdrew from Cologne, Germany, marking the end of their occupation following World War I. This event was part of the broader process of demilitarization and normalization of relations in post-war Europe.
events.name: Troops leave Cologne

events.enhanced_description: On February 1, 1926, land on Broadway and Wall Street in New York City was sold at a record price of $7 per square inch. This sale highlighted the booming real estate market in New York during the 1920s, a period characterized by economic prosperity.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Record land sale in New York City

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1926, Kevin O'Higgins, the Irish Minister for Justice, appointed the Committee on Evil Literature. This committee was tasked with reviewing and regulating literature deemed harmful or immoral, reflecting the cultural tensions in post-independence Ireland.
events.name: Committee on Evil Literature appointed

events.enhanced_description: On February 20, 1926, the Berlin International Green Week debuted, becoming an important agricultural and food fair in Germany. This event has continued annually, showcasing innovations in agriculture and food production.
events.name: Berlin International Green Week debuts

events.enhanced_description: On February 25, 1926, Francisco Franco was promoted to General in Spain. This promotion would later play a crucial role in his rise to power during the Spanish Civil War and the establishment of his dictatorship.
events.name: Francisco Franco becomes General

events.enhanced_description: On March 6, 1926, the Shakespeare Memorial Theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon was destroyed by fire. This theatre was a significant cultural landmark dedicated to the works of William Shakespeare, and its loss was deeply felt in the arts community.
events.name: Shakespeare Memorial Theatre destroyed by fire

events.enhanced_description: On March 14, 1926, the El Virilla train accident occurred in Costa Rica, resulting in the deaths of 248 people and injuring 93 others. This tragic event highlighted the safety issues surrounding rail travel in the region.
events.name: El Virilla train accident

events.enhanced_description: On March 16, 1926, Robert H. Goddard successfully launched the first liquid-fuel rocket in Auburn, Massachusetts. This groundbreaking achievement laid the foundation for modern rocketry and space exploration.
events.name: Robert H. Goddard launches liquid-fuel rocket

events.enhanced_description: On March 23, 1926, Éamon de Valera organized the political party Fianna Fáil in Ireland. This party would become one of the dominant political forces in the country, shaping Irish politics for decades.
events.name: Éamon de Valera organizes Fianna Fáil

events.enhanced_description: The Haidbauer incident on April 1, 1926, involved the physical assault of a child by philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein in Otterthal, Austria. This incident raised questions about Wittgenstein's character and the philosophical implications of his actions.
events.name: Haidbauer incident

events.enhanced_description: On April 4, 1926, Theodoros Pangalos won the Greek presidential election with an overwhelming 93.3% of the vote. The election was characterized by low voter turnout, as many viewed the outcome as predetermined due to the political climate of the time.
events.name: Greek presidential election won by Theodoros Pangalos

events.enhanced_description: On April 6, 1926, Aarón Joaquín experienced a vision in Nuevo León, Mexico, which led to the founding of La Luz del Mundo, a nontrinitarian charismatic restorationist Christian church. This event marked a significant moment in the religious landscape of Mexico.
events.name: Vision of Aarón Joaquín in Nuevo León

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1926, an assassination attempt against Italian Fascist leader Benito Mussolini failed, highlighting the growing tensions and opposition to his regime. This incident underscored the volatile political climate in Italy during the 1920s.
events.name: Assassination attempt against Benito Mussolini

events.enhanced_description: On April 17, 1926, Zhang Zuolin's army successfully captured Beijing, marking a significant moment in the power struggles during the Warlord Era in China. This event contributed to the ongoing conflicts that characterized Chinese politics in the early 20th century.
events.name: Zhang Zuolin's army captures Beijing

events.enhanced_description: On April 25, 1926, Reza Khan was crowned Shah of Iran, adopting the name Pahlavi. This event marked the formal establishment of the Pahlavi dynasty, which would significantly influence Iran's political landscape for decades.
events.name: Reza Khan crowned Shah of Iran

events.enhanced_description: On May 4, 1926, the United Kingdom general strike commenced at midnight, initiated in support of striking coal miners. This nationwide labor action was one of the largest in British history, reflecting the intense class struggles of the time.
events.name: United Kingdom general strike begins

events.enhanced_description: On May 9, 1926, following the general strike that began on May 4, martial law was declared in the United Kingdom. This drastic measure was taken to restore order amidst the widespread unrest and labor disputes.
events.name: Martial law declared in the United Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1926, planes piloted by Major Harold Geiger and Horace Meek Hickam collided in mid-air at Langley Field, Virginia. This incident highlighted the risks associated with early aviation training and operations.
events.name: Mid-air collision at Langley Field

events.enhanced_description: On May 12, 1926, Roald Amundsen and his crew successfully flew over the North Pole in the airship Norge. This achievement marked a significant milestone in the history of polar exploration and aviation.

image.caption: Portrait of Roald Amundsen at Ny-Ålesund, Svalbard.
image.credit: Preus Museum Anders Beer Wilse — Preus Museum on Flickr
image.date_qualification: Depicted in 1925; the North Pole flight occurred on 12 May 1926.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Roald Amundsen flies over the North Pole

events.enhanced_description: On May 12, 1926, the May Coup led by Józef Piłsudski resulted in his takeover of the Polish government. This coup significantly altered the political landscape of Poland and established Piłsudski's authoritarian regime.
events.name: May Coup in Poland

events.enhanced_description: On May 18, 1926, evangelist Aimee Semple McPherson disappeared while visiting a beach in Venice, California. Her mysterious disappearance garnered significant media attention and public speculation, impacting her ministry and the Pentecostal movement.
events.name: Aimee Semple McPherson disappears

events.enhanced_description: On May 20, 1926, the United States Congress passed the Air Commerce Act, which established regulations for the licensing of pilots and aircraft. This legislation was a critical step in the development of civil aviation in the United States.
events.name: Air Commerce Act passed by the United States Congress

events.enhanced_description: On May 23, 1926, the first Lebanese constitution was established, laying the groundwork for Lebanon's political framework. This constitution was a significant step towards national governance and independence.
events.name: First Lebanese constitution established

events.enhanced_description: On May 26, 1926, the Rif War concluded when the Rif rebels surrendered in Morocco, ending a prolonged conflict that had significant implications for Spanish and Moroccan relations. This surrender marked the end of a fierce struggle for autonomy in the Rif region.

image.caption: Map showing the Republic of the Rif’s territory within Spanish Morocco.
image.credit: Tyk — Own work
image.date_qualification: A 2011 map of the Republic of the Rif, not a depiction of the surrender or the war’s end.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Rif War ends with surrender of Rif rebels

events.enhanced_description: On May 28, 1926, a coup d'état led by Manuel Gomes da Costa resulted in the establishment of the Ditadura Nacional (National Dictatorship) in Portugal. This event set the stage for António de Oliveira Salazar's Estado Novo regime, which would dominate Portuguese politics for decades.
events.name: 1926 coup d'état in Portugal

events.enhanced_description: On June 4, 1926, Ignacy Mościcki was elected president of Poland, succeeding Stanisław Wojciechowski. His presidency occurred during a tumultuous period marked by political instability and the aftermath of the May Coup.
events.name: Ignacy Mościcki becomes president of Poland

events.enhanced_description: On June 7, 1926, Carl Gustaf Ekman succeeded Rickard Sandler as Prime Minister of Sweden. His leadership marked a shift in Swedish politics during a period of social and economic change.
events.name: Carl Gustaf Ekman becomes Prime Minister of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1926, Arthur Meighen briefly returned to office as Prime Minister of Canada during the King-Byng Affair. This political crisis highlighted the tensions between the Governor General and the elected government.
events.name: Arthur Meighen returns as Prime Minister of Canada

events.enhanced_description: The Northern Expedition was a military campaign led by the Kuomintang (KMT) to unify China under its control, beginning in July 1926. This campaign aimed to defeat warlords and establish a central government, marking a significant step in the Chinese Nationalist movement.
events.name: Northern Expedition

events.enhanced_description: On July 3, 1926, a Caudron C.61 aircraft operated by Compagnie Internationale de Navigation Aérienne crashed in Czechoslovakia, highlighting the risks associated with early aviation. The incident raised concerns about aviation safety standards at the time.
events.name: Caudron C.61 Crash

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1926, General Óscar Carmona led a military coup in Portugal, resulting in the establishment of a military dictatorship that lasted for several years. This coup marked a significant turning point in Portuguese politics, leading to the eventual rise of the Estado Novo regime.
events.name: Coup d'état in Portugal

events.enhanced_description: On July 10, 1926, a bolt of lightning struck Picatinny Arsenal in New Jersey, igniting a fire that led to a series of explosions over the next few days. This incident caused significant damage and raised awareness about the safety of munitions storage.
events.name: Picatinny Arsenal Explosion

events.enhanced_description: On July 15, 1926, the Bombay Electric Supply and Transport Company introduced motor buses in Mumbai, revolutionizing public transport in the city. This development marked a significant advancement in urban mobility and contributed to the modernization of Bombay.
figures: Bombay Electric Supply and Transport Company
events.name: Introduction of Motor Buses in India

events.enhanced_description: On July 26, 1926, the National Bar Association was incorporated in the United States, aimed at promoting the interests of African American lawyers and judges. This organization played a crucial role in advocating for civil rights and equality in the legal profession.
events.name: Incorporation of the National Bar Association

events.enhanced_description: The Cristero War began on August 1, 1926, in Mexico as a response to the anticlerical measures enforced by the 1917 Constitution. This conflict pitted the Mexican government against Catholic rebels, leading to significant violence and social upheaval.

image.caption: Photograph of suspects belonging to the National League for the Defense of Religious Liberty at a police inspection.
image.credit: The original author of that photograph is Casasola (a photographer from the Casasola Archive). — This work was found on the Mediateca INAH website, the official digital repository of the Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia (INAH), México, specifically in the Fototeca Nacional within the Archivo Casasola collection. Source: https://mediateca.inah.gob.mx/islandora_74/islandora/object/fotografia%3A63509
image.date_qualification: Circa 1928–1929; this is a photograph from during the war, not an image of its beginning on August 3, 1926.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Cristero War Begins

events.enhanced_description: On August 2, 1926, the Western Australian Secession League was founded, advocating for the secession of Western Australia from the Commonwealth of Australia. Although short-lived, the league reflected regional discontent and aspirations for greater autonomy.
events.name: Western Australian Secession League Founded

events.enhanced_description: On August 5, 1926, audiences in New York City witnessed the debut of the Warner Brothers' Vitaphone system in the film 'Don Juan,' starring John Barrymore. This marked a significant advancement in sound technology in cinema, paving the way for the future of talkies.
events.name: Vitaphone System Debut

events.enhanced_description: On August 6, 1926, Gertrude Ederle became the first woman to swim across the English Channel, completing the challenging journey from France to England. Her achievement not only set a record but also inspired women and athletes worldwide.
events.name: Gertrude Ederle Swims the English Channel

events.enhanced_description: On August 18, 1926, the first televised weather map was broadcast from NAA Arlington to the Weather Bureau office in Washington, D.C. This event marked a significant milestone in the field of meteorology and broadcasting technology.
events.name: First Weather Map Televised

events.enhanced_description: On August 22, 1926, Georgios Kondylis ousted Theodoros Pangalos in a coup, leading to a shift in power in Greece. This event was part of the broader political instability that characterized the country during the interwar period.
events.name: Georgios Kondylis Ousts Theodoros Pangalos

events.enhanced_description: On August 25, 1926, Pavlos Kountouriotis announced the end of dictatorship in Greece, declaring himself president. This proclamation marked a significant political transition in the country, moving towards a more democratic governance.
events.name: Pavlos Kountouriotis Announces End of Dictatorship

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1926, Lebanon, under the French Mandate, adopted its first constitution, establishing itself as a republic with Charles Debbas as its president. This event marked a significant step towards national sovereignty and governance.
events.name: Lebanon's First Constitution

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1926, the Weimar Republic of Germany joined the League of Nations, marking a significant moment in international relations post-World War I. This membership aimed to foster cooperation and peace in Europe.
events.name: Germany Joins the League of Nations

events.enhanced_description: On September 11, 1926, an assassination attempt was made on Italian Prime Minister Benito Mussolini when Gino Lucetti threw a bomb at his car in Rome. Mussolini escaped unharmed, but the incident underscored the political tensions of the era.
events.name: Assassination Attempt on Mussolini

events.enhanced_description: On September 14, 1926, the Locarno Treaties were ratified in Geneva, solidifying agreements aimed at ensuring peace in post-World War I Europe. These treaties represented a significant diplomatic effort to stabilize the continent.
events.name: Ratification of the Locarno Treaties

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1926, the Great Miami Hurricane struck, causing catastrophic damage and resulting in over 100 fatalities. The hurricane's impact was devastating, leading to extensive destruction and financial loss in the region.
events.name: Great Miami Hurricane

events.enhanced_description: On September 19, 1926, the Giuseppe Meazza Stadium, also known as San Siro, officially opened in Milan, becoming one of the most iconic sports venues in Italy. The stadium has since hosted numerous significant sporting events and concerts.
events.name: Opening of Giuseppe Meazza Stadium

events.enhanced_description: On September 20, 1926, the North Side Gang attempted to assassinate mobster Al Capone by spraying his Cicero headquarters with over a thousand rounds of machine gun fire. Capone miraculously escaped unharmed, highlighting the violent gang rivalries of the era.
events.name: Assassination Attempt on Al Capone

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1926, French war ace René Fonck and his crew attempted to fly across the Atlantic in pursuit of the Orteig Prize. Tragically, their modified Sikorsky S-35 crashed during take-off, resulting in the death of two crew members.
events.name: René Fonck's Atlantic Flight Attempt

events.enhanced_description: On September 23, 1926, Gene Tunney defeated Jack Dempsey to become the heavyweight boxing champion of the world. This match was highly publicized and marked a significant moment in boxing history.
events.name: Gene Tunney Defeats Jack Dempsey

events.enhanced_description: On September 25, 1926, the League of Nations Slavery Convention was adopted, aiming to abolish all forms of slavery worldwide. This convention represented a significant step towards international human rights advocacy.
events.name: League of Nations Slavery Convention

events.enhanced_description: On October 2, 1926, Józef Piłsudski, a key figure in Polish politics and military leader, assumed the role of Prime Minister of Poland, marking a significant shift in the country's governance following a coup d'état that he orchestrated.

image.caption: Portrait of Polish marshal Józef Piłsudski.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Z działalności Wielkopolskiego Związku Powstańców i Strzelców w roku 1929/30, Poznań 1930(?) wolnedzwieki.pl
image.date_qualification: Portrait of Piłsudski, not a depiction of his appointment as prime minister. The original date is qualified as before 1930.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Józef Piłsudski becomes prime minister of Poland

events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1926, British miners reached an agreement to end their strike, which had lasted for several months and was part of a larger general strike that aimed to protest against wage cuts and poor working conditions in the coal industry.
events.name: British miners agree to end their strike

events.enhanced_description: On October 14, 1926, A. A. Milne's beloved children's book 'Winnie-the-Pooh' was published in London, introducing readers to the charming adventures of the titular bear and his friends in the Hundred Acre Wood, becoming a classic of children's literature.
events.name: Winnie-the-Pooh is published

events.enhanced_description: On October 16, 1926, an ammunition explosion occurred on the troopship Kuang Yuang near Jiujiang, China, resulting in the tragic loss of approximately 1,200 lives, highlighting the dangers associated with military transport during this period.
events.name: Ammunition explosion on troopship Kuang Yuang

events.enhanced_description: The 1926 Imperial Conference opened on October 19, 1926, in London, where leaders from the British Empire gathered to discuss issues of governance and the relationship between the dominions and the British government, leading to significant constitutional changes.
events.name: The 1926 Imperial Conference opens

events.enhanced_description: On October 20, 1926, a devastating hurricane struck Cuba, resulting in the deaths of approximately 650 people and causing widespread destruction across the island, marking one of the deadliest natural disasters in Cuban history.
events.name: Hurricane kills 650 in Cuba

events.enhanced_description: On October 23, 1926, Leon Trotsky and Lev Kamenev were expelled from the Politburo of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, a significant political maneuver that reflected the growing power of Joseph Stalin and the consolidation of his control over the party.
events.name: Leon Trotsky and Lev Kamenev removed from the Politburo

events.enhanced_description: On October 31, 1926, the famous magician and escape artist Harry Houdini died in Detroit, Michigan, from complications related to a ruptured appendix, marking the end of an era for one of the most renowned entertainers of the early 20th century.
events.name: Harry Houdini dies

events.enhanced_description: On November 10, 1926, Earle Nelson, a necrophiliac serial killer known as the 'Gorilla Man,' committed his ninth murder in San Francisco, targeting a boarding house landlady, which shocked the community and drew significant media attention.
events.name: Earle Nelson kills his 9th victim

events.enhanced_description: On November 11, 1926, the United States Numbered Highway System was officially established, including iconic routes such as U.S. Route 66, which facilitated national travel and commerce, shaping the American landscape for decades to come.
events.name: The United States Numbered Highway System is established

events.enhanced_description: On November 15, 1926, the NBC Radio Network officially opened in New York City, featuring 24 stations and marking a significant milestone in the development of American broadcasting and the rise of radio as a dominant medium for entertainment and information.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: The NBC Radio Network opens

events.enhanced_description: On November 24, 1926, the village of Rocquebillier in the French Riviera was nearly destroyed by a massive hailstorm, causing extensive damage to property and agriculture in the region.
events.name: Rocquebillier is almost destroyed in a hailstorm

events.enhanced_description: On November 25, 1926, the Fascist regime in Italy, led by Benito Mussolini, re-established the death penalty, reflecting the government's increasing authoritarian measures and crackdown on dissent.
events.name: The death penalty is re-established in Italy

events.enhanced_description: On November 26, 1926, all Italian Communist deputies were arrested under the orders of Benito Mussolini's government, marking a significant escalation in the repression of political opposition in Fascist Italy.
events.name: All Italian Communist deputies are arrested

events.enhanced_description: On November 27, 1926, the restoration of Colonial Williamsburg began, aiming to preserve and interpret the historical significance of this colonial capital, which would later become a major tourist attraction and educational site.
events.name: Restoration of Colonial Williamsburg begins

events.enhanced_description: On December 2, 1926, British Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin announced the end of martial law that had been declared during the general strike, signaling a return to normalcy and the resolution of the labor unrest that had gripped the nation.
events.name: British prime minister Stanley Baldwin ends martial law

events.enhanced_description: On December 3, 1926, renowned English detective story writer Agatha Christie mysteriously disappeared from her home in Surrey, sparking a nationwide search that captivated the public and media; she was found on December 14 at a hotel under an assumed name.
events.name: Agatha Christie disappears

events.enhanced_description: The Council for the Preservation of Rural England, later known as the Campaign to Protect Rural England (CPRE), was established to combat urban sprawl and preserve the countryside. Founded by Patrick Abercrombie, the organization aimed to promote sustainable development and protect rural landscapes from unchecked expansion.
events.name: The Council for the Preservation of Rural England founded

events.enhanced_description: On December 13, 1926, Miina Sillanpää made history by becoming Finland's first female government minister. Her appointment marked a significant step towards gender equality in Finnish politics and inspired future generations of women leaders.
events.name: Miina Sillanpää becomes Finland's first female government minister

events.enhanced_description: On December 17, 1926, a coup d'état in Lithuania resulted in the overthrow of the democratically elected government. Antanas Smetona seized power, leading to an authoritarian regime that would last until the onset of World War II.
events.name: 1926 Lithuanian coup d'état

events.enhanced_description: On December 18, 1926, Turkey officially adopted the Gregorian calendar, transitioning from the Julian calendar. This reform was part of a series of modernization efforts under Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, aimed at aligning Turkey more closely with Western practices.
events.name: Turkey converts to the Gregorian calendar

events.enhanced_description: On December 23, 1926, Nicaraguan President Adolfo Díaz requested U.S. military assistance amid a civil war. In response, American troops established neutral zones in Puerto Cabezas to protect foreign nationals and property, marking a significant intervention in Nicaraguan affairs.

locations.name: Puerto Cabezas, North Caribbean Coast Autonomous Region, Nicaragua

events.name: Nicaraguan President Adolfo Díaz requests U.S. military assistance

events.enhanced_description: The Shōwa period in Japan commenced on December 26, 1926, following the death of Emperor Taishō. His son, Hirohito, ascended to the throne, marking a new era that would last until 1989 and encompass significant political and social changes in Japan.
events.name: Shōwa period begins in Japan

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1927, the British Broadcasting Company transitioned into the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) following the enactment of its Royal Charter. John Reith became the first Director-General, setting the foundation for the BBC's future as a leading public broadcaster.
events.name: The British Broadcasting Company becomes the British Broadcasting Corporation

events.enhanced_description: In 1927, the Harlem Globetrotters exhibition basketball team played their first-ever road game in Hinckley, Illinois. This marked the beginning of their journey to becoming a globally recognized sports and entertainment phenomenon.
events.name: The Harlem Globetrotters play their first road game

events.enhanced_description: In 1927, the silent romantic comedy film 'It', starring Clara Bow, was released, popularizing the concept of the 'It girl' and becoming a cultural phenomenon of the era.
events.name: Release of the film 'It'

events.enhanced_description: In 1927, João Ribeiro de Barros became the first non-European to complete a transatlantic flight, traveling from Genoa, Italy, to Fernando de Noronha, Brazil, marking a significant achievement in aviation history.
events.name: João Ribeiro de Barros transatlantic flight

events.enhanced_description: In May 1927, Philo Farnsworth transmitted his first experimental electronic television motion pictures, advancing the technology beyond previous electromechanical systems.
events.name: Philo Farnsworth's television transmission

events.enhanced_description: In 1927, inventor Philo Farnsworth achieved a groundbreaking milestone by developing the first fully electronic television system. This innovation laid the foundation for modern television broadcasting and revolutionized the way visual media is consumed.
events.name: The first fully electronic television system

events.enhanced_description: In October 1927, physicist Niels Bohr presented his theoretical principle of complementarity at the Fifth Solvay Conference on Physics. This principle became a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, influencing the understanding of wave-particle duality.
events.name: Niels Bohr presents principle of complementarity

events.enhanced_description: In 1927, Australian cricketer Bill Ponsford scored an astonishing 437 runs in a single innings at the Melbourne Cricket Ground, setting a new world record for the highest first-class cricket score. This remarkable achievement not only broke his own previous record but also solidified his place in cricket history.

locations.name: Melbourne Cricket Ground, Melbourne, Victoria, Australia

events.name: Bill Ponsford's World Record

events.enhanced_description: The dismantled pieces of the White Chapel were found inside the Third Pylon at Karnak in 1927. Between 1927 and 1930, the pieces were carefully removed and later assembled in the Karnak Open Air Museum.
events.name: White Chapel pieces removed from Karnak’s Third Pylon

events.enhanced_description: On January 7, 1927, the first transatlantic telephone call was successfully made via radio from New York City to London. This groundbreaking achievement marked a significant advancement in telecommunications and international communication.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: First transatlantic telephone call made

events.enhanced_description: On January 9, 1927, a devastating fire broke out at the Laurier Palace Theatre in Montreal, resulting in the tragic deaths of 78 children. This incident raised significant concerns about fire safety regulations in public venues.

image.caption: Facade of the Laurier Palace Theatre after the fire.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — http://www.cinemamuetquebec.ca/content/theme_cap/5?lang=fr
image.date_qualification: Image description dates the aftermath photograph to 1927; it does not establish the exact date it was taken.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Laurier Palace Theatre fire

events.enhanced_description: On January 10, 1927, Fritz Lang's iconic science fiction film Metropolis premiered in Germany. The film is renowned for its groundbreaking special effects and its exploration of themes such as class struggle and industrialization.
events.name: Release of Fritz Lang's Metropolis

events.enhanced_description: On January 11, 1927, Louis B. Mayer announced the creation of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences at a banquet in Los Angeles. This organization would later become famous for the annual Academy Awards, celebrating excellence in the film industry.
events.name: Creation of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences

events.enhanced_description: On January 19, 1927, Great Britain dispatched troops to Shanghai, China, to protect foreign nationals amid rising anti-foreign riots. This military intervention highlighted the tensions between foreign powers and Chinese nationalists during this period.
events.name: British troops sent to China

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1927, U.S. Marines invaded Nicaragua under orders from President Calvin Coolidge, intervening in the ongoing civil war. This military presence would continue until 1933, reflecting U.S. interests in Central America during this era.

image.caption: A map of Nicaragua published by Richard Mayer (Firm).
image.credit: Norman B. Leventhal Map Center — Nicaragua
image.date_qualification: Map of Nicaragua published by Richard Mayer (Firm), dated 1920 in the source description. It provides geographic context; the later metadata date is omitted.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: U.S. Marines invade Nicaragua

events.enhanced_description: In February 1927, physicist Werner Heisenberg formulated his famous uncertainty principle while working as a lecturer at Niels Bohr's Institute for Theoretical Physics in Copenhagen. This principle fundamentally changed the understanding of quantum mechanics.
events.name: Werner Heisenberg formulates uncertainty principle

events.enhanced_description: On February 7, 1927, an attempted military coup in Lisbon, Portugal, was successfully suppressed. This event reflected the political instability in Portugal during the early 20th century, leading to significant changes in governance.
events.name: Attempted military coup in Lisbon

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1927, British troops landed in Shanghai due to concerns from the UK government regarding the safety of British residents in the settlement amidst rising tensions in China.
events.name: British troops land in Shanghai

events.enhanced_description: On February 14, 1927, a magnitude 6.1 earthquake struck Yugoslavia, resulting in significant damage and the loss of 50 lives, marking one of the notable seismic events in the region.
events.name: Yugoslav earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On February 19, 1927, a general strike erupted in Shanghai as a protest against the presence of British troops, reflecting the growing anti-imperialist sentiment among the Chinese population.
events.name: General strike in Shanghai

events.enhanced_description: On February 23, 1927, the U.S. Federal Radio Commission was established to regulate radio frequencies, marking a significant step in the development of broadcasting in the United States.
events.name: U.S. Federal Radio Commission established

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1927, a diamond rush occurred in South Africa, attracting trained athletes hired by major companies to stake claims, reflecting the economic opportunities of the time.
events.name: Diamond rush in South Africa

events.enhanced_description: On March 7, 1927, the Kita Tango earthquake struck western Honshu, Japan, with a magnitude of 7.0 Mw, resulting in at least 2,925 fatalities and extensive damage in the Toyooka and Mineyama areas.
events.name: Kita Tango earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On March 11, 1927, the Roxy Theatre opened in New York City, founded by Samuel Roxy Rothafel, becoming a landmark venue for film and entertainment.
events.name: Opening of the Roxy Theatre

events.enhanced_description: On March 14, 1927, Pan American World Airways was founded by Juan T. Trippe, marking a significant development in international air travel.
events.name: Founding of Pan American World Airways

events.enhanced_description: On March 24, 1927, during the Nanking Incident, U.S. Navy and British Royal Navy warships fired shells to disperse crowds after six foreigners were killed, highlighting the tensions between foreign powers and local forces.
events.name: Nanking Incident

events.enhanced_description: On March 29, 1927, Henry Segrave broke the land speed record by driving the Sunbeam 1000 hp at Daytona Beach, Florida, showcasing advancements in automotive engineering.
events.name: Henry Segrave breaks land speed record

events.enhanced_description: The Nanjing–Wuhan split in April 1927 marked a significant political division within the Kuomintang (KMT) government in China, with leftist factions in Wuhan opposing the rightist factions in Nanjing. This split contributed to the fragmentation of Chinese nationalism and the rise of regional warlords.
events.name: Nanjing–Wuhan split

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1927, Bell Telephone Co. successfully transmitted an image of Herbert Hoover, marking the first long-distance demonstration of television technology.
events.name: First successful long-distance television transmission

events.enhanced_description: On April 12, 1927, the Royal and Parliamentary Titles Act renamed the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland to the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, reflecting the political changes following the establishment of the Irish Free State.
events.name: Royal and Parliamentary Titles Act 1927

events.enhanced_description: On April 12, 1927, during the Shanghai Massacre, Kuomintang troops killed numerous communist-supporting workers, effectively ending the First United Front and igniting the Chinese Civil War.
events.name: Shanghai Massacre

events.enhanced_description: On April 18, 1927, the Kuomintang established a government in Nanking, marking a significant moment in the Chinese Civil War and the consolidation of Nationalist power.
events.name: Kuomintang government established in Nanking

events.enhanced_description: On April 21, 1927, Japan faced a banking crisis that had significant implications for the country's economy and financial stability.
events.name: Banking crisis in Japan

events.enhanced_description: On April 22, 1927, the Great Mississippi Flood struck, affecting 700,000 people and becoming the most significant natural disaster in American history up to that point.
events.name: Great Mississippi Flood

events.enhanced_description: On April 23, 1927, Cardiff City made history by winning the FA Cup, defeating Arsenal 1-0, marking the only time a team from outside England has won the prestigious competition.
events.name: Cardiff City wins FA Cup

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1927, the Carabineros de Chile, the national police force and gendarmerie, were created, establishing a significant institution for law enforcement in the country.
events.name: Creation of Carabineros de Chile

events.enhanced_description: On May 9, 1927, the Australian Parliament convened for the first time in Canberra, Australian Capital Territory, marking a significant moment in the nation's political history.

image.caption: Old Parliament House in Canberra, Australia.
image.credit: JJ Harrison ( https://www.jjharrison.com.au/ ) — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2009-08-07, decades after the first Parliament convened in Canberra on 1927-05-09.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: First Australian Parliament convenes in Canberra

events.enhanced_description: The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences was founded in Los Angeles to mediate labor disputes and establish standards for the film industry. It later became famous for presenting the Academy Awards, which honor outstanding achievements in cinema.
events.name: Founding of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences

events.enhanced_description: British police conducted a raid on the Soviet trade delegation's office in London, reflecting the growing tensions between the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union during the interwar period. This incident was part of a broader context of suspicion and espionage.
events.name: Raid on Soviet Trade Delegation in London

events.enhanced_description: Major Harold Geiger, a pioneer in U.S. Army aviation, tragically died in a plane crash while flying his Airco DH.4 aircraft at Olmsted Field. His contributions to military aviation were significant during the early years of flight.

image.caption: Portrait of Lieutenant Harold E. Geiger, a pioneer aviator.
image.credit: Bain News Service, publisher. — This image is available from the United States Library of Congress 's Prints and Photographs division under the digital ID ggbain.11254 . This tag does not indicate the copyright status of the attached work. A normal copyright tag is still required. See Commons:Licensing .
image.date_qualification: Image dated 1912-08-10, fifteen years before the event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Death of Major Harold Geiger

events.enhanced_description: The Bath School disaster occurred when Andrew Kehoe, a disgruntled school official, orchestrated a series of violent attacks that resulted in the deaths of 45 people, primarily children. This tragic event remains one of the deadliest school attacks in U.S. history.
events.name: Bath School Disaster

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Jeddah was signed between the United Kingdom and Ibn Saud, recognizing his sovereignty over the Kingdom of Hejaz and Nejd, which later became Saudi Arabia. This treaty marked a significant step in the establishment of modern Saudi statehood.
events.name: Treaty of Jeddah

events.enhanced_description: On May 20, 1927, Charles Lindbergh completed the first solo, nonstop transatlantic flight from New York City to Paris in his aircraft, the Spirit of St. Louis. This historic achievement made him an international hero and significantly advanced the field of aviation.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Charles Lindbergh's Transatlantic Flight

events.enhanced_description: The Gulang earthquake, measuring 7.6 Mw, struck Gansu province in northwest China, causing widespread devastation and resulting in over 40,000 fatalities. It is remembered as one of the deadliest earthquakes in Chinese history.
events.name: Gulang Earthquake

events.enhanced_description: Nearly 600 members of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers and the Institute of Radio Engineers attended a live demonstration of television at the Bell Telephone Building in New York City. This event marked a significant milestone in the development of television technology.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Television Demonstration

events.enhanced_description: The United Kingdom severed diplomatic relations with the Soviet Union following revelations of espionage and underground agitation, reflecting the deteriorating relationship between the two nations during the 1920s.
events.name: UK Cuts Diplomatic Relations with the Soviet Union

events.enhanced_description: In August 1930, the volcanic island of Anak Krakatau began to form permanently in the Sunda Strait, following a series of eruptions. This event marked the emergence of a new geological feature in a region known for its volcanic activity.
events.name: Formation of Anak Krakatau

events.enhanced_description: Yugoslavia severed diplomatic relations with Albania amid rising tensions and political disputes in the Balkans. This decision reflected the complex geopolitical landscape of the region during the interwar period.
events.name: Yugoslavia Sever Diplomatic Relations with Albania

events.enhanced_description: On June 4, 1927, aviators Clarence Chamberlin and Charles Albert Levine took off from Roosevelt Field, New York, and successfully flew to Eisleben, Germany, in the Wright-Bellanca WB-2 Columbia aircraft. This flight occurred just weeks after Charles Lindbergh's historic solo transatlantic flight.

image.caption: Clarence Chamberlin and Charles Albert Levine standing in front of their Wright-Bellanca aircraft.
image.credit: FOTO:Fortepan — ID 132700 : Adományozó/Donor: MAGYAR MŰSZAKI ÉS KÖZLEKEDÉSI MÚZEUM / ARCHÍVUM / NEGATÍVTÁR / MAGYAR NEMZETI MÚZEUM GYŰJTEMÉNYE. — https://download.fortepan.hu/_photo/download/fortepan_132700.jpg
image.date_qualification: 1928; the image postdates the 1927 flight.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

locations.name: Roosevelt Field, New York, United States

events.name: Chamberlin and Levine Flight

events.enhanced_description: In retaliation for the assassination of Pyotr Voykov, the Soviet ambassador to Poland, the Soviet Union executed 20 individuals accused of espionage. This event highlighted the intense political climate and retaliatory actions during the period.
events.name: Execution of 20 for Espionage

events.enhanced_description: Léon Daudet, a prominent leader of the French monarchists, was arrested in France, reflecting the political tensions and conflicts within the country during the interwar period.
events.name: Arrest of Léon Daudet

events.enhanced_description: The Association football club Persebaya Surabaya was founded in the Dutch East Indies, now Indonesia. It has since become one of the most prominent football clubs in the region, contributing to the development of the sport in Indonesia.
events.name: Foundation of Persebaya Surabaya

events.enhanced_description: Iberia, the Spanish airline, was established in 1927, marking a significant development in the aviation industry in Spain. It has since grown to become one of the largest airlines in the country.
events.name: Establishment of Iberia Airlines

events.enhanced_description: A total solar eclipse occurred on June 29, 1927, visible across parts of Wales, northern England, southern Scotland, Norway, and northern Sweden. This astronomical event captivated the public and scientists alike, contributing to the study of solar phenomena.
events.name: Solar Eclipse of June 29, 1927

events.enhanced_description: On July 1, 1927, Commander Richard E. Byrd and his crew took off from Roosevelt Field in New York in the Fokker Trimotor airplane America, aiming to cross the Atlantic. They were forced to ditch in France due to bad weather but survived the emergency landing.

locations.name: Roosevelt Field, New York, United States

events.name: Byrd's Transatlantic Flight Attempt

events.enhanced_description: The Food, Drug, and Insecticide Administration (FDIA) was established as a federal agency in the United States, tasked with overseeing food safety and drug regulation. This agency played a crucial role in public health and consumer protection.
events.name: Establishment of the FDIA

events.enhanced_description: On July 10, 1927, Kevin O'Higgins, the Vice-President of the Executive Council of the Irish Free State, was assassinated by members of the anti-Treaty Irish Republican Army. This event underscored the ongoing political violence in Ireland during this period.
events.name: Assassination of Kevin O'Higgins

events.enhanced_description: The Jericho earthquake struck on July 11, 1927, and is noted for being the largest ever recorded in the region, resulting in approximately 300 fatalities. The earthquake caused significant damage across Palestine and Transjordan.
events.name: Jericho Earthquake

events.enhanced_description: Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn was freed from imprisonment in Kostroma, Russia, on July 13, 1927, after being detained for his religious activities. His release was celebrated by many in the Jewish community.
events.name: Release of Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn

events.enhanced_description: The July Revolt of 1927 in Austria was a significant uprising against the government, culminating in violent clashes at the Palace of Justice. This event reflected the growing tensions between socialist and conservative factions in Austrian society during the interwar period.
events.name: July Revolt of 1927

events.enhanced_description: The Menin Gate Memorial, dedicated on July 24, 1927, serves as a tribute to the British and Commonwealth soldiers who died in World War I and have no known grave. It features over 54,000 names inscribed on its walls, symbolizing the profound loss experienced during the war.
events.name: The Menin Gate is dedicated as a war memorial

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1927, during the Nanchang Uprising, the Communist Chinese People's Liberation Army was formed as a response to the Kuomintang's anti-communist purge. This event marked a significant turning point in the Chinese Civil War and laid the foundation for the eventual establishment of the People's Republic of China.
events.name: Formation of the People's Liberation Army

events.enhanced_description: On August 2, 1927, U.S. President Calvin Coolidge publicly announced his decision not to seek re-election in 1928, a move that surprised many political observers. His announcement marked a significant moment in American politics, as it opened the field for other candidates in the upcoming presidential election.
events.name: Calvin Coolidge announces he will not run for president

events.enhanced_description: The Peace Bridge, connecting Fort Erie, Ontario, and Buffalo, New York, officially opened on August 7, 1927. This bridge symbolizes the friendship and cooperation between Canada and the United States, facilitating trade and travel across the border.
events.name: The Peace Bridge opens

events.enhanced_description: On August 10, 1927, Mount Rushmore Park was rededicated, with President Calvin Coolidge promising national funding for the completion of the iconic presidential sculptures. This event highlighted the significance of the monument as a symbol of American democracy and history.
events.name: Mount Rushmore Park is rededicated

events.enhanced_description: On August 22, 1927, around 200 people gathered in Hyde Park, London, to protest against the death sentences of Italian American anarchists Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo Vanzetti. This demonstration was part of a larger international outcry against their controversial trial and execution.
events.name: Demonstration against Sacco and Vanzetti's death sentences

events.enhanced_description: On August 23, 1927, Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo Vanzetti were executed at Charlestown State Prison in Boston, Massachusetts. Their trial and execution became emblematic of the era's anti-immigrant sentiment and raised significant questions about justice and fairness in the American legal system.

image.caption: Coffins of Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo Vanzetti being carried out of a funeral room in Boston.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — https://beeldbank.spaarnestadphoto.com/search.pp?flush=1&multikeyword=SFA022004132&searchtype=0#ctr-thumbnails
image.date_qualification: Image description dates the photograph to 1927; this depicts the aftermath, not the executions themselves.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Sacco and Vanzetti executed

events.enhanced_description: On August 24, 1927, the Nova Scotia hurricane struck the Atlantic Provinces of Canada, causing extensive damage and resulting in at least 56 fatalities. This hurricane was one of the most devastating natural disasters to hit the region in the early 20th century.
events.name: The 1927 Nova Scotia hurricane

events.enhanced_description: On August 26, 1927, aviator Paul Redfern departed from Brunswick, Georgia, in his Stinson Detroiter named 'Port of Brunswick' to attempt a solo nonstop flight to Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. His journey ended in tragedy when he crashed in the Venezuelan jungle, with the crash site never being located.
events.name: Paul Redfern's flight attempt

events.enhanced_description: On September 7, 1927, the University of Minas Gerais was founded in Brazil, marking a significant development in higher education in the region. The establishment of this institution aimed to enhance educational opportunities and contribute to the intellectual growth of the state.
events.name: The University of Minas Gerais is founded

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1927, the Columbia Phonographic Broadcasting System, which would later become known as CBS, was formed in the United States. This marked a significant moment in the history of broadcasting, as CBS would go on to become one of the largest television and radio networks in the world.
events.name: Formation of CBS

events.enhanced_description: On September 25, 1927, a treaty signed by the League of Nations Slavery Commission abolished all types of slavery. This landmark agreement represented a significant step towards global human rights and the fight against human trafficking.
events.name: League of Nations treaty abolishes slavery

events.enhanced_description: On September 29, 1927, the East St. Louis Tornado struck, resulting in 79 fatalities and injuring 550 people. This tornado became known as the second costliest and at least the 24th deadliest tornado in U.S. history, highlighting the devastating impact of natural disasters.
events.name: East St. Louis Tornado

events.enhanced_description: On October 4, 1927, the carving of the iconic sculptures at Mount Rushmore National Memorial began. This monumental project aimed to honor four U.S. presidents and has since become a symbol of American history and artistry.
events.name: Carving of Mount Rushmore begins

events.enhanced_description: On October 6, 1927, 'The Jazz Singer,' starring Al Jolson, premiered at the Warner Theater in New York City. This film is recognized as the first significant 'talkie,' marking a pivotal moment in cinematic history and the transition from silent films to sound films.
events.name: The Jazz Singer premieres

events.enhanced_description: On October 8, 1927, the New York Yankees, famously known as the 'Murderers' Row' team, completed a four-game sweep of the Pittsburgh Pirates in the World Series. This victory solidified their dominance in baseball during the 1920s.
events.name: New York Yankees sweep World Series

events.enhanced_description: On October 9, 1927, the Mexican government successfully crushed a rebellion in Veracruz, demonstrating its authority and control over the region. This event was part of the broader context of political instability and conflict in Mexico during the post-revolutionary period.
events.name: Mexican government crushes rebellion in Veracruz

events.enhanced_description: On October 18, 1927, the first flight of Pan American Airways took off from Key West, Florida, bound for Havana, Cuba. This marked the beginning of a new era in commercial aviation, connecting the United States and Cuba and expanding air travel opportunities.
events.name: First flight of Pan American Airways

events.enhanced_description: On October 25, 1927, the Italian ocean liner Principessa Mafalda capsized off the coast of Porto Seguro, Brazil, resulting in the tragic loss of at least 314 lives. This maritime disaster highlighted the dangers of sea travel during that era.
events.name: Principessa Mafalda capsizes

events.enhanced_description: On October 27, 1927, Queen Wilhelmina of the Netherlands officially opened the Maas–Waal Canal in Nijmegen, a significant infrastructure project aimed at improving navigation and flood control in the region.
events.name: Queen Wilhelmina of the Netherlands opens the Maas–Waal Canal

events.enhanced_description: On November 1, 1927, İsmet İnönü formed the fifth government of Turkey, continuing the reforms initiated by Mustafa Kemal Atatürk and shaping the modern Turkish state.
events.name: İsmet İnönü forms a new government in Turkey

events.enhanced_description: The Great Vermont Flood of November 1927 caused catastrophic flooding across the state, resulting in significant damage and loss of life, marking it as the worst natural disaster in Vermont's history.
events.name: Great Vermont Flood of 1927

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1927, Frank Heath and his horse Gypsy Queen completed an extraordinary two-year journey of 11,356 miles, visiting all 48 states of the U.S., showcasing the spirit of adventure and exploration.
events.name: Frank Heath returns to Washington, D.C.

events.enhanced_description: On November 12, 1927, Mahatma Gandhi made his only visit to Ceylon (now Sri Lanka), where he engaged with local leaders and discussed the Indian independence movement, emphasizing non-violent resistance.
events.name: Mahatma Gandhi visits Ceylon

events.enhanced_description: On November 14, 1927, a catastrophic explosion occurred at three Equitable Gas storage tanks in the North Side of Pittsburgh, resulting in the deaths of 26 people and causing extensive damage estimated between $4 million and $5 million.
events.name: Pittsburgh gasometer explosion

events.enhanced_description: On November 21, 1927, during a miners' strike, Colorado state police opened fire on a group of unarmed miners in Ludlow, resulting in the deaths of six individuals and highlighting the tensions between labor and law enforcement.
events.name: Columbine Mine massacre

events.enhanced_description: On December 17, 1927, the United States Navy submarine S-4 was accidentally rammed and sunk by the Coast Guard cutter John Paulding off the coast of Provincetown, resulting in the loss of all hands aboard despite several rescue attempts.
events.name: United States Navy submarine S-4 sinking

events.enhanced_description: On December 17, 1927, the United States Navy submarine S-4 was accidentally rammed and sunk by the United States Coast Guard cutter John Paulding off the coast of Provincetown, Massachusetts. Despite several attempts to rescue the crew, all 40 men aboard the submarine perished in the incident, highlighting the dangers of naval operations during this era.
events.name: Sinking of the USS S-4

events.enhanced_description: On December 19, 1927, three prominent members of the Indian independence movement—Pandit Ram Prasad Bismil, Thakur Roshan Singh, and Ashfaqulla Khan—were executed by the British Raj, igniting further resistance against colonial rule.
events.name: Three Indian revolutionaries executed

events.enhanced_description: On December 27, 1927, the musical play Show Boat, based on Edna Ferber's novel, premiered on Broadway, marking a pivotal moment in American musical theater as it addressed serious themes and showcased a diverse cast.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Show Boat opens on Broadway

events.enhanced_description: On December 29, 1927, the eruption of the Perboewatan and Danan undersea volcanoes near Krakatoa led to the formation of Anak Krakatau Island, a significant geological event in the region.

image.caption: Anak Krakatau volcano in Indonesia.
image.credit: Lord Mountbatten — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2013-10-20; the article states Anak Krakatoa first emerged on 29 December 1927.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Eruption of the Perboewatan and Danan volcanoes

events.enhanced_description: On December 30, 1927, the Tokyo Metro Ginza Line opened, becoming the first commuter metro line in Asia and marking a significant advancement in urban transportation in Japan.
events.name: Tokyo Metro Ginza Line opens

events.enhanced_description: In January 1928, British bacteriologist Frederick Griffith published the results of his experiments, which indirectly demonstrated that DNA is the genetic material responsible for heredity. This groundbreaking work laid the foundation for future genetic research and the understanding of molecular biology.
events.name: Griffith's Experiment

events.enhanced_description: In 1928, Boris Bazhanov, who served as Joseph Stalin's personal secretary, made a daring escape from the Soviet Union by crossing the border into Iran. His defection marked a significant moment in the context of Soviet politics and the growing discontent among former allies of Stalin.
events.name: Boris Bazhanov's Defection

events.enhanced_description: In August 1928, Margaret Mead's groundbreaking work, 'Coming of Age in Samoa,' was published, challenging Western notions of adolescence and gender roles. This influential text brought attention to the field of cultural anthropology and highlighted the importance of cultural context in understanding human behavior.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Publication of Coming of Age in Samoa

events.enhanced_description: In October 1928, the women's organization Gruaja Shiqiptare was founded in Tirana, Albania, with Princess Senije serving as its chair. This organization aimed to promote women's rights and social issues in Albania during a time of significant political change.
events.name: Foundation of Gruaja Shiqiptare

events.enhanced_description: In 1928, Josemaría Escrivá founded Opus Dei, a personal prelature of the Catholic Church, aimed at promoting the sanctification of ordinary life through work and the pursuit of holiness. The organization emphasizes the importance of integrating faith into daily activities and has grown to have a significant global presence.
events.name: Josemaría Escrivá founds Opus Dei

events.enhanced_description: In 1928, Arvid Lindman returned to the role of Prime Minister of Sweden, marking a significant political shift as he led a right-wing government. His rival, Ernst Trygger, served as Foreign Minister, indicating a coalition of conservative forces during a time of political realignment in Sweden.
events.name: Arvid Lindman returns as Prime Minister of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: Boston Garden officially opened in 1928, becoming a prominent venue for sports and entertainment in Boston, Massachusetts. It served as the home for the Boston Celtics and the Boston Bruins, and hosted numerous concerts and events over the decades.
events.name: Opening of Boston Garden

events.enhanced_description: In 1928, the women's organization Anjuman-i Himayat-i-Niswan was founded in Kabul, Afghanistan, aimed at promoting women's rights and education. This organization played a crucial role in advocating for women's issues in a rapidly changing socio-political landscape.
events.name: Founding of Anjuman-i Himayat-i-Niswan

events.enhanced_description: On January 17, 1928, Leon Trotsky was arrested by the OGPU in Moscow, leading to his eventual exile. Trotsky's arrest was part of a broader campaign by Stalin to eliminate political rivals and consolidate power within the Soviet Union.
events.name: Arrest of Leon Trotsky

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1928, the volcanic island Anak Krakatau emerged from the sea in the Sunda Strait, Indonesia. This event marked the reawakening of the Krakatoa volcanic system, which had been dormant since the catastrophic eruption of 1883.
events.name: Emergence of Anak Krakatau

events.enhanced_description: In February 1928, the Ford River Rouge Complex in Dearborn, Michigan, was completed, becoming the world's largest integrated factory. This monumental achievement in industrial engineering revolutionized automobile manufacturing and set new standards for production efficiency.
events.name: Completion of Ford River Rouge Complex

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1928, Scottish inventor John Logie Baird successfully broadcast a transatlantic television signal from London to Hartsdale, New York. This pioneering achievement marked a significant milestone in the development of television technology and international broadcasting.
events.name: John Logie Baird's Transatlantic Broadcast

events.enhanced_description: The 1928 Winter Olympics were held in St. Moritz, Switzerland, from February 11 to February 19, marking the first time the Winter Games were conducted as a separate event from the Summer Olympics. Notably, Norwegian figure skater Sonja Henie won her first gold medal during these games.
events.name: 1928 Winter Olympics

events.enhanced_description: On December 5, 1976, Japan held a general election in which the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) lost its majority in the House of Representatives, securing only 249 out of 511 seats. This marked a significant shift in Japanese politics and set the stage for a more competitive political landscape.
events.name: Japanese General Election

events.enhanced_description: On February 25, 1928, Charles Jenkins Laboratories in Washington, D.C., became the first holder of a television license from the Federal Radio Commission. This milestone marked the beginning of regulated television broadcasting in the United States.
events.name: First Television License

events.enhanced_description: The March 15 incident in 1928 involved a crackdown on socialists and communists by the Japanese government, particularly targeting activists imprisoned at Ichigaya Prison. This event was part of a broader trend of increasing repression against leftist movements in Japan during the 1920s.
events.name: March 15 incident

events.enhanced_description: On March 21, 1928, Charles Lindbergh was awarded the Medal of Honor for his historic transatlantic flight in 1927. This recognition celebrated his significant contribution to aviation and his role in popularizing air travel.
events.name: Charles Lindbergh's Medal of Honor

events.enhanced_description: On March 22, 1928, the Muslim Brotherhood was founded in Ismailia, Egypt, by Islamic scholar Hassan al-Banna. The organization aimed to promote Islamic values and social reform, and it would go on to play a significant role in Egyptian and Middle Eastern politics.
events.name: Founding of the Muslim Brotherhood

events.enhanced_description: On March 24, 1928, excavation work began at the site of the ancient Canaanite city of Ugarit, which had been accidentally rediscovered. This archaeological endeavor would uncover significant artifacts and texts that contributed to the understanding of ancient Near Eastern cultures.
events.name: Rediscovery of Ugarit

events.enhanced_description: On April 10, 1928, the Republican Party primary elections in Chicago, known as the Pineapple Primary, were marred by violence, bombings, and assassination attempts, resulting in the deaths of two politicians. This event highlighted the intense political rivalries and corruption within the party during this period.
events.name: Pineapple Primary Violence

events.enhanced_description: On April 12, 1928, a bomb attack targeting Italian Fascist leader Benito Mussolini in Milan resulted in the deaths of 17 bystanders. This assassination attempt underscored the growing opposition to Mussolini's regime and the violent political climate of the time.
events.name: Bomb Attack on Mussolini

events.enhanced_description: On April 12, 1928, the first east-west transatlantic flight took place from Dublin, Ireland, to Greenly Island, Canada, using the German Junkers W 33 Bremen. This historic flight demonstrated the advancements in aviation technology and the potential for international air travel.
events.name: First East-West Transatlantic Flight

events.enhanced_description: On April 13, 1928, an explosion occurred at a dance hall in West Plains, Missouri, resulting in significant casualties and damage. The incident raised concerns about safety regulations and the risks associated with public gatherings.
events.name: West Plains Dance Hall Explosion

events.enhanced_description: On April 14, 1928, a significant earthquake struck Chirpan, Bulgaria, followed by another quake in Plovdiv four days later. The two earthquakes resulted in the destruction of over 21,000 buildings and nearly 130 fatalities, highlighting the region's vulnerability to seismic activity.
events.name: Chirpan and Plovdiv Earthquakes

events.enhanced_description: On April 19, 1928, the original Oxford English Dictionary was completed after 70 years of work, with the publication of the last section covering words from 'wise' to 'wyze'. This monumental achievement in lexicography established a comprehensive record of the English language.
events.name: Publication of the Oxford English Dictionary

events.enhanced_description: On April 22, 1928, a magnitude 6.0 earthquake struck Corinth, Greece, causing widespread destruction and resulting in 20 fatalities. The quake also triggered a non-destructive tsunami, further impacting the coastal region.
events.name: Corinth Earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On April 28, 1928, southern-central Pennsylvania experienced an unprecedented snowfall of 28 inches. This extreme weather event disrupted daily life and highlighted the region's susceptibility to severe winter storms.
events.name: Snowfall in Pennsylvania

events.enhanced_description: The Jinan incident was a significant armed conflict on May 3, 1928, between the Imperial Japanese Army, allied with Northern Chinese warlords, and the Kuomintang's southern army. This clash marked a critical moment in the struggle for control over China during a period of warlordism and rising nationalism.
events.name: Jinan incident

events.enhanced_description: On May 7, 1928, the Representation of the People Act was passed in the United Kingdom, lowering the voting age for women from 30 to 21. This landmark legislation granted women equal suffrage with men, significantly advancing gender equality in British politics.
events.name: Passage of the Representation of the People Act

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1928, General Electric's television station W2XB in Schenectady, New York, began the first regular schedule of television programming. This event marked a pivotal moment in the history of broadcasting and the development of television as a medium.
events.name: First regular television programming schedule

events.enhanced_description: On May 15, 1928, Disney Studios released the animated short Plane Crazy in Los Angeles, featuring the first appearances of Mickey and Minnie Mouse. Although it was not widely distributed at the time, it laid the groundwork for the future success of Disney's animated characters.
events.name: Release of Plane Crazy

events.enhanced_description: On May 23, 1928, a bomb attack against the Italian consulate in Buenos Aires resulted in the deaths of 22 individuals and injuries to 43 others. This tragic event highlighted the political tensions and violence prevalent in Argentina during this period.
events.name: Bomb attack on Italian consulate

events.enhanced_description: On May 24, 1928, the airship Italia crashed at the North Pole, with Italian general Umberto Nobile among the occupants. A subsequent rescue expedition was launched on May 30, but tragically, Roald Amundsen was among those who lost their lives during the search for survivors.
events.name: Crash of the airship Italia
