events.enhanced_description: On May 30, 1928, rookie driver Louis Meyer won his first Indianapolis 500, a prestigious automobile race. Meyer would go on to win this iconic event two more times, in 1933 and 1936, solidifying his legacy in motorsport history.
events.name: Louis Meyer wins Indianapolis 500

events.enhanced_description: On May 31, 1928, South Africa adopted a new national flag based on the Van Riebeeck flag, replacing the Red Ensign. This flag later became infamously known as the 'apartheid flag' for its association with the country's apartheid regime from 1948 to 1994.
events.name: South Africa adopts new national flag

events.enhanced_description: On June 4, 1928, the Huanggutun incident occurred when warlord Zhang Zuolin was assassinated by Japanese agents in Shenyang, China. This event significantly impacted the power dynamics in China and escalated tensions between Japan and Chinese nationalists.
events.name: Huanggutun incident

events.enhanced_description: On June 8, 1928, the National Revolutionary Army seized Beijing and renamed it Běipíng, effectively ending the Beiyang government's control by the 'Fengtian warlords.' This event marked a significant step in the Kuomintang's efforts to unify China.
events.name: National Revolutionary Army seizes Beijing

events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1928, Australian aviator Charles Kingsford Smith and his crew completed the first flight across the Pacific Ocean, traveling from Oakland, California, to Brisbane, Australia, via Honolulu and Fiji. This historic flight showcased the advancements in aviation and opened new possibilities for transoceanic travel.

image.caption: Vintage gelatin silver print of Charles Kingsford-Smith and Charles Ulm after landing at Mascot following the first trans-Pacific flight.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — State Library of New South Wales
image.date_qualification: Photographed 1928-06-10, the day after the flight was completed on 1928-06-09.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: First flight across the Pacific Ocean

events.enhanced_description: On June 14, 1928, students took over the medical wing of Rosario University in Argentina, reflecting the growing student activism and demands for educational reform during this period. This event was part of a broader movement for change within Argentine universities.
events.name: Students take over Rosario University

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1928, Amelia Earhart became the first woman to successfully complete a transatlantic flight as a passenger in a Fokker F.VIIb/3m piloted by Wilmer Stultz, flying from Newfoundland to Wales. This achievement marked a significant milestone in aviation history and women's participation in the field.
events.name: Amelia Earhart's transatlantic flight

events.enhanced_description: On June 20, 1928, Puniša Račić, a Yugoslav politician, carried out a gun attack in the Yugoslavian Parliament, killing three opposition representatives and injuring three others. This violent act underscored the intense political strife and instability in Yugoslavia during this period.
events.name: Puniša Račić's attack in Yugoslavian Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1928, a Swedish aeroplane successfully rescued some survivors of the Italian North Pole expedition, including Umberto Nobile. The Soviet icebreaker Krasin later saved the remaining survivors on July 12, highlighting the international efforts in Arctic exploration and rescue.
events.name: Rescue of survivors from the Italian North Pole expedition

events.enhanced_description: On June 28, 1928, the keel of the Oceanic, the first 1,000 ft (300 m)-long ocean liner for the British White Star Line, was laid by Harland and Wolff in Belfast. Although construction faced delays and was ultimately canceled in 1929, this project represented significant advancements in shipbuilding technology.

image.caption: Artist’s illustration of the planned White Star Line ocean liner Oceanic.
image.credit: Ercoka — Own work
image.date_qualification: Retrospective illustration of the planned ship, not a photograph of the 1928 keel-laying; the saved image date is 2025-08-07.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Keel laying of the Oceanic

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1928, at the Democratic National Convention in Houston, Governor of New York Al Smith became the first Catholic nominated by a major political party for President of the United States. His nomination marked a significant moment in American political history, reflecting changing attitudes towards religion in politics.
events.name: Al Smith nominated for President

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1928, President Herbert Hoover announced the recall of U.S. troops from China, marking a significant shift in American foreign policy as the nation sought to reduce its military presence abroad. This decision was influenced by the changing political landscape in China and the desire to promote diplomatic relations.
events.name: The United States recalls its troops from China

events.enhanced_description: The 1928 Summer Olympics, held in Amsterdam, opened on July 28 with the ceremonial lighting of the Olympic flame. This event marked the debut of women's athletics and gymnastics in the Olympic Games, with Polish discus thrower Halina Konopacka becoming the first female Olympic gold medalist in a track and field event.
events.name: 1928 Summer Olympics Opening Ceremony

events.enhanced_description: On August 2, 1928, Italy and Ethiopia signed the Italo-Ethiopian Treaty, which aimed to resolve tensions between the two nations. This treaty was part of Italy's broader imperial ambitions in Africa and set the stage for future conflicts, including the Second Italo-Ethiopian War.
events.name: Italo-Ethiopian Treaty

events.enhanced_description: On August 16, 1928, notorious serial killer Carl Panzram was arrested in Washington, D.C., initially for burglary. His subsequent confessions revealed a history of violent crimes, including multiple murders, making him one of America's most infamous criminals.
events.name: Arrest of Carl Panzram

events.enhanced_description: On August 22, 1928, Al Smith accepted the Democratic nomination for the U.S. presidential election, making history as the first Catholic nominee from a major party. This event was notable for its simultaneous broadcast on radio and television, showcasing the growing influence of media in politics.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Al Smith accepts Democratic nomination

events.enhanced_description: On August 26, 1928, the landmark negligence case Donoghue v Stevenson was initiated in Scotland when May Donoghue discovered a snail in her ginger beer. This case established the modern principles of negligence and duty of care in tort law.

image.caption: Retrospective illustration of the “snail in the bottle” case.
image.credit: Lairich Rig — From geograph.org.uk
image.date_qualification: The image date is 2013-05-20; it does not date the 1928 case.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Donoghue v Stevenson case

events.enhanced_description: On August 27, 1928, the Kellogg-Briand Pact was signed in Paris, representing a significant diplomatic effort to outlaw aggressive war. This treaty, initiated by U.S. Secretary of State Frank B. Kellogg and French Foreign Minister Aristide Briand, aimed to promote peace and prevent future conflicts.
events.name: Signing of the Kellogg-Briand Pact

events.enhanced_description: On August 29, 1928, F.C. Motagua was founded in Tegucigalpa, Honduras, as an association football club. The club has since become one of the most successful and popular teams in Honduran football history.
events.name: Foundation of F.C. Motagua

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1928, Ahmet Zogu, the President of the Albanian Republic, declared the establishment of a constitutional monarchy, naming himself King Zog I. This transition marked a significant shift in Albania's governance and its aspirations for modernization.
events.name: Establishment of the Albanian Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: On September 3, 1928, inventor Philo Farnsworth demonstrated the world's first working all-electronic television system in San Francisco. This groundbreaking technology utilized electronic scanning for both the pickup and display devices, paving the way for the future of television broadcasting.
events.name: Philo Farnsworth's television demonstration

events.enhanced_description: On September 11, 1928, the first broadcast of a play by television, titled 'The Queen's Messenger,' was transmitted from General Electric's W2XAD in Schenectady, New York. This event utilized innovative techniques developed by Ernst Alexanderson, marking a significant milestone in television history.
events.name: First television play broadcast

events.enhanced_description: On September 12, 1928, the Okeechobee hurricane struck Guadeloupe, resulting in the deaths of approximately 1,200 people. This catastrophic event highlighted the vulnerability of Caribbean islands to severe weather and the need for improved disaster preparedness.

image.caption: Synoptic weather map of the Okeechobee hurricane nearing landfall in Puerto Rico on September 13, 1928; it provides regional storm context, rather than depicting the hurricane’s September 12 strike on Guadeloupe.
image.credit: NOAA Library — https://library.noaa.gov/weather-climate/synoptic-map
image.date_qualification: Map dated September 13, 1928; one day after the hurricane struck Guadeloupe.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Okeechobee hurricane strikes Guadeloupe

events.enhanced_description: On September 16, 1928, the Okeechobee hurricane made landfall in Florida, resulting in the deaths of at least 2,500 people. This disaster remains one of the deadliest hurricanes in U.S. history, prompting changes in hurricane forecasting and emergency response.
events.name: Okeechobee hurricane impacts Florida

events.enhanced_description: On September 25, 1928, Paul and Joseph Galvin incorporated the Galvin Manufacturing Corporation in Chicago, Illinois. This company would later evolve into Motorola, a pioneer in telecommunications and consumer electronics.
events.name: Incorporation of Galvin Manufacturing Corporation

events.enhanced_description: On September 28, 1928, Scottish microbiologist Alexander Fleming made a groundbreaking discovery at St Mary's Hospital in London when he accidentally rediscovers penicillin. This antibiotic would later revolutionize medicine and save countless lives.
events.name: Discovery of Penicillin

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1928, Joseph Stalin launched the first five-year plan aimed at rapidly industrializing the Soviet Union. This ambitious initiative resulted in significant economic changes, but also led to widespread hardship as the average nonfarm wage fell by 50%.
events.name: Launch of Stalin's first five-year plan

events.enhanced_description: On October 2, 1928, Josemaría Escrivá founded Opus Dei, a personal prelature of the Catholic Church, in Madrid, Spain. This organization emphasizes the universal call to holiness and the importance of integrating faith into everyday life.
events.name: Foundation of Opus Dei

events.enhanced_description: On October 7, 1928, Haile Selassie was crowned king of Abyssinia (Ethiopia), marking the beginning of his reign. His leadership would later play a crucial role in the resistance against Italian invasion and the establishment of Ethiopia as a symbol of African independence.

image.caption: Portrait of Haile Selassie I in coronation regalia.
image.credit: Beatrice Playne — [1]
image.date_qualification: The source dates the image to the 1950s; it does not depict the 1928 coronation.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Haile Selassie's coronation

events.enhanced_description: On October 8, 1928, Chiang Kai-shek was named Generalissimo of the Nationalist Government of the Republic of China, solidifying his leadership role in the Kuomintang. This position enabled him to consolidate power and lead the country during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Chiang Kai-shek named Generalissimo

events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1928, the iron lung respirator was used for the first time at Children's Hospital in Boston, Massachusetts. This medical innovation provided life-saving support for patients suffering from respiratory failure, particularly during polio outbreaks.
events.name: First use of iron lung respirator

events.enhanced_description: On October 22, 1928, the Phi Sigma Alpha fraternity was founded at the University of Puerto Rico, Río Piedras Campus. This organization aimed to promote academic excellence and leadership among its members.

image.caption: Sigma Club House in Hato Rey, Puerto Rico.
image.credit: El Johnson ( talk ) — I ( El Johnson ( talk )) created this work entirely by myself.
image.date_qualification: A later photograph of the fraternity’s club house, not a photograph of its 1928 founding.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Foundation of Phi Sigma Alpha fraternity

events.enhanced_description: On October 25, 1928, the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement (ICRM) was formally established with the adoption of the 'Statutes of the International Red Cross.' This organization aimed to provide humanitarian assistance and protect the rights of individuals during conflicts.
events.name: Establishment of the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement

events.enhanced_description: On October 28, 1928, the Second Youth Congress was held in Batavia (now Jakarta), where young Indonesian nationalists gathered to discuss their aspirations for independence. The congress resulted in the Youth Pledge, a declaration of unity and commitment to the Indonesian nation, and introduced the national anthem 'Indonesia Raya.'
events.name: Second Youth Congress in Batavia

events.enhanced_description: In November 1928, Turkey enacted a law to replace the Arabic script with a Latin-based alphabet, a key reform initiated by Mustafa Kemal Atatürk as part of his broader modernization efforts. This change aimed to increase literacy and facilitate communication in the rapidly changing Turkish Republic.
events.name: Turkey passes a law switching to the Latin-based modern Turkish alphabet

events.enhanced_description: The 1928 United States presidential election culminated on November 6, where Republican candidate Herbert Hoover won decisively against Democratic opponent Al Smith. This election was notable for its reflection of the changing political landscape and the growing influence of urban voters.
events.name: 1928 United States presidential election

events.enhanced_description: On November 9, 1928, Radclyffe Hall's novel The Well of Loneliness was tried and convicted of obscenity in London due to its themes of lesbian love. This landmark case highlighted the societal tensions surrounding sexuality and literature in the early 20th century.
events.name: Trial of The Well of Loneliness

events.enhanced_description: The enthronement ceremony of Emperor Hirohito took place on November 10, 1928, two years after he ascended the throne following the death of Emperor Taishō. This grand event marked a significant moment in Japanese history, symbolizing continuity and the imperial tradition.
events.name: Enthronement of Emperor Hirohito

events.enhanced_description: On November 12, 1928, the liner SS Vestris developed a severe starboard list and sank approximately 200 miles off Hampton Roads, Virginia. The tragic incident resulted in an estimated 110 to 127 deaths, highlighting the dangers of maritime travel during this period.
events.name: Sinking of SS Vestris

events.enhanced_description: The 1928 Australian federal election, held on November 17, saw Stanley Bruce's Nationalist/Country Coalition Government re-elected, albeit with a reduced majority against the Labor Party led by James Scullin. This election reflected the shifting political dynamics in Australia during the late 1920s.
events.name: 1928 Australian federal election

events.enhanced_description: On November 18, 1928, Mickey Mouse made his first appearance in Steamboat Willie, which was notable for being the first synchronized sound cartoon. This groundbreaking film marked a significant milestone in animation and established Mickey Mouse as a cultural icon.

image.caption: Poster for the animated short film Steamboat Willie, featuring Mickey Mouse.
image.credit: Walt Disney / Ub Iwerks — Original poster: https://kith.com/blogs/kith/kith-x-disney-journal
image.date_qualification: The poster represents the film associated with Mickey Mouse’s official debut; it is not evidence of the premiere itself. The supplied image date is 1928-11-18.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False; Restrictions: trademarked

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Mickey Mouse appears in Steamboat Willie

events.enhanced_description: The one-movement ballet Boléro, composed by Maurice Ravel and choreographed by Bronislava Nijinska, premiered at the Paris Opéra on November 22, 1928. This performance showcased Ravel's innovative orchestration and has since become one of the most famous pieces in the classical repertoire.
events.name: Premiere of Boléro

events.enhanced_description: On November 28, 1928, the Persija Jakarta football club was founded, originally known as Voetbalbond Indonesische Jacatra. This establishment marked a significant development in Indonesian sports, contributing to the growth of football in the region.

locations.name: Jakarta, Special Capital Region of Jakarta, Indonesia

events.name: Founding of Persija Jakarta

events.enhanced_description: On December 3, 1928, a seaplane sent to greet aviation pioneer Alberto Santos-Dumont crashed in Rio de Janeiro, resulting in the tragic deaths of all on board. The incident occurred as the pilot attempted to avoid a collision with another aircraft, underscoring the risks of early aviation.

locations.name: Rio de Janeiro, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

events.name: Seaplane crash in Rio de Janeiro

events.enhanced_description: On December 4, 1928, Cosmo Gordon Lang was enthroned as the Archbishop of Canterbury, becoming the first bachelor to hold the position in 150 years. His appointment marked a significant moment in the Church of England's history, reflecting changing attitudes towards clergy and leadership.
events.name: Enthronement of Cosmo Gordon Lang

events.enhanced_description: On December 6, 1928, the Colombian government deployed military forces to suppress a month-long strike by United Fruit Company workers, resulting in an unknown number of deaths. This event highlighted the tensions between labor rights and corporate interests in Colombia during this period.
events.name: Colombian military intervention against United Fruit Company workers

events.enhanced_description: On December 21, 1928, the United States Congress approved the construction of Boulder Dam, which would later be renamed Hoover Dam. This monumental project was part of a broader effort to manage water resources and provide hydroelectric power in the American Southwest.
events.name: Approval of Boulder Dam construction

events.enhanced_description: In 1929, King Alexander of the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes suspended the constitution, establishing a dictatorship that centralized power and curtailed political freedoms. This move was part of a broader strategy to stabilize the kingdom amid rising ethnic tensions and political fragmentation.
events.name: Dictatorship in Yugoslavia

events.enhanced_description: In 1929, Albanian missionary sister Agnes Gonxha Bojaxhiu, later known as Mother Teresa, arrived in Kolkata from Ireland to begin her humanitarian work. Her dedication to serving the poor and sick would eventually lead to her becoming a global symbol of compassion and charity.
events.name: Arrival of Mother Teresa in Calcutta

events.enhanced_description: Union Airways Pty. Ltd. was founded in 1929, eventually becoming South African Airways by 1934. This establishment marked a significant development in the aviation industry in South Africa, contributing to the growth of air travel in the region.

image.caption: South African Airways Airbus A340-300 ZS-SXE taking off from Washington Dulles International Airport.
image.credit: Joe Ravi — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2011-10-05; not a photograph of the 1929 founding.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Union Airways Pty. Ltd. is founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1929, the Red Crescent was officially adopted as an additional emblem of the League of Red Cross Societies, symbolizing the organization's commitment to humanitarian aid across various cultures and religions. This decision marked an important step in the evolution of international humanitarian law.
events.name: The Red Crescent is adopted as an emblem

events.enhanced_description: In 1929, conscription in Australia officially ended, marking a significant shift in the country's military policy following World War I. This decision reflected changing attitudes towards military service and the role of the state in conscripting citizens.
events.name: Conscription in Australia Ends

events.enhanced_description: In 1929, slavery was officially abolished in Jordan, marking a significant step towards social reform in the region. This legislative change reflected broader trends in the Middle East and around the world towards the recognition of human rights.
events.name: Abolition of Slavery in Jordan

events.enhanced_description: The National Revolutionary Party (Partido Nacional Revolucionario) was established in Mexico by ex-President Plutarco Elías Calles, aiming to consolidate political power and influence in the post-revolutionary landscape. This party would dominate Mexican politics for decades under various names.
events.name: Establishment of the National Revolutionary Party

events.enhanced_description: On January 6, 1929, King Alexander of the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes suspended the constitution, initiating the 6 January Dictatorship. This authoritarian regime aimed to centralize power and suppress political opposition in the newly formed kingdom.
events.name: 6 January Dictatorship in Yugoslavia

events.enhanced_description: On January 10, 1929, Hergé's comic book hero Tintin made his first appearance in Tintin in the Land of the Soviets, serialized in the children's newspaper supplement Le Petit Vingtième. This marked the beginning of a beloved series that would become a cornerstone of European comic culture.
events.name: First appearance of Tintin

events.enhanced_description: On January 17, 1929, the comic strip character Popeye made his debut in Elzie Crisler Segar's Thimble Theatre. This introduction of the spinach-loving sailor would lead to a significant cultural phenomenon in American comic strips and animation.

image.caption: The first Popeye comic strip, published in the East Liverpool Review.
image.credit: E. C. Segar (1894–1938) — East Liverpool Review , 1929-01-17, p. 12
image.date_qualification: Depicted/published date: January 17, 1929 (not the 2025 upload date).
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: First appearance of Popeye

events.enhanced_description: On January 17, 1929, Kabul fell to the forces of Habibullah Kalakani, marking the beginning of a nine-month period of Saqqawist rule amid the ongoing Afghan Civil War. This event underscored the instability and power struggles within Afghanistan during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Fall of Kabul to Saqqawist forces

events.enhanced_description: On January 29, 1929, Erich Maria Remarque's novel All Quiet on the Western Front was published in book form. This powerful anti-war narrative provided a poignant perspective on the experiences of soldiers during World War I, resonating deeply with readers and critics alike.
events.name: Publication of All Quiet on the Western Front

events.enhanced_description: The Litvinov Pact was a significant diplomatic agreement signed in Moscow, where the Soviet Union, Poland, Estonia, Romania, and Latvia committed to resolving disputes through peaceful means rather than military force. This pact was part of a broader effort to stabilize relations in Eastern Europe during the interwar period.
events.name: Litvinov's Pact

events.enhanced_description: The Lateran Treaty was a landmark agreement between the Kingdom of Italy and the Holy See, establishing Vatican City as an independent sovereign state. This treaty resolved the longstanding 'Roman Question' regarding the political status of the papacy and its territories.
events.name: Lateran Treaty

events.enhanced_description: The Saint Valentine's Day Massacre was a notorious gangland shooting that took place in Chicago, where five members of a rival gang were murdered in a brutal attack attributed to the ongoing gang wars of the Prohibition era. This event highlighted the violent power struggles among organized crime groups in the city.

locations.name: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois, United States

events.name: Saint Valentine's Day Massacre

events.enhanced_description: The first battle of the Warlord Rebellion occurred in Zhifu, Shandong, where a large rebel force led by Zhang Zongchang faced off against National Revolutionary Army troops. The battle resulted in a decisive defeat for the rebels, marking a significant moment in the ongoing conflict between warlords and the Nationalist government.
events.name: First Battle of the Warlord Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: Grand Teton National Park was established by the United States Congress, preserving the stunning landscapes of the Teton Range and the surrounding ecosystems. This park has since become a vital area for conservation and recreation, attracting visitors from around the world.

locations.name: Grand Teton National Park, Wyoming, United States

events.name: Establishment of Grand Teton National Park

events.enhanced_description: The San Francisco Bay Toll-Bridge opened as the longest bridge in the world at the time, symbolizing a significant achievement in engineering and infrastructure. This bridge facilitated transportation and commerce across the San Francisco Bay, reshaping the region's connectivity.
events.name: Opening of the San Francisco Bay Toll-Bridge

events.enhanced_description: A revolt led by Generals José Gonzalo Escobar and Jesús María Aguirre in Mexico failed to achieve its objectives, reflecting the ongoing political instability and military conflicts in the country during this period. The revolt was part of the larger context of post-revolutionary Mexico.
events.name: Failed revolt by Generals Escobar and Aguirre

events.enhanced_description: Herbert Hoover was sworn in as the 31st president of the United States, taking office during a time of economic prosperity that would soon be overshadowed by the Great Depression. His presidency would be marked by significant challenges as the nation faced unprecedented economic turmoil.
events.name: Herbert Hoover sworn in as President

events.enhanced_description: The second Davos University Conference opened in Switzerland, featuring a notable philosophical debate between Ernst Cassirer and Martin Heidegger. This event highlighted the intellectual currents of the time and the clash between different philosophical perspectives.
events.name: Second Davos University Conference

events.enhanced_description: The withdrawal of Japanese forces from Shandong province to their garrison in Qingdao marked the end of the Jinan Incident, a conflict that arose from tensions between Chinese nationalists and foreign powers. This event was significant in the context of Japanese imperial ambitions in China.
events.name: End of the Jinan Incident

events.enhanced_description: Imperial Airways began operating the first commercial flights between London and Karachi, marking a significant development in international air travel. This service opened new avenues for commerce and connectivity between Europe and South Asia.
events.name: First commercial flights by Imperial Airways

events.enhanced_description: Persia signed the Litvinov Protocol, which was part of a series of agreements aimed at promoting peace and cooperation among nations in the aftermath of World War I. This protocol was significant in the context of international relations in the early 20th century.
events.name: Persia signs the Litvinov Protocol

events.enhanced_description: The first edition of the Monaco Grand Prix was held, establishing one of the most prestigious automobile races in the world. This event has since become a hallmark of motorsport, attracting top drivers and teams from around the globe.
events.name: First Monaco Grand Prix

events.enhanced_description: The 7.2 Mw Kopet Dag earthquake struck the Iran-Turkmenistan border region, causing widespread devastation and resulting in significant loss of life. With a maximum intensity of IX on the Mercalli scale, it highlighted the seismic risks in this geologically active area.
events.name: Kopet Dag earthquake

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Blood Alley was a violent confrontation between rival gangs in Sydney, Australia, reflecting the intense gang rivalries of the time. This event underscored the challenges of law enforcement in dealing with organized crime.
events.name: Battle of Blood Alley

events.enhanced_description: The first Academy Awards ceremony took place at the Hollywood Roosevelt Hotel, celebrating the best films of 1927 and 1928. This event marked the beginning of an annual tradition that would become a hallmark of the film industry.

locations.name: Hollywood, Los Angeles, California, United States

events.name: First Academy Awards

events.enhanced_description: The first Conference of the Communist Parties of Latin America was held in Buenos Aires, gathering various communist leaders to discuss strategies and solidarity among leftist movements in the region. This conference was significant in the context of the rising influence of communism in Latin America.
events.name: 1st Conference of the Communist Parties of Latin America

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Lima was signed to resolve a border dispute between Peru and Chile, establishing a framework for peaceful relations between the two nations. This treaty was a crucial step in stabilizing diplomatic ties in South America.
events.name: Treaty of Lima

events.enhanced_description: The ratification of the Lateran Treaty solidified Vatican City's status as a sovereign state, further entrenching the relationship between the Catholic Church and the Italian government. This event marked a significant moment in the history of church-state relations.
events.name: Ratification of the Lateran Treaty

events.enhanced_description: Ramsay MacDonald formed the second Labour government in the United Kingdom, marking a significant moment in British political history as the Labour Party sought to implement its policies during a time of economic uncertainty. This government faced numerous challenges, including the onset of the Great Depression.
events.name: Formation of the second Labour government

events.enhanced_description: An agreement brokered by U.S. Ambassador Dwight Whitney Morrow helped to bring an end to the Cristero War in Mexico, a conflict rooted in religious and political tensions. This resolution was significant in stabilizing the country after years of violence.
events.name: End of the Cristero War

events.enhanced_description: The first public demonstration of color television took place at Bell Telephone Laboratories in New York, showcasing the technological advancements in broadcasting. This event marked a pivotal moment in the evolution of television, paving the way for future developments in media.
events.name: First public demonstration of color TV

events.enhanced_description: The Kellogg–Briand Pact, signed by numerous leading world powers, officially went into effect on January 1, 1929, aiming to renounce war as a means of resolving conflicts. This landmark agreement was a significant step towards international diplomacy and peace efforts in the interwar period.
events.name: The Kellogg–Briand Pact goes into effect

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1929, Pope Pius XI made a historic appearance in St. Peter's Square, marking the end of nearly 60 years of the papacy's self-imposed isolation known as the 'Prisoner in the Vatican.' This event was witnessed by approximately 250,000 people and symbolized a new era for the Catholic Church.
events.name: Pope Pius XI emerges from the Apostolic Palace

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1929, the Geneva Convention was revised to address the treatment of prisoners of war, establishing important humanitarian standards. This convention aimed to ensure the humane treatment of individuals captured during armed conflicts, reflecting a growing international commitment to human rights.
events.name: The Geneva Convention addresses the treatment of prisoners of war

events.enhanced_description: On July 29, 1929, French Prime Minister Raymond Poincaré resigned, paving the way for Aristide Briand to take over leadership. This political shift was significant in the context of France's domestic and foreign policy during a tumultuous period in European history.
events.name: Raymond Poincaré resigns as French Prime Minister

events.enhanced_description: On August 8, 1929, the German rigid airship LZ 127 Graf Zeppelin embarked on a historic circumnavigation of the Northern Hemisphere, departing from Lakehurst, New Jersey. This journey included the first nonstop flight across the Pacific Ocean from Tokyo to Los Angeles, showcasing advancements in air travel.
events.name: LZ 127 Graf Zeppelin circumnavigates the Northern Hemisphere

events.enhanced_description: The Cannock Chase murders on August 13, 1929, involved the tragic deaths of three young girls in England, which shocked the nation and drew significant media attention. The case highlighted issues of child safety and the public's response to violent crime.
events.name: Cannock Chase murders

events.enhanced_description: On August 16, 1929, the 1929 Palestine riots erupted between Palestinians and Jews in Mandatory Palestine, resulting in significant violence and loss of life. The riots continued until the end of the month, with a total of 133 Jews and 116 Palestinians killed, highlighting the escalating tensions in the region.
events.name: The 1929 Palestine riots break out

events.enhanced_description: On August 23, 1929, the 1929 Hebron massacre occurred, resulting in the deaths of 65 to 68 Jews at the hands of Palestinians. This tragic event forced the remaining Jewish population to flee the city, further exacerbating tensions in the region during a period of violent conflict.

image.caption: Image identified as depicting a Jewish child victim of the 1929 Arab riots in Hebron.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — www.sephardiccouncil.org , IsraCast
image.date_qualification: Image date supplied as 1929; no more specific date is supported.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The 1929 Hebron massacre

events.enhanced_description: On August 29, 1929, during the ongoing Palestine riots, 18 to 20 Jews were killed in Safed by Palestinian Arabs. This incident was part of a broader wave of violence that characterized the region during this tumultuous period.
events.name: The 1929 Palestine riots: Jews killed in Safed

events.enhanced_description: On August 31, 1929, the Young Plan was finalized, establishing the total reparations owed by Germany after World War I at $26.35 billion to be paid over 58.5 years. This plan aimed to ease the financial burden on Germany and stabilize the post-war economy.
events.name: The Young Plan is finalized

events.enhanced_description: On September 3, 1929, the Dow Jones Industrial Average reached a peak of 381.17, a record it would not surpass until November 1954. This peak was indicative of the economic prosperity of the late 1920s, just before the onset of the Great Depression.

image.caption: Logarithmic graph of the Dow Jones Industrial Average’s historical values.
image.credit: Lalala666 at English Wikipedia — Transferred from en.wikipedia to Commons.
image.date_qualification: A retrospective graph of index values, not a contemporary photograph of the 1929 peak. The original upload date is not a depicted date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: The Dow Jones Industrial Average peaks

events.enhanced_description: On September 5, 1929, Aristide Briand presented his ambitious plan for the United States of Europe, advocating for greater political and economic unity among European nations. This proposal was part of a broader vision for peace and cooperation in the aftermath of World War I.
events.name: Aristide Briand presents his plan for the United States of Europe

events.enhanced_description: On September 7, 1929, the steamship SS Kuru sank in Lake Näsijärvi near Tampere, Finland, resulting in the tragic drowning of 138 people. This disaster highlighted the dangers of maritime travel and prompted discussions on safety regulations.
events.name: The steamship SS Kuru sank

events.enhanced_description: On September 17, 1929, a coup d'état ousted Augustinas Voldemaras from his position as Prime Minister of Lithuania, replacing him with Juozas Tūbelis, the brother-in-law of President Antanas Smetona. This political shift reflected the instability in Lithuanian politics during the interwar period.

image.caption: Portrait of Lithuanian Prime Minister Augustinas Voldemaras.
image.credit: George Grantham Bain Collection (Library of Congress) — This image is available from the United States Library of Congress 's Prints and Photographs division under the digital ID ggbain.34434 . This tag does not indicate the copyright status of the attached work. A normal copyright tag is still required. See Commons:Licensing .
image.date_qualification: Depicted date unrecorded; the upload date is not the image date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: A coup ousts Augustinas Voldemaras in Lithuania

events.enhanced_description: On September 30, 1929, Fritz von Opel piloted the Opel RAK.1, the first rocket-powered aircraft, in front of a large crowd in Frankfurt am Main. This pioneering flight marked a significant milestone in aviation history and the development of rocket technology.
events.name: Fritz von Opel pilots the first rocket-powered aircraft

events.enhanced_description: On October 3, 1929, the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes officially changed its name to the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. This rebranding was part of a broader effort to unify the diverse ethnic groups within the kingdom under a single national identity.

locations.historical_name: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes
locations.name: Belgrade, Belgrade, Serbia

events.name: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes changes name to Kingdom of Yugoslavia

events.enhanced_description: On October 6, 1929, Serie A was established as the top-class professional football league in Italy, replacing the previous Divisione Nazionale. This change marked a significant development in Italian football, leading to the formation of a more structured league system.
events.name: Serie A replaces Divisione Nazionale

events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1929, the Australian federal election resulted in a victory for the Labor Party, led by James Scullin, over the Nationalist/Country Coalition Government, headed by Prime Minister Stanley Bruce. This election was notable for being the first instance in Australian history where a sitting prime minister lost his own seat.
events.name: 1929 Australian federal election

events.enhanced_description: On October 13, 1929, the Afghan Civil War came to an end, concluding a period of significant internal conflict in Afghanistan. This resolution was crucial for the stability of the country and set the stage for future political developments.

image.caption: Animated map of the Afghan Civil War of 1928–1929, showing Saqqawist and anti-Saqqawist forces.
image.credit: Koopinator — Own work , Information from Kabul under siege: Fayz Muhammad's account of the 1929 Uprising
image.date_qualification: Created 2019-09-20; depicts the 1928–1929 civil war.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Afghan Civil War ends

events.enhanced_description: In the landmark case of Edwards v. Canada (Attorney General), the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council ruled that women are considered 'persons' under the British North America Acts, allowing them eligibility for appointment to the Senate of Canada. This pivotal decision was a significant victory for women's rights in Canada, championed by the Famous Five, a group of women activists.
events.name: Edwards v. Canada (Attorney General)

events.enhanced_description: On October 22, 1929, the government of Aristide Briand fell in France, marking a significant political shift during a turbulent period in French politics. Briand, a prominent statesman known for his efforts in promoting peace in Europe, faced challenges that ultimately led to his resignation.
events.name: Fall of Aristide Briand's government

events.enhanced_description: The Wall Street Crash of 1929, which began on October 24, saw three significant drops in stock prices that wiped out more than $30 billion from the New York Stock Exchange. This catastrophic event marked the beginning of the Great Depression, profoundly impacting the global economy.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Wall Street Crash of 1929

events.enhanced_description: On October 25, 1929, former U.S. Interior Secretary Albert B. Fall was convicted of bribery for his involvement in the Teapot Dome scandal, becoming the first cabinet member in U.S. history to be imprisoned for actions taken while in office. This scandal highlighted issues of corruption and mismanagement within the federal government.
events.name: Albert B. Fall Convicted

events.enhanced_description: In November 1929, Vladimir Zworykin took out the first patent for color television, marking a significant advancement in broadcasting technology. This invention laid the groundwork for the development of color television, which would revolutionize the media landscape.
events.name: Patent for Color Television

events.enhanced_description: On November 1, 1929, an annual solar eclipse was observed over the Atlantic Ocean and parts of Africa. Such astronomical events have historically captivated human interest and contributed to advancements in the understanding of celestial mechanics.
events.name: Annual Solar Eclipse

events.enhanced_description: On November 7, 1929, the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) opened its doors to the public in New York City. The inaugural exhibition featured works by renowned artists such as Cézanne, Gauguin, van Gogh, and Seurat, attracting 47,000 visitors and establishing MoMA as a leading institution in modern art.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Opening of the Museum of Modern Art

events.enhanced_description: On November 15, 1929, the film 'Atlantic', a drama about the sinking of the RMS Titanic, was released in the United Kingdom. This film was notable for its simultaneous German-language version, marking a significant moment in the history of sound films.
events.name: Release of 'Atlantic'

events.enhanced_description: On November 18, 1929, the Grand Banks earthquake struck off the coast of Newfoundland, Canada. This significant seismic event caused considerable damage and triggered a tsunami, impacting coastal communities and highlighting the region's vulnerability to natural disasters.
events.name: 1929 Grand Banks Earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On November 29, 1929, Bernt Balchen, U.S. Admiral Richard E. Byrd, Captain Ashley McKinley, and Harold June made history by becoming the first individuals to fly over the South Pole. This monumental achievement in aviation and exploration expanded the boundaries of human knowledge about the polar regions.
events.name: First Flight Over the South Pole

events.enhanced_description: On December 27, 1929, Soviet General Secretary Joseph Stalin ordered the 'liquidation of the kulaks as a class', initiating a campaign against wealthier peasants in the Soviet Union. This brutal policy aimed to consolidate state control over agriculture and led to widespread repression and suffering.
events.name: Liquidation of the Kulaks

events.enhanced_description: On December 28, 1929, known as 'Black Saturday', New Zealand colonial police killed 11 unarmed demonstrators in Samoa. This tragic event galvanized the Mau movement, which sought independence for Samoa, highlighting the tensions between colonial authorities and indigenous populations.

image.caption: New Zealand police in Samoa during the Mau movement.
image.credit: Alfred John Tattersall (1861 - 1951) — http://mp.natlib.govt.nz/detail/?id=27816&l=en
image.date_qualification: Circa 1930; the image date does not establish that it depicts the events of 28 December 1929.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Black Saturday in Samoa

events.enhanced_description: On December 29, 1929, the All India Congress convened in Lahore, where it formally demanded Indian independence from British rule. This pivotal moment in the Indian independence movement marked a significant escalation in the struggle for self-governance.
events.name: All India Congress in Lahore

events.enhanced_description: In early 1930, Mahatma Gandhi informed the British Viceroy of India that a campaign of civil disobedience would commence the following week, marking a pivotal moment in the Indian independence movement. This announcement set the stage for widespread protests against British rule.
events.name: Civil Disobedience Announcement

events.enhanced_description: In 1930, André Tardieu began his second term as Prime Minister of France, a role he had previously held during a tumultuous period marked by economic challenges and political instability. His leadership was characterized by efforts to stabilize the French economy.
events.name: André Tardieu's Second Term

events.enhanced_description: In 1930, the first frozen foods developed by Clarence Birdseye went on sale in Springfield, Massachusetts. This innovation revolutionized food preservation and distribution, paving the way for the modern frozen food industry.
events.name: First Frozen Foods Sale

events.enhanced_description: In 1930, the International Left Opposition (ILO) was founded in Paris, France, as a faction within the Communist movement that opposed the policies of the Soviet Union under Joseph Stalin. This organization aimed to promote a more democratic and internationalist approach to socialism.
events.name: International Left Opposition Founded

events.enhanced_description: The Turkestan–Siberia Railway was completed in 1930, connecting Central Asia with Siberia and facilitating trade and transportation across the region. This railway was a significant infrastructure project that contributed to the economic development of the Soviet Union.
events.name: Turkestan–Siberia Railway Completion

events.enhanced_description: The construction of the Boulder Dam, later known as the Hoover Dam, began in 1930 on the Colorado River, a monumental engineering project aimed at providing hydroelectric power and water management for the southwestern United States.
events.name: Construction of Boulder Dam

events.enhanced_description: In 1930, Cecil George Paine, a pathologist at the Sheffield Royal Infirmary, achieved the first recorded cure of an eye infection using penicillin. This groundbreaking achievement marked a significant milestone in the development of antibiotics and their medical applications.
events.name: Cecil George Paine's Penicillin Cure

events.enhanced_description: In 1930, Bernhard Schmidt invented the Schmidt camera, a type of catadioptric telescope that uses a combination of lenses and mirrors to produce wide-field images. This invention has had a lasting impact on astronomical photography and observation.
events.name: Invention of the Schmidt Camera

events.enhanced_description: On January 15, 1930, the Moon reached its nearest point to Earth, known as perigee, coinciding with its fullest phase. This event marked a significant astronomical occurrence, with the Moon being at a distance of 356,397 km from Earth.
events.name: Perigee of the Moon

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1930, the Indian National Congress declared this date as Independence Day, or Purna Swaraj, symbolizing the demand for complete independence from British rule. This declaration was a pivotal moment in the Indian independence movement.

image.caption: Retrospective illustration of the Indian National Congress moving toward independence.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — http://www.columbia.edu/itc/mealac/pritchett/00routesdata/1900_1999/partition/negotiations/negotiations.html
image.date_qualification: Image dated 1929; the event described is dated 26 January 1930.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Independence Day Declared by Indian National Congress

events.enhanced_description: On January 28, 1930, the first patent for a field-effect transistor was granted to Julius Edgar Lilienfeld in the United States. This invention laid the foundation for modern electronics and semiconductor technology.
events.name: First Patent for Field-Effect Transistor

events.enhanced_description: On January 30, 1930, Pavel Molchanov launched a radiosonde from Slutsk in the Soviet Union, marking a significant advancement in meteorological technology. This device allowed for the collection of atmospheric data, enhancing weather forecasting capabilities.
events.name: Radiosonde Launch by Pavel Molchanov

events.enhanced_description: On February 10, 1930, the Việt Nam Quốc Dân Đảng launched the Yên Bái mutiny in an attempt to end French colonial rule in Vietnam. This uprising was a significant event in the struggle for Vietnamese independence and highlighted the growing nationalist sentiment.
events.name: Yên Bái Mutiny

events.enhanced_description: On February 18, 1930, Clyde Tombaugh confirmed the existence of Pluto while studying photographs taken earlier in the month. This discovery expanded our understanding of the solar system and Pluto was classified as a planet until its reclassification as a dwarf planet in 2006.
events.name: Discovery of Pluto

events.enhanced_description: On March 2, 1930, Mahatma Gandhi informed the British Viceroy of India that a campaign of civil disobedience would commence the following week. This announcement marked a pivotal moment in the Indian independence movement, as Gandhi sought to challenge British authority through nonviolent resistance.
events.name: Gandhi's Civil Disobedience Announcement

events.enhanced_description: On March 6, 1930, International Unemployment Day was observed in various countries around the world, highlighting the global economic crisis and the struggles faced by unemployed individuals during the Great Depression. This day served as a platform for advocating workers' rights and social justice.
events.name: International Unemployment Day

events.enhanced_description: On March 12, 1930, Mahatma Gandhi commenced a 200-mile march to the Arabian Sea at Dandi to protest the British monopoly on salt, symbolizing the Indian struggle for independence. This act of civil disobedience galvanized the Indian populace and drew international attention to the Indian independence movement.
events.name: Salt March

events.enhanced_description: On March 28, 1930, the Turkish government formally requested that the international community recognize 'Istanbul' and 'Ankara' as the official names for the historically known 'Constantinople' and 'Angora', respectively. This request marked a significant step in the modernization and national identity of Turkey.
events.name: Request for Name Change

events.enhanced_description: On March 29, 1930, Heinrich Brüning was appointed Chancellor of Germany during a period marked by economic turmoil and political instability. His policies aimed at addressing the Great Depression would lead to significant changes in German politics.
events.name: Appointment of Heinrich Brüning

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1930, the Motion Picture Production Code, commonly known as the Hays Code, was instituted by film studios in the United States. This code imposed strict guidelines on the portrayal of sex, crime, religion, and violence in films, significantly shaping American cinema for the next four decades.
events.name: Hays Code Instituted

events.enhanced_description: On April 6, 1930, Mahatma Gandhi made salt from seawater at Dandi, directly violating British salt laws in a bold act of civil disobedience. This act symbolized the Indian struggle for independence and inspired many to join the movement.
events.name: Gandhi's Salt Law Violation

events.enhanced_description: On April 17, 1930, DuPont announced the invention of neoprene, a synthetic rubber that would have a profound impact on various industries, including automotive and consumer goods. This innovation marked a significant advancement in materials science.
events.name: Invention of Neoprene

events.enhanced_description: The Chittagong Rebellion began on April 18, 1930, with the Chittagong armoury raid, where revolutionaries attempted to seize arms to fight against British colonial rule in India. This event was a significant moment in the Indian independence movement.
events.name: Chittagong Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On April 21, 1930, a devastating fire at the Ohio Penitentiary in Columbus resulted in the deaths of 320 inmates, making it one of the deadliest prison fires in U.S. history. The tragedy raised questions about prison safety and management.

image.caption: Historic view of the Ohio Penitentiary in Columbus.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — https://digital-collections.columbuslibrary.org/digital/collection/ohio/id/15146
image.date_qualification: The image depicts the penitentiary site circa 1897, decades before the 1930 fire; it is contextual site imagery, not a photograph of the fire.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Ohio Penitentiary Fire

events.enhanced_description: On April 22, 1930, the United Kingdom, Japan, and the United States signed the London Naval Treaty, aimed at regulating submarine warfare and limiting naval shipbuilding. This treaty was part of broader efforts to promote peace and stability in the interwar period.
events.name: London Naval Treaty

events.enhanced_description: On May 6, 1930, a powerful 7.1 magnitude earthquake struck northwestern Iran and southeastern Turkey, resulting in widespread destruction and an estimated 3,000 fatalities. This disaster highlighted the region's vulnerability to seismic activity.
events.name: Salmas Earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1930, the National Pan-Hellenic Council was founded in Washington, D.C., as a collaborative organization for the nine historically African American sororities and fraternities. This council aimed to promote unity and support among these organizations.
events.name: National Pan-Hellenic Council Founded

events.enhanced_description: On May 15, 1930, nurse Ellen Church became the world's first flight attendant while working for Boeing Air Transport. Her role marked the beginning of a new profession in the aviation industry, enhancing passenger safety and comfort.
events.name: First Flight Attendant

events.enhanced_description: On May 16, 1930, Rafael Trujillo was elected president of the Dominican Republic, marking the beginning of his long and controversial rule characterized by authoritarianism and repression.
events.name: Rafael Trujillo Elected

events.enhanced_description: On May 17, 1930, French Prime Minister André Tardieu announced the withdrawal of the remaining French troops from the Rhineland, a significant step in post-World War I relations between France and Germany.
events.name: Withdrawal from the Rhineland

events.enhanced_description: On May 24, 1930, Amy Johnson landed in Darwin, Australia, becoming the first woman to fly solo from England to Australia, a remarkable achievement in aviation history that showcased her pioneering spirit and determination.
events.name: Amy Johnson's Solo Flight

events.enhanced_description: On June 7, 1930, Carl Gustaf Ekman became Prime Minister of Sweden for the second and final time, leading the country during a period of economic challenges and political change.
events.name: Carl Gustaf Ekman's Second Term

events.enhanced_description: On June 14, 1930, the Federal Bureau of Narcotics was established under the United States Department of the Treasury, replacing the Narcotics Division of the Prohibition Unit. This agency was tasked with regulating and enforcing drug laws in the U.S.
events.name: Federal Bureau of Narcotics Established

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1930, President Herbert Hoover signed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act into law, which raised duties on numerous imports to protect American industries during the Great Depression. The act is often criticized for exacerbating the economic downturn by prompting retaliatory tariffs from other countries.
events.name: Smoot–Hawley Tariff Act

events.enhanced_description: The First Eastern Women's Congress took place on July 3, 1930, in Damascus, Syria, bringing together women from various Eastern countries to discuss issues related to women's rights and social reform. This event marked a significant step in the women's movement in the region.
events.name: First Eastern Women's Congress

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1930, the dedication ceremony for the sculpted head of George Washington at Mount Rushmore took place, a monumental project led by sculptor Gutzon Borglum. This iconic site symbolizes American democracy and has become a national landmark.

locations.name: Mount Rushmore, South Dakota, United States

events.name: Dedication of George Washington's head at Mount Rushmore

events.enhanced_description: The Seventh Lambeth Conference of Anglican bishops opened on July 5, 1930, in Canterbury, England. This conference was notable for approving the use of birth control in limited circumstances, reflecting a shift in the Church's stance on family planning.
events.name: Seventh Lambeth Conference

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1930, the far-right Lapua Movement conducted a march in Helsinki, Finland, showcasing their growing influence in Finnish politics. The movement was known for its nationalist and anti-communist sentiments during a period of political instability.
events.name: Lapua Movement March

events.enhanced_description: On July 11, 1930, Australian cricketer Don Bradman scored a world record 309 runs in a single day during a Test match against England, ultimately achieving the highest individual Test innings of 334. This performance solidified his reputation as one of cricket's greatest players.
events.name: Don Bradman's World Record

events.enhanced_description: The first FIFA World Cup commenced on July 13, 1930, with Lucien Laurent scoring the first goal for France against Mexico. This inaugural tournament marked a significant milestone in the history of international football.
events.name: First FIFA World Cup

events.enhanced_description: On July 19, 1930, Georges Simenon's detective character Inspector Jules Maigret made his first appearance in print in the serialized novel 'Pietr-le-Letton' in a French weekly magazine. This character would go on to become one of the most famous figures in detective fiction.
events.name: Inspector Maigret's First Appearance

events.enhanced_description: On July 28, 1930, R. B. Bennett defeated William Lyon Mackenzie King in the federal elections, becoming the Prime Minister of Canada. His leadership would be marked by challenges related to the Great Depression.
events.name: R. B. Bennett Becomes Prime Minister

events.enhanced_description: On July 29, 1930, the British airship R100 embarked on a successful 78-hour passage to Canada, showcasing advancements in air travel technology during the interwar period. This journey was part of efforts to explore the potential of airships for transatlantic travel.

image.caption: The English airship R100 moored at a mast in Canada.
image.credit: Theodor Horydczak — U.S. Library of Congress
image.date_qualification: The image shows R100 at its Canadian mooring site during 1930; it is not established as a photograph of the transatlantic passage itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: British Airship R100 Passage

events.enhanced_description: On July 30, 1930, Uruguay defeated Argentina 4–2 to win the first FIFA World Cup final at Estadio Centenario in Montevideo. This historic match marked the culmination of the inaugural tournament and established Uruguay as a football powerhouse.
events.name: First FIFA World Cup Final

events.enhanced_description: On August 7, 1930, R. B. Bennett officially took office as the eleventh Prime Minister of Canada, succeeding William Lyon Mackenzie King. His tenure would be marked by the challenges of the Great Depression.
events.name: R. B. Bennett Takes Office

events.enhanced_description: On August 12, 1930, Turkish troops moved into Persia to combat Kurdish insurgents, reflecting the ongoing tensions and conflicts in the region during this period. This military action was part of Turkey's efforts to maintain control over its borders.
events.name: Turkish Troops in Persia

events.enhanced_description: The first British Empire Games opened on August 16, 1930, in Hamilton, Ontario, Canada, featuring athletes from various countries of the British Empire. This event laid the foundation for what would later become the Commonwealth Games.
events.name: First British Empire Games

events.enhanced_description: On August 27, 1930, a military junta took control in Peru, marking a significant shift in the country's political landscape. This coup was part of a broader trend of military interventions in Latin America during this period.
events.name: Military Junta in Peru

events.enhanced_description: On September 3, 1930, the San Zenón hurricane struck the Caribbean, causing widespread destruction in Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic. This devastating storm highlighted the vulnerability of Caribbean nations to natural disasters.
events.name: San Zenón Hurricane

events.enhanced_description: On September 6, 1930, José Félix Uriburu led a military coup in Argentina, overthrowing President Hipólito Yrigoyen. This coup marked the beginning of a series of military governments in Argentina during the early 20th century.
events.name: 1930 Argentine Coup d'état

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1930, Scotch Tape, invented by Richard Gurley Drew, was sold by the 3M company for the first time in the United States. This innovative adhesive tape would become a staple in households and industries worldwide.
events.name: Invention of Scotch Tape

events.enhanced_description: On September 14, 1930, the German federal election resulted in the National Socialists winning 107 seats in the Reichstag, making them the second largest party. This election was a pivotal moment in the rise of the Nazi Party in Germany.
events.name: 1930 German Federal Election

events.enhanced_description: On September 17, 1930, Turkish forces suppressed the Kurdish Ararat rebellion, which was part of a broader conflict involving Kurdish nationalism and Turkish state authority. This suppression highlighted the ongoing ethnic tensions in the region.
events.name: Suppression of the Kurdish Ararat Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On September 20, 1930, the Eastern Catholic Rite Syro-Malankara Catholic Church was formed, representing a significant development in the history of Eastern Catholicism. This church emerged from the Syro-Malabar Catholic Church and sought to maintain its traditions while being in communion with the Pope.
events.name: Formation of Syro-Malankara Catholic Church

events.enhanced_description: On September 27, 1930, İsmet İnönü formed a new government in Turkey, marking the sixth government since the establishment of the Republic. His leadership was characterized by efforts to modernize Turkey and navigate the challenges of the interwar period.
events.name: İsmet İnönü Forms New Government

events.enhanced_description: In October 1930, the Indochinese Communist Party was formed in Hanoi, Vietnam, marking a significant step in the Vietnamese struggle for independence from colonial rule. This party would later play a crucial role in the fight against French colonialism and the establishment of a communist government in Vietnam.
events.name: Formation of the Indochinese Communist Party

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1930, British rule over Weihaiwei, a territory leased to the United Kingdom, officially ended as it was returned to China. This event marked the conclusion of foreign colonial control in the region, reflecting the broader trend of decolonization in the early 20th century.
events.name: End of British rule of Weihaiwei

events.enhanced_description: On October 3, 1930, the German Socialist Labour Party in Poland – Left was founded in Łódź following a split in the German Socialist Workers' Party. This event highlighted the political fragmentation within the socialist movement in Poland during a time of rising tensions and economic challenges.
events.name: Founding of the German Socialist Labour Party in Poland – Left

events.enhanced_description: On October 5, 1930, the British airship R101, the world's largest flying craft at the time, tragically crashed in France during its maiden overseas voyage to India. The disaster resulted in the loss of 48 lives, including Britain's Air Minister, Christopher Thomson, highlighting the risks associated with early air travel.
events.name: Crash of British airship R101

events.enhanced_description: On October 14, 1930, Kaarlo Juho Ståhlberg, the first President of Finland, and his wife, Ester, were kidnapped from their home in Helsinki by members of the far-right Lapua Movement. They were released unharmed, but the incident underscored the political tensions and extremist movements in Finland during this period.
events.name: Kidnapping of Kaarlo Juho Ståhlberg

events.enhanced_description: On October 20, 1930, the British government issued the Passfield white paper, which called for restrictions on Jewish immigration into Mandatory Palestine. This document was a response to growing tensions between Jewish and Arab communities and reflected the complexities of British colonial policy in the region.
events.name: British Passfield white paper

events.enhanced_description: On October 24, 1930, Getúlio Vargas led a successful coup against President Washington Luís, marking the beginning of the Vargas Era in Brazil. This revolution was fueled by widespread discontent with the political elite and economic instability, leading to significant changes in Brazilian governance.

locations.name: Rio de Janeiro, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

events.name: Brazilian Revolution of 1930

events.enhanced_description: On October 27, 1930, ratifications were exchanged in London for the first London Naval Treaty, which modified the Washington Naval Treaty of 1922. This treaty aimed to limit naval armaments among the major powers and was a response to the escalating naval arms race of the time.
events.name: First London Naval Treaty Ratifications

events.enhanced_description: On November 2, 1930, Haile Selassie was crowned Emperor of Ethiopia in a grand ceremony in Addis Ababa. His reign would become symbolic of African independence and resistance against colonialism, particularly during the Italian invasion of Ethiopia in the 1930s.
events.name: Crowning of Haile Selassie

events.enhanced_description: On November 3, 1930, Getúlio Vargas officially assumed the presidency of Brazil following his successful coup against Washington Luís. His presidency would be marked by significant social and economic reforms, as well as authoritarian measures.

locations.name: Rio de Janeiro, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

events.name: Getúlio Vargas becomes President of Brazil

events.enhanced_description: On November 25, 1930, a devastating earthquake struck the Izu Peninsula in Japan, resulting in the deaths of 223 people and the destruction of approximately 650 buildings. This natural disaster highlighted the seismic vulnerabilities of the region, which is known for its geological activity.
events.name: Izu Peninsula Earthquake

events.enhanced_description: The Futian incident in December 1930 involved a purge within the Chinese Red Army, where suspected traitors were executed in a brutal crackdown. This event illustrated the internal conflicts and power struggles within the Communist Party during the Chinese Civil War.
events.name: Futian incident

events.enhanced_description: In December 1930, Turkey granted all adult women the right to vote in elections, a significant step towards gender equality in the country. This reform was part of a series of progressive changes implemented by Mustafa Kemal Atatürk's government in the early years of the Republic.
events.name: Turkish Women's Right to Vote

events.enhanced_description: On December 19, 1930, Mount Merapi, one of Indonesia's most active volcanoes, erupted, resulting in the destruction of numerous villages and the tragic loss of approximately 1,300 lives. This eruption underscored the geological hazards faced by communities living near active volcanoes.
events.name: Eruption of Mount Merapi

events.enhanced_description: The Menemen Incident on December 23, 1930, was a revolt by Islamist factions against the secularization policies of the Turkish government. This uprising underscored the tensions between secular and religious forces in Turkey during the early years of the Republic.
events.name: Menemen Incident

events.enhanced_description: On December 24, 1930, inventor Harry Grindell Matthews demonstrated his innovative device designed to project images onto clouds in London. This invention showcased the creative possibilities of early 20th-century technology and garnered public interest.
events.name: Harry Grindell Matthews' Cloud Projection Device

events.enhanced_description: On December 29, 1930, Sir Muhammad Iqbal delivered a pivotal presidential address in Allahabad, introducing the two-nation theory which laid the groundwork for the creation of Pakistan. His vision significantly influenced the political landscape of the Indian subcontinent.

image.caption: Portrait of Muhammad Iqbal, British-Indian philosopher, poet and politician.
image.credit: Iqbal Academy Pakistan
image.date_qualification: The image is identified as a depiction of Iqbal, with a latest possible date of 1938; it is a portrait, not evidence of the 1930 Allahabad Address itself. The original image date is given as “by 1938.”
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Sir Muhammad Iqbal's Presidential Address

events.enhanced_description: On December 31, 1930, Pope Pius XI issued the encyclical Casti Connubii, which emphasized the sanctity of marriage and prohibited Roman Catholics from using artificial birth control. This document reaffirmed the Catholic Church's stance on family and moral issues.
events.name: Papal Encyclical Casti Connubii

events.enhanced_description: The Iowa Cow War in 1931 was a conflict between farmers and state authorities over the enforcement of bovine tuberculosis testing regulations. This dispute highlighted the tensions between agricultural practices and government intervention during the Great Depression.
events.name: Iowa Cow War

events.enhanced_description: In early 1931, the Chinese Communist Party achieved a significant military victory against the Nationalist Kuomintang forces, marking a pivotal moment in the Chinese Civil War. This defeat weakened the Kuomintang's control and emboldened the Communist forces, setting the stage for further conflicts.
events.name: The Chinese Communists inflict a sharp defeat on the Kuomintang forces

events.enhanced_description: From June to November 1931, catastrophic flooding of the Yangtze and Huai Rivers devastated large areas of China, resulting in an estimated 422,000 deaths. The floods caused widespread destruction, leading to famine and disease in the affected regions.
events.name: June–November 1931 China flood

events.enhanced_description: In 1931, anti-Chinese riots erupted in Pyongyang, resulting in the deaths of approximately 127 Chinese individuals and injuries to 393 others. The violence reflected the rising tensions between Korean residents and the Chinese community during a period of nationalistic fervor.
events.name: Anti-Chinese rioting in Pyongyang

events.enhanced_description: The Geneva Convention of 1929, which established standards for the treatment of prisoners of war, officially entered into force in 1931. This convention marked a significant advancement in international humanitarian law.
events.name: Geneva Convention (1929) enters into force

events.enhanced_description: In 1931, the Red China News Agency, a predecessor of the Xinhua News Agency, was officially founded in Ruijin, Jiangxi Province. This agency played a crucial role in disseminating information and propaganda during the Chinese Communist Party's rise to power.
events.name: Foundation of the Red China News Agency

events.enhanced_description: In 1931, the Panama Canal was closed for a couple of weeks due to damage caused by earthquakes. This incident highlighted the vulnerabilities of significant infrastructure to natural disasters.

image.caption: Map of the Panama Canal, English version.
image.credit: Thoroe — Own work Map created using: Generic Mapping Tools (GMT) with SRTM3 V2 data OpenStreetMap data File:CanalZone.gif File:Panama Canal Rough Diagram-non annotated.png Proposal for the expansion of the Panama Canal Panama Canal Profile Map
image.date_qualification: Map created in 2012; it provides geographic context, not a depiction of the 1931 earthquake-related closure.

events.name: Closure of the Panama Canal Due to Earthquakes

events.enhanced_description: On February 4, 1931, Soviet leader Joseph Stalin delivered a pivotal speech advocating for rapid industrialization in the Soviet Union. He emphasized the need to close the technological gap with advanced nations, asserting that failure to do so would lead to the country's downfall in future conflicts.
events.name: Stalin's Speech on Industrialization

events.enhanced_description: The official inauguration ceremonies for New Delhi as the capital of India commenced on February 10, 1931. This marked a significant transition in the administrative center of British India, symbolizing a new era in governance.
events.name: Inauguration of New Delhi

events.enhanced_description: On February 16, 1931, Pehr Evind Svinhufvud was elected as the president of Finland. His presidency would play a crucial role in navigating Finland through the challenges of the interwar period.
events.name: Election of Pehr Evind Svinhufvud

events.enhanced_description: On February 21, 1931, Peruvian revolutionaries hijacked a Ford Trimotor aeroplane, demanding that the pilot drop propaganda leaflets over Lima. This act was part of a broader revolutionary movement against the government.
events.name: Aeroplane Hijacking in Peru

events.enhanced_description: On March 5, 1931, the British viceroy of India and Mohandas Gandhi signed the Gandhi–Irwin Pact, which marked a significant step towards Indian independence by addressing civil disobedience and political negotiations.
events.name: Gandhi–Irwin Pact

events.enhanced_description: The Finnish Parliament House was officially opened on March 7, 1931, serving as the seat of the Finnish Parliament and symbolizing the country's democratic governance.
events.name: Opening of the Finnish Parliament House

events.enhanced_description: On March 11, 1931, the Soviet Union introduced the Ready for Labour and Defence of the USSR programme, known as GTO, aimed at promoting physical fitness and preparedness among citizens.
events.name: Introduction of GTO Programme

events.enhanced_description: On March 23, 1931, Indian revolutionary leaders Bhagat Singh, Shivaram Rajguru, and Sukhdev Thapar were hanged for their involvement in a conspiracy to murder, igniting widespread protests and furthering the independence movement.
events.name: Execution of Indian Revolutionaries

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1931, a devastating earthquake struck Managua, Nicaragua, resulting in the deaths of approximately 2,000 people and causing widespread destruction in the city.
events.name: Earthquake in Managua

events.enhanced_description: On April 1, 1931, the Kuomintang government launched the Second Encirclement Campaign against the Jiangxi Soviet, aiming to eliminate Communist forces in the region. This campaign was part of the ongoing Chinese Civil War.
events.name: Second Encirclement Campaign

events.enhanced_description: On April 6, 1931, the Portuguese government declared martial law in Madeira and the Azores in response to the Madeira uprising in Funchal, reflecting the political unrest in the region.
events.name: Martial Law in Portugal

events.enhanced_description: On April 12, 1931, municipal elections in Spain were held, which were interpreted as a referendum on the monarchy. The elections resulted in a significant victory for republican parties, paving the way for political change.
events.name: Municipal Elections in Spain

events.enhanced_description: On April 14, 1931, the Second Spanish Republic was proclaimed in Madrid following the municipal elections. This event marked a significant shift in Spanish politics and governance.
events.name: Proclamation of the Second Spanish Republic
