events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1933, Franklin D. Roosevelt was inaugurated as the 32nd president of the United States, delivering his famous line, 'The only thing we have to fear is fear itself.' This marked the beginning of his 'first 100 days' and significant New Deal reforms.
events.name: Franklin D. Roosevelt's inauguration

events.enhanced_description: On March 5, 1933, President Franklin D. Roosevelt declared a 'Bank holiday,' closing all banks in the United States to prevent further financial collapse during the Great Depression. This action was part of his broader strategy to stabilize the economy.
events.name: Bank holiday declaration

events.enhanced_description: The real-estate trading board game Monopoly was invented in the United States in 1933, becoming one of the most popular board games in history. Its gameplay reflects economic principles and has been enjoyed by millions worldwide.
events.name: Monopoly game invention

events.enhanced_description: On March 10, 1933, a 6.4 magnitude earthquake struck Long Beach, California, causing significant damage and resulting in 115 fatalities. The earthquake underscored the seismic risks in Southern California and prompted improvements in building codes.
events.name: Long Beach earthquake

events.enhanced_description: Giuseppe Zangara, who attempted to assassinate President Franklin D. Roosevelt, was executed in the electric chair at Florida State Prison. His assassination attempt occurred on February 15, 1933, but he was convicted and executed within a month, highlighting the urgency and severity of political violence during this period.
events.name: Execution of Giuseppe Zangara

events.enhanced_description: On March 12, 1933, Franklin D. Roosevelt delivered his first 'Fireside chat,' addressing the American public directly via radio. This innovative communication strategy helped to build public trust and support for his New Deal policies during the Great Depression.
events.name: Fireside chat

events.enhanced_description: On March 14, 1933, the Indonesian football club Persib Bandung was founded, originally known as Bandoeng Inlandsche Voetbal Bond. The club has since become one of the most successful and popular football teams in Indonesia.
events.name: Persib Bandung founded

events.enhanced_description: On March 15, 1933, the Dow Jones Industrial Average experienced a remarkable rise from 53.84 to 62.10, marking a 15.34% gain, the largest one-day percentage increase in the index's history during the Great Depression. This event signaled a potential turning point in the economic crisis.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Dow Jones Industrial Average rise

events.enhanced_description: Dachau, the first Nazi concentration camp, was completed on March 20, 1933, and opened on March 22 to detain political prisoners. It became a model for subsequent camps and a symbol of the Nazi regime's brutal repression.
events.name: Dachau concentration camp completion

events.enhanced_description: On March 22, 1933, President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed the Cullen–Harrison Act, amending the Volstead Act to allow the manufacture and sale of 3.2% beer and light wines. This legislation marked a significant step towards the end of Prohibition in the United States.
events.name: Cullen–Harrison Act

events.enhanced_description: On March 23, 1933, the Reichstag passed the Enabling Act, granting Adolf Hitler the authority to enact laws without parliamentary consent, effectively establishing his dictatorship. This act was a critical step in the consolidation of Nazi power in Germany.
events.name: Enabling Act passage

events.enhanced_description: On March 27, 1933, Japan announced its intention to leave the League of Nations, a decision that reflected its growing militarism and dissatisfaction with international diplomacy. This withdrawal would become effective in 1935.
events.name: Japan leaves the League of Nations

events.enhanced_description: On March 29, 1933, Welsh journalist Gareth Jones made the first report in the West about the Holodomor famine genocide in Ukraine, bringing international attention to the devastating effects of Soviet policies. His reporting played a crucial role in raising awareness of the famine.
events.name: Gareth Jones reports on Holodomor

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1933, the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) was established in the United States as part of the New Deal, aimed at providing jobs and relief for the unemployed during the Great Depression. The program focused on environmental conservation and infrastructure development.
events.name: Civilian Conservation Corps establishment

events.enhanced_description: On April 1, 1933, the Nazi Party, led by Julius Streicher, organized a nationwide boycott of Jewish-owned businesses in Germany. This event marked a significant escalation in the anti-Semitic policies of the Nazi regime, setting the stage for further discrimination and violence against Jewish communities.
events.name: Boycott of Jewish-owned businesses in Germany

events.enhanced_description: On April 2, 1933, English cricketer Wally Hammond scored a remarkable 336 runs in a test match against New Zealand at Eden Park, Auckland. This record-breaking performance remains one of the highest individual scores in Test cricket history.
events.name: Wally Hammond's record score in cricket

events.enhanced_description: On April 3, 1933, an anti-monarchist rebellion erupted in Siam (modern-day Thailand), reflecting growing discontent with the monarchy. This event was part of a broader movement towards modernization and political reform in the country.
events.name: Anti-monarchist rebellion in Siam

events.enhanced_description: On April 4, 1933, the American airship USS Akron crashed off the coast of New Jersey, resulting in the deaths of 73 of its 76 crew members. This tragedy marked one of the deadliest airship accidents in history and raised questions about the safety of airship travel.

locations.name: Off the coast of New Jersey

events.name: Crash of the USS Akron

events.enhanced_description: On April 5, 1933, the International Court of Justice in The Hague ruled that Greenland belongs to Denmark, condemning Norwegian landings on the eastern part of the island. This decision was significant in establishing international legal precedents regarding territorial claims.
events.name: International Court of Justice ruling on Greenland

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1933, the Cullen-Harrison Act was enacted, allowing the sale of certain types of beer in the United States, marking a significant step towards the end of Prohibition. This legislation was a precursor to the full repeal of Prohibition later that year.
events.name: Legalization of beer sales in the United States

events.enhanced_description: On April 11, 1933, aviator Bill Lancaster took off from Lympne Airport in England in an attempt to set a speed record to the Cape of Good Hope. Unfortunately, he vanished during the flight, and his body was not discovered until 1962 in the Sahara Desert.
events.name: Bill Lancaster's flight attempt

events.enhanced_description: On April 13, 1933, the Children and Young Persons Act was passed in the United Kingdom, aimed at improving the welfare of children and young people. This legislation was part of a broader movement towards social reform in the early 20th century.
events.name: Children and Young Persons Act in the UK

events.enhanced_description: On April 21, 1933, the Nazi regime in Germany outlawed the kosher ritual of shechita, which is the Jewish method of slaughtering animals for food. This law was part of a broader campaign against Jewish practices and rights in the country.
events.name: Outlawing of kosher shechita in Nazi Germany

events.enhanced_description: On April 24, 1933, the persecution of Jehovah's Witnesses in Nazi Germany began with the seizure of the Bible Students' office in Magdeburg. This marked the start of systematic oppression against religious minorities under the Nazi regime.
events.name: Persecution of Jehovah's Witnesses in Nazi Germany

events.enhanced_description: On April 26, 1933, Hermann Göring established the Gestapo, the secret police of Nazi Germany. This organization played a crucial role in the regime's oppressive tactics against political opponents and minority groups.
events.name: Establishment of the Gestapo

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1933, the Stahlhelm, a paramilitary organization of World War I veterans, officially joined the Nazi Party. This integration signified the consolidation of power by the Nazis and the alignment of various nationalist groups with their agenda.
events.name: Stahlhelm joins the Nazi Party

events.enhanced_description: On May 2, 1933, Adolf Hitler enacted Gleichschaltung, a policy that prohibited trade unions in Germany. This move was part of the Nazis' broader strategy to eliminate opposition and consolidate control over all aspects of German society.
events.name: Gleichschaltung: Prohibition of trade unions

events.enhanced_description: On May 3, 1933, Dáil Éireann, the parliament of the Irish Free State, abolished the oath of allegiance to the British Crown. This legislative change marked a significant step towards full sovereignty and independence for Ireland.
events.name: Abolition of the oath of allegiance in the Irish Free State

events.enhanced_description: On May 5, 1933, the detection of radio waves from the center of the Milky Way Galaxy by Karl Jansky was reported in The New York Times. This groundbreaking discovery is considered the birth of radio astronomy, paving the way for future astronomical research.
events.name: Detection of radio waves by Karl Jansky

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, Mohandas Gandhi, imprisoned by British authorities in Pune as part of the Quit India Movement, initiated a hunger strike to protest his detention. This act of nonviolent resistance highlighted the struggle for Indian independence and garnered significant national and international attention.
events.name: Gandhi's hunger strike

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1933, Paraguay officially declared war on Bolivia, marking the beginning of the Chaco War, a conflict primarily over control of the Chaco region, believed to be rich in oil. The war lasted until 1935 and resulted in significant casualties and territorial changes.
events.name: Chaco War: Paraguay formally declares war on Bolivia

events.enhanced_description: On May 17, 1933, Vidkun Quisling and Johan Bernhard Hjort established the Nasjonal Samling (National Gathering Party) in Norway, a far-right political party that would later collaborate with Nazi Germany during World War II. The party aimed to promote nationalism and fascist ideologies in Norway.
events.name: Formation of the Nasjonal Samling in Norway

events.enhanced_description: On May 18, 1933, President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed an act creating the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA), aimed at addressing the economic devastation of the Great Depression by providing jobs, electricity, and flood control in the Tennessee Valley region. The TVA became a model for regional planning and development.
events.name: Creation of the Tennessee Valley Authority

events.enhanced_description: On May 26, 1933, the Nazi Party in Germany introduced a law to legalize eugenic sterilization, targeting individuals deemed 'unfit' to reproduce. This law was part of the broader eugenics movement that aimed to improve the genetic quality of the population and laid the groundwork for future atrocities.
events.name: Nazi Germany legalizes eugenic sterilization

events.enhanced_description: On May 27, 1933, as part of the New Deal, President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed the Federal Securities Act into law, which mandated the registration of securities with the Federal Trade Commission. This legislation aimed to restore public confidence in the financial markets following the 1929 stock market crash.
events.name: Federal Securities Act signed into law

events.enhanced_description: In June 1933, the Holodomor famine-genocide in Ukraine reached its peak, with an estimated 30,000 deaths per day due to man-made starvation policies imposed by the Soviet government. This tragic event had a devastating impact on the Ukrainian population and is recognized as a genocide.
events.name: Holodomor famine-genocide reaches peak

events.enhanced_description: On June 5, 1933, the U.S. Congress enacted a joint resolution abrogating the gold standard, nullifying creditors' rights to demand payment in gold. This significant economic policy shift was part of the broader New Deal efforts to combat the Great Depression.
events.name: U.S. Congress abrogates the gold standard

events.enhanced_description: On June 6, 1933, the first drive-in movie theater opened in Pennsauken Township, New Jersey, revolutionizing the way audiences experienced films. This innovative concept allowed viewers to watch movies from the comfort of their cars, paving the way for the drive-in culture that became popular in the following decades.

locations.name: Pennsauken Township, New Jersey, United States

events.name: First drive-in movie theater opens

events.enhanced_description: The London Economic Conference was held in June 1933, gathering representatives from various nations to address the global economic crisis stemming from the Great Depression. The conference aimed to promote international cooperation and stabilize currencies but ultimately failed to achieve its goals.
events.name: London Economic Conference held

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1933, the Union Station massacre occurred in Kansas City, Missouri, when notorious gangster Pretty Boy Floyd killed an FBI agent, three local police officers, and bank robber Frank Nash during a botched rescue attempt. This violent incident highlighted the growing power of organized crime during the Great Depression.
events.name: Union Station massacre

events.enhanced_description: On June 22, 1933, the Nazi regime in Germany officially outlawed the Social-Democratic Party (SPD), effectively eliminating one of the last major political opponents to Hitler's government. This action was part of a broader campaign to consolidate power and suppress dissent.
events.name: Nazi Germany outlaws the Social-Democratic Party

events.enhanced_description: On June 25, 1933, delegates convened at the Wilmersdorfer Tennishallen in Berlin to protest against the persecution of Jehovah's Witnesses under the Nazi regime. This gathering highlighted the growing concern over religious freedoms and human rights violations in Germany.
events.name: Protest against persecution of Jehovah's Witnesses

events.enhanced_description: On June 26, 1933, the American Totalisator Company unveiled its first electronic pari-mutuel betting machine at Arlington Park race track near Chicago. This innovation revolutionized the betting industry by automating the process and enhancing the experience for bettors.
events.name: First electronic pari-mutuel betting machine unveiled

events.enhanced_description: On July 1, 1933, the London Passenger Transport Board commenced operations, consolidating various transport services in London to improve efficiency and service. This marked a significant development in public transportation in the capital.
events.name: London Passenger Transport Board begins operation

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1933, Mahatma Gandhi was sentenced to prison in India for his role in the civil disobedience movement against British colonial rule. His imprisonment sparked widespread protests and highlighted the struggle for Indian independence.
events.name: Gandhi sentenced to prison

events.enhanced_description: On July 6, 1933, the first Major League Baseball All-Star Game was played at Comiskey Park in Chicago, featuring the best players from the American League and National League. This event has since become an annual tradition in professional baseball.
events.name: First Major League Baseball All-Star Game

events.enhanced_description: On July 8, 1933, the first rugby union test match was played between the Wallabies of Australia and the Springboks of South Africa at Newlands in Cape Town. This historic match marked the beginning of a fierce rivalry in international rugby.
events.name: First rugby union test match between Australia and South Africa

events.enhanced_description: The Shinpeitai Incident on July 11, 1933, involved an attempt by nationalist military factions in Japan to establish a regime through a coup. This event highlighted the rising militarism and political instability in Japan during the 1930s.
events.name: Shinpeitai Incident

events.enhanced_description: On July 14, 1933, Nazi Germany enacted the Law for the Prevention of Hereditarily Diseased Offspring, which mandated the sterilization of individuals with certain genetic conditions. This law was part of the regime's eugenics policies and had devastating effects on many lives.
events.name: Law for the Prevention of Hereditarily Diseased Offspring enacted

events.enhanced_description: On July 15, 1933, the Four-Power Pact was signed by Britain, France, Germany, and Italy, aiming to promote peace and stability in Europe. However, the pact ultimately failed to prevent the rise of tensions leading to World War II.
events.name: Four-Power Pact signed

events.enhanced_description: On July 20, 1933, Vatican state secretary Eugenio Pacelli, who later became Pope Pius XII, signed the Reichskonkordat with Nazi Germany. This concordat aimed to regulate the relationship between the Catholic Church and the Nazi state, but it also raised ethical concerns regarding the Church's stance during the regime's atrocities.
events.name: Reichskonkordat signed

events.enhanced_description: On July 22, 1933, Wiley Post became the first person to fly solo around the world, landing at Floyd Bennett Field in Brooklyn, New York, after completing a journey of 15,596 miles in 7 days, 18 hours, and 45 minutes. This remarkable feat showcased advancements in aviation and inspired future explorers.
events.name: Wiley Post flies solo around the world

events.enhanced_description: The Blue Eagle emblem of the National Recovery Administration was publicly displayed for the first time in August 1933, symbolizing the New Deal's efforts to promote fair competition and labor rights during the Great Depression.
events.name: The Blue Eagle emblem is displayed

events.enhanced_description: The Stalin White Sea–Baltic Canal opened in August 1933, connecting the White Sea with Lake Onega and the Baltic Sea. Constructed using forced labor, it exemplified the Soviet regime's ambitious infrastructure projects.
events.name: Opening of the Stalin White Sea–Baltic Canal

events.enhanced_description: The Simele massacre occurred in August 1933, when Iraqi government troops killed more than 3,000 Assyrian Iraqis. This tragic event highlighted the ethnic tensions and violence in the region during this period.
events.name: Simele massacre

events.enhanced_description: On August 12, 1933, Winston Churchill delivered a speech warning about the dangers of German rearmament, emphasizing the need for vigilance against the growing threat posed by Nazi Germany.
events.name: Winston Churchill warns of German rearmament

events.enhanced_description: In August 1933, loggers accidentally ignited a forest fire in the Coast Range of Oregon, known as the first forest fire of the Tillamook Burn, which ultimately destroyed 240,000 acres before being extinguished.
events.name: Tillamook Burn forest fire

events.enhanced_description: The Diexi earthquake struck Mao County in Sichuan, China, on August 25, 1933, resulting in the deaths of approximately 9,000 people. It was one of the deadliest earthquakes in Chinese history.
events.name: Diexi earthquake

events.enhanced_description: German-Jewish philosopher Theodor Lessing was shot in Mariánské Lázně, Czechoslovakia, on August 30, 1933, and died the following day. His assassination was part of the broader wave of violence against Jews and intellectuals during the rise of Nazism.

locations.name: Mariánské Lázně, Karlovy Vary, Czech Republic

events.name: Assassination of Theodor Lessing

events.enhanced_description: Alejandro Lerroux formed a new government in Spain on January 1, 1933, during a time of political upheaval and social change, as various factions sought to influence the direction of the Spanish Republic.
events.name: Formation of new government in Spain

events.enhanced_description: In September 1933, a devastating hurricane struck the town of Tampico, Mexico, causing widespread destruction and loss of life. The event highlighted the vulnerability of coastal communities to natural disasters.
events.name: Hurricane destroys Tampico

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1933, Engelbert Dollfuss, the leader of the Fatherland's Front in Austria, was seriously injured in a failed assassination attempt. This event underscored the political tensions and violence in Austria during the rise of fascism.
events.name: Assassination attempt on Engelbert Dollfuss

events.enhanced_description: Air France was formed on October 7, 1933, through the merger of five French airline companies, marking a significant development in the aviation industry and establishing a major player in international air travel.
events.name: Formation of Air France

events.enhanced_description: On October 10, 1933, a bomb exploded on a United Airlines Boeing 247 during a transcontinental flight near Chesterton, Indiana, killing all seven people on board. This incident marked the first proven case of sabotage in civil aviation.
events.name: United Airlines Boeing 247 mid-air explosion

events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1933, the United States Department of Justice acquired the United States Army Disciplinary Barracks on Alcatraz Island, planning to convert it into a federal penitentiary. This marked the beginning of Alcatraz's infamous history as a maximum-security prison.
events.name: Acquisition of Alcatraz by the Department of Justice

events.enhanced_description: On October 14, 1933, Germany announced its withdrawal from the League of Nations and the World Disarmament Conference, following the denial of its request to increase its military capabilities. This decision reflected the growing tensions in Europe leading up to World War II.
events.name: Germany withdraws from the League of Nations

events.enhanced_description: On October 14, 1933, the new constitution of Estonia was approved after three consecutive referendums, marking a significant step in the establishment of democratic governance in the country.
events.name: Approval of new constitution in Estonia

events.enhanced_description: On October 16, 1933, Victor Licata committed a series of parricides in Tampa, Florida, which sparked a nationwide debate about the legalization of cannabis. This tragic event was used by some lawmakers as a rallying point to push for stricter drug laws, linking cannabis to violent crime.
events.name: Parricides committed in the United States by Victor Licata lead to calls for the legal prohibition of cannabis

events.enhanced_description: On October 17, 1933, renowned physicist Albert Einstein arrived in the United States as a refugee from Nazi Germany. He took a position at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey, where he would continue his groundbreaking work in theoretical physics.
events.name: Albert Einstein arrives in the United States

events.enhanced_description: On November 5, 1933, the Basque people in Spain voted for autonomy, marking a significant step in their quest for self-governance. This vote was part of a broader movement for regional autonomy within Spain during the Second Spanish Republic.
events.name: Spanish Basque people vote for autonomy

events.enhanced_description: On November 8, 1933, U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt unveiled the Civil Works Administration, a New Deal program aimed at providing jobs for over 4 million unemployed Americans during the Great Depression. This initiative was part of Roosevelt's broader strategy to revive the economy and reduce unemployment.
events.name: New Deal: Civil Works Administration unveiled

events.enhanced_description: On November 11, 1933, a severe dust storm, known as 'the great black blizzard,' swept through South Dakota, stripping topsoil from already desiccated farmlands. This event was part of the Dust Bowl phenomenon that devastated agricultural regions in the United States during the 1930s.
events.name: Dust Bowl: The great black blizzard in South Dakota

events.enhanced_description: On November 12, 1933, the Japan Precision Optical Industry was founded in Tokyo, Japan. This company would later evolve into the globally recognized Canon brand, known for its cameras and photocopiers.
events.name: Japan Precision Optical Industry founded

events.enhanced_description: On November 16, 1933, the United States and the Soviet Union formally established diplomatic relations, marking a significant shift in international relations during the interwar period. This move was part of a broader strategy by the Roosevelt administration to engage with the Soviet Union amidst rising global tensions.
events.name: United States and Soviet Union establish diplomatic relations

events.enhanced_description: On November 19, 1933, general elections in the Second Spanish Republic resulted in a victory for right-wing parties, significantly altering the political landscape of Spain. This election was a pivotal moment leading up to the Spanish Civil War.
events.name: Second Spanish Republic: General elections result in a victory by the right-wing parties

events.enhanced_description: On November 22, 1933, the Fujian People's Government was declared in Fujian Province, China, amidst the backdrop of political upheaval and the struggle for power during the Chinese Civil War. This government was part of a series of regional governments that emerged during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Fujian People's Government declared

events.enhanced_description: On December 5, 1933, the Twenty-first Amendment to the United States Constitution was ratified, officially repealing Prohibition. This marked a significant shift in American law and society, allowing for the legal sale and consumption of alcohol.
events.name: Twenty-first Amendment to the United States Constitution ratified

events.enhanced_description: On December 15, 1933, the Twenty-first Amendment officially went into effect, making alcohol legal in the United States once again. This event marked the end of over a decade of Prohibition and was celebrated by many across the nation.
events.name: Twenty-first Amendment officially goes into effect

events.enhanced_description: On December 17, 1933, the first NFL Championship game was played in New York City, where the Chicago Bears defeated the New York Giants 23-21. This game marked a significant moment in the history of American football, establishing the NFL as a major professional sports league.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: First NFL Championship game played

events.enhanced_description: On December 21, 1933, Newfoundland returned to Crown colony status following a financial collapse. This marked a significant change in governance for the territory, which had previously been a dominion of Canada.

locations.name: St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada

events.name: Newfoundland returns to Crown colony status

events.enhanced_description: On December 23, 1933, a tragic train crash occurred in Lagny-Pomponne, France, resulting in the deaths of over 200 people. This disaster highlighted the need for improved safety measures in rail transportation.
events.name: Lagny-Pomponne rail accident

events.enhanced_description: On December 26, 1933, the Nissan Motor Company was organized in Tokyo, Japan. This company would go on to become one of the largest automobile manufacturers in the world.
events.name: Nissan Motor Company organized

events.enhanced_description: On December 29, 1933, Ion Gheorghe Duca, the Prime Minister of Romania, was assassinated by members of the Iron Guard. This politically motivated murder underscored the rising tensions and violence in Romania during the interwar period.

image.caption: Portrait of Romanian politician Ion Gheorghe Duca.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — http://www.gov.ro/upload/articles/198/thumbs/ion-g-duca.jpg
image.date_qualification: The image description identifies Duca; no depicted image date is supplied. It is a portrait, not a depiction of the assassination.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Ion Gheorghe Duca assassinated

events.enhanced_description: The International Telecommunication Union (ITU) was established in 1934 as a specialized agency of the League of Nations to coordinate international telecommunication standards and policies. This organization plays a crucial role in the development and regulation of global telecommunications.
events.name: The International Telecommunication Union is established

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1934, President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed the Gold Reserve Act, mandating that all gold held by the Federal Reserve be surrendered to the U.S. Treasury. This act effectively raised the gold price from $20.67 to $35 per ounce, a significant move during the Great Depression.
events.name: Gold Reserve Act signed by Franklin D. Roosevelt

events.enhanced_description: In 1934, Greece, Romania, Turkey, and Yugoslavia formed the Balkan Pact, aimed at mutual defense and cooperation among the Balkan states. This alliance was a response to the rising threat of fascism in Europe and sought to promote regional stability.
events.name: Balkan Pact formation

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1934, the Soviet Union officially joined the League of Nations, marking a significant moment in international relations as it sought to engage with the global community despite its revolutionary ideology.
events.name: Soviet Union Joins League of Nations

events.enhanced_description: In 1934, Bruno Richard Hauptmann was arrested in connection with the infamous Lindbergh kidnapping case, which had captivated the nation and raised concerns about child safety and crime in America.
events.name: Arrest of Bruno Richard Hauptmann

events.enhanced_description: In winter 1934, Tadj ol-Molouk, the Empress consort of Iran, and her daughters publicly appeared in Tehran without a veil, a significant act that contributed to the eventual abolition of the veil in the country, reflecting changing social norms.
events.name: Empress Consort of Iran Appears Without Veil

events.enhanced_description: In 1934, Abidjan was designated as the capital of the French colony of Ivory Coast, a decision that would shape the city's development and significance in West Africa.
events.name: Abidjan Becomes Capital of Ivory Coast

events.enhanced_description: In 1934, the phenomenon of sonoluminescence was discovered at the University of Cologne, where bubbles in a liquid emit short bursts of light when exposed to intense sound waves, leading to further research in acoustics and physics.
events.name: Discovery of Sonoluminescence

events.enhanced_description: In 1934, the Australian frontier wars, which lasted for 146 years, came to an end, marking a significant moment in the history of Indigenous Australian resistance against colonial expansion.
events.name: End of the Australian Frontier Wars

events.enhanced_description: In 1934, the Yomiuri Giants, one of Japan's most successful professional baseball clubs, was founded in Tokyo, contributing to the growth of baseball as a popular sport in the country.
events.name: Founding of the Yomiuri Giants

events.enhanced_description: On January 15, 1934, an 8.0 Mw earthquake struck the Nepal–Bihar region, causing catastrophic destruction and resulting in an estimated 6,000 to 10,700 fatalities. This earthquake is one of the deadliest in the region's history, highlighting the seismic vulnerability of the area.

image.caption: Historical image of the Old Darbhanga Raj Palace, damaged in the 1934 earthquake.
image.credit: P. C. Roy Chaudhury — Bihar District Gazetteers: Darbhanga
image.date_qualification: Depicted damage is attributed to the 1934 earthquake; image_date is 2021-06-04 16:47:51 and does not establish when the original photograph was made.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Nepal–Bihar earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1934, Nazi Germany and the Second Polish Republic signed a ten-year declaration of non-aggression, aimed at stabilizing relations between the two nations. This agreement was significant in the context of rising tensions in Europe leading up to World War II.
events.name: German–Polish declaration of non-aggression

events.enhanced_description: On January 30, 1934, the Law on the Reconstruction of the Reich was enacted in Nazi Germany, significantly diminishing the political power of federal states, including Prussia. This law was part of Hitler's broader strategy to centralize power and eliminate regional autonomy.
events.name: Law on the Reconstruction of the Reich

events.enhanced_description: On February 6, 1934, far-right leagues rallied in front of the Palais Bourbon in Paris, attempting a coup d'état against the Third Republic. This political crisis highlighted the growing tensions and instability within France during the interwar period.
events.name: French political crisis

events.enhanced_description: On February 9, 1934, Gaston Doumergue was tasked with forming a new government in France amidst political turmoil. His leadership was crucial in navigating the challenges facing the Third Republic during a period of significant instability.
events.name: Gaston Doumergue forms a new government in France

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1934, the Fatherland Front engaged in a series of clashes across Austria, consolidating its power during the Austrian Civil War. This conflict was marked by violent confrontations between the government and socialist factions.
events.name: Austrian Civil War

events.enhanced_description: On February 16, 1934, the Commission of Government was sworn in as a form of direct rule for the Dominion of Newfoundland. This marked a significant shift in governance as Newfoundland faced economic challenges and sought assistance from Britain.
events.name: Commission of Government sworn in Newfoundland

events.enhanced_description: On February 21, 1934, Augusto César Sandino, a prominent Nicaraguan revolutionary leader, was assassinated in Managua by the National Guard. His death marked a pivotal moment in Nicaraguan history, as he had been a symbol of resistance against U.S. intervention.

image.caption: Portrait of Nicaraguan revolutionary Augusto César Sandino.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — https://mediateca.inah.gob.mx/islandora_74/islandora/object/fotografia%3A449874 http://quepasoestamosvivos.blogspot.com/2013/02/el-asesinato-de-sandino.html?m=1
image.date_qualification: June 1929, before the assassination on 21 February 1934.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Assassination of Augusto César Sandino

events.enhanced_description: On February 23, 1934, King Leopold III ascended to the throne of Belgium following the death of his father, King Albert I, on February 17. His reign would be marked by the challenges of World War II and the complexities of Belgian politics.
events.name: King Leopold III of Belgium succeeds to the throne

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1934, Manchukuo, a puppet state established by Japan in Manchuria, proclaimed a monarchy under Puyi, the last Emperor of China. This move was part of Japan's efforts to legitimize its control over the region.
events.name: Proclamation of monarchy in Manchukuo

events.enhanced_description: On March 12, 1934, Prime Minister Konstantin Päts declared a state of emergency in Estonia, effectively staging a self-coup with parliamentary approval. This action marked the beginning of the Era of Silence, during which political dissent was suppressed.
events.name: Estonian self-coup by Konstantin Päts

events.enhanced_description: On March 13, 1934, notorious American outlaw John Dillinger and his gang robbed the First National Bank in Mason City, Iowa, stealing $52,000. This robbery was part of Dillinger's infamous crime spree during the Great Depression.
events.name: John Dillinger bank robbery

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1934, the Great Hakodate Fire devastated the city of Hakodate in southern Hokkaido, Japan, killing at least 2,166 people. This catastrophic event led to significant changes in fire safety regulations in Japan.
events.name: Great Hakodate Fire

events.enhanced_description: On March 24, 1934, the Tydings–McDuffie Act was passed by the United States Congress, granting the Philippines a greater degree of self-government. This act was a significant step towards Philippine independence, which would be fully realized in 1946.
events.name: Tydings–McDuffie Act passed

events.enhanced_description: On April 21, 1934, the 'surgeon's photograph' of the Loch Ness Monster was published in the Daily Mail, taken by London gynaecologist Robert Kenneth Wilson. This photograph sparked widespread interest and speculation about the existence of the mythical creature, although it was later revealed to be a hoax.
events.name: Surgeon's photograph of Loch Ness Monster published

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1934, the May Constitution was enacted in Austria, marking the establishment of the Austrofascist Federal State. This constitution consolidated power under the Fatherland Front and curtailed democratic processes in the country.
events.name: May Constitution of 1934

events.enhanced_description: On May 15, 1934, Kārlis Ulmanis established an authoritarian government in Latvia, effectively ending the democratic system that had been in place since independence. His regime would last until the Soviet occupation in 1940.
events.name: Establishment of authoritarian government in Latvia

events.enhanced_description: On May 19, 1934, Kimon Georgiev staged a coup d'état in Bulgaria, overthrowing the government of Georgi Kyoseivanov. This coup was part of a broader trend of political instability and authoritarianism in Eastern Europe during the interwar period.

image.caption: Memorial plaque to Kimon Georgiev at 11 Geneva Street in Sofia.
image.credit: Spiritia — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed 5 March 2018, according to Exif data; not the event date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Kimon Georgiev stages coup d'état in Bulgaria

events.enhanced_description: On May 23, 1934, infamous American outlaws Bonnie Parker and Clyde Barrow were ambushed and killed by law enforcement in Bienville Parish, Louisiana. Their violent crime spree had captivated the nation, and their deaths marked the end of an era in American criminal history.
events.name: Ambush and killing of Bonnie and Clyde

events.enhanced_description: On May 28, 1934, the Dionne quintuplets were born near Callander, Ontario, Canada, to parents Oliva and Elzire Dionne. They became the first known quintuplets to survive infancy, capturing international attention and leading to significant media coverage and public fascination.
events.name: Birth of the Dionne Quintuplets

events.enhanced_description: On May 31, 1934, the Barmen Declaration was signed by a group of Protestant Christians in Nazi Germany, largely drafted by theologian Karl Barth. This declaration opposed the pro-Nazi German Christian movement and asserted the independence of the church from state control.
events.name: Signing of the Barmen Declaration

events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1934, Donald Duck made his film debut in Walt Disney's Silly Symphony cartoon 'The Wise Little Hen.' This marked the beginning of Donald Duck's rise to fame as one of Disney's most beloved characters.
events.name: Donald Duck's Film Debut

events.enhanced_description: On June 10, 1934, Italy defeated Czechoslovakia 2-1 after extra time in the final match of the first-ever FIFA World Cup held in Italy. This victory marked Italy's first World Cup title, establishing the nation as a formidable force in international football.
events.name: 1934 FIFA World Cup Final

events.enhanced_description: On June 14, 1934, Adolf Hitler and Benito Mussolini met for the first time at the Venice Biennale. This meeting symbolized the growing alliance between Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy, which would have significant implications for European politics.
events.name: First Meeting of Hitler and Mussolini

events.enhanced_description: On June 18, 1934, the Indian Reorganization Act was enacted in the United States, aimed at reversing the assimilationist policies of the Dawes Act and restoring some degree of self-governance to Native American tribes. This act marked a significant shift in U.S. policy towards Indigenous peoples.
events.name: Enactment of the Indian Reorganization Act

events.enhanced_description: On June 27, 1934, Imam Yahya of Yemen and Ibn Saud of Saudi Arabia concluded a peace treaty, which helped to stabilize relations between the two nations. This agreement was significant in the context of regional politics and tribal dynamics.
events.name: Peace Treaty between Yemen and Saudi Arabia

events.enhanced_description: On June 30, 1934, the Nazi Party's SA camp in Oranienburg was taken over by the Schutzstaffel (SS), marking a significant shift in power within the Nazi regime. This takeover was part of the broader purges during the Night of the Long Knives.
events.name: SA Camp Oranienburg Taken Over by SS

events.enhanced_description: On July 1, 1934, the Hays Code began to be strictly enforced in the Hollywood film industry, establishing guidelines for film content that would last until 1968. This code aimed to ensure that films adhered to moral standards and reflected societal values.
events.name: Enforcement of the Hays Code

events.enhanced_description: On July 13, 1934, Adolf Hitler delivered a speech to the Reichstag justifying the recent purge of the SA during the Night of the Long Knives. In this address, he sought to legitimize his actions and consolidate his power within the Nazi regime.
events.name: Hitler's Speech to the Reichstag

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1934, Austrian Nazis assassinated Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss during a failed coup attempt known as the July Putsch. This event highlighted the tensions between the Austrian government and Nazi sympathizers within the country.
events.name: July Putsch

events.enhanced_description: On August 2, 1934, following the death of President Paul von Hindenburg, Adolf Hitler combined the offices of Chancellor and President, declaring himself Führer of Germany. This consolidation of power marked a critical moment in the establishment of a totalitarian regime.
events.name: Hitler Becomes Führer

events.enhanced_description: On August 8, 1934, the Wehrmacht, Germany's armed forces, swore a personal oath of loyalty to Adolf Hitler. This act further solidified Hitler's control over the military and ensured the loyalty of the armed forces to his regime.
events.name: Wehrmacht Oath of Loyalty

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1934, the United States Marine Corps completed its withdrawal from Haiti after nearly two decades of military presence. This marked the end of U.S. occupation, which had significant implications for Haitian sovereignty and U.S.-Haitian relations.
events.name: U.S. Marines Leave Haiti

events.enhanced_description: On August 19, 1934, a German referendum was held in which 90% of the population approved of Adolf Hitler's assumption of presidential powers, combining the roles of Führer and Reichskanzler. This referendum was a key moment in consolidating Hitler's totalitarian regime.

image.caption: Ballot for the 1934 German referendum on merging the offices of Chancellor and President.
image.credit: The Nazis — https://www.alexautographs.com/auction-lot/1934-german-referendum_888421495F
image.date_qualification: The supplied image date is August 1934; the referendum was held on 19 August 1934.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: 1934 German Referendum

events.enhanced_description: On September 4, 1934, Evelyn Waugh's novel 'A Handful of Dust' was published in full, receiving critical acclaim for its satirical portrayal of British society. The novel is considered one of Waugh's major works and a significant contribution to 20th-century literature.
events.name: Publication of A Handful of Dust

events.enhanced_description: On September 10, 1934, the 6th Nuremberg Rally was staged by the German Nazi Party, showcasing the party's power and propaganda. This rally was a significant event in the Nazi regime's efforts to promote its ideology and consolidate support.
events.name: 6th Nuremberg Rally

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1934, a fire aboard the passenger liner SS Morro Castle off the coast of New Jersey resulted in the deaths of 134 people. This tragic incident raised concerns about maritime safety and led to changes in regulations for passenger ships.

locations.name: Off the coast of New Jersey, United States

events.name: Fire on SS Morro Castle

events.enhanced_description: On September 15, 1934, the Australian federal election resulted in the re-election of Joseph Lyons' United Australia Party (UAP) with a decreased majority, defeating the Labor Party led by former Prime Minister James Scullin. This election marked a significant moment in Australian political history.
events.name: 1934 Australian Federal Election

events.enhanced_description: On September 19, 1934, the Soviet Union officially joined the League of Nations, marking a significant moment in international relations. This membership was part of the Soviet strategy to gain legitimacy and influence in global politics.
events.name: Soviet Union Joins the League of Nations

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1934, the Muroto typhoon struck Honshū, Japan, killing 3,036 people and causing widespread destruction, including damage to temples and schools in Osaka. This disaster highlighted the vulnerability of the region to natural calamities.
events.name: Muroto Typhoon

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1934, a gas explosion at Gresford Colliery in Wrexham, north-east Wales, resulted in the deaths of 266 miners and rescuers. This tragic event raised awareness about mining safety and led to calls for improved regulations in the industry.
events.name: Gresford Colliery Explosion

events.enhanced_description: On September 28, 1934, Afghanistan officially joined the League of Nations, marking its entry into the international community. This membership was part of Afghanistan's efforts to gain recognition and support on the global stage.
events.name: Afghanistan Joins the League of Nations

events.enhanced_description: On October 2, 1934, a typhoon struck Osaka and Kyoto, Japan, resulting in 1,660 deaths and injuring 5,400 people while destroying the rice harvest. This disaster had significant implications for food security and the economy in the region.
events.name: Typhoon in Osaka and Kyoto

events.enhanced_description: On October 6, 1934, Lluís Companys, the President of Catalonia, declared the Catalan State of the Spanish Federal Republic. This declaration was met with swift military action from the Spanish government, leading to the arrest of Companys and members of his government, and the suspension of Catalonia's autonomy until 1936.
events.name: Catalan State Declaration

events.enhanced_description: On October 9, 1934, during a state visit to France, King Alexander of Yugoslavia and French Foreign Minister Louis Barthou were assassinated in Marseille. This event marked a significant political upheaval in the Balkans and strained relations between Yugoslavia and other European nations.
events.name: Assassination of King Alexander of Yugoslavia

events.enhanced_description: The Long March began on October 16, 1934, as the People's Liberation Army of the Chinese Communist Party embarked on a strategic retreat from Jiangxi to Yan'an. This monumental journey covered thousands of miles and became a symbol of the Communist Party's resilience and determination.
events.name: Beginning of the Long March

events.enhanced_description: On November 3, 1934, Charles Kingsford Smith completed the first eastward crossing of the Pacific Ocean, flying from Brisbane, Australia, to San Francisco in the Lockheed Altair, Lady Southern Cross. This historic flight included the first eastward leg from Hawaii to North America.
events.name: First Eastward Crossing of the Pacific Ocean

events.enhanced_description: On November 5, 1934, the MacRobertson Air Race commenced from RAF Mildenhall in England to Melbourne, Australia, celebrating the centenary of Victoria. The race was won by the British de Havilland DH.88 Comet, Grosvenor House, piloted by C. W. A. Scott and Tom Campbell Black.
events.name: MacRobertson Air Race

events.enhanced_description: On November 6, 1934, the attempted exclusion of Egon Kisch, a prominent journalist and anti-fascist activist, from Australia began, highlighting the tensions surrounding immigration and political dissent during this period.
events.name: Attempted Exclusion of Egon Kisch

events.enhanced_description: On November 23, 1934, an Anglo-Ethiopian boundary commission discovered an Italian garrison at Walwal, which was well within Ethiopian territory. This incident contributed to the escalating tensions that led to the Abyssinia Crisis.
events.name: Discovery of Italian Garrison at Walwal

events.enhanced_description: On November 27, 1934, Daniel Salamanca Urey was deposed in a military coup and replaced by José Luis Tejada Sorzano, marking a significant shift in Bolivia's political landscape during a period of instability.
events.name: Deposition of Daniel Salamanca Urey

events.enhanced_description: On December 2, 1934, the Quintette du Hot Club de France, a pioneering jazz group, performed for the first time in Paris, led by guitarist Django Reinhardt and violinist Stéphane Grappelli. This group played a crucial role in the development of European jazz.
events.name: First Performance of Quintette du Hot Club de France

events.enhanced_description: On December 5, 1934, during the Abyssinia Crisis, Ethiopian and Italian troops exchanged gunfire, resulting in significant casualties. This conflict marked a critical point in the escalating tensions between Ethiopia and Italy.
events.name: Abyssinia Crisis: Gunfire Exchange

events.enhanced_description: On December 21, 1934, the orchestral suite Lieutenant Kijé, composed by Sergei Prokofiev, premiered in Leningrad. This work is one of Prokofiev's best-known compositions and showcases his innovative style.
events.name: Premiere of Lieutenant Kijé

events.enhanced_description: On December 27, 1934, the country formerly known as Persia officially adopted the name Iran, reflecting a shift towards a more nationalistic identity under the rule of Reza Shah Pahlavi.
events.name: Persia Becomes Iran

events.enhanced_description: On December 29, 1934, Japan officially renounced the Washington Naval Treaty of 1922 and the London Naval Treaty of 1930, signaling its intent to expand its naval power and marking a significant shift in international relations leading up to World War II.
events.name: Japan Renounces Naval Treaties

events.enhanced_description: In 1935, Robert Watson-Watt first demonstrated the use of radar to detect aircraft at Daventry, England. This groundbreaking technology would later play a crucial role in air defense during World War II.
events.name: Robert Watson-Watt demonstrates radar

events.enhanced_description: In 1935, İsmet İnönü formed the new government in Turkey, marking his eighth term as Prime Minister during Mustafa Kemal Atatürk's presidency. His leadership was pivotal in shaping modern Turkey's political landscape.
events.name: İsmet İnönü forms the new government in Turkey

events.enhanced_description: In 1935, the London and North Eastern Railway commenced the Silver Jubilee, marking the introduction of Britain's first streamline train service. This innovative service represented a significant advancement in railway technology and design, aiming to enhance speed and efficiency in passenger transport.
events.name: The London and North Eastern Railway Silver Jubilee

events.enhanced_description: Samuel Hoare resigned as the British Foreign Secretary, a position he held since 1931, amidst increasing criticism over his handling of foreign affairs, particularly regarding Italy's aggression in Ethiopia. He was succeeded by Anthony Eden, who would later play a significant role in British foreign policy leading up to World War II.
events.name: Samuel Hoare resigns as British foreign secretary, and is replaced by Anthony Eden

events.enhanced_description: The Lanka Sama Samaja Party (LSSP) was founded in Colombo, marking a significant moment in Sri Lankan politics as it became the first socialist party in the country. The party aimed to represent the working class and promote socialist ideals in the face of colonial rule and social inequality.
events.name: The socialist party of Sri Lanka, the Lanka Sama Samaja Party, is founded

events.enhanced_description: Regina Jonas made history in 1935 by becoming the first woman to receive semikhah (rabbinical ordination) in Judaism. Her groundbreaking achievement paved the way for future generations of female rabbis, although she tragically perished in the Holocaust.

image.caption: Colorized portrait of Regina Jonas.
image.credit: See — Hand colored version of

events.enhanced_description: On January 7, 1935, Italian premier Benito Mussolini and French Foreign Minister Pierre Laval concluded an agreement in Rome, wherein both powers agreed not to oppose each other's colonial claims, reflecting the geopolitical dynamics of the time.
events.name: Mussolini-Laval Agreement

events.enhanced_description: On January 8, 1935, the legendary rock and roll artist Elvis Presley was born in Tupelo, Mississippi. His music and cultural impact would go on to shape the landscape of American music and popular culture.
events.name: Birth of Elvis Presley

events.enhanced_description: On January 12, 1935, Amelia Earhart became the first person to successfully complete a solo flight from Hawaii to California, covering a distance of 2,408 miles. This achievement marked a significant milestone in aviation history.
events.name: Amelia Earhart's Solo Flight

events.enhanced_description: On January 13, 1935, a plebiscite in the Saar Basin revealed that 90.3% of voters wished to join Germany, a significant event that reflected the shifting political landscape in Europe during the interwar period.
events.name: Saar Basin Plebiscite

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1935, the first canned beer was sold in Richmond, Virginia, by Gottfried Krueger Brewing Company, revolutionizing the beverage industry and paving the way for the modern beer market.
events.name: First Canned Beer Sold

events.enhanced_description: On February 6, 1935, Parker Brothers began selling the board game Monopoly, which was created by Charles Darrow. The game quickly gained popularity and became a staple of American culture, symbolizing capitalism and economic competition.
events.name: Parker Brothers begins selling the board game Monopoly in the United States

events.enhanced_description: On February 13, 1935, Richard Hauptmann was convicted and sentenced to death for the kidnapping and murder of Charles Lindbergh Jr., the infant son of famous aviator Charles Lindbergh. The case garnered national attention and raised significant public interest in crime and justice.
events.name: Richard Hauptmann is convicted and sentenced to death for the kidnapping and murder of Charles Lindbergh Jr.

events.enhanced_description: On February 15, 1935, Gerhard Domagk and colleagues published their findings on Prontosil, the first widely effective antibiotic, in the Deutsche Medizinische Wochenschrift. This discovery marked a significant advancement in medical science and the treatment of bacterial infections.
events.name: Discovery and clinical development of Prontosil published

events.enhanced_description: On February 26, 1935, Adolf Hitler ordered the reinstatement of the Luftwaffe, Germany's air force, in direct violation of the Treaty of Versailles. This move was a significant step in Germany's military rearmament and foreshadowed the aggressive expansionist policies that would lead to World War II.
events.name: Hitler orders reinstatement of the Luftwaffe

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1935, a coup d'état attempt led by Nikolaos Plastiras and Anastasios Papoulas aimed to overthrow the People's Party government in Greece. The coup was suppressed by March 11, resulting in the leaders being condemned to death for treason.
events.name: 1935 Greek coup d'état attempt

events.enhanced_description: On March 2, 1935, King Prajadhipok (Rama VII) of Siam abdicated the throne, passing the crown to his 9-year-old nephew, Ananda Mahidol (Rama VIII). This transition marked a significant moment in Thai history, as it ushered in a new era of monarchy.
events.name: King Prajadhipok abdicates the throne

events.enhanced_description: On March 16, 1935, Adolf Hitler publicly announced Germany's re-armament, a direct violation of the Treaty of Versailles. This announcement was a pivotal moment in the lead-up to World War II, signaling Germany's intent to rebuild its military strength.
events.name: Hitler announces German re-armament

events.enhanced_description: On March 19, 1935, a race riot erupted in Harlem, New York City, following rumors that a teenage Puerto Rican shoplifter had been brutally beaten by police. The incident highlighted racial tensions and sparked discussions about police brutality and civil rights.

locations.name: Harlem, New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Harlem riot of 1935

events.enhanced_description: On March 21, 1935, Reza Shah of Iran requested that the international community formally adopt the name 'Iran' to refer to the country, replacing the historical name 'Persia'. This change reflected a growing sense of national identity and pride.
events.name: Reza Shah asks for the name change to Iran

events.enhanced_description: On March 22, 1935, the world's first regular television program was transmitted from the Funkturm in Berlin, Germany, by Fernsehsender Paul Nipkow. This event marked a significant milestone in the development of television as a medium for mass communication.
events.name: First regular television program transmitted

events.enhanced_description: On April 11, 1935, the Danish general election was held, resulting in Thorvald Stauning becoming the first Social Democratic Prime Minister of Denmark. His leadership marked a significant shift in Danish politics towards social democracy.
events.name: Danish general election results in Social Democratic Prime Minister

events.enhanced_description: On April 14, 1935, a massive dust storm known as 'Black Sunday' struck eastern New Mexico, Colorado, and western Oklahoma, exacerbating the Dust Bowl crisis. This event became emblematic of the environmental disaster that devastated American agriculture during the 1930s.

locations.name: Eastern New Mexico, Colorado, and Western Oklahoma, United States

events.name: Black Sunday Dust Bowl storm

events.enhanced_description: On April 15, 1935, the Roerich Pact, a Pan-American treaty aimed at the protection of cultural artifacts, was signed in Washington, D.C. This treaty emphasized the importance of safeguarding cultural heritage during times of conflict.
events.name: The Roerich Pact signed

events.enhanced_description: On April 17, 1935, Sun Myung Moon, a teenage Presbyterian convert in Korea under Japanese rule, claimed to have received a revelation from Jesus instructing him to complete a mission from nearly 2,000 years prior. This event marked the beginning of his religious movement.
events.name: Sun Myung Moon claims revelation

events.enhanced_description: On April 24, 1935, William Christian Bullitt Jr., the United States Ambassador to the Soviet Union, hosted the Spring Ball of the Full Moon, which was noted for its extravagant preparations and was said to surpass all previous embassy parties in Moscow's history.
events.name: William Christian Bullitt Jr. hosts Spring Ball

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1935, Sheffield Wednesday defeated West Bromwich Albion 4-2 at Wembley Stadium in London to win the FA Cup final. This victory marked a significant achievement in English football history.
events.name: Sheffield Wednesday wins FA Cup final

events.enhanced_description: On April 29, 1935, the first edition of the Vuelta a España was raced, establishing it as one of the three Grand Tours of road bicycle racing. This event has since become a prestigious annual cycling competition.
events.name: First edition of the Vuelta a España

events.enhanced_description: On May 14, 1935, Northamptonshire County Cricket Club achieved a victory over Somerset at Taunton by 48 runs, marking what would become their last win for 99 matches, a record in the County Championship.
events.name: Northamptonshire County Cricket Club's record

events.enhanced_description: On May 15, 1935, Joseph Stalin officially opened the Moscow Metro to the public, marking a significant advancement in urban transportation in the Soviet Union. The Metro became a symbol of Soviet engineering and modernization.
events.name: Moscow Metro opens to the public

events.enhanced_description: On May 19, 1935, T. E. Lawrence, famously known as 'Lawrence of Arabia', was involved in a motorcycle accident near his home in Dorset, England. He succumbed to his injuries a few days later, marking the end of the life of a notable figure in British history.
events.name: T. E. Lawrence motorcycle accident

events.enhanced_description: On May 21, 1935, Adolf Hitler announced the reintroduction of conscription to the Wehrmacht, violating the Treaty of Versailles. This decision further escalated tensions in Europe and contributed to the onset of World War II.
events.name: Hitler announces reintroduction of conscription

events.enhanced_description: In the landmark case Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States, the Supreme Court ruled that the National Industrial Recovery Act was unconstitutional, marking a significant setback for President Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal policies aimed at economic recovery during the Great Depression.
events.name: Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States

events.enhanced_description: The French ocean liner SS Normandie embarked on her maiden voyage from Le Havre to New York City, achieving the Blue Riband for the fastest transatlantic crossing at the time. This voyage marked a significant achievement in maritime travel and luxury.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Maiden voyage of SS Normandie

events.enhanced_description: The 1935 Quetta earthquake, registering a magnitude of 7.1, devastated the city of Quetta in Balochistan, Pakistan, resulting in the deaths of approximately 40,000 people and causing widespread destruction.
events.name: 1935 Quetta earthquake

events.enhanced_description: The He–Umezu Agreement was a significant accord in which China's Kuomintang government conceded military control of northeastern China to Japan, reflecting the increasing influence of Japanese imperialism in the region during the 1930s.
events.name: He–Umezu Agreement

events.enhanced_description: Alcoholics Anonymous was founded in Akron, Ohio, by William G. Wilson and Dr. Robert Smith, marking the beginning of a global movement aimed at helping individuals struggling with alcoholism through mutual support and shared experiences.
events.name: Founding of Alcoholics Anonymous

events.enhanced_description: The Chaco War, fought between Paraguay and Bolivia over control of the Chaco region, concluded in 1935, resulting in significant territorial gains for Paraguay and highlighting the geopolitical tensions in South America during the early 20th century.
events.name: End of the Chaco War

events.enhanced_description: In a historic boxing match at Madison Square Garden, James J. Braddock defeated Max Baer to win the heavyweight championship of the world, a victory that symbolized hope during the Great Depression.

image.caption: Portrait of boxer James J. Braddock, photographed by Alan Fisher for the New York World-Telegram & Sun Collection.
image.credit: Alan Fisher, World Telegram staff photographer — Library of Congress. New York World-Telegram & Sun Collection. https://hdl.loc.gov/loc.pnp/cph.3f05862
image.date_qualification: Image date: 1935 (as supplied); not established as the date of the bout photograph.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

locations.name: Madison Square Garden, New York City, New York, United States

events.name: James J. Braddock defeats Max Baer

events.enhanced_description: The Anglo-German Naval Agreement was signed, allowing Germany to expand its navy to 35% of the British naval tonnage, a significant step in the rearmament of Germany prior to World War II.
events.name: Anglo-German Naval Agreement

events.enhanced_description: Carlos Gardel, the legendary Franco-Argentine singer and composer known as the 'Father of Tango', tragically died in a plane crash in Medellín, Colombia, leaving a lasting legacy in the world of music.
events.name: Death of Carlos Gardel

events.enhanced_description: The RMS Mauretania, once the fastest ocean liner in the world, set sail from Southampton to Rosyth to be broken up, marking the end of an era in maritime history.
events.name: RMS Mauretania sails for breaking up

events.enhanced_description: The Brazilian radiophonic program A Voz do Brasil was inaugurated, becoming a significant medium for government communication and cultural dissemination throughout the country.
events.name: Inauguration of A Voz do Brasil

events.enhanced_description: The seventh and final congress of the Comintern was held, marking the end of an era for the international communist movement as it faced increasing challenges and changes in the global political landscape.
events.name: Seventh Congress of the Comintern

events.enhanced_description: A catastrophic dam burst near Ovada, Italy, resulted in the tragic loss of approximately 250 lives, highlighting the dangers of infrastructure failures.
events.name: Dam burst near Ovada

events.enhanced_description: President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed the Social Security Act into law, establishing a social insurance program designed to provide financial assistance to the elderly and unemployed, a cornerstone of the New Deal.
events.name: Signing of the Social Security Act

events.enhanced_description: Representatives from France, Britain, and Italy convened in Paris in an unsuccessful attempt to negotiate a resolution to the Abyssinia Crisis, reflecting the growing tensions in Europe and the challenges of collective security.
events.name: Abyssinia Crisis negotiations

events.enhanced_description: The 1935 Labor Day hurricane, the strongest hurricane ever to strike the United States, made landfall in the Upper Florida Keys as a Category 5 storm, causing widespread destruction and claiming 423 lives.

locations.name: Upper Florida Keys, Florida, United States

events.name: 1935 Labor Day hurricane

events.enhanced_description: American aviator Howard Hughes set a new airspeed record of 352 mph while flying the Hughes H-1 Racer, showcasing advancements in aviation technology and engineering during the 1930s.
events.name: Howard Hughes sets airspeed record

events.enhanced_description: The Nuremberg Laws were enacted in Germany, stripping Jews of their citizenship and laying the groundwork for systemic discrimination and persecution, a pivotal moment in the lead-up to the Holocaust.
events.name: Nuremberg Laws enacted

events.enhanced_description: Manuel L. Quezon was elected as the 2nd President of the Philippines, marking a significant moment in the country's political history as it moved towards greater autonomy from American colonial rule.
events.name: Manuel L. Quezon elected President

events.enhanced_description: Earl W. Bascom and his brother Weldon produced the first night rodeo held outdoors under electric lights in Columbia, Mississippi, revolutionizing the way rodeos were presented and enjoyed.
events.name: First night rodeo under electric lights

events.enhanced_description: The London and North Eastern Railway's first A4 Class streamlined steam locomotive, A4 2509 Silver Link, made her inaugural journey from London King's Cross, marking a significant advancement in railway technology and design.
events.name: Inaugural journey of A4 2509 Silver Link

events.enhanced_description: On September 30, 1935, U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt dedicated the Hoover Dam, a monumental feat of engineering that harnessed the Colorado River for hydroelectric power and flood control. The dam, originally named Boulder Dam, symbolizes the New Deal's efforts to combat the Great Depression through large-scale public works projects.
events.name: Dedication of the Hoover Dam

events.enhanced_description: The Second Italo-Ethiopian War began on October 3, 1935, when Italian General Emilio De Bono invaded Ethiopia, marking a significant conflict in the lead-up to World War II. This invasion was part of Italy's imperial ambitions and resulted in widespread condemnation from the international community.

image.caption: Italian troops with a machine gun.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Abbysinian War October 1935, Italian machine gun, mediastorehouse.com

events.name: Beginning of the Second Italo-Ethiopian War

events.enhanced_description: On October 6, 1935, the wreckage of the RMS Lusitania, a British ocean liner sunk by a German U-boat in 1915, was discovered off the coast of Ireland. This discovery reignited interest in the ship's tragic sinking and its implications for maritime law and warfare.
events.name: Discovery of the wreckage of the RMS Lusitania

events.enhanced_description: On October 10, 1935, a tornado struck Langenberg, Germany, destroying the 160-meter tall wooden radio tower. This event marked a turning point in radio tower design, leading to the phasing out of wooden structures in favor of more durable materials.
events.name: Destruction of the wooden radio tower in Langenberg

events.enhanced_description: On October 11, 1935, the RMS Olympic, once the largest ocean liner in the world, sailed from Southampton for the last time before being sold for scrap. This marked the end of an era for the White Star Line and the age of ocean liners.
events.name: Final voyage of the RMS Olympic

events.enhanced_description: On October 14, 1935, the Liberal Party, led by William Lyon Mackenzie King, won a majority government in the Canadian federal election, defeating the Conservative Party led by R. B. Bennett. This election was pivotal in shaping Canada's political landscape during the Great Depression.
events.name: 1935 Canadian federal election

events.enhanced_description: On October 21, 1935, the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the United Kingdom delivered a landmark decision in Grant v Australian Knitting Mills, which significantly impacted consumer law and established important precedents regarding product liability.

locations.name: Judicial Committee of the Privy Council

events.name: Grant v Australian Knitting Mills decision

events.enhanced_description: On October 22, 1935, after the Long March, the Chinese Communist Party established its base in Shaanxi province, specifically in the city of Xi'an. This settlement marked a crucial turning point in the Chinese Civil War, allowing the party to regroup and strategize for future conflicts.
events.name: Chinese Communist Party settles in Shaanxi

events.enhanced_description: On November 14, 1935, the United Kingdom held a general election in which Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin returned to office leading a National Government formed by the Conservative Party. This election resulted in a large but reduced majority, reflecting the changing political landscape in Britain.
events.name: 1935 United Kingdom general election

events.enhanced_description: On November 22, 1935, the flying boat China Clipper took off from Alameda, California, marking the first airmail delivery across the Pacific Ocean. This historic flight underscored the advancements in aviation and international mail services, reaching Manila with over 110,000 pieces of mail.
events.name: China Clipper's first airmail flight

events.enhanced_description: On November 23, 1935, researchers Jacques and Thérèse Tréfouël, Daniel Bovet, and Federico Nitti at the Pasteur Institute in Paris discovered that sulfanilamide was the active component of Prontosil, paving the way for the development of sulfa drugs and revolutionizing the treatment of bacterial infections.
events.name: Discovery of sulfanilamide as active component of Prontosil

events.enhanced_description: On November 25, 1935, after 11 years in exile, King George II returned to Greece, landing in Corfu. His return marked a significant moment in Greek history, as it followed a controversial referendum favoring the monarchy's restoration.
events.name: Return of King George II of Greece

events.enhanced_description: On December 10, 1935, the Hanshin Tigers, a prominent professional baseball club in Japan, was founded in Osaka. The team has since become a significant part of Japanese sports culture and has a passionate fan base.
events.name: Founding of the Hanshin Tigers

events.enhanced_description: On December 12, 1935, Heinrich Himmler founded the Lebensborn program in Germany, aimed at promoting Aryan birth rates in line with Nazi eugenics policies. This program was part of the broader racial ideology that characterized the Nazi regime.
events.name: Founding of the Lebensborn program

events.enhanced_description: On December 17, 1935, the Douglas DST, the prototype of the Douglas DC-3 airliner, made its first flight in the United States. This aircraft would go on to become one of the most significant and widely used airliners in aviation history.
events.name: First flight of the Douglas DST

events.enhanced_description: On December 18, 1935, British Foreign Secretary Samuel Hoare resigned and was replaced by Anthony Eden. This change in leadership reflected the shifting political dynamics in Britain during a tumultuous period leading up to World War II.
events.name: Resignation of Samuel Hoare

events.enhanced_description: In 1935, Mao Zedong issued the Wayaobu Manifesto, which called for a united front against Japanese imperialism in China. This manifesto was pivotal in rallying various factions within China to resist the growing threat of Japanese invasion during a period of national crisis.
events.name: Mao Zedong issues the Wayaobu Manifesto

events.enhanced_description: On December 28, 1935, the Soviet newspaper Pravda published a letter from Pavel Postyshev, reviving the New Year tree tradition in the Soviet Union. This revival was part of a broader cultural shift under Stalin's regime, aiming to promote state-sanctioned festivities.
events.name: Revival of the New Year tree tradition in the Soviet Union

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1936, Per Albin Hansson resigned as Prime Minister of Sweden due to disagreements over defense policy. His resignation led to Axel Pehrsson-Bramstorp taking over as Prime Minister, marking a significant shift in Swedish politics during a turbulent period in Europe.
events.name: Per Albin Hansson resigns as Prime Minister of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: In 1936, the Mästermyr chest, a remarkable artifact from the Viking Age, was discovered in the Mästermyr mire near Hemse on Gotland, Sweden. This chest, believed to have belonged to a craftsman, contained various tools and items that provide insight into Viking craftsmanship and daily life.
events.name: Discovery of the Mästermyr chest

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of his father, King George V, Edward VIII ascended to the throne on January 20, 1936. His reign was marked by controversy, particularly regarding his relationship with Wallis Simpson, which ultimately led to his abdication later that year.
events.name: King Edward VIII ascends the throne

events.enhanced_description: The state funeral of King George V took place on January 28, 1936, following a grand procession through London. He was interred at St George's Chapel in Windsor Castle, marking a significant moment in British royal history.

locations.name: St George's Chapel, Windsor Castle, Berkshire, United Kingdom

events.name: State funeral of George V of the United Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: On February 4, 1936, Radium E, also known as bismuth-210, was synthesized, marking a significant milestone in the field of nuclear chemistry. This achievement demonstrated the capabilities of scientists to create radioactive elements artificially.
events.name: Radium E becomes the first synthetic radioactive element

events.enhanced_description: The IV Olympic Winter Games officially opened on February 6, 1936, in Garmisch-Partenkirchen, Germany. This event was notable not only for its athletic competitions but also for the political climate of the time, as it was held under the Nazi regime.
events.name: IV Olympic Winter Games open

events.enhanced_description: On February 10, 1936, during the Second Italo-Ethiopian War, Italian forces achieved a decisive victory at the Battle of Amba Aradam, effectively neutralizing the Ethiopian army. This battle was part of Italy's aggressive campaign to annex Ethiopia.
events.name: Battle of Amba Aradam

events.enhanced_description: The 1936 Spanish general election, held on February 16, resulted in a majority for the left-wing Popular Front coalition. This election was a pivotal moment leading up to the Spanish Civil War, reflecting the deep political divisions in the country.
events.name: 1936 Spanish general election

events.enhanced_description: The February 26 Incident, which occurred on February 26, 1936, was a failed coup attempt by the Imperial Way Faction against the Japanese government. The incident resulted in the assassination of several politicians and highlighted the growing militarism in Japan.

image.caption: Rebel soldiers guard Hanzomon Gate of the Imperial Palace.

events.name: February 26 Incident

events.enhanced_description: The construction of the Hoover Dam was completed on March 1, 1936, marking a significant engineering achievement of the time. The dam, located on the border between Nevada and Arizona, was crucial for water management and hydroelectric power generation in the southwestern United States.
