events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1938, representatives of the British and French governments informed Czechoslovak President Edvard Beneš that they would not intervene if Hitler annexed the Sudetenland by force. This ultimatum led to the capitulation of the Czechoslovak government.
events.name: Czechoslovak Government's Capitulation

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1938, Czechoslovak Premier Milan Hodža resigned following the government's capitulation to the demands of Britain and France. He was succeeded by General Jan Syrový, marking a significant shift in the Czechoslovak leadership during a critical period.

image.caption: Portrait photograph of Milan Hodža by Robert Sennecke.
image.credit: Robert Sennecke — Photographs available at www.audiovis.nac.gov.pl are public domain or the owner of the copyrights is the State Treasury of Poland, represented by the National Digital Archive and which grant free of charge licence for free use of the materials on all known exploitation fields.
image.date_qualification: Portrait dated November 1935; it predates his resignation in September 1938 and is not a photograph of that event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Resignation of Milan Hodža

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1938, British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain arrived in Bad Godesberg to negotiate with Adolf Hitler regarding the Sudetenland crisis. Hitler escalated his demands, insisting on the occupation of all German Sudeten territories by October 1, prompting Chamberlain to advise Czechoslovakia to mobilize its forces that night.
events.name: Neville Chamberlain arrives in Bad Godesberg for talks with Hitler

events.enhanced_description: On September 23, 1938, the Czechoslovak army mobilized in response to the escalating tensions and the threat of invasion by Nazi Germany. This mobilization was a critical step in preparing the nation for potential conflict.
events.name: Czechoslovak Army Mobilization

events.enhanced_description: In response to the escalating tensions and demands from Nazi Germany, the Czechoslovak army was mobilized in late September 1938. This mobilization was a direct reaction to the threats posed by Hitler regarding the Sudetenland, marking a significant moment in the lead-up to World War II.
events.name: The Czechoslovak army mobilizes

events.enhanced_description: On September 24, 1938, Sir Eric Phipps, the British Ambassador to France, reported that the majority of French sentiment was against war, raising doubts about France's willingness to engage militarily in the Sudetenland crisis. This report highlighted the challenges of forming a united front against Nazi aggression.
events.name: Phipps's Report on French Sentiment

events.enhanced_description: On September 25, 1938, the British Royal Navy was ordered to sea as tensions escalated in Europe, signaling a potential military response to the threats posed by Nazi Germany. This action was part of the broader mobilization of forces in anticipation of conflict.
events.name: British Royal Navy Orders

events.enhanced_description: As tensions rose in late September 1938, the Soviet Union issued a warning to Poland concerning its military buildup along the Czechoslovak border. The Soviet leadership indicated that any aggression against Czechoslovakia would nullify the non-aggression pact signed between the two nations in 1932.
events.name: Soviet Union warns Poland regarding Czech border

events.enhanced_description: On September 26, 1938, Adolf Hitler delivered a vitriolic speech at Berlin's Sportpalast, defiantly implying that war with Czechoslovakia could begin at any moment. This speech further escalated tensions in Europe and foreshadowed the impending conflict.
events.name: Hitler's Speech at Sportpalast

events.enhanced_description: On September 28, 1938, as his deadline for occupying the Sudetenland approached, Adolf Hitler invited Italian Duce Benito Mussolini, French Premier Édouard Daladier, and British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain to a conference in Munich, excluding the Czechs from the discussions.
events.name: Munich Conference Invitation

events.enhanced_description: In late September 1938, Sir Eric Phipps, the British Ambassador to France, reported to London that the majority of the French populace was against war, with only a small faction advocating for military action. This report raised significant concerns about France's willingness to support Britain in the event of a conflict with Nazi Germany.
events.name: Sir Eric Phipps reports on French opposition to war

events.enhanced_description: On September 29, 1938, Colonel Graham Christie was informed by Carl Friedrich Goerdeler that the mobilization of the Royal Navy had negatively impacted the popularity of the Nazi regime, as the German public began to realize the potential for a world war due to the Sudetenland crisis.
events.name: Public Sentiment in Germany

events.enhanced_description: In late September 1938, Colonel Graham Christie, a former British military attaché in Berlin, was informed by Carl Friedrich Goerdeler that the mobilization of the Royal Navy had negatively impacted the popularity of the Nazi regime. The German public began to realize that the impending conflict could lead to a world war.
events.name: Colonel Graham Christie reports on Nazi regime popularity

events.enhanced_description: On September 30, 1938, Neville Chamberlain returned to Britain from a meeting with Adolf Hitler, declaring 'Peace for our time.' This statement was emblematic of the policy of appeasement that characterized British foreign policy in the lead-up to World War II.
events.name: Chamberlain's Declaration of Peace

events.enhanced_description: On September 30, 1938, Neville Chamberlain and Adolf Hitler concluded their discussions regarding the Sudetenland. Chamberlain agreed to present Hitler's demands to the Czechoslovak government, which ultimately rejected the terms, leading to increased tensions in Europe.
events.name: Chamberlain and Hitler conclude talks on the Sudetenland

events.enhanced_description: On September 30, 1938, the Munich Agreement was signed by leaders from Germany, Italy, Britain, and France, allowing for the annexation of the Sudetenland by Germany. The Czechoslovak government was notably excluded from the negotiations, highlighting the disregard for its sovereignty.
events.name: Munich Agreement signed

events.enhanced_description: In October 1938, the Imperial Japanese Army launched a significant offensive, largely overrunning the city of Canton (Guangzhou) during the Second Sino-Japanese War. This event marked a critical moment in the conflict, showcasing Japan's military dominance in the region.
events.name: Imperial Japanese Army overruns Canton

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1938, German troops marched into the Sudetenland following the Munich Agreement. This military action was part of Hitler's broader strategy to expand German territory and was met with little resistance from the Czechoslovak forces.
events.name: German troops march into the Sudetenland

events.enhanced_description: On October 2, 1938, the Tiberias massacre occurred when Arab raiders attacked Jewish immigrants, resulting in the deaths of 19 individuals. This event highlighted the escalating tensions and violence in the region during this period.
events.name: Tiberias massacre

events.enhanced_description: On October 4, 1938, the Republican forces in the Spanish Civil War began the withdrawal of foreign volunteers from combat, adhering to an agreement made earlier in July. This decision reflected the changing dynamics of the conflict as external support diminished.
events.name: Republican forces withdraw foreign volunteers

events.enhanced_description: On October 5, 1938, Edvard Beneš, the president of Czechoslovakia, resigned from his position amid the growing crisis over the Sudetenland. His resignation marked a significant turning point in Czechoslovak history as the country faced imminent threats from Nazi Germany.
events.name: Edvard Beneš resigns

events.enhanced_description: On October 16, 1938, Winston Churchill delivered a broadcast address to the United States, condemning the Munich Agreement as a significant defeat for Western democracies. He urged America and Europe to prepare for potential armed resistance against Adolf Hitler's aggressive expansion.
events.name: Winston Churchill condemns Munich Agreement

events.enhanced_description: On October 18, 1938, the German government expelled 12,000 Polish Jews living in Germany. While the Polish government accepted 4,000 of these individuals, the remaining 8,000 were left stranded in no-man's land along the German-Polish border, highlighting the growing anti-Semitic policies of the Nazi regime.
events.name: German expulsion of Polish Jews

events.enhanced_description: On October 21, 1938, Adolf Hitler circulated a secret memorandum among his high command, outlining plans for the 'liquidation of the rest of Czechoslovakia' and the occupation of Memel. This document revealed Hitler's aggressive intentions and disregard for the Munich Agreement.
events.name: Hitler's secret memorandum on Czechoslovakia

events.enhanced_description: On October 24, 1938, French Foreign Minister Georges Bonnet initiated a major purge of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, dismissing or exiling several officials who opposed appeasement policies. This action reflected the internal political struggles in France regarding its stance towards Nazi Germany.
events.name: Georges Bonnet's purge of Foreign Affairs Ministry

events.enhanced_description: On October 27, 1938, DuPont announced the name for its new synthetic yarn: 'nylon.' This innovation marked a significant advancement in materials science and would later become a staple in various industries, including textiles and fashion.
events.name: DuPont announces nylon

events.enhanced_description: On November 7, 1938, Ernst vom Rath, a Third Secretary at the German Embassy in Paris, was assassinated by Herschel Grynszpan, a Jewish teenager. This act of violence was a response to the persecution of Jews in Germany and served as a catalyst for the subsequent Kristallnacht pogrom.
events.name: Assassination of Ernst vom Rath

events.enhanced_description: On the night of November 9-10, 1938, Kristallnacht, or the 'Night of Broken Glass,' erupted across Germany, resulting in widespread violence against Jewish communities. Approximately 7,500 Jewish businesses were vandalized, 267 synagogues were set ablaze, and around 30,000 Jewish men were arrested and sent to concentration camps.
events.name: Kristallnacht

events.enhanced_description: On November 10, 1938, İsmet İnönü was elected as the second President of Turkey following the death of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk. His presidency marked a significant period in Turkish history as he continued to implement Atatürk's reforms and navigate the challenges of the interwar period.
events.name: İsmet İnönü becomes President of Turkey

events.enhanced_description: On November 11, 1938, Celâl Bayar formed the 10th government of Turkey, having previously served as Prime Minister twice. His government was tasked with continuing the modernization efforts initiated by Atatürk and addressing the economic challenges facing the nation.
events.name: Formation of Celâl Bayar's government

events.enhanced_description: On November 12, 1938, French Finance Minister Paul Reynaud implemented a series of economic reforms aimed at boosting productivity and reversing the economic decline that followed the Munich Agreement. These reforms were controversial and faced opposition from various political factions.
events.name: Paul Reynaud's economic reforms

events.enhanced_description: On November 16, 1938, Swiss chemist Albert Hofmann first synthesized LSD (lysergic acid diethylamide) at the Sandoz Laboratories in Basel. This groundbreaking discovery would later have profound implications for psychology, psychiatry, and popular culture.
events.name: Synthesis of LSD

events.enhanced_description: On November 18, 1938, John L. Lewis was elected as the first president of the Congress of Industrial Organizations (CIO) in the United States. His leadership marked a pivotal moment in the labor movement, advocating for the rights of industrial workers.
events.name: John L. Lewis elected as CIO president

events.enhanced_description: On November 25, 1938, French Foreign Minister Georges Bonnet informed Léon Noël, the French Ambassador to Poland, that France should seek an excuse to terminate the 1921 Franco-Polish alliance. This decision reflected the shifting geopolitical landscape in Europe leading up to World War II.
events.name: Georges Bonnet's Franco-Polish alliance termination

events.enhanced_description: On November 30, 1938, the Czechoslovak parliament elected Emil Hácha as the new president of Czechoslovakia. His presidency came at a tumultuous time as the country faced increasing pressure from Nazi Germany.
events.name: Election of Emil Hácha as President of Czechoslovakia

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1938, Slovakia was granted the status of an autonomous state under the leadership of Catholic priest Fr. Joseph Tiso. This marked a significant shift in the political landscape of Czechoslovakia as tensions with Hungary and Germany escalated.
events.name: Slovakia granted autonomous status

events.enhanced_description: On December 6, 1938, German Foreign Minister Joachim von Ribbentrop visited Paris, where he allegedly received a statement from French Foreign Minister Georges Bonnet regarding France's recognition of Germany's influence in Eastern Europe. This interaction was pivotal in shaping German foreign policy in the lead-up to World War II.
events.name: Ribbentrop's visit to Paris

events.enhanced_description: On December 11, 1938, parliamentary elections were held in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, where the opposition gained votes but failed to secure any seats. This election highlighted the political tensions and the challenges faced by the opposition in a repressive political environment.
events.name: Yugoslavia parliamentary election

events.enhanced_description: On December 13, 1938, the Neuengamme concentration camp opened near Hamburg, Germany. This facility became one of the many sites of imprisonment and forced labor during the Holocaust, reflecting the escalating brutality of the Nazi regime.
events.name: Opening of Neuengamme concentration camp

events.enhanced_description: On December 15, 1938, the Netherlands closed its borders to refugees, a decision that reflected the growing anti-Semitic sentiment in Europe and the challenges faced by those fleeing persecution in Nazi Germany.
events.name: Netherlands closes border to refugees

events.enhanced_description: On December 17, 1938, German chemist Otto Hahn discovered nuclear fission of uranium, a breakthrough that laid the groundwork for the development of nuclear energy and weapons. This discovery marked the beginning of the Atomic Age and had profound implications for science and global politics.

image.caption: Photograph of the Deutsches Museum reconstruction of the experimental apparatus associated with Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann’s discovery of nuclear fission.
image.credit: J Brew — originally posted to Flickr as Nuclear Fission Deutsches Museum
image.date_qualification: The apparatus is presented as a reconstruction of the 1938 experimental setup; the image itself dates to 2006-05-28.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Discovery of nuclear fission by Otto Hahn

events.enhanced_description: On December 23, 1938, a coelacanth, a fish believed to have been extinct for 66 million years, was caught off the coast of South Africa near the Chalumna River. This remarkable discovery astonished the scientific community and provided valuable insights into evolutionary biology.

locations.name: Chalumna River, Eastern Cape, South Africa

events.name: Coelacanth caught off South Africa

events.enhanced_description: On December 24, 1938, leading Korean dancer Choi Seung-hee arrived in Le Havre, France, after her tour in the United States. This marked the beginning of her European tour, making her one of the first Korean entertainers to gain international recognition.
events.name: Choi Seung-hee arrives in France

events.enhanced_description: On December 27, 1938, a massive avalanche struck a construction worker dormitory site in Kurobe, Japan, resulting in the tragic deaths of 87 people. This disaster highlighted the dangers faced by workers in mountainous regions.
events.name: Avalanche in Kurobe, Japan

events.enhanced_description: World War II crimes in Poland encompass a range of atrocities committed by both Nazi and Soviet forces during the occupation of Poland from 1939 onwards. These crimes included mass executions, forced labor, and the systematic extermination of the Jewish population.
events.name: World War II crimes in Poland

events.enhanced_description: Various laws and regulations come into effect in Nazi Germany, further entrenching the regime's oppressive policies. These measures reflect the increasing control of the state over various aspects of life in Germany.
events.name: Coming into effect in Nazi Germany of:

events.enhanced_description: Several oppressive laws come into effect in Nazi Germany, including the Protection of Young Persons Act and regulations affecting small businesses and Jewish citizens. These laws exemplify the regime's systematic discrimination and control over society.
events.name: Coming into effect in Nazi Germany of various laws

events.enhanced_description: Bill Hewlett and David Packard establish Hewlett-Packard in a garage in Palo Alto, California, marking the inception of what would become a major player in technology and innovation. This event is often regarded as the birth of Silicon Valley.
events.name: Hewlett-Packard founded

events.enhanced_description: Philipp Etter assumes the presidency of the Swiss Confederation, leading the country during a time of neutrality amidst the growing tensions of World War II. His leadership is characterized by Switzerland's commitment to maintaining its independence.
events.name: Philipp Etter takes over as President of the Swiss Confederation

events.enhanced_description: The Third Five-Year Plan is initiated in the Soviet Union, focusing on rapid industrialization and military buildup. This plan reflects the regime's ambitions to strengthen the economy and prepare for potential conflicts.
events.name: The Third Soviet Five Year Plan is launched

events.enhanced_description: The Protection of Young Persons Act, originally passed in April 1938, comes into effect in Nazi Germany, further entrenching the regime's control over youth and education. This act is part of a broader strategy to indoctrinate young people.
events.name: The Protection of Young Persons Act comes into effect

events.enhanced_description: New regulations come into effect in Nazi Germany requiring small businesses to maintain adequate accounting records. This measure reflects the regime's increasing control over the economy and its efforts to monitor financial activities.
events.name: Small businesses obligation to maintain accounting

events.enhanced_description: A decree in Nazi Germany mandates that Jews must change their names to reflect their ethnicity, furthering the regime's oppressive policies against Jewish citizens. This reflects the systematic discrimination and dehumanization faced by the Jewish community.
events.name: The Jews name change decree

events.enhanced_description: In Paris, French Foreign Minister Georges Bonnet delivers a speech affirming the government's commitment to the cordon sanitaire, a strategy aimed at containing the spread of fascism in Eastern Europe. This reflects the geopolitical tensions leading up to World War II.
events.name: Georges Bonnet's speech in Paris

events.enhanced_description: In a pivotal speech in the House of Commons, British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain declared that any German aggression against France would be viewed as an attack on Britain itself. This statement underscored Britain's commitment to collective security in Europe and foreshadowed the alliances that would shape the early stages of World War II.
events.name: British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain states in the House of Commons that any German attack on France will be automatically considered an attack on Britain

events.enhanced_description: In response to a speech by French Foreign Minister Georges Bonnet, German Foreign Minister Joachim von Ribbentrop asserted that all French security commitments in Eastern Europe were now void. This statement reflected the escalating tensions between Germany and France as Europe edged closer to war.
events.name: German Foreign Minister Joachim von Ribbentrop protests French security commitments

events.enhanced_description: The Arab revolt in Palestine, which began in 1936, concluded in 1939 after years of conflict between Arab nationalists and British authorities. The revolt was fueled by opposition to British rule and Jewish immigration, and its end marked a significant moment in the history of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
events.name: The 1936–39 Arab revolt in Palestine ends

events.enhanced_description: In January 1939, French Foreign Minister Georges Bonnet proposed to Lord Halifax during an emergency meeting in London that Poland could serve as a buffer state to protect Romania from a potential German invasion. This meeting highlighted the growing tensions in Europe as nations sought to navigate the impending threat of World War II.
events.name: Emergency meeting in London regarding Romanian crisis

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1939, General Francisco Franco officially assumed power in Spain following the conclusion of the Spanish Civil War. His regime would last until his death in 1975, marking a significant period of authoritarian rule in Spanish history.
events.name: General Francisco Franco assumes power

events.enhanced_description: In 1939, American adventurer Richard Halliburton sent a last message from a Chinese junk before disappearing during a voyage across the Pacific Ocean. His disappearance sparked intrigue and speculation, and in 1945, wreckage believed to be from his vessel washed ashore in San Diego.
events.name: Richard Halliburton's last message

events.enhanced_description: In 1939, Refik Saydam formed the 12th government of Turkey, marking his second term as Prime Minister. His leadership came during a critical period in Turkish history as the nation navigated the complexities of international relations in the lead-up to World War II.
events.name: Refik Saydam forms new government in Turkey

events.enhanced_description: Polish Foreign Minister Colonel Józef Beck signed a treaty in London that aimed to formalize Neville Chamberlain's 'Polish Guarantee' on March 31, 1939. This treaty was part of the efforts to secure alliances against the growing threat of Nazi Germany.
events.name: Polish Foreign Minister signs treaty in London

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of his father, King Ghazi, in an automobile accident, Faisal II ascended to the throne of Iraq at the tender age of three in 1939. His reign would be marked by political instability and the influence of foreign powers in Iraqi affairs.
events.name: Faisal II becomes King of Iraq

events.enhanced_description: In 1939, Robert Menzies was elected leader of the United Australia Party, subsequently becoming the 12th Prime Minister of Australia. His leadership marked a significant shift in Australian politics, although he would not be sworn in until later that April.

image.caption: Portrait of Robert Menzies.
image.credit: National Library of Australia — http://nla.gov.au/nla.obj-136636422
image.date_qualification: Dated 1939; the source does not establish a more precise date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Robert Menzies becomes leader of the United Australia Party

events.enhanced_description: In 1939, the All India Forward Bloc was formed by Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose as a faction within the Indian National Congress. This organization aimed to consolidate nationalist forces and promote a more radical approach to achieving independence from British rule.
events.name: Formation of the All India Forward Bloc

events.enhanced_description: In 1939, the British government issued the White Paper of 1939, which sharply restricted Jewish immigration to Mandatory Palestine. This policy was controversial and had significant implications for Jewish refugees fleeing Europe during the rise of Nazism.
events.name: British government issues White Paper of 1939

events.enhanced_description: In 1939, Sweden, Norway, and Finland collectively refused Germany's offer of non-aggression pacts. This decision reflected their desire to maintain neutrality amidst the growing tensions in Europe leading up to World War II.
events.name: Sweden, Norway, and Finland refuse Germany's offer

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1939, the Reichstag passed a statement designating Hermann Göring as Adolf Hitler's successor in the event of Hitler's death during World War II. This decision reflected the consolidation of power within the Nazi regime and the importance of Göring in the hierarchy of the Third Reich.
events.name: Reichstag statement on Hitler's succession

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1939, Britain and France issued ultimatums to Germany, demanding the cessation of its aggressive actions in Europe. This marked a significant escalation in tensions leading up to World War II, as nations began to take a firmer stance against Nazi expansionism.
events.name: Britain and France deliver ultimatums to Germany

events.enhanced_description: Following the invasion of Poland, the Free City of Danzig was annexed to Nazi Germany on January 1, 1939. This event was part of Hitler's broader strategy to reclaim territories lost after World War I and to assert German dominance in Eastern Europe.
events.name: Annexation of the Free City of Danzig

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1939, both Spain and Ireland declared their neutrality in the impending conflict of World War II. This decision reflected their desire to avoid the devastation of war and maintain sovereignty amidst the rising tensions in Europe.
events.name: Spain and Ireland declare neutrality

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1939, the United Kingdom, France, New Zealand, Australia, and India declared war on Nazi Germany, marking the official start of their military engagement in World War II. This collective action was a response to Germany's aggressive expansion and violation of international agreements.
events.name: Allied declaration of war on Nazi Germany

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1939, U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt delivered a nationwide radio address advocating for neutrality as the United States faced the growing threat of World War II. His message aimed to reassure the American public and maintain the nation's isolationist stance.
events.name: FDR advocates neutrality

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1939, the ocean liner SS Athenia became the first British civilian casualty of World War II when it was torpedoed and sunk by the German submarine U-30 in the eastern Atlantic. Of the 1,418 people aboard, 98 passengers and 19 crew members lost their lives, marking a tragic escalation in the conflict.
events.name: SS Athenia torpedoed

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1939, Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain offered Winston Churchill the position of First Lord of the Admiralty, marking Churchill's return to government after a decade. This appointment would prove significant as Churchill later became a key leader during World War II.
events.name: Churchill appointed First Lord of the Admiralty

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1939, the British Royal Air Force conducted the first bombing raid on Wilhelmshaven during World War II. This marked the beginning of aerial warfare in the conflict, as the Allies sought to disrupt German military operations.
events.name: First bombing of Wilhelmshaven

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1939, the defense of Katowice by irregular Polish militia failed as German Wehrmacht forces secured the city, leading to the Katowice massacre. This event highlighted the brutal tactics employed by the Nazis during their invasion of Poland.
events.name: Defense of Katowice

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1939, Nepal declared war on Germany, aligning itself with the Allies in response to the growing threat posed by the Axis powers. This declaration was part of a broader effort by various nations to oppose Nazi aggression.
events.name: Nepal declares war on Germany

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1939, the Little Sisters of Jesus was founded in Algeria by Little Sister Magdeleine. This religious community aimed to live among the poor and marginalized, reflecting a commitment to social justice and service.
events.name: Little Sisters of Jesus founded

events.enhanced_description: In September 1939, following the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, the Soviet Union invaded Poland from the east, occupying significant territories. This invasion was part of a secret agreement with Nazi Germany to divide Poland between the two powers.
events.name: Soviet invasion of Poland

events.enhanced_description: On September 17, 1939, the Royal Navy aircraft carrier HMS Courageous was torpedoed and sunk by the German submarine U-29 in the Western Approaches, resulting in the loss of 519 crew members. This marked the first significant loss of a British warship in World War II.
events.name: Sinking of HMS Courageous

events.enhanced_description: In late 1939, Reinhard Heydrich, head of the Security Police, issued the Schnellbrief directive, which mandated the transfer of Jews from towns and villages in occupied Poland to ghettos. This directive laid the groundwork for the systematic persecution of Jews during the Holocaust.
events.name: Schnellbrief directive by Reinhard Heydrich

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1939, Romanian Prime Minister Armand Călinescu was assassinated in Bucharest by members of the fascist Iron Guard. His death marked a significant turning point in Romanian politics, leading to increased instability and the rise of extremist groups.
events.name: Assassination of Armand Călinescu

events.enhanced_description: In September 1939, following their respective invasions of Poland, Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union reached an agreement to divide Polish territories between them. This pact was a significant factor in the early stages of World War II.

image.caption: Map of territorial disputes and claims regarding Lithuania.
image.credit: Renata3 This W3C-unspecified vector image was created with Inkscape . — Self-made using Inkscape; used Image:LithuaniaPhysicalMap-Clean.svg by Knutux for some background features; Source map: (2001) Lietuvos istorijos atlasas , Vilnius: Vaga, p. 44 & 45
image.date_qualification: The map depicts the 1939–1940 territorial context; the supplied image date is 2008-03-28 and is not the date of the events shown.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Nazi-Soviet agreement on Poland

events.enhanced_description: On September 28, 1939, Warsaw surrendered to German forces after weeks of intense fighting. This marked a significant defeat for Poland and a crucial victory for Germany in the early stages of World War II.
events.name: Surrender of Warsaw

events.enhanced_description: In late 1939, the Piotrków Trybunalski Ghetto was established as the first Jewish ghetto in Nazi-occupied Europe. This marked the beginning of systematic segregation and persecution of Jews in occupied territories.
events.name: Establishment of Piotrków Trybunalski Ghetto

events.enhanced_description: In November 1939, Nazi Germany initiated the Lebensborn program in occupied Poland, aimed at the systematic kidnapping of Polish children deemed racially valuable. This policy was part of a broader strategy of ethnic cleansing and Germanization.
events.name: Lebensborn policy initiated

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1939, Hedda Hopper's Hollywood premiered on radio, hosted by the influential gossip columnist Hedda Hopper. The show ran until 1951, solidifying Hopper's status as a powerful figure in Hollywood.
events.name: Hedda Hopper's Hollywood Debut

events.enhanced_description: In early 1939, the Germans initiated Sonderaktion Krakau, targeting scientists and intellectuals from the University of Kraków and other institutions. This operation was part of a broader campaign to suppress Polish culture and intellectualism.
events.name: Sonderaktion Krakau

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1939, CBS television station W2XAB resumed test transmissions from the top of the Chrysler Building in New York City. This marked a significant step in the development of television broadcasting in the United States.

locations.name: Chrysler Building, New York City, New York, United States

events.name: CBS Test Transmission Resumes

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1939, the British battleship HMS Nelson struck a mine laid by U-31 off the coast of Scotland, resulting in significant damage and leading to repairs that lasted until August 1940.

locations.name: Off the coast of Scotland, United Kingdom

events.name: HMS Nelson Strikes a Mine

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1939, the German submarine U-36 was torpedoed and sunk by the British submarine HMS Salmon off the coast of Stavanger, marking the first enemy submarine lost to a British submarine during World War II.
events.name: U-36 Sunk by HMS Salmon

events.enhanced_description: In 1939, Semyon Kirlian invented Kirlian photography, a technique that captures the electrical coronal discharge of objects, leading to significant interest in the fields of photography and parapsychology.
events.name: Kirlian Photography Invented

events.enhanced_description: In 1939, Enzo Ferrari founded Auto Avio Construzioni in Modena, Italy, which would later evolve into the iconic Ferrari brand known for its luxury sports cars and racing heritage.
events.name: Enzo Ferrari Founds Auto Avio Construzioni

events.enhanced_description: After an extensive search and eighteen months of uncertainty following her disappearance, pioneering aviator Amelia Earhart is officially declared dead. Her legacy as a trailblazer for women in aviation continues to inspire generations.
events.name: Amelia Earhart is officially declared dead

events.enhanced_description: Otto Hahn's groundbreaking discoveries in nuclear fission are published in the journal Naturwissenschaften, laying the foundation for future developments in nuclear physics and energy. His work would eventually lead to significant advancements in both energy production and weaponry.
events.name: Otto Hahn's discoveries in nuclear fission published

events.enhanced_description: French physicist Marguerite Perey identifies francium, the last chemical element to be discovered in nature. This discovery adds to the periodic table and enhances the understanding of radioactive elements.
events.name: Marguerite Perey identifies francium

events.enhanced_description: Norway formally claims Queen Maud Land in Antarctica, asserting its territorial rights in the region. This claim is part of a broader trend of national interests in Antarctica during the early 20th century.
events.name: Norway claims Queen Maud Land in Antarctica

events.enhanced_description: Admiral Wilhelm Canaris of the Abwehr leaks false information suggesting that Germany plans to invade the Netherlands, leading to heightened tensions and a shift in British military policy. This incident reflects the strategic maneuvering of intelligence during the prelude to World War II.
events.name: "Dutch War Scare" misinformation leak

events.enhanced_description: The 1939 Chillán earthquake strikes Chile, resulting in an estimated 30,000 fatalities and widespread destruction across approximately 130,000 square kilometers. This disaster highlights the seismic vulnerability of the region and its impact on local communities.
events.name: 1939 Chillán earthquake

events.enhanced_description: Refik Saydam is appointed as the Prime Minister of Turkey, forming the 11th government of the Republic. His leadership comes during a period of significant political and social change in Turkey.
events.name: Refik Saydam forms the new government of Turkey

events.enhanced_description: During the Spanish Civil War, Nationalist troops, supported by Italy, capture Barcelona, marking a decisive victory in the conflict. This event signifies the collapse of Republican resistance in Catalonia.
events.name: Spanish Civil War: Spanish Nationalist troops take Barcelona

events.enhanced_description: Adolf Hitler orders Plan Z, a comprehensive naval expansion program aimed at building a formidable German fleet to challenge the British Royal Navy by 1944. This initiative reflects Germany's militaristic ambitions leading up to World War II.
events.name: Hitler orders Plan Z

events.enhanced_description: In a speech to the Reichstag, Adolf Hitler calls for an 'export battle' to bolster Germany's foreign exchange reserves. He also makes a chilling prophecy regarding the consequences of a war instigated by 'Jewish financiers', reflecting the regime's anti-Semitic ideology.
events.name: Hitler's speech before the Reichstag

events.enhanced_description: British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain addresses the House of Commons, declaring that any German attack on France will be viewed as an attack on Britain. This statement underscores the growing tensions in Europe and the UK's commitment to its allies.
events.name: Neville Chamberlain's statement in the House of Commons

events.enhanced_description: John Ford's iconic Western film 'Stagecoach', starring John Wayne, premieres in New York City and Los Angeles. This film is credited with revitalizing the Western genre and establishing John Wayne as a leading star.
events.name: Stagecoach premieres

events.enhanced_description: The Golden Gate International Exposition, held on Treasure Island in San Francisco Bay, celebrated the city's recovery from the Great Depression and showcased advancements in technology and culture. The exposition featured pavilions from various countries and was a significant event in promoting international goodwill.
events.name: The Golden Gate International Exposition opens in San Francisco

events.enhanced_description: On February 27, 1939, the United Kingdom and France officially recognized Francisco Franco's regime in Spain, marking a significant shift in international relations following the Spanish Civil War. This recognition solidified Franco's position as the leader of Spain and was part of the broader context of European politics leading up to World War II.
events.name: The United Kingdom and France recognize Franco's government in Spain

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1939, an explosion at an Imperial Japanese Army ammunition dump on the outskirts of Osaka resulted in the deaths of 94 individuals. This tragic incident highlighted the dangers associated with military operations and the management of munitions during a period of escalating militarization in Japan.
events.name: Imperial Japanese Army ammunition dump explosion in Osaka

events.enhanced_description: On March 2, 1939, Cardinal Eugenio Pacelli was elected as Pope Pius XII, succeeding Pope Pius XI. His papacy would last until 1958 and was marked by significant events, including World War II and the post-war reconstruction of Europe.
events.name: Pope Pius XII succeeds Pope Pius XI

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1939, the Timeless Test, a historic cricket match between England and South Africa, commenced in Durban. The match is notable for being the longest in cricket history, lasting 12 days before being abandoned due to the English team's need to depart for their ship home.
events.name: The Timeless Test begins in Durban, South Africa

events.enhanced_description: On March 13, 1939, Adolf Hitler advised Slovak leader Jozef Tiso to declare Slovakia's independence to prevent its partition by Hungary and Poland. This advice was part of Hitler's broader strategy to expand German influence in Central Europe.
events.name: Adolf Hitler advises Jozef Tiso to declare Slovakia's independence

events.enhanced_description: On March 14, 1939, the Slovak provincial assembly declared independence from Czechoslovakia, with priest Jozef Tiso becoming the president of the newly formed Slovak government. This event marked the establishment of the Slovak Republic, which aligned itself with Nazi Germany.
events.name: The Slovak provincial assembly proclaims independence

events.enhanced_description: On March 15, 1939, German troops occupied the remaining territories of Bohemia and Moravia, effectively ending the existence of Czechoslovakia. This occupation was part of Hitler's aggressive expansionist policies leading up to World War II.
events.name: German troops occupy Bohemia and Moravia; Czechoslovakia ceases to exist

events.enhanced_description: On March 16, 1939, Hungary invaded Carpatho-Ukraine, leading to the swift collapse of the region's defenses. The invasion marked the end of any significant resistance and was part of the broader territorial ambitions of Hungary during the interwar period.
events.name: Hungary invades Carpatho-Ukraine

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1939, the nationalist governments of Spain and Portugal signed the Iberian Pact in Lisbon, pledging mutual defense of the Iberian Peninsula and maintaining neutrality in the event of a broader European conflict. This agreement was significant in the context of rising tensions in Europe leading up to World War II.
events.name: The Iberian Pact is signed in Lisbon

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1939, Germany issued an ultimatum to Lithuania demanding the return of the Klaipėda Region (Memel Territory). This ultimatum was part of Nazi Germany's aggressive expansionist policies and set the stage for further territorial acquisitions.
events.name: German ultimatum to Lithuania regarding Klaipėda Region

events.enhanced_description: Following the ultimatum on March 20, 1939, Lithuania ceded the Klaipėda Region to Nazi Germany, which was subsequently occupied by German forces on March 22. This event was a significant step in the lead-up to World War II, as it demonstrated the effectiveness of Nazi diplomacy and intimidation.
events.name: Nazi Germany granted the Klaipėda Region by Lithuania

events.enhanced_description: The Slovak–Hungarian War began on March 23, 1939, following tensions between Slovakia and Hungary over territorial disputes. This conflict was part of the broader instability in Central Europe during the interwar period and was influenced by the shifting alliances and national aspirations of the time.
events.name: The Slovak–Hungarian War begins

events.enhanced_description: On March 24, 1939, members of the pro-Nazi German National Movement in Liechtenstein attempted a coup to provoke the annexation of the country into Germany. This event highlighted the political tensions in Europe and the influence of Nazi ideology in smaller nations.
events.name: 1939 Liechtenstein putsch

events.enhanced_description: On March 26, 1939, the Nationalists launched their final offensive in the Spanish Civil War, leading to the collapse of the Republican forces. This offensive marked the end of the war and solidified Francisco Franco's dictatorship in Spain.
events.name: Final offensive of the Spanish Civil War launched by the Nationalists

events.enhanced_description: On March 27, 1939, the University of Oregon defeated Ohio State University 46-33 in Evanston, Illinois, to win the championship of the inaugural NCAA men's basketball tournament. This victory marked a significant milestone in college basketball history.
events.name: The University of Oregon wins the first NCAA men's basketball tournament

events.enhanced_description: On March 28, 1939, General Francisco Franco officially assumed power in Madrid following the victory of Nationalist forces in the Spanish Civil War. His regime would last until his death in 1975, characterized by authoritarian rule and repression of dissent.
events.name: General Francisco Franco assumes power in Madrid

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1939, British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain delivered a speech in the House of Commons, offering a guarantee of British support for Polish independence. This commitment was a crucial step in the lead-up to World War II, as it signaled Britain's willingness to confront German aggression.
events.name: Neville Chamberlain offers British guarantee of Polish independence

events.enhanced_description: The Spanish Civil War officially came to an end on April 1, 1939, when the last Republican forces surrendered to Franco's Nationalists. This marked the culmination of a brutal conflict that had significant implications for Spain and Europe as a whole.
events.name: End of the Spanish Civil War

events.enhanced_description: On April 3, 1939, Adolf Hitler ordered the German military to begin planning for Fall Weiß, the code name for the invasion of Poland. This directive was a crucial step leading to the outbreak of World War II later that year.

image.caption: German military map showing the planned invasion of Poland (Fall Weiß).
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — https://static.dw.com/image/50105792_303.jpg
image.date_qualification: Image date is 1939; the record does not establish that the map was created on 3 April 1939.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Hitler orders planning for Fall Weiß

events.enhanced_description: The Slovak–Hungarian War concluded on April 4, 1939, with Slovakia ceding eastern territories to Hungary. This conflict was part of the broader territorial disputes in Central Europe during the interwar period.
events.name: End of the Slovak–Hungarian War

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1939, Italy launched an invasion of Albania, prompting King Zog to flee into exile in Greece with his family. This invasion marked a significant escalation in Italian expansionism under Mussolini.
events.name: Italian invasion of Albania begins

events.enhanced_description: On April 9, 1939, African-American singer Marian Anderson performed before a crowd of 75,000 at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C. This historic concert followed her denial of performance rights at Constitution Hall, highlighting the racial discrimination of the time.
events.name: Marian Anderson's concert at Lincoln Memorial

events.enhanced_description: On April 11, 1939, Hungary officially withdrew from the League of Nations, reflecting the growing isolationist and nationalist sentiments in Europe as tensions escalated leading up to World War II.
events.name: Hungary leaves the League of Nations

events.enhanced_description: On April 14, 1939, French Foreign Minister Georges Bonnet met with Soviet Ambassador Jakob Suritz in Paris to discuss the formation of a 'peace front' involving France, the Soviet Union, Great Britain, Poland, and Romania to deter German aggression. This meeting underscored the diplomatic efforts to prevent the looming conflict in Europe.
events.name: Meeting in Paris regarding peace front

events.enhanced_description: On April 18, 1939, the Soviet Union proposed a 'peace front' aimed at resisting aggression in Europe. This proposal was part of the broader geopolitical maneuvering as tensions escalated towards World War II.
events.name: Soviet Union proposes a peace front

events.enhanced_description: On April 25, 1939, the Federal Security Agency (FSA) was established in the United States, alongside the Civilian Conservation Corps and the Public Health Service. This agency was part of the New Deal reforms aimed at addressing the economic challenges of the Great Depression.
events.name: Founding of the Federal Security Agency

events.enhanced_description: On April 28, 1939, Adolf Hitler delivered a speech before the Reichstag in which he renounced the Anglo-German Naval Agreement and the German-Polish declaration of non-aggression. This act signaled a further deterioration of diplomatic relations in Europe.
events.name: Hitler renounces agreements

events.enhanced_description: The 1939 New York World's Fair opened on April 30, 1939, showcasing innovations and cultural exhibits from around the world. The fair was a reflection of optimism and progress during a time of global uncertainty.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Opening of the 1939 New York World's Fair

events.enhanced_description: On May 3, 1939, Vyacheslav Molotov succeeded Maxim Litvinov as the Soviet Foreign Commissar. This change in leadership came during a critical time as the Soviet Union navigated its foreign relations in the lead-up to World War II.
events.name: Vyacheslav Molotov succeeds Maxim Litvinov

events.enhanced_description: On May 6, 1939, German anti-Nazi Carl Friedrich Goerdeler informed the British government about the secret rapprochement between Germany and the Soviet Union, aimed at dividing Eastern Europe. His insights highlighted the precarious political landscape in Europe as tensions escalated towards war.
events.name: Carl Friedrich Goerdeler informs British government

events.enhanced_description: On May 9, 1939, Spain officially withdrew from the League of Nations, a move that reflected its isolationist stance following the Spanish Civil War and the rise of Francisco Franco's regime. This departure marked a significant moment in Spain's diplomatic history as it distanced itself from international cooperation during a tumultuous period in Europe.
events.name: Spain leaves the League of Nations

events.enhanced_description: On May 14, 1939, Lina Medina, a five-year-old girl from Pueblo Libre, Peru, made medical history by giving birth to a baby boy, becoming the youngest confirmed mother. Her case raised significant ethical and medical discussions regarding child welfare and the implications of early pregnancy.
events.name: Lina Medina gives birth

events.enhanced_description: On May 17, 1939, King George VI and Queen Elizabeth of the United Kingdom arrived in Quebec City, marking the first-ever royal tour of Canada by a reigning monarch. This historic visit strengthened ties between Canada and Britain and was part of a broader effort to promote Canadian unity and identity.
events.name: King George VI and Queen Elizabeth arrive in Quebec City

events.enhanced_description: On May 18, 1939, the Hòa Hảo religious sect was established in Vietnam by Huỳnh Phú Sổ. This sect emerged as a significant spiritual movement, emphasizing a blend of Buddhism and local beliefs, and played a crucial role in the socio-political landscape of Vietnam during the colonial period.
events.name: Establishment of the Hòa Hảo sect

events.enhanced_description: On May 20, 1939, Pan American Airways inaugurated its transatlantic mail service with the first flight of the Boeing 314 flying boat, Yankee Clipper, from Port Washington, New York, to Marseille, France. This marked a significant advancement in international air travel and mail delivery, paving the way for future commercial aviation.
events.name: Pan American Airways begins transatlantic mail service

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1939, Germany and Italy formalized their alliance by signing the Pact of Steel, which solidified their military and political cooperation. This pact was a crucial step in the lead-up to World War II, aligning the two fascist regimes against the Allied powers.

image.caption: Photograph of the signing of the Pact of Steel in Berlin.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Istituto Luce Id:A00113852
image.date_qualification: Described as taken on 22 May 1939; the supported display date is 1939.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Germany and Italy sign the Pact of Steel

events.enhanced_description: On May 24, 1939, the first issue of Fashizmi, a publication promoting fascist ideology, was published in Tirana, Albania. This publication played a role in disseminating fascist propaganda during a time of political upheaval in the region.
events.name: First issue of Fashizmi published

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1939, Tefik Mborja, an Albanian fascist leader, was appointed as a member of the Italian Chamber of Fasces and Corporations. This appointment highlighted the increasing influence of Italian fascism in Albania during this period.
events.name: Tefik Mborja appointed to Italian Chamber

events.enhanced_description: On June 3, 1939, the Soviet government presented its definition of aggression, which was accepted by French Foreign Minister Georges Bonnet but rejected by the British. This disagreement highlighted the complexities of forming an alliance against the Axis powers.
events.name: Soviet government offers definition of aggression

events.enhanced_description: On June 4, 1939, the St. Louis, a ship carrying 907 Jewish refugees, was denied permission to land in Florida and only a few passengers were allowed to enter Cuba. Forced to return to Europe, many of its passengers later perished in Nazi death camps, highlighting the dire consequences of restrictive immigration policies during the Holocaust.
events.name: The St. Louis incident

events.enhanced_description: The Pringsheim Sale on June 7, 1939, at Sotheby & Co. in London featured the auction of Italian Majolica from the collection of Alfred Pringsheim. This event illustrated the art market's dynamics and the cultural significance of collecting in pre-World War II Europe.
events.name: Pringsheim Sale, June 7, 1939 at Sotheby & Co.

events.enhanced_description: On June 14, 1939, the Tientsin Incident occurred when Japanese forces blockaded the British concession in Tianjin, China. This event escalated tensions between Japan and Western powers, nearly leading to an Anglo-Japanese war.
events.name: Tientsin Incident

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1939, Eugen Weidmann was guillotined in Versailles, marking the last public execution in France. This event sparked debates about the morality of capital punishment and the public's role in such proceedings.

image.caption: Anthropometric portrait of Eugène Weidmann.
image.credit: Unknown, SRIJ de Paris. Uploaded and restored by Jebulon — Courtesy of Head of Service Regional d'Identité Judiciaire de Paris
image.date_qualification: A 1937 portrait of Weidmann, not a photograph of the execution; the upload and restoration date is not the image date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Last public execution in France

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1939, talks in Ankara between French Ambassador René Massigli and Turkish Foreign Minister Şükrü Saracoğlu concluded with the resolution of the Hatay dispute in Turkey's favor, leading to Turkey's annexation of Hatay. This event was significant in shaping the geopolitical landscape of the region.
events.name: Hatay dispute resolution

events.enhanced_description: In 1949, Siam officially changed its French name to 'Thaïlande' and its English name to 'Thailand', reflecting the country's desire to assert its national identity. This change followed the earlier adoption of the name 'Prated Thai' in 1939.
events.name: Siam changes name to Thailand

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1939, the Ford 9N tractor, featuring the innovative Ferguson hydraulic three-point hitch, was first demonstrated in Dearborn, Michigan. This tractor revolutionized agricultural practices by allowing for more efficient use of farm implements.
events.name: Ford 9N tractor demonstration

events.enhanced_description: The 1939 Degenerate Art auction in Switzerland was a controversial event where artworks deemed 'degenerate' by the Nazi regime were sold to raise funds for the regime. This auction was part of a broader campaign to rid German culture of modernist influences, reflecting the oppressive political climate of the time.
events.name: 1939 Degenerate Art auction

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1939, the Neuengamme concentration camp in Germany became an autonomous facility. This marked a significant development in the Nazi regime's system of forced labor and imprisonment, contributing to the horrors of the Holocaust.

image.caption: Archival photograph of forced labor at Neuengamme concentration camp.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — https://collections.ushmm.org/search/catalog/pa1060376 https://collections.ushmm.org/search/catalog/pa1060335
image.date_qualification: The image is dated 1941–1942, later than the camp’s reported autonomy in 1939; it depicts activity at the camp, not the 1939 change in status.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Neuengamme concentration camp becomes autonomous

events.enhanced_description: On July 6, 1939, the last remaining Jewish enterprises in Germany were closed by the Nazis as part of their systematic campaign against Jewish businesses. This action further marginalized the Jewish community and foreshadowed the more severe measures that would follow during the Holocaust.
events.name: Closure of Jewish enterprises in Germany

events.enhanced_description: On July 8, 1939, the Pan American Airways Boeing 314 flying boat, Yankee Clipper, inaugurated the world's first heavier-than-air North Atlantic air passenger service between the United States and Britain. This milestone in aviation history marked the beginning of transatlantic commercial air travel.
events.name: Yankee Clipper inaugurates North Atlantic air service

events.enhanced_description: On July 23, 1939, Mahatma Gandhi wrote a personal letter to Adolf Hitler from India, addressing him as 'My friend' and urging him to prevent any possible war. This unusual correspondence highlighted Gandhi's commitment to peace and his hope for dialogue amidst rising global tensions.
events.name: Gandhi's letter to Hitler

events.enhanced_description: On July 27, 1939, Auckland, New Zealand, experienced its first recorded snowfall since records began in 1853. This rare meteorological event captivated the local population and was noted in weather history.
events.name: First recorded snow in Auckland

events.enhanced_description: On August 2, 1939, physicist Albert Einstein and his colleague Leo Szilard signed a letter addressed to President Franklin D. Roosevelt, warning about the potential for Nazi Germany to develop atomic weapons using uranium. This letter prompted the U.S. government to initiate research into atomic energy, leading to the establishment of the Manhattan Project.
events.name: Einstein–Szilard letter signed

events.enhanced_description: On August 4, 1939, British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain dismissed the Parliament of the United Kingdom until October 3, amidst rising tensions in Europe as World War II loomed. This decision reflected the urgent political climate as the UK prepared for potential conflict.
events.name: Parliament dismissal by Neville Chamberlain

events.enhanced_description: The musical film 'The Wizard of Oz', starring Judy Garland, premiered on August 15, 1939, at Grauman's Chinese Theatre in Los Angeles. The film has since become a classic, celebrated for its innovative use of Technicolor and its enduring themes of friendship and courage.
events.name: Premiere of The Wizard of Oz

events.enhanced_description: On August 19, 1939, Adolf Hitler ordered the Kriegsmarine to commence operations for Fall Weiß, the planned invasion of Poland. This decision marked a significant escalation in the lead-up to World War II, as Germany prepared to execute its aggressive military strategy.
events.name: Fall Weiß ordered by Hitler

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1939, Soviet armored forces under General Georgy Zhukov achieved a decisive victory against the Imperial Japanese Army during the Japanese-Soviet border conflict in Inner Mongolia. This battle underscored the tensions between the two nations prior to World War II.
events.name: Soviet victory in Inner Mongolia

events.enhanced_description: On August 23, 1939, the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact was signed between Germany and the Soviet Union, establishing a neutrality treaty and outlining the division of Eastern Europe into spheres of influence. This agreement significantly impacted the geopolitical landscape leading into World War II.
events.name: Signing of the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact

events.enhanced_description: On August 24, 1939, following the public revelation of the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain recalled Parliament to address the escalating crisis in Europe. This led to significant military preparations and legislative actions in anticipation of war.
events.name: Recall of Parliament by Neville Chamberlain

events.enhanced_description: On August 25, 1939, the German Foreign Ministry severed all telecommunication links with the outside world as part of the preparations for Fall Weiß. This action was a precursor to the imminent invasion of Poland, highlighting the secrecy and urgency of Nazi plans.
events.name: German communication cut-off

events.enhanced_description: On August 26, 1939, the first televised Major League Baseball games were broadcast from experimental station W2XBS, featuring a double-header between the Cincinnati Reds and the Brooklyn Dodgers at Ebbets Field in Brooklyn, New York. This event marked a significant milestone in the history of sports broadcasting.
events.name: First televised Major League Baseball games

events.enhanced_description: On August 27, 1939, the Heinkel He 178, the world's first turbojet-powered aircraft, made its inaugural flight with Captain Erich Warsitz at the controls. This groundbreaking achievement marked a significant advancement in aviation technology.
events.name: First flight of the Heinkel He 178

events.enhanced_description: On August 28, 1939, the French ocean liner SS Normandie entered New York Harbor, where it would later be interned and ultimately scrapped after World War II. The ship was renowned for its luxurious design and speed, symbolizing the golden age of transatlantic travel.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: SS Normandie enters New York Harbor

events.enhanced_description: On August 30, 1939, Poland began mobilizing its military forces in response to the growing threat from Nazi Germany. This mobilization was a critical step in preparing for the impending invasion that would mark the start of World War II.
events.name: Poland mobilizes against Nazi Germany

events.enhanced_description: On August 31, 1939, Operation Himmler was executed, where Nazi German troops disguised as Poles staged a series of false flag operations, including the Gleiwitz incident. This operation provided a pretext for Germany to invade Poland, igniting World War II.
events.name: Operation Himmler false flag operations

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1939, the German battleship Schleswig-Holstein opened fire on Polish positions at Westerplatte, marking the beginning of World War II. This attack followed a series of provocations and was part of Germany's invasion of Poland, which would lead to widespread conflict across Europe.
events.name: Beginning of World War II

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1939, the German battleship Schleswig-Holstein fired upon Polish positions at Westerplatte, marking the opening shots of World War II. This attack initiated a series of military confrontations that would engulf Europe in conflict.
events.name: Opening shots of World War II

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1939, the Battle of Westerplatte concluded with Polish troops surrendering after a week-long defense against overwhelming German forces. This battle became a symbol of Polish resistance during the early days of World War II.
events.name: Battle of Westerplatte ends

events.enhanced_description: On September 4, 1939, the conflict continued as the United Kingdom and France mobilized their forces against Germany, following their declarations of war. The situation in Europe was rapidly deteriorating, leading to a full-scale war.
events.name: Continuation of WWII hostilities

events.enhanced_description: On September 3, 1939, the United Kingdom and France declared war on Germany in response to its invasion of Poland, marking a significant escalation in the conflict that would become World War II. This declaration united the Allies against the Axis powers.
events.name: Declaration of war by the UK and France

events.enhanced_description: On September 5, 1939, the United States officially declared its neutrality in the escalating conflict of World War II. This decision reflected the isolationist sentiment prevalent in American society at the time.
events.name: U.S. declares neutrality in WWII

events.enhanced_description: On September 6, 1939, South Africa declared war on Germany, aligning itself with the Allies in response to the invasion of Poland. This declaration marked South Africa's entry into World War II.
events.name: South Africa declares war on Germany

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1939, forward elements of General Hermann Höppner's XVI Panzerkorps positioned themselves outside Warsaw, showcasing the rapid German advance during the invasion of Poland. The Polish High Command found itself isolated, struggling to mount an effective defense.
events.name: German advance towards Warsaw

events.enhanced_description: On September 9, 1939, Polish troops under General Tadeusz Kutrzeba launched the Battle of the Bzura, the largest counter-attack mounted by Polish forces during the invasion. Initially successful, the operation soon bogged down due to German mechanized units and air support.
events.name: Battle of the Bzura begins

events.enhanced_description: On September 10, 1939, Canada declared war on Germany, marking its first independent declaration of war. This decision was made by Prime Minister Mackenzie King and reflected Canada's commitment to support the Allied cause in World War II.
events.name: Canada declares war on Germany

events.enhanced_description: On September 13, 1939, during the Zambrów massacre, German Wehrmacht soldiers executed over 200 Polish prisoners of war. This brutal act exemplified the atrocities committed by Nazi forces during their invasion of Poland.
events.name: Zambrów massacre

events.enhanced_description: On September 15, 1939, diverse elements of the German Wehrmacht surrounded Warsaw, demanding its surrender. The Polish defenders refused, leading to a prolonged siege that would become one of the most significant battles of the war.
events.name: Siege of Warsaw begins

events.enhanced_description: On September 16, 1939, a ceasefire was declared, ending the Battles of Khalkhin Gol, an undeclared border war between the Soviet Union and Japan. This conflict had significant implications for both nations and their military strategies in the lead-up to World War II.
events.name: Ceasefire at Khalkhin Gol

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1939, the Polish submarine ORP Orzeł escaped internment from Tallinn Harbour, Estonia, raising concerns for both the Soviet Union and Germany regarding Estonia's neutrality. This incident highlighted the complexities of international relations during the early stages of World War II.
events.name: Orzeł incident

events.enhanced_description: On September 19, 1939, the Poznań pocket collapsed, resulting in the capture of over 150,000 Polish troops by German forces. This event marked a significant turning point in the invasion of Poland, as German forces continued their advance toward Warsaw.
events.name: Collapse of the Poznań pocket

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1939, Reinhard Heydrich issued the Schnellbrief directive, mandating the transfer of Jews in Polish occupation zones to ghettos and the establishment of Jewish councils, known as Judenräte. This directive marked the beginning of systematic persecution of Jews in Nazi-occupied territories.
events.name: Heydrich's directive on Jewish councils

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1939, a joint victory parade was held in Brest-Litovsk by the Wehrmacht and the Red Army, celebrating the successful completion of the Invasion of Poland. This event symbolized the cooperation between Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union in their territorial ambitions.
events.name: Joint victory parade in Brest-Litovsk

events.enhanced_description: On September 24, 1939, the Soviet Union issued an ultimatum to Estonia, demanding the establishment of Soviet military bases on its territory. Estonia accepted the ultimatum, which marked a significant shift in the balance of power in the Baltic region.

image.caption: Red Army troops enter Estonia in a historical photograph.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — http://entsyklopeedia.ee/meedia/eesti_iseseisvuse_häving_1939–1940/1_473_punaarmee_eesti_piir
image.date_qualification: The described entry occurred on 18 October 1939, after the Soviet ultimatum and the treaty allowing Soviet bases; it depicts aftermath, not the ultimatum itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Soviet ultimatum to Estonia

events.enhanced_description: World War II officially began on September 1, 1939, when Germany invaded Poland, leading to widespread conflict across Europe and eventually the world. This marked a significant escalation in global tensions that had been building since the end of World War I.
events.name: Start of World War II

events.enhanced_description: On September 30, 1939, General Władysław Sikorski was appointed Prime Minister of the Polish government-in-exile, which was established following the invasion of Poland by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union. His leadership was crucial in maintaining Polish sovereignty and coordinating resistance efforts during the war.
events.name: General Władysław Sikorski becomes Prime Minister of the Polish government-in-exile

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Kock, which concluded on October 6, 1939, marked the end of organized Polish resistance during the September Campaign. Following this battle, Polish forces transitioned to underground resistance against the occupying powers.
events.name: Battle of Kock

events.enhanced_description: On October 7, 1939, the British Royal Navy cruiser HMS Emerald departed from Plymouth in convoy for Halifax, Nova Scotia, carrying £2 million in gold bars intended for the purchase of military supplies in North America. This operation was a precursor to the larger Operation Fish.
events.name: HMS Emerald departs for Halifax

events.enhanced_description: On October 8, 1939, Germany formally annexed Western Poland following its invasion. This annexation was part of a broader strategy to integrate occupied territories into the German Reich.
events.name: Germany annexes Western Poland

events.enhanced_description: On October 14, 1939, the German submarine U-47 sank the British battleship HMS Royal Oak while it was anchored in Scapa Flow, resulting in the loss of 833 crew members. This event highlighted the vulnerability of British naval forces early in the war.
events.name: Sinking of HMS Royal Oak

events.enhanced_description: In November 1939, physicist Hans Ferdinand Mayer authored the Oslo Report, detailing German advancements in weapons systems. He passed this critical intelligence to the British Secret Intelligence Service, contributing to the Allied understanding of German military capabilities.
events.name: Oslo Report by Hans Ferdinand Mayer

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1939, U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt ordered the implementation of the Neutrality Act of 1939, which allowed cash-and-carry purchases of weapons by non-belligerent nations. This marked a shift in U.S. foreign policy as the country began to support Allied nations.
events.name: U.S. Neutrality Act of 1939

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1939, Stewart Menzies was appointed as the head of the British Secret Intelligence Service (SIS). His leadership would play a crucial role in intelligence operations throughout World War II.
events.name: Stewart Menzies appointed head of SIS

events.enhanced_description: On November 6, 1939, Hedda Hopper's Hollywood premiered on radio in the United States, hosted by the influential gossip columnist Hedda Hopper. The show ran until 1951, solidifying Hopper's status as a powerful figure in Hollywood.
events.name: Hedda Hopper's Hollywood debuts

events.enhanced_description: On November 8, 1939, an assassination attempt was made on Adolf Hitler by Georg Elser during a speech commemorating the Beer Hall Putsch in Munich. Although the bomb detonated, Hitler escaped unharmed, allowing him to continue his leadership during the war.
events.name: Assassination attempt on Adolf Hitler

events.enhanced_description: On November 8, 1939, Georg Elser attempted to assassinate Adolf Hitler during a speech commemorating the Beer Hall Putsch in Munich. The bomb failed to kill Hitler, who escaped unharmed, leading to severe repercussions for those suspected of involvement.

image.caption: Archival personnel-file photograph of Georg Elser.
image.credit: Weißkunig — File:Gestapo-Akte_Georg_Elser_(Delikt).jpg
image.date_qualification: Portrait of Georg Elser, taken before 1 December 1939; it is not a photograph of the assassination attempt.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Assassination Attempt on Hitler

events.enhanced_description: On November 9, 1939, two British agents from the Secret Intelligence Service were captured by German forces in what became known as the Venlo Incident. This event heightened tensions between Britain and Germany and showcased the risks faced by intelligence operatives.
events.name: Venlo Incident

events.enhanced_description: On November 14, 1939, U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt laid the cornerstone of the Jefferson Memorial in Washington, D.C. This memorial was dedicated to Thomas Jefferson, the third President of the United States and a key figure in American history.
events.name: Laying of the cornerstone of the Jefferson Memorial

events.enhanced_description: On November 16, 1939, notorious gangster Al Capone was released from Terminal Island due to deteriorating health caused by syphilis. His release marked the end of a significant chapter in organized crime in America.
events.name: Release of Al Capone

events.enhanced_description: On November 17, 1939, in response to protests against the Nazi occupation, German forces stormed the University of Prague, resulting in the murder of nine Czech students and the imprisonment of over 1,200 others. This brutal crackdown would be commemorated as International Students' Day.

image.caption: Black-and-white image identifying nine executed student association leaders.
image.credit: Skot — Own work
image.date_qualification: Retrospective image documenting people executed on 17 November 1939; the saved image date is 2020-11-17, not the date of the executions.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Nazi crackdown on Czech students

events.enhanced_description: On November 23, 1939, the British armed merchantman HMS Rawalpindi was sunk in the GIUK gap during an engagement with the German battleships Scharnhorst and Gneisenau. This event underscored the ongoing naval conflict between Britain and Germany.
events.name: Sinking of HMS Rawalpindi

events.enhanced_description: On November 26, 1939, the Soviet Red Army shelled the village of Mainila, claiming that the fire originated from Finland. This incident was used as a pretext to justify the invasion of Finland, marking the beginning of the Winter War.
events.name: Shelling of Mainila

events.enhanced_description: On November 30, 1939, Soviet forces launched an attack against Finland, breaching the Mannerheim Line, which was a key defensive fortification. This marked the official start of the Winter War, with Finland fiercely resisting the invasion.
events.name: Winter War Begins

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1939, the Soviet Union established the Finnish Democratic Republic in Terijoki, a puppet state intended to legitimize Soviet control over Finland during the Winter War.
events.name: Establishment of Finnish Democratic Republic

events.enhanced_description: On December 6, 1939, during the Winter War, Finnish forces successfully halted the Soviet advance at the Mannerheim Line during the Battle of Taipale. This battle showcased the resilience of Finnish troops against overwhelming odds.
events.name: Battle of Taipale

events.enhanced_description: On December 9, 1939, Corporal Thomas Priday became the first soldier of the British Expeditionary Force to be killed in World War II after triggering a French land mine in France.
events.name: First British Soldier Killed

events.enhanced_description: On December 12, 1939, the British destroyer HMS Duchess sank after colliding with the battleship HMS Barham off the coast of Scotland, resulting in the loss of 124 men.

locations.name: Off the coast of Scotland, United Kingdom

events.name: HMS Duchess Sinks

events.enhanced_description: On December 13, 1939, during the Battle of the River Plate, the German heavy cruiser Admiral Graf Spee was trapped by British cruisers HMS Ajax, HMNZS Achilles, and HMS Exeter after a running battle. The Graf Spee was scuttled by its crew off Montevideo Harbor on December 17.
events.name: Battle of the River Plate

events.enhanced_description: On December 14, 1939, the League of Nations expelled the Soviet Union for its aggression against Finland during the Winter War. This marked a significant diplomatic shift and highlighted the international community's response to Soviet expansionism.
events.name: League of Nations Expels USSR

events.enhanced_description: On December 15, 1939, the epic historical romance film 'Gone with the Wind' premiered at Loew's Grand Theatre in Atlanta. Based on Margaret Mitchell's novel, it became the highest-grossing film of its time and remains a classic in American cinema.

locations.name: Loew's Grand Theatre, Atlanta, Georgia, United States

events.name: Premiere of Gone with the Wind

events.enhanced_description: On December 18, 1939, during the Battle of the Heligoland Bight, the RAF Bomber Command attempted a daylight mission to attack Kriegsmarine ships but was repulsed by Luftwaffe fighter aircraft.
